parts.problemMd:
A sealed container A has the shape of a rectangular prism and contains an ideal gas. The dimensions of the container are *x*, *y *and z as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![15-2-1a-h-derivation-cube-hsq-cie-a-level](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/15-ideal-gases/15-3-kinetic-theory-of-gases/assets/011-15-2-1a-h-derivation-cube-hsq-cie-a-level.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

- The average force exerted by the gas on the bottom wall of the container is *F*
- There are *n *moles of gas in the container
- The temperature of the gas is *T *

Obtain an expression for the height of the container in terms of* F,* *n *and *T*.
parts.solutionMd:
Obtain an expression in terms of* F,* *n *and *T *for the height of the container:

- Surface pressure:  $P=\frac{F}{A}$
- Ideal gas equation:  $PV=nRT$
- Combine the equations:  $( \frac{F}{A} ) V = n R T$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute and rearrange the dimensions *l*, *h*, and *w *into the equation:

- Area:  $A=xy$
- Volume:  $V=xyz$*  *
- Substitute:   $\frac{F\timesxyz}{xy}=nRT\RightarrowFz=nRT$

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A second container B contains the same ideal gas.

The following information is known:

- The pressure in B is a quarter of the pressure in A
- The volume of B is five times the volume of A
- Container B contains half the number of molecules as A
- The temperature of container B is 800 K

Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules in the gas of container A.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules in the gas of container A:

List the known quantities:

- Pressure of gas in B:  $P_{B}=\frac{1}{4}P_{A}$
- Volume of B:  $V_{B}=5V_{A}$
- Number of molecules in B:  $n_{B}=\frac{1}{2}n_{A}$
- Temperature of gas in B:  *T*<sub>B</sub> = 800 K
- Molar gas constant, *R *= 8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Boltzmann constant, *k *= 1.38 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J K<sup>−1</sup>

Write expressions in terms of the ideal gas equation for the gas contained in A and B:

- Gas in container A:  $P_{A}V_{A}=n_{A}RT_{A}$
- Gas in container B:  `P _ B V _ B = n _ B R T _ B <-> ( P _ A / 4 ) x ( 5 V _ A ) = ( n _ A / 2 ) R x 800` **[1 mark]**
- Simplify:  $\frac{5}{4}P_{A}V_{A}=400n_{A}R\RightarrowP_{A}V_{A}=320n_{A}R$

Equate the equations in terms of *R *to find the temperature in container A:

- Gas in container A:  $P_{A}V_{A}=n_{A}RT_{A}\RightarrowR=\frac{P_{A}V_{A}}{n_{A}T_{A}}$
- Gas in container B:  $P_{A}V_{A}=320n_{A}R\RightarrowR=\frac{P_{A}V_{A}}{320n_{A}}$
- Equate & simplify:  $\frac{P_{A}V_{A}}{n_{A}T_{A}}=\frac{P_{A}V_{A}}{320n_{A}}$
- Temperature of gas A:  $T_{A}=320K$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules in the gas of container A:

- Average kinetic energy:  $E_{k}=\frac{3}{2}kT$
- $E_{k} = \frac{3}{2} \times ( 1.38 \times 10^{- 23} ) \times 320$
- $E_{k}=6.624\times10^{-21}J$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The kinetic theory of gases assumes that collisions between particles and between particles and the walls of their container are perfectly elastic.

(i) Describe what is meant by a *perfectly elastic collision*

[1]

(ii) Describe the nature of the forces between the molecules

[1]

(iii) Describe, with a reason, the type of speed of the molecules considered in the kinetic theory.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) A perfectly elastic collision is when:

- Kinetic energy is conserved during the collision **OR**
- No kinetic energy is permanently transformed into internal energy (heat, deformation, sound); **[1 mark]**

(ii) The forces between the molecules are:

- There are no long-range intermolecular forces **OR**
- Forces between molecules are negligible except during collisions **[1 mark]**

(iii) The speed of the molecules considered in the kinetic theory is:

- The Root Mean Square (RMS) speed; **[1 mark]**

This is because:

- Because the macroscopic properties of the gas (like Temperature and Pressure) are related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules, which depends on the square of the speed;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A gas collimator is used to measure the average velocity of particles in a gas.

The collimator in Fig. 1.1 controls the pressure and the volume and it maintains a gas at a constant temperature.

![15-2-2b-h-collimator-kinetic-theory-hsq-cie-a-level](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/15-ideal-gases/15-3-kinetic-theory-of-gases/assets/010-15-2-2b-h-collimator-kinetic-theory-hsq-cie-a-le.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Explain why two narrow apertures are required in the collimator to measure the velocity of the particles inside.
parts.solutionMd:
Two narrow apertures are required in the collimator to measure the velocity of the particles inside because:

- Particles in the main chamber move in a constant random  thermal motion; **[1 mark]**
- Only particles travelling in a straight line along the axis / parallel to the beam can pass through both apertures to reach the detector; **[1 mark]**
- This ensures the velocity measured is strictly the velocity in the direction of the beam; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A paint manufacturer is measuring the root mean square speed of a sample of propane particles used to make spray paint. At a temperature of 9 °C the propane molecules have a velocity of 399.00 m s<sup>−1</sup>  with an uncertainty of 0.5 %.

Propane has a molecular mass of 44.097 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.

Determine whether the propane sample behaves as an ideal gas.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine whether the propane sample behaves as an ideal gas:

- Molar mass of propane, *M*<sub>*r*</sub> = 44.097 g mol<sup>−1</sup> = 44.097 × 10<sup>−3</sup> kg mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Average velocity of particles, *c* = 399.00 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Uncertainty in velocity = 0.5 %
- Temperature, *T *= 9 °C = 9 + 273.15 = 282.15 K
- Avogadro constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Boltzmann constant, *k* = 1.38 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J K<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the mass of one molecule, $m$

- $m=\frac{M_{r}}{N_{A}}=\frac{44.097\times10^{-3}}{6.02\times10^{23}}$
- $m=7.325\times10^{-26}\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the RMS speed, $c_{rms}$

- $c_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{3kT}{m}}$
- $c_{r m s} = \sqrt{ \frac{3 \times ( 1.38 \times 10^{- 23} ) \times 282.15}{7.325 \times 10^{- 26} } }$
- $c_{rms}=399.20ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Compare to the measured value

- Measured value = 399.00 m s<sup>-1</sup>
- Calculated value = 399.20 m s<sup>-1</sup>
- $\% \text{uncertainty} = \frac{calculated \text{velocity} - \text{known} \text{velocity} }{known \text{velocity} } \times 100$
- $\% \text{uncertainty} = \frac{399.20 - 399.00}{399.00} \times 100$
- $\% \text{uncertainty} = 0.05 \%$ **[1 mark]**
- The difference between the theoretical and measured speeds is about 0.05%, which is much smaller than the 0.5% experimental uncertainty, therefore, the measured speed is consistent with the value predicted for an ideal gas; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A sealed box contains 3.0 moles of a monatomic ideal gas. The average translational kinetic energy of the gas is 1 × 10<sup>4</sup> J.

Calculate the average temperature of the gas.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the average temperature of the gas:

List the known quantities:

- Number of moles, *n *= 3.0
- Pressure, *p *= 6.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Average translational kinetic energy of the molecules in the gas, *E*<sub>*k-total*</sub> = 1 × 10<sup>4</sup> J
- Avogadro constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Boltzmann constant, *k *= 1.38 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J K<sup>−1</sup>
- Molar gas constant, *R *= 8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the translational kinetic energy of one molecule in the gas, *E*<sub>*k-total*</sub>:

- The gas contains 3 moles, so *n *= 3
- Each mole of gas contains Avogadro's number of molecules, *N*<sub>*A*</sub>
- Therefore, the translational kinetic energy of one molecule in the gas is given by the equation: $E_{k}=\frac{E_{k-total}}{nN_{A}}$
- $E_{k} = \frac{1 \times 10^{4} }{3 \times ( 6.02 \times 10^{23} )}$
- $E_{k}=5.537\times10^{-21}J$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the temperature of the gas:

- Average kinetic energy:  $E_{k}=\frac{3}{2}kT\RightarrowT=\frac{2E_{k}}{3k}$
- $T = \frac{2 E_{k} }{3 k} = \frac{2 \times ( 5.537 \times 10^{- 21} )}{3 \times ( 1.38 \times 10^{- 23} )} = 267.5 \mathrm{K}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A sealed box contains 3.0 moles of a monatomic ideal gas. The average translational kinetic energy of the gas is 1 × 10^4 J.

Calculate the translational kinetic energy of one molecule in the gas: E_k = E_k-total / (n N_A) = (1 × 10^4) / (3 × (6.02 × 10^23)) = 5.537 × 10^−21 J

The molar mass of the gas in the box is 5.9 g mol<sup>−1</sup>. Assume that there are perfectly elastic collisions between the particles and the box walls and that the particles travel perpendicular to the walls.

Calculate the magnitude of the impulse when one gas atom collides with one wall of the box.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the magnitude of the impulse when a gas atom collides with the walls of the box:

List the known quantities:

- Number of moles, *n *= 3.0 (From part (a))
- Average translational kinetic energy of one molecule, *E*<sub>*k*</sub> = 5.54 × 10<sup>−21</sup> J (From part (a))
- Molar mass, *M*<sub>*r*</sub> = 5.9 g mol<sup>−1</sup> = 5.9 × 10<sup>−3</sup> kg mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Avogadro constant, *N*<sub>*A*</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the mass of one molecule, *m*:

- $m=\frac{M_{r}}{N_{A}}$
- $m = \frac{( 5.9 \times 10^{- 3} )}{( 6.02 \times 10^{23} )}$
- $m=9.8\times10^{-27}\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the average translational kinetic energy of one molecule to calculate the average velocity, *c*:

- $E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} m ( \text{angle} \text{brackets} c^{2} ) \text{angle} \text{brackets}$
- $c=\sqrt{\frac{2E_{k}}{m}}$
- $c = \sqrt{ \frac{2 \times ( 5.54 \times 10^{- 21} )}{9.8 \times 10^{- 27} } }$
- $c=1063ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the magnitude of the impulse of the gas atoms:

- The collision of the particles with the walls is perfectly elastic, so kinetic energy is conserved before and after each collision
- Consider the change in direction of the particle before and after the collision

  - Before the collision: the particle moves towards the wall and the velocity is positive
  - After the collision: the particle moves away from the wall and the velocity is negative

- Impulse = change in momentum = *mv *− *mu*
- Impulse =* mc − *(−*mc*)* *= 2*mc*
- Impulse = 2 × (9.8 × 10<sup>−27</sup>) × (1063)
- Impulse = 2.08 × 10<sup>−23</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A sealed box contains 3.0 moles of a monatomic ideal gas. The average translational kinetic energy of the gas is 1 × 10^4 J. Calculate the average temperature of the gas. [Answer: T = 267.5 K]

The pressure of the ideal gas in the box is 6.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa. The box is opened and additional molecules enter. The number of gas atoms is increased by *y *%.

The box is then resealed and the temperature of the remaining gas atoms increased by 102.5 °C. The new pressure in the box is 2% of the original pressure. The box has a volume 0.819 m<sup>3</sup>.

Find the value of *y*.
parts.solutionMd:
Find the value of *y:*

List the known quantities:

- Original number of moles, *n *= 3.0
- Original pressure, *p*<sub>*1*</sub>* *= 6.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Volume of gas, *V* = 0.819 m<sup>3</sup>
- Original temperature, *T*<sub>*1*</sub> = 267.5 K (from **(a)**)
- New temperature, *T*<sub>*2*</sub> = 267.5 + 102.5 = 370 K
- New pressure, *p*<sub>*2*</sub> = 0.02 × *p*<sub>*1*</sub> = 0.02 × (6.1 × 10<sup>5</sup>) = 1.22 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa
- Molar gas constant, *R *= 8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the new number of moles, *n*:

- Ideal gas equation: $pV=nRT\Rightarrown=\frac{p_{2}V}{RT_{2}}$
- $n = \frac{( 1.22 \times 10^{4} ) \times 0.819}{8.31 \times 370} = 3.25 \text{mol}$** [1 mark]**

Calculate *y*:

- $y = \frac{d i f f e r e n c e i n m o l e s}{o r i g i n a l n u m b e r o f m o l e s} \times 100 \%$
- $y = \frac{3.25 - 3}{3} \times 100 = 8.3 \%$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Δ**T** can be in °C or K, as the temperature difference is the **same** for both scales, as it is **linear**.*

parts.problemMd: Define internal energy.
parts.solutionMd:
Internal energy is defined as:

- The sum of (the random distribution of) kinetic and potential energies within a system of molecules; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Describe the change in internal energy if a system's temperature decreases.
parts.solutionMd:
If the temperature decreases:

parts.problemMd:

For an ideal gas, temperature is .................... proportional to ................... kinetic energy.

|---|---|---|
| **total** | **directly** | **average** |
parts.solutionMd:
To complete the sentence:

**One**** mark for each correct word:**

- For an ideal gas, temperature is **directly**** **proportional to **average **kinetic energy

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Explain why the following statement made by a student is only true for an ideal gas:

'*internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energies of all the particles*'.
parts.solutionMd:
This is only true for an ideal gas because:

- Ideal gases have no potential energy; **[1 mark]**
- Because there are no interactions / forces between the particles; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The statement above omits the potential energy from the definition of internal energy.*

> *In this topic, you must be familiar with the assumptions made in the ideal gas model. An ideal gas has particles that collide but have no intermolecular interactions.*

> *In a solid, liquid, or real gas, however, there are interactions between particles. These make up the system's potential energy, which contributes to internal energy. *

parts.problemMd:
For an ideal gas, internal energy is directly proportional to temperature in kelvin.

A sample of ideal gas is in a perfectly insulated box of fixed volume.

The temperature of the sample rises from 400 K to 600 K. Its internal energy was initially 2800 J.

Calculate its new internal energy.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the new internal energy:

List the known quantities:

- Initial temperature, *T*<sub>*i*</sub>  = 400 K
- Final temperature, *T*<sub>*f*</sub>  = 600 K
- Initial internal energy, *U*<sub>*i*</sub>  = 2800 J

Use direct proportionality:

- $T\proptoU$
- Therefore, $\frac{T_{f}}{T_{i}}=\frac{U_{f}}{U_{i}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities to find the new internal energy, *U*<sub>*f*</sub> :

- $U_{f}=U_{i}\times\frac{T_{f}}{T_{i}}=2800\times\frac{600}{400}$ **[1 mark]**
- $U_{f}=4200J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The equation *$\frac{T_{f}}{T_{i}}=\frac{U_{f}}{U_{i}}$* is essentially saying 'if temperature doubles, internal energy also doubles'. This is direct proportionality, but you could have also used the initial temperature and initial internal energy to find a constant of proportionality and found final internal energy that way. Both methods are equivalent.*

parts.problemMd:
State and explain, in molecular terms, whether the internal energy of the following increases, decreases or does not change.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:

(ii) The internal energy of some water as it evaporates at a constant temperature:

- The kinetic energy remains constant because the temperature remains constant; **[1 mark]**
- So the internal energy increases; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A container of fixed volume holds 15.0 moles of a monatomic ideal gas. This is 9.03 × 10<sup>24</sup> atoms in total.

Each atom has a mass of 6.64 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg.

The gas is held at a temperature such that the root-mean-square speed is 1680 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate this temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the temperature:

List the known quantities:

- Number of moles, *n*  = 15.0 mol
- Number of atoms, *N* = 9.03 × 10<sup>24</sup>
- Root-mean-square speed, $\sqrt{( \text{angle} \text{brackets} c^{2} ) \text{angle} brackets}$ = 1680 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Mass of an individual atom, *m* = 6.64 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg
- Molar gas constant, *R*  = 8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>

Recall the ideal gas law:

- $pV=nRT$

Use the pressure of an ideal gas equation from the formulae page:

- $p = 1 \frac{1}{3} \frac{N m}{V} ( \text{angle} \text{brackets} c^{2} ) \text{angle} \text{brackets}$

Combine the two to eliminate pressure and volume:

- $p V = ( 1 \frac{1}{3} \frac{N m}{ \cancel{V} } ( \text{angle} \text{brackets} c^{2} ) \text{angle} \text{brackets} ) \times \cancel{V} = n R T$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange for temperature:

- $n R T = \frac{N m ( \text{angle} \text{brackets} c^{2} ) \text{angle} brackets}{3}$
- $T = \frac{N m ( \text{angle} \text{brackets} c^{2} ) \text{angle} brackets}{3 n R} = \frac{( 9.03 \times 10^{24 ) \times ( 6.64 \times 10^{-27} } ) \times 1680^{2}}{3 \times 15 \times 8.31}$ **[1 mark]**
- $T=453K$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Combining these two known equations requires some careful algebra. Additionally, a common pitfall is to forget to square the root-mean-square speed when using the pressure of an ideal gas equation. You had to square the 1680 m s*<sup>*−1*</sup>* to get the correct answer.*

> *Root-mean-square speed is written as *$\sqrt{( \text{angle} \text{brackets} c^{2} ) \text{angle} brackets}$* and has units of speed,  m s*<sup>*−1*</sup>*.*

> *Mean-square speed is written as *`< c ^2 >`* and has units of speed-squared, m*<sup>*2*</sup>* s*<sup>*−2*</sup>*.*

parts.problemMd:

Calculate the new temperature of the gas.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the new temperature:

List the known quantities:

- Number of moles, *n*  = 15 mol (from (a))
- Molar gas constant, *R*  = 8.31 J K<sup>−1</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>
- Pressure, *p*  = 150 kPa = 150 × 10<sup>3</sup> Pa
- Volume, *V*  = 0.300 m<sup>3</sup>

Rearrange the ideal gas equation for temperature:

- $pV=nRT$
- $T=\frac{pV}{nR}$

Substitute the known quantities:

- $T = \frac{( 150 \times 10^{3} ) \times 0.300}{15 \times 8.31}$ **[1 mark]**
- $T=361K$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

(ii) Describe the process which caused this:

Explain your answer:

- The volume was fixed / constant; **[1 mark]**
- No work was done; **[1 mark]**

> *Recall that internal energy can be decreased either by the gas doing work (i.e. expanding) or heat being transferred away from the gas. The container has a fixed volume, so the gas cannot expand or be compressed.*

> *This leaves only heat transfer as a means of reducing internal energy. This is a less formal way of stating the first law of thermodynamics - a concept you will come a cross in the next topic.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A container of fixed volume holds 15.0 moles of a monatomic ideal gas.

The boiling point of this gas is 350 K. Explain why the potential energy of this ideal gas does not change.
parts.solutionMd:
The potential energy is unchanged because:

- (For an ideal gas) there are no intermolecular forces; **[1 mark]**
- (Additionally) no phase changes occur; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Of course, in reality there are intermolecular forces between gaseous particles. For an ideal gas, however, these interactions are ignored and all internal energy is assumed to be derived from the average kinetic energy of the particles.*

> *This is why internal energy is directly proportional to temperature for an ideal gas. *

> *Potential energy changes if the gas condenses, as bonds form between the particles in a liquid phase, but that is not occurring here.*

parts.problemMd:
A monatomic gas, contained within a balloon, gains 43 kJ of internal energy.

This process involves 25 kJ of thermal energy being transferred to the gas.

Calculate the work done through this process, including the whether work is done on or by the balloon.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculating the work done by the gas:

List the known quantities:

- Change in internal energy, Δ*U* = +43 kJ
- Thermal energy transferred, *Q* = +25 kJ

Recall the first law of thermodynamics:

- $ΔU=q+W$

Substitute the known quantities and find *W *:

- $43=25+W$ **[1 mark]**
- $W=+18\mathrm{kJ}$ **[1 mark]**
- Work is done <u>on the balloon</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In thermodynamics, the sign in front of an energy implies a direction of transfer. In CIE, the convention is:*

- *Work done **on** the system (gas compressed) is positive*
- *Work done **by** the system (gas expands) is negative*

> *Not every website or exam board uses CIE's sign convention for thermodynamics, so be aware of this if attempting practice questions from a range of exam boards or websites.*

A monatomic gas, contained within a balloon, gains 43 kJ of internal energy. This process involves 25 kJ of thermal energy being transferred to the gas. Calculate the work done through this process... W = +18 kJ. Work is done on the balloon.

parts.problemMd: Suggest, with a reason, how the specific latent heat of vapourisation of water at a pressure greater than atmospheric pressure compares with its value at atmospheric pressure.

| **Final answer:** **0** | + *q* | **Final answer:** **+ ΔU** |

- The water remains at atmospheric pressure, and the only energy supplied is thermal energy, so the internal energy of the water increases by *+ΔU;* **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A fixed mass of water is in a beaker at atmospheric pressure. The initial temperature of the water is 0 \u00b0C. The water is supplied with thermal energy q, so that its temperature increases to 10 \u00b0C. There is no net change in the volume of the water.

Determine the work done and the increase in internal energy of the water by completing Table 1.1, considering the first law of thermodynamics.

Table 1.1: work done on water = 0; thermal energy supplied to water = +q; increase in internal energy of water = +\u0394U. The volume of the water does not change, so the work done on the water = 0. The water remains at atmospheric pressure, and the only energy supplied is thermal energy, so the internal energy of the water increases by +\u0394U.

The water from part (b) is now heated so it's temperature increases by a further 10 °C to a final temperature of 20 °C. This process causes the volume of the water to increase so that work *W *is done.

Assume that the change in internal energy is the same as in part (b).

Determine the work done, thermal energy supplied and the increase in internal energy of the water by completing **Table 1.2**, considering the first law of thermodynamics.

**Table 1.2**

| Work done on water | thermal energy supplied to water | increase in internal energy of water |
|---|---|---|
|   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
A table that would score 2 marks should look like this:

| Work done on water | thermal energy supplied to water | increase in internal energy of water |
|---|---|---|
| **Final answer:** **−W** | **Final answer:** **+W +ΔU** | **Final answer:** **+ΔU** |

- Work, *W* is done on the water to increase the volume, so the work done by the water = −*W* **AND**
- The change in internal energy = same as part (b) = *+*Δ*U*; **[1 mark]**

- Work done + thermal energy supplied = increase in internal energy

  - So −*W* + thermal energy supplied = +Δ*U*
  - Hence, thermal energy supplied = +*W* +Δ*U*;* ***[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A fixed mass of an ideal gas is initially at a temperature of 20 °C. The gas has a volume of 0.12 m^3 and a pressure of 0.6 × 10^5 Pa.

The gas undergoes three successive changes, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![16-1-2b-m-thermodynamics-cycle-of-change-grid-sq-cie-a-level](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/16-thermodynamics/16-2-the-first-law-of-thermodynamics/assets/001-16-1-2b-m-thermodynamics-cycle-of-change-grid-sq.png)

The initial state of the gas is represented by point X. The gas is cooled at constant pressure to point Y by the removal of 24.0 kJ of thermal energy.

The gas is then heated at constant volume to point Z.

Finally, the gas expands at constant temperature back to its original pressure and volume at point X. During the expansion, the gas does 15.8 kJ of work.

Calculate the magnitude of the work done in kJ during the change XY.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the magnitude of the work done in kJ during the change XY

List the known quantities:

- For X and Y pressure, *p *= 0.6 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- For X, volume, *V*<sub>*X*</sub> = 0.12 m<sup>3</sup>
- For Y, volume, *V*<sub>*Y*</sub> = 0.04 m<sup>3</sup>

Use the work done on a gas equation:

- $W=p\DeltaV$ **[1 mark]**
- $W = p ( V_{X} - V_{Y} )$
- $W = ( 0.6 \times 10^{5} ) \times ( 0.12 - 0.04 )$
- $W=4800J=4.8\mathrm{kJ}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The gas undergoes three successive changes, as shown in Fig. 1.1. The initial state of the gas is represented by point X. The gas is cooled at constant pressure to point Y by the removal of 24.0 kJ of thermal energy. The gas is then heated at constant volume to point Z. Finally, the gas expands at constant temperature back to its original pressure and volume at point X. During the expansion, the gas does 15.8 kJ of work.
Calculate the magnitude of the work done in kJ during the change XY: W = pΔV = (0.6 × 10^5) × (0.12 − 0.04) = 4800 J = 4.8 kJ

Complete Table 1.1 to show the work done on the gas, the thermal energy supplied to the gas and the increase in internal energy of the gas, for each of the changes XY, YZ and ZX.

**Table 1.1**

| change | increase in internal energy of gas / kJ | thermal energy supplied to gas / kJ | work done on gas / kJ |
|---|---|---|---|
| XY |   | −24.0 |   |
| YZ |   |   |   |
| ZX |   |   | −15.8 |
parts.solutionMd:
**During XY**

- Work done on gas for XY = +4.8 kJ (from (b))
- Increase in internal energy Δ*U* = − 24 + 4.8 = −19.2 kJ calculated from the equation $\DeltaU=q+W$

**During YZ**

- Work done for YZ = 0 kJ (as there is no change in volume)
- Increase in internal energy Δ*U* =  +19.2 kJ because the total increase in internal energy of the system (XYZX) = 0
- Hence, thermal energy gained = 19.2 kJ

**During ZX**

- Work done for ZX = −15.8 kJ (given in table)
- Increase in internal energy = 0 kJ (temperature and state do not change along ZX so the system is not heated . For the isothermal expansion ZX, the internal energy does not change (Δ*U* = 0), so by $\DeltaU=q+W$, $q=-W=+15.8$ kJ — thermal energy is supplied to maintain constant temperature)
- Hence, thermal energy = 15.8 kJ

A correctly completed table should look like this:

| change | increase in internal energy of gas / kJ | thermal energy supplied to gas / kJ | work done on gas / kJ |
|---|---|---|---|
| XY | **Final answer:** **−19.2** | −24.0 | **Final answer:** **4.8** |
| YZ | **Final answer:** **19.2** | **Final answer:** **19.2** | **Final answer:** **0** |
| ZX | **Final answer:** **0** | **Final answer:** **15.8** | −15.8 |

- **1 mark for each correct row**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The curved line ZX is called an isotherm. It is common for you to be asked to recognise that, if temperature and state of an **ideal gas **do not change, the internal energy does not change. The particles of an ideal gas do not interact so the only internal energy is the sum of kinetic energies (i.e. temperature).*

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows a chamber containing 5.2 kg of a gas, with a 0.75 kg piston above the gas.

![thermodynamics-1ah-ib-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/16-thermodynamics/16-2-the-first-law-of-thermodynamics/assets/002-thermodynamics-1ah-ib-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

When the gas is supplied with 32.4 kJ of heat, the piston experiences an average upwards acceleration 3.5 m s<sup>−2</sup> over a distance of 12 cm.

Calculate the work done by the gas.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the work done by the gas:

List the known quantities:

- Heat supplied to gas, *q*  = 32.4 kJ
- Upwards acceleration, *a*  = 3.5 m s<sup>−2</sup>
- Mass of piston, *m*  = 0.75 kg
- Distance moved, *s*  = 12 cm = 0.12 m
- Acceleration of free fall, *g*  = 9.81 m s<sup>−2 </sup>(from the data page)

Apply Newton's second law:

- The resultant force, *F*<sub>*res*</sub> , on the piston is:

  - $F_{res}=ma$
- The gas exerts an upward force, *F*<sub>*res*</sub> , and the piston's weight, *mg* , acts downwards

  - $F_{res}=F_{gas}-mg$
- Combine the two equations

  - $F_{gas}-mg=ma$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the force from the gas:

- $F_{g a s} = m ( a + g ) = 0.75 ( 3.5 + 9.81 )$
- $F_{gas}=9.983N$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the work done, *W *:

- Recall that distance moved parallel to the force was 12 cm
- $W=F_{gas}s=9.983\times0.12$
- $W=1.2J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Work done pops up in a lot of different areas of physics - you may have gone to the first law of thermodynamics initially. This question, however, makes use of Newton's second law to find a resultant force and then calculate mechanical work.  Annotate the diagram, list your known quantities, and the method will become much clearer.*

parts.problemMd:
A mass of 0.42 kg is attached to a spring and the system is made to oscillate with simple harmonic motion (SHM) on a horizontal, frictionless surface. The mass passes through the equilibrium position 200 times per minute.

The kinetic energy of the mass as it passes through the equilibrium position is 500 mJ. There are two points where the restoring force acting on the mass is at its maximum.

Show that the distance between these points is approximately 29 cm.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m* = 0.42 kg
- Passes through equilibrium 200 minute<sup>–1</sup>
- Kinetic Energy at *x* = 0, $E_{k}$= 500 mJ = 0.5 J

Determine the time period of the mass:

- The mass passes through the equilibrium position twice in one time period

  - There are 100 complete oscillations per minute
- *T* = $\frac{1}{f}$where *f* = $\frac{100}{60}$ s<sup>-1</sup>
- *T* = $\frac{60}{100}$= 0.6 s **[1 mark]**

Determine the angular velocity of the mass:

- *ω *= $\frac{2π}{T}$= $\frac{2π}{0.6}$ = 10.472 rad s<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Kinetic energy (and velocity) is maximum when displacement is zero:

- $E_{k}$=$\frac{1}{2}$*mv*<sup>2</sup>
- $v_{max}=ωx_{0}$* * where *x*<sub>0</sub>  is amplitude
- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$
- 0.5 = $\frac{1}{2}$× 0.42 × (10.472)<sup>2 </sup>× *x*<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>

Rearrange for amplitude *x*<sub>0</sub> and substitute in the values:

- Amplitude, *x*<sub>0 </sub>=$\sqrt{ \frac{2 \times 0.5}{0.42 \times ( 10.472 )^{2}} }$ = 0.147 m = 14.7 cm **[1 mark]**

Calculate the distance:

- Distance between the two maxima is twice the amplitude
- *d *= 14.7 × 2 = 29.3 = 29 cm (2 sf) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *There are several useful formulae for the simple harmonic oscillation on the formula page. The equation *$v_{max}=ωx_{0}$* can be derived from:*

$v=\pmω\sqrt{x_{0}^{2}-x^{2}}$

> *by realising that speed is at a maximum at the equilibrium position, when **x**  is zero. Here, **x*<sub>*0*</sub>*  is maximum displacement (the amplitude).*

$T=2π\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$

parts.solutionMd:
Derive equation for frequency of a pendulum:

- *f =*$\frac{1}{T}$* *=  $\frac{1}{2π}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$

Consider the effect of a stronger gravitational field:

- Period is independent of gravitational acceleration / there is no *g* term, so change in *g* will not affect frequency; **[1 mark]**

Consider the effect of 3 additional springs in parallel:

- 4 springs will require 4 times the force to extend the same distance, so <u>*k*</u><u> in this experiment is quadrupled</u> (× 4); **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
The amplitude of the pendulum is 60 cm when it swings with a frequency of 0.7 Hz. During this oscillation, the maximum kinetic energy of the pendulum is 23 J.

Determine the mass of the pendulum bob.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the mass of the pendulum bob:

List the known quantities:

- Amplitude, $A=x_{0}=60\mathrm{cm}=0.6m$
- Frequency, $f=0.7\mathrm{Hz}$
- Maximum kinetic energy, $E_{Kmax}=23J$

Recall the total energy equation and rearrange to solve for *m*:

- $E=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}$
- $m=\frac{2E}{ω^{2}x_{0}^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the equation for angular velocity into the total energy equation:

- $ω=\frac{2π}{T}=2πf$
- $m = \frac{2 E}{( 2 \mathrm{\pi } f )^{2} x_{0}^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate mass:

- $E_{Kmax}=E$ **[1 mark]**
- $m = \frac{2 \times 23}{( 2 \mathrm{\pi } \times 0.7 )^{2} \times ( 0.6 )^{2}}$
- $m=6.6\mathrm{kg}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The amplitude of the pendulum is 60 cm when it swings with a frequency of 0.7 Hz. During this oscillation, the maximum kinetic energy of the pendulum is 23 J.
Determine the mass of the pendulum bob. (m = 6.6 kg)

Calculate the kinetic energy of the pendulum when the pendulum bob is at a distance of $0.4x_{0}$ from its point of maximum displacement.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the kinetic energy of the pendulum bob:

List the known quantities:

- Maximum kinetic energy, $E_{Kmax}=\frac{1}{2}mω^{2}x_{0}^{2}=23J$ (from part (b))
- Amplitude, $A=x_{0}=0.6m$ (from part (a))
- Frequency, $f=0.7\mathrm{Hz}$ (from part (a))
- Mass of pendulum, $m=6.6\mathrm{kg}$ (from part (b))

Determine the displacement from the equilibrium position:

- The question states that the pendulum is $0.4x_{0}$ from its maximum displacement ![9-1-hl-mcq-m5-ms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/17-oscillations/17-2-energy-in-simple-harmonic-motion/assets/023-9-1-hl-mcq-m5-ms.jpg)

  - Therefore, it is $0.6x_{0}$ from its equilibrium position **OR** $x=0.6\times0.6=0.36m$ **[1 mark]**

Using the kinetic energy equation to determine the kinetic energy at this displacement:

- $E_{K } = 1 \frac{1}{2} m \\omega ^{2} ( x_{0}^{2} - x^{2} ) = 1 \frac{1}{2} m ( 2 \pi f )^{2} ( x_{0}^{2} - x^{2} )$
- $E_{K } = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 6.6 \times ( 2 \pi \times 0.7 )^{2} \times ( 0.6^{2} - 0.36^{2} )$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{K}=14.72J$** [1 mark]**

**OR**

- $E_{K } = 1 \frac{1}{2} m \\omega ^{2} ( x_{0}^{2} - x^{2} ) = 1 \frac{1}{2} m \\omega ^{2} ( x_{0}^{2} - ( 0.6 x_{0} )^{2} )$
- $E_{K } = 1 \frac{1}{2} m \\omega ^{2} x_{0}^{2} ( 1 - 0.6^{2} ) = 23 ( 1 - 0.6^{2} )$ **[1 mark]**

- $E_{K}=14.72J$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *We can use the total energy equation in this instance because we know the value of the maximum kinetic energy which is equal to the total energy of the system. Always choose equations based on the known quantities you are given (or can calculate from what you are given!)*

A U shaped tube with cross-sectional area *A *contains a liquid of mass *m*, density *ρ* and volume *V *as shown in Fig. 1.1. When the water of length *L* is in equilibrium in the tube the levels of water on either side are equal. When the water is pushed down a distance *x*<sub>*max*</sub> on one side of the tube then the water on the opposite side rises. Upon release the water undergoes simple harmonic motion as the water levels on each side rise and fall about the equilibrium position.

![17-2-q1a-h-sq-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/17-oscillations/17-2-energy-in-simple-harmonic-motion/assets/026-17-2-q1a-h-sq-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Obtain an expression for the maximum kinetic energy of the liquid in terms of its cross-sectional area *A, *density *ρ, *maximum velocity *v*<sub>max </sub>and length of water *L*.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Cross-sectional area of liquid = *A*
- Mass of liquid = *m*
- Density of liquid = *ρ*
- Volume of liquid = *V*
- Length of liquid column =* L*

Recall the equations for maximum kinetic energy *E*<sub>*k (max)*</sub>, volume *V* and density *ρ*:

- $E_{k ( m a x )} = 1 \frac{1}{2} m v_{m a x}^{2}$ **AND**
- *V *= *AL* **AND**
- $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange and substitute the equations for mass *m *and volume *V*:

- $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$ $\rightarrow$ $m=ρV$
- $m = \\rho \times ( A L )$
- $E_{k ( m a x )} = 1 \frac{1}{2} ( \\rho A L ) v_{m a x}^{2}$
- $E_{k ( m a x )} = 1 \frac{1}{2} A L \\rho v_{m a x}^{2}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *To answer this question correctly take time to think about all the equations you know that can help you express the quantity you want with those you need. Even though the water is curved it is a cylinder of length **L, **so volume = cross-sectional area **A **× **L**. *

- Density of liquid = *ρ*
- Volume of liquid = *V*

- *m *= *Vρ*

- So, *m *= *Ax*<sub>*max*</sub>*ρ ***[1 mark]**

Obtain an expression for gravitational potential energy *E*<sub>*p*</sub><sub> (max)</sub> in terms of cross-sectional area *A *and density of liquid *ρ*:

- *E*<sub>*p (max)*</sub> = (*Ax*<sub>*max*</sub>*ρ*) × *gx*<sub>*max*</sub>

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Gravtiational potential energy is gained when the water is a height of **x*<sub>*max*</sub>* above the equilibrium position hence the equation for the mass of the water moving above this position contains **x*<sub>*max*</sub>*. The SHM equation for **v*<sub>*max*</sub>* is **v*<sub>*max*</sub>* = **ωA** where **A **is amplitude and not cross-sectional area. Don't let this confuse you! *

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A U shaped tube with cross-sectional area A contains a liquid of mass m, density ρ and volume V as shown in Fig. 1.1. When the water of length L is in equilibrium in the tube the levels of water on either side are equal. When the water is pushed down a distance x_max on one side of the tube then the water on the opposite side rises. Upon release the water undergoes simple harmonic motion as the water levels on each side rise and fall about the equilibrium position.
E_k(max) = 1/2 ALρ(v_max)^2 (From part a)
E_p(max) = Aρg(x_max)^2 (From part b)

Show that the time period of the oscillation of the liquid in the U shaped tube of Fig. 1.1 is given by the equation

$T=2π\sqrt{\frac{l}{2g}}$
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- $E_{k ( m a x )} = 1 \frac{1}{2} A L \\rho v_{m a x}^{2}$ (From part a))
- *E*<sub>*p (max)*</sub> = *Aρgx*<sub>*max*</sub><sup>*2 *</sup>(From part b))

Combine the expressions and rearrange to get an expression for $\frac{x_{max}}{v_{max}}$:

- $\frac{1}{2}ALρv_{max}^{2}=Aρgx_{max}^{2}$
- $\frac{v_{max}^{2}}{x_{max}^{2}}=\frac{2Aρg}{ALρ}$
- $\frac{v_{max}^{2}}{x_{max}^{2}}=\frac{2g}{L}$
- $\frac{v_{max}}{x_{max}}=\sqrt{\frac{2g}{L}}$
- $\frac{x_{max}}{v_{max}}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the equation for *v*<sub>*max*</sub> to substitute in for *ω*:

- Recall: *v*<sub>*max *</sub>= *ωx*<sub>*max *</sub>(for amplitude *x*<sub>*max*</sub>)
- $ω=\frac{v_{max}}{x_{max}}$ $\rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{ω}=\frac{x_{max}}{v_{max}}$
- $\frac{1}{ω}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$ **[1 mark]**

Recall the equation for angular velocity, *ω *in terms of time period *T *and obtain the required equation:

- Recall: $ω=\frac{2π}{T}$
- So, $\frac{1}{ω}=\frac{T}{2π}$
- $\frac{T}{2π}=\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$ **[1 mark]**
- So, $T=2π\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}$

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You do not need to know this equation for your course, so don't learn it. These types of hard questions are common when they take you beyond the syllabus. *

- <u>Energy is transferred away</u> from the oscillating system; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the amplitude decreases; **[1 mark]**

> *When answering an 'explain' question, make sure you use either 'because', 'due to' or 'therefore' in your answer to ensure you fully answer the question.*

> *Another way to phrase this answer would be:*

parts.problemMd:
A student investigates the vertical oscillations of the mass–spring system shown in Fig. 1.1.

![6-3-s-q--q4a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/17-oscillations/17-3-damped-and-forced-oscillations-resonance/assets/001-6-3-s-q-q4a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The system is suspended from one end of a thread passing over a pulley. The other end of the thread is tied to a weight. The system is shown in Fig. 1.1 with the mass at the equilibrium position, denoted by the fiducial mark. The spring constant is the same for each spring.

The table below shows the measurements recorded by the student over the course of 5 repeats of the experiment.

**Table 1.1**

| **Time for 40 oscillations of the mass-spring system / s** |   |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 45.8 | 44.6 | 45.6 | 45.8 | 45.2 |

Determine the natural frequency of the mass-spring system and the percentage uncertainty in the data. Hence quote the natural frequency with its uncertainty to an appropriate number of significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the mean time period, *T*:

- Sum of times = 45.8 + 44.6 + 45.6 + 45.8 + 45.2 = 227
- Mean time for 40 oscillations, 40*T* =$\frac{227}{5}$ = 45.4 s
- Mean time period, *T* =$\frac{45.4}{40}$ = 1.135 s **[1 mark]**

Calculate the natural frequency:

- There is no driving force, so the natural frequency is $f_{0}$  =$\frac{1}{T}$
- Natural frequency, $f_{0}$ = $\frac{1}{1.135}$  = 0.881 Hz **[1 mark]**

Determine the percentage uncertainty in the data:

- For a set of data, the uncertainty = ± half of the range
- Uncertainty in data, Δ(40*T*) = $\frac{45.8-44.6}{2}$ = 0.6 s
- Percentage uncertainty = $\frac{\Delta ( 40 T )}{40 T}$ × 100%
- Percentage uncertainty = $\frac{0.6}{45.4}$ × 100% = 1.3 % **[1 mark]**

Calculate the uncertainty in natural frequency and quote the final answer to 3 s.f:

- $\frac{\Deltaf_{0}}{f_{0}}$ =$\frac{\DeltaT}{T}$
- Δ$f_{0}$ = $f_{0}$  ×$\frac{\DeltaT}{T}$
- Uncertainty in natural frequency, Δ$f_{0}$ = 0.881 × $\frac{0.6}{45.4}$ = 0.012 Hz
- Therefore, $f_{0}$ = 0.881 ± 0.012 Hz (3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *It is easy to get confused when combining uncertainties in formulae, especially when we have the reciprocal of period here.*

> *In this equation:*

$\mathrm{speed}=\frac{\mathrm{distance}}{\mathrm{time}}$

> *the percentage uncertainty of speed is simply the sum of the percentage uncertainties of distance and time.*

> *For the equation in this question:*

$f=\frac{1}{T}$

> *we are combining the percentage uncertainty of time period and the number 1. Obviously, the number 1 has no uncertainty so the percentage uncertainty of frequency is just 0 + the percentage uncertainty of period - this is why we can say:*

$\frac{Δf}{f}=\frac{ΔT}{T}$

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
A bar magnet is suspended on a spring as shown in Fig. 1.1. A pole of the magnet is located near to one end of a solenoid.

**Fig. 1.1**

The observations made are summarised in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Supply** | **Observation** |
|---|---|
| Direct current (d.c.) | 1. The magnet moves vertically |
| Alternating current (a.c.) | 2. The magnet oscillates |
| 3. When the frequency of the alternating current (a.c) is changed, the amplitude of vibration of the magnet is associated with the applied frequency |   |

parts.solutionMd:
Why the magnet moves vertically when subjected to a direct current:

Any **two** from:

- When a d.c. supply is switched on, the solenoid produces a magnetic field; **[1 mark]**
- (Depending on the orientation of the bar magnet,) the magnetic field either attracts or repels the magnet; **[1 mark]**
- The magnetic field causes the magnet to move either towards or away from the solenoid; **[1 mark]**

Why the magnet oscillates when subjected to an alternating current:

Any **two** from:

- When a.c. passes through the solenoid, an <u>alternating</u> magnetic field is produced; **[1 mark]**
- The alternating magnetic field alternately attracts and repels the magnet; **[1 mark]**
- The alternating magnetic field causes the magnet to periodically move towards and away from the solenoid, hence oscillations occur; **[1 mark]**

Why the amplitude is associated with the applied frequency:

Any **two** from:

- The magnet undergoes <u>forced oscillations</u> as a result of the a.c. passing through the solenoid; **[1 mark]**
- The amplitude varies with the applied frequency of the driving oscillations; **[1 mark]**
- Frequency of magnet oscillations originate from the frequency of the alternating current supply; **[1 mark]**** **

parts.problemMd: Calculate the acceleration of the proton when placed in a uniform electric field of field strength 6.0 × 10<sup>–2</sup> V m<sup>–1</sup><sub>.</sub>
parts.solutionMd:
The acceleration is:

List the known quantities:

- Electric field strength, *E* = 6.0 × 10<sup>–2</sup> V m<sup>–1</sup>

From the formulae page:

- Rest mass of proton, *m*<sub>p </sub>= 1.67 × 10<sup>–27</sup> kg
- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C

Determine an equation for the acceleration, *a*:

- $F=Eq=ma$
- $a=\frac{Eq}{m}$ **[1 mark]**

- $a = \frac{( 6.0 \times 10^{- 2} ) \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{- 19} ) }{1.67 \times 10^{- 27} }$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The metal plates are 50 mm apart. When the switch is closed, the plates are charged by a 200 V dc supply, as shown in Fig 1.2.

![7-4-s-q--q3c-easy-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-2-uniform-electric-fields/assets/003-7-4-s-q-q3c-easy-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Calculate the electric field strength between the plates when the switch is closed.

State an appropriate unit for your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the electric field strength between the plates:

List the known quantities:

- Potential difference between the plates, *V* = 200 V
- Separation between the plates, *d* = 50 mm = 50 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m

Use the equation for electric field strength:

- Electric field strength:  $E=\frac{V}{d}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $E=\frac{200}{50\times10^{-3}}$* *
- Evaluate: * *$E$ = 4000 **[1 mark]**
- Unit:  V m<sup>–1 </sup>**OR**** **N C<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *There are two ways of calculating electric field strength, but it is important to understand the difference between them. *

> *The equation:*

$E=\frac{V}{d}$

> *is used to calculate the electric field strength between **parallel plates**, where **V** is the potential difference between the plates and **d** is the separation of the plates. This is a uniform field *

> *The equation: *

> $E=\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{Q}{r^{2}}$*  *

> *is used to calculate the electric field strength around a **point charge**, where **Q** is the charge which produces the electric field and **r** is the distance between the charge producing the electric field to the point where the electric field strength is being calculated. This is a radial (a type of non-uniform) field.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A uniform electric field is produced between two charged parallel plates, A and B. A positively charged alpha particle enters the electric field and deflects, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

State and explain the effect on the deflection of the alpha particle when

(i) the potential difference applied between A and B is increased

[2]

(ii) the separation of A and B is increased.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Increasing the potential difference between the plates causes:

- A greater electric field strength / force (on the alpha particle); **[1 mark]**
- (Hence) a greater deflection; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Increasing the separation between the plates causes:

- A smaller electric field strength / force (on the alpha particle); **[1 mark]**
- (Hence) a smaller deflection; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

> *The stronger the electric field strength between the two parallel plates, the more a charged particle will deflect. The equation used to calculate the electric field strength, **E**, between two parallel charged plates is:*

$E=\frac{V}{d}$

> *where **V** is the voltage across the plates and **d** is the separation distance. *

> *From this equation, we can see that the electric field strength is inversely proportional to the distance between the plates *$( E \propto \frac{1}{d} )$*. Therefore, if the distance between the charged plates **increases**, the electric field strength will **decrease**.*

**Extract:**

The alpha particle is replaced by a beta particle. The separation of the plates and the potential difference applied across them is kept the same.

State and explain **two** properties of alpha and beta particles that can affect the amount these particles deflect in an electric field.
parts.solutionMd:
The properties of alpha and beta particles that can cause differences in deflections are:

**Final answer:** **Any two ****pairs from:**

- Charge; **[1 mark]**
- Opposite charges deflect in opposite directions **OR **the greater the charge, the greater the deflection **OR** alpha deflects more than beta due to greater charge; **[1 mark]**

- Mass; **[1 mark]**
- The greater the mass, the smaller the deflection **OR** alpha deflects less than beta due to larger mass; **[1 mark]**

- Speed; **[1 mark]**
- The greater the speed, the smaller the deflection; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The faster a charged particle enters the electric field, the smaller the deflection. This is because it will spend **less** **time** in the electric field. *

> *The **smaller** the potential difference applied between the charged parallel plates, the smaller the electric field strength. This is because electric field strength and potential difference are directly proportional *$( E = \frac{V}{d} )$*.*

> *This means that less force will be acting on a charged particle due to the electric field (since *$F=qE$*), and therefore less deflection.*

parts.problemMd:
The force on a proton placed between the plates is 50 nN and the separation of the plates is 24 mm.

Calculate the potential difference between the plates.
parts.solutionMd:
The potential difference between the plates is:

List the known quantities:

- Electric force, *F = *50 nN = 50 × 10<sup>–9</sup> N
- Separation of the plates, *d* = 24 mm = 24 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m

From the formulae page:

- Elementary charge, *e*  = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C

Determine the equation for the potential difference between the plates, *V*:

- $F=Eq$ and $E=\frac{V}{d}$
- $F=\frac{Vq}{d}$
- $V=\frac{Fd}{q}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the values:

- $V = \frac{( 50 \times 10^{- 9} ) \times ( 24 \times 10^{- 3} ) }{1.60 \times 10^{- 19} }$ **[1 mark]**
- $V=7.5\times10^{9}V=7.5\mathrm{GV}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

**Fig 1.3**

Calculate the charge of the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
The charge of the particle is:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of the particle, *m* = 5.0 g = 5 × 10<sup>–3</sup> kg
- Separation of the plates, *d* = 24 mm = 24 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- Potential difference between the plates, *V* = 7.5 × 10<sup>9</sup> V

Determine an equation for the charge of the particle, *q*:

- To remain stationary, the electric force upwards = weight downwards
- $F=Eq=mg$
- $q=\frac{mg}{E}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the electric field strength, *E*:

- $E=\frac{\DeltaV}{\Deltad}=\frac{7.5\times10^{9}}{24\times10^{-3}}=3.125\times10^{11}Vm^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the values into the charge equation, *q*:

- $q = \frac{( 5.0 \times 10^{- 3} ) \times 9.81}{3.125 \times 10^{11} }$ **[1 mark]**
- $q=1.5696\times10^{-13}C=1.6\times10^{-13}C$ **[1 mark]**

> *Remember you **cannot** use the same electric force **F** as in part (b), because this is a different particle to the proton. We can use the same potential difference and separation between the plates because these are the property of the plates itself (which haven't changed), instead of the particle.*

parts.problemMd: State Coulomb’s law.
parts.solutionMd:
Coulomb’s law states:

- The (electric) force between <u>two point charges</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Many definitions in A–level physics involve describing an equation in words. Remember that Coulomb’s law is equal to*

$F=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$

> *Therefore, *$F\proptoQ_{1}Q_{2}$* (force is proportional to the product of the **two **charges) and *$F\propto\frac{1}{r^{2}}$*  (force is inversely proportional to the square of their separation)*

Use Coulomb’s law to calculate the force between the point charges:

> *In this question, you are asked to calculate the **magnitude** of the electric force acting on each point charge. This means that you do **not** need to include the negative sign in your answer. A negative sign simply indicates that the electric force between the positive and negative point charges is **attractive**.*

parts.solutionMd:

- Separation between the two charges, *r* = 67 mm = 67 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- $Q_{1}$= +10.0 nC
- $Q_{2}$= +6.0 nC

From the formulae page:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup>** OR **$\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$** **= 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup>

- Coulomb’s Law: *F* = $\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

> *Remember that the charges must be in Coulombs and the separation **r**  must be in metres for Coulomb's law**. *

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the electric force between the alpha and aluminium nuclei:

List the known quantities

- Distance between nuclei, *r* = 2.0 nm = 2.0 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m
- Coulomb constant, $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup> (from the data page)
- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C (from the data page)

- Charge on aluminium nucleus, *Q*<sub>*2*</sub> = 13*e* = 13 × (1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) C

Use Coulomb's law to calculate the electric force:

- Coulomb's law:  $F=\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $F = \frac{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) \times 2 \times 13 \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{-19} } )^{2}}{( 2.0 \times 10^{- 9} )^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

An alpha particle and an aluminium nucleus are isolated in a vacuum, as shown in Fig. 1.1. Each nucleus may be considered to be a point mass with a point charge.

An aluminium nucleus contains 13 protons. The alpha particle and the aluminium nucleus are separated by a distance of 2.0 nm. Calculate the electric force between the alpha particle and the aluminium nucleus. Electric force: F = 1.5 × 10^–9 N

The aluminium nucleus contains 27 nucleons in total.

(i) Calculate the gravitational force between the two nuclei.

[2]

(ii) Suggest why gravitational effects do not need to be accounted for in electric field calculations involving nuclei.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the gravitational force between the alpha and aluminium nuclei:

List the known quantities

- Distance between nuclei, *r* = 2.0 nm = 2.0 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m
- Gravitational constant, $G$ = 6.67 × 10<sup>–11</sup> N m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>–2</sup> (from the formula sheet)
- Atomic mass unit, u = 1.66 × 10<sup>–27</sup> kg
- Mass of alpha particle, *m*<sub>*1*</sub> = 4u = 4 × (1.66 × 10<sup>–27</sup>)
- Mass of aluminium nucleus, *m*<sub>*2*</sub> = 27u = 27 × (1.66 × 10<sup>–27</sup>)

parts.problemMd:
Two charged objects X and Y are made to circle a point O. X and Y are at a distance, *d* = 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m and they have equal masses, where *m* = 1.7 × 10<sup>−9</sup> kg as shown in Fig. 1.1.

The objects carry an equal but opposite charge, where the magnitude *q* = 3.2 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C.

![dae17afb-852e-4b5a-8723-1796e5ba2bd7-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-3-electric-force-between-point-charges/assets/001-dae17afb-852e-4b5a-8723-1796e5ba2bd7-1.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Calculate the acceleration of X and Y.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Distance, *d* = 1.8 × 10<sup>−8</sup> m
- Mass*, m* = 1.7 × 10<sup>−9</sup> kg
- Charge, *q* = 3.2 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C
- Gravitational constant, *G* = 6.67 × 10<sup>−11</sup> N m<sup>2</sup> kg<sup>−2</sup>
- Permittivity of free space, *ε*<sub>*o*</sub> = 8.85 × 10<sup>−12</sup> C<sup>2</sup> N<sup>−1</sup> m<sup>−2</sup>

Deduce an expression for the resultant force:

- X and Y are in a circular motion around O
- The forces which hold the particle in motion are gravity and the Coulomb force
- Resultant centripetal force, $F_{R}=F_{g}+F_{c}$

  - Where *F*<sub>*R*</sub> = resultant force, *F*<sub>*g*</sub> = force due to gravity, *F*<sub>*c*</sub> = Coulomb force

Find *F*<sub>*g*</sub>, the force due to gravity:

- $F_{g}=G\frac{Mm}{r^{2}}$
- Therefore $F_{g}=(6.67\times10^{-11})\times\frac{(1.7\times10^{-9})^{2}}{(1.8\times10^{-8})^{2}}=5.950\times10^{-13}N$ **[1 mark]**

Find *F*<sub>*c*</sub>, the Coulomb force by combining the equations for Coulomb's law and Coulomb's constant:

- $F_{c}=\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$
- Therefore $F_{c}=\frac{(3.2\times10^{-19})^{2}}{4π\times(8.85\times10^{-12})\times(1.8\times10^{-8})^{2}}=2.842\times10^{-12}N$ **[1 mark]**

Add the forces to find the resultant and use *F = ma* to find acceleration:

- $F_{R}=ma$
- Therefore, $a=\frac{(F_{g}+F_{c})}{m}$
- Therefore $a=\frac{(5.950\times10^{-13})+(2.842\times10^{-12})}{(1.7\times10^{-9})}=2.022\times10^{-3}$
- *a* = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m s<sup>−2</sup> (2 s.f.); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In many situations gravity can be taken as negligible, however in this situation the particles are close enough together that gravity plays a part.*

> *An alternative method to find the time period would use the equation  *$F_{R}=mω^{2}r$*, which introduces one extra step but still ends at the same place and same answer.*

> *Once the force has been found, acceleration can be obtained from circular motion equations.*

> *Finally, the last equation can be found two ways, either by deriving as suggested in the solution above, or, using quick dimensional analysis as a reminder. Notice that angular velocity is measured in 'per seconds', therefore time period must be, in effect, 'per angular velocity'.*

> *Remember that electric field lines show the direction in which a positive charge would move if placed at a particular point. Therefore, the field lines point **away** from a **positive** charge and **towards** a **negative** charge.*

> *The strength of the electric field is shown by the **spacing** of the electric field lines.  The closer the field lines are together, the stronger the electric field. The further apart the electric field lines are, the weaker the electric field.*

parts.problemMd: State the formula for the electric field strength $E$ at the surface of the sphere and state the meaning of any other symbols used.
parts.solutionMd:
The formula for electric field strength at the surface of the sphere is:

- $E=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Where $ε_{0}$ is the permittivity of free space, *Q* is the charge on the sphere, and* r* is the radius of the sphere; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The formula for electric field strength at the surface of the sphere is: E = Q/(4πε₀r²) Where ε₀ is the permittivity of free space, Q is the charge on the sphere, and r is the radius of the sphere.

The field strength at the surface of sphere A is 2.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> V cm<sup>–1</sup>, and the field strength at the surface of sphere B is 1.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> V cm<sup>–1</sup>.

The magnitude of the charge stored on the surface of sphere B is 7.5 µC.

(i) Show that the radius of sphere B is about 7 cm.

[2]

(ii) Calculate the magnitude of the charge stored on the surface of sphere A. Assume both spheres have an equal radius.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Electric field strength at surface of A = 2.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> V cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Electric field strength at surface of B = 1.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> V cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Charge on surface of sphere B = 7.5 µC = 7.5 × 10<sup>–6</sup> C
- Coulomb constant, $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup> (from data page)

(i) Calculate the radius of sphere B:

- Electric field strength:  $E=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$
- Rearrange:  $r^{2}=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}E}\Rightarrowr=\sqrt{\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}E}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $r_{B} = \sqrt{ \frac{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) \times ( 7.5 \times 10^{-6} } )}{1.3 \times 10^{3}} }$
- Radius of B:  $r_{B}$ = 7.2 cm ≈ 7 cm **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the magnitude of the charge stored on the surface of sphere A:

- If the spheres have the same radius, then $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$ = constant for both A and B
- Therefore, $\frac{E_{A}}{E_{B}}=\frac{Q_{A}}{Q_{B}}$
- The ratio of the field strengths is $\frac{E_{A}}{E_{B}}=\frac{2.6\times10^{3}}{1.3\times10^{3}}=2$ **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, $\frac{E_{A}}{E_{B}}=\frac{Q_{A}}{Q_{B}}=2$
- So, the charge on the surface of A is $Q_{A}=7.5\times2=15\mathrm{μC}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Notice that the field strength has been given in V cm*<sup>*–1*</sup>*, and the answer to (i) is required in cm. Look out for units in questions like this so you don't waste time converting units when you don't need to! *

> *In part (ii), if you are confident using ratios, you will be able to obtain the relationship between field strength and charge quickly and this can save a lot of time compared to carrying out two sets of calculations!*

parts.problemMd: State the relationship between electric field strength $E$ and the distance $r$ from a point charge.
parts.solutionMd:
The relationship between electric field strength and distance are related by:

parts.problemMd:

This charge may be assumed to act as a point charge situated at the centre of sphere X.

Calculate the electric field strength at a distance of

(i) 2 cm from the centre of sphere X

[2]

(ii) 10 cm from the centre of sphere X.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Charge on sphere X, $Q$ = 2.0 × 10<sup>−9</sup> C
- Coulomb constant, $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup> (from data page)

(i) Calculate the electric field strength at a distance of 2 cm:

- Electric field strength:  $E=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Distance from charge = 2 cm = 0.02 m
- Substitute:  $E = \frac{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) ( 2.0 \times 10^{-9} } )}{0.02^{2}}$

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *For part (ii), you could take your answer to (i) and divide it by 25 as the distance has increased by a factor of 5, so from the inverse square law, the electric field strength will decrease by a factor of 5*<sup>*2*</sup>

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Sphere X is a small conducting sphere that carries a charge of +2.0 × 10^−9^ C. This charge may be assumed to act as a point charge situated at the centre of sphere X. Calculate the electric field strength at a distance of (i) 2 cm from the centre of sphere X (ii) 10 cm from the centre of sphere X.

Coulomb constant, 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10^9 m F^–1. At 10 cm = 0.1 m: E = (8.99 × 10^9)(2.0 × 10^−9)/0.1^2 = 1800 V m^–1 (1.8 kV m^–1).

Sphere X is placed at a distance of 20 cm from sphere Y, which is identical to sphere X but carries a negative charge.

At the midpoint between the spheres X and Y:

(i) Calculate the magnitude of the electric field strength

[2]

(ii) State the direction of the electric field.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the magnitude of the electric field strength at the midpoint:

List the known quantities:

- Charge on sphere X, $Q_{X}$ = +2.0 × 10<sup>−9</sup> C
- Charge on sphere Y, $Q_{Y}$ = –2.0 × 10<sup>−9</sup> C
- Midpoint between spheres, $r$ = 10 cm
- Electric field strength at 10 cm = 1800 V m<sup>–1</sup> (from part b)

Add the field strengths to find the value at the midpoint:

- Electric field strength:  $E=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$
- Field at midpoint, $E=E_{X}+E_{Y}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E$ = 2 × 1800 = 3600 V m<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) The direction of the electric field at the midpoint is

- Towards sphere Y; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *This is a simple question when you realise that the midpoint is 10 cm from both spheres, and they both have the same charge, so you simply need to use the value of field strength from the previous sub-part and multiply it by 2 to find the combined field strength due to both charges*

> *The easiest mistake to make with this question is to subtract E*<sub>*Y*</sub>* from E*<sub>*X*</sub>* as it carries a negative charge. However, remember that an electric field is understood by describing it as a region where a **positive charge** will be moved. Therefore, both charges would move a positive charge to the right (towards Y), hence the values add up and the overall field is **stronger**.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Sphere X is a small conducting sphere that carries a charge of +2.0 × 10^−9^ C.
Sphere X is placed at a distance of 20 cm from sphere Y, which is identical to sphere X but carries a negative charge. At the midpoint between the spheres X and Y: (i) Calculate the magnitude of the electric field strength (ii) State the direction of the electric field.

Sphere Y is replaced with a sphere which is positively charged and identical to sphere X.

Explain why the value of electric field strength at the midpoint between the spheres would be zero.
parts.solutionMd:
The electric field strength at the midpoint between the spheres would be zero because:

- Both spheres have equal, positive charges which repel each other; **[1 mark]**
- At the midpoint, the magnitude of the electric fields are equal and the directions are opposite **OR** at the midpoint, the overall electric field is $E=E_{X}-E_{X}=0$; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *This question follows logically from the previous part, as now both spheres have the **same charge** and **repel **each other, so it makes sense that there must be a point between them where the electric field cancels out*

> *Remember that an electric field describes a region where a **positive charge** will be moved. Therefore, at the midpoint, both charges would move a positive charge to the right, but one would move it towards the midpoint and one would move it away from the midpoint, hence the values cancel out by the same amount*

parts.problemMd: Calculate the distance *d* from a point charge of 6.0 µC where the electric field strength is 96 kV m<sup>–1</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
The distance *d* where the electric field strength is 96 kV m<sup>–1</sup> is:

List the known quantities:

- Charge, *Q* = 6.0 µC = 6.0 × 10<sup>–6</sup> C
- Electric field strength, *E* = 96 kV m<sup>–1</sup> = 96 × 10<sup>3</sup> V m<sup>–1</sup>

From the formulae page:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup>
- Coulomb constant,** **$k=\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$** **= 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup>

Determine the equation for the distance *d*:

- For a point charge, $E=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}=\frac{kQ}{r^{2}}$ (in this case *d* = *r*)

parts.solutionMd:

- Initial distance, $r_{1}=d$ = 0.75 m (from part a)

> *There are a few different ways to answer this question, you could substitute this number back into the electric field strength equation. Both methods will gain full marks.*

parts.problemMd:
An α-particle is moving directly towards a stationary gold nucleus (${}_{79}^{197}{Au}$).

The α-particle and the gold nucleus may be considered to be solid spheres with the charge and mass concentrated at the centre of each sphere.

The α-particle approaches to 0.75 × 10<sup>–14</sup> m from the gold nucleus where it is momentarily stationary.

Calculate the electric field strength the α-particle experiences at the point.
parts.solutionMd:
The electric field strength the α-particle experiences is:

List the known quantities:

- Atomic number of the gold nucleus = 79
- Distance of closest approach, *r* = 0.75 × 10<sup>–14</sup> m

From the formulae page:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup>** OR **$\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$** **= 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>–1</sup>
- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C

Determine the equation for the electric field strength of the gold nucleus, *E*:

- $E=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r^{2}}$

Determine *Q*, the charge of the gold nucleus:

- $Q = 79 e = 79 \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{- 19} ) = 1.264 \times 10^{- 17} \mathrm{C}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the values into the electric field equation:

- $E = \frac{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) \times ( 1.264 \times 10^{-17} } ) }{( 0.75 \times 10^{- 14} )^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E=2.02\times10^{21}Vm^{-1}=2.0\times10^{21}Vm^{-1}$ **OR **$NC^{-1}$**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember that the charge of a nucleus is just the total charge of the protons. Each proton has a charge, **e**, the elementary charge (the same charge as an electron, which makes atoms neutral). This is then multiplied by the **atomic** or **proton** number to get the total charge. The mass number, 197, is not used in this question.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows the electric field lines around a particle with charge q.

A stationary proton is placed at point A, which is a distance of 0.1 nm from the particle. The proton is released and moves to point B, which is a distance of 0.5 nm from the particle.

The potential difference between A and B is 23 V.

Show that the particle has the same charge as two protons.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the particle has the same charge as two protons:

List the known quantities:

- Distance from the particle to A, $r_{1}$ = 0.1 nm = 0.1 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m
- Distance from the particle to B, $r_{2}$ = 0.5 nm = 0.5 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m
- Potential difference between A and B, $\DeltaV$ = 23 V
- Coulumb constant, $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>−1</sup>
- Elementary charge, $e$ = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C (from the data page)

Use the equation for change in electric potential:

- Electric potential:  $V=\frac{q}{4πε_{0}r}$ (from the data page)
- Change in electric potential:  $\Delta V = \frac{q}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \epsilon_{0} } ( \frac{1}{r} _{1} - \frac{1}{r} _{2} )$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation and substitute the values to calculate the charge:

acceleration = ................................. m s<sup>–2</sup> [3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Use Fig. 4.2 to explain whether the two spheres have charges of the same, or opposite, sign:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one ****from:**

- According to the graph the electric field E close to sphere A is positive and close to sphere B is negative; **[1 mark]**
- The electric fields are in opposite directions; **[1 mark]**
- There is a point on the graph between the spheres where the field strength is zero; **[1 mark]** **AND**
- So the charges on the spheres have the same sign; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Use data from Fig. 4.2 to determine the magnitude of the acceleration of the proton:

- Distance from sphere x = 5.0 cm

parts.problemMd:
Two charges are separated by a distance of 23 cm, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![18-2-3c-m-point-charge-and-elec-field-sq-cie-a-level](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-5-electric-potential/assets/005-18-2-3c-m-point-charge-and-elec-field-sq-cie-a-l.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the distance, in mm, from the −22.1 μC to the point between the two charges, where the resultant electric potential is zero:

List the known quantities:

- Separation, *r *= 23 cm = 0.23 m
- Charge 1, *Q*<sub>*1*</sub> = −22.1 μC =  −22.1 × 10<sup>−6</sup> C
- Charge 2, *Q*<sub>*2*</sub> = +5.4 μC = 5.4 × 10<sup>−6</sup> C
- $\frac{1}{4πε_{0}}$ = 8.99 × 10<sup>9</sup> m F<sup>−1</sup>

Draw a diagram of the situation:

![ddc09216-64df-473f-aa57-7fcb4f7bdc63](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-5-electric-potential/assets/006-ddc09216-64df-473f-aa57-7fcb4f7bdc63.jpeg)

Use the equation for the electric potential to obtain an expression for the electric potential when it is zero:

- $V=\frac{Q}{4πε_{0}r}$
- Potential due to −22.1 μC charge is: $\frac{( - 22.1 \times 10^{- 6} )}{( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) x}$
- Potential due to +5.4 μC charge is: $\frac{( + 5.4 \times 10^{- 6} )}{( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) ( 0.23 - x )}$
- So, $\frac{( - 22.1 \times 10^{- 6} )}{( 8.99 \times 10^{9 ) x} + \frac{( + 5.4 \times 10^{-6} } )}{( 8.99 \times 10^{9} ) ( 0.23 - x )} = 0$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation to obtain a value for *x*:

- $\frac{( - 22.1 \times 10^{- 6} )}{ x} = \frac{( - 5.4 \times 10^{- 6} )}{ ( 0.23 - x )}$
- $( - 22.1 \times 10^{- 6} ) ( 0.23 - x ) = ( - 5.4 \times 10^{- 6} ) x$
- $( - 5.083 \times 10^{- 6} ) + ( 22.1 \times 10^{- 6} ) x = ( - 5.4 \times 10^{- 6} ) x$
- $( - 5.083 \times 10^{- 6} ) = ( - 2.75 \times 10^{- 5} ) x$ **[1 mark]**
- So, $x = \frac{( - 5.083 \times 10^{- 6} )}{( - 2.75 \times 10^{- 5} )} = 0.184 \mathrm{m} = 184 \text{mm}$** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Electric potential is a scalar quantity, so the sum of the **resultant electric potential = 0**. In the method shown above the quantities from the question are substituted into the equation for electric potential. You could **rearrange and substitute at the end** too, sometimes it is easier to see a rearrangement with **numbers**. *

Calculate the kinetic energy of an α particle travelling at a speed of 3.50 × 10^7 m s^–1. Ek = 4.09 × 10^–12 J

Calculate the closest distance of approach for a head-on collision between an  $α$ particle travelling at a speed of 3.50 × 10<sup>7</sup> m s<sup>–1 </sup>and a gold nucleus for which the proton number is 79.

Assume that the gold nucleus remains stationary during the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Kinetic energy of particle, *E*<sub>*k*</sub> = 4.09 × 10<sup>–12</sup> J (from part a)

From data page:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>–12</sup> F m<sup>–1</sup>
- Charge of an electron, *e* = 1.60 × 10<sup>–19 </sup>C

Calculate charge of alpha particle and gold nucleus:

- An alpha particle is a helium nucleus with 2 protons and 2 neutrons
- Charge of alpha particle, $Q_{α}$= +2*e* **AND** Charge of gold nucleus, $Q_{gold}$ = +79*e ***[1 mark]**

Calculate the closest distance of approach:

- The kinetic energy lost by the alpha particle = gain in electric potential energy as it approaches the gold nucleus
- Gain in potential energy, *E*<sub>*P*</sub>  =$\frac{Q_{α}Q_{gold}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$ = loss in *E*<sub>*k*</sub>* ***[1 mark]**
- *E*<sub>*k*</sub>* *=$\frac{Q_{α}Q_{gold}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$ therefore, *r *=$\frac{Q_{α}Q_{gold}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}E_{k}}$
- *r* =$\frac{2 \times 79 \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{- 19} )^{2}}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 8.85 \times 10^{- 12} ) \times ( 4.09 \times 10^{- 12} )}$ **[1 mark]**
- *r* = 8.89 × 10<sup>–15</sup> m = 8.89 fm **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The equation for electric potential energy is given at the start of your paper on the formula page. This is the energy involved in bringing a charge **q ** from infinity to a distance **r**  from a point charge **Q.*

parts.problemMd:
Three charges are fixed at the corners of a right-angled triangle as shown in Fig. 1.1. The length of the horizontal and vertical sides are both *d. *

![7-5-s-q--q3a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-5-electric-potential/assets/012-7-5-s-q-q3a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Show that the electric potential at point P, halfway between the −2Q and −6Q charge is:

$V_{p}=-\frac{2Q}{\sqrt{2}d\mathrm{πε}_{0}}$
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Charge on Q<sub>1</sub> = −2Q
- Charge on Q<sub>2 </sub>= +4Q
- Charge on Q<sub>3</sub> = −6Q
- Distance from Q<sub>1</sub> to Q<sub>2</sub> = *d*
- Distance from Q<sub>2</sub> to Q<sub>3</sub> = *d*

From the data sheet:

- Electric potential, *V* =$\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}$

Calculate the distance from each charge to point P, *h*:

- (2*h*)<sup>2</sup> = *d*<sup>2</sup> + *d*<sup>2</sup> **OR** *h*<sup>2</sup> = $( \frac{d}{2} )^{2} + ( \frac{d}{2} )^{2}$
- *h*<sup>2</sup> =$\frac{2d^{2}}{4}$
- *h* =$\frac{\sqrt{2}d}{2}$  **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total electric potential at the point P, $V_{p}$ :

- $V_{p}$= $V_{1}+V_{2}+V_{3}$
- $V_{p}$ =  $( - \frac{2 Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} ( \text{bevelled} \frac{ \sqrt{2} d}{2} )} ) + ( \frac{4 Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} ( \text{bevelled} \frac{ \sqrt{2} d}{2} )} ) + ( - \frac{6 Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_{0} ( \text{bevelled} \frac{ \sqrt{2} d}{2} )} )$  **[1 mark]**
- $V_{p}$ =  $( - \frac{2 Q}{2 \sqrt{2} d \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} } ) + ( \frac{4 Q}{2 \sqrt{2} d \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} } ) + ( - \frac{6 Q}{2 \sqrt{2} d \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} } )$
- $V_{p}$= $( - \frac{4 Q}{2 \sqrt{2} d \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} } )$ =$( - \frac{2 Q}{ \sqrt{2} d \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} } )$  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Make sure to label the diagram if this makes it easier to calculate the correct lengths. The key is to realise that P is equidistant from all the charges. Remember that electric potential is scalar so the direction doesn’t matter!*
