parts.problemMd:
Before the discovery of quarks, scientists speculated that the subatomic particles might be made up of smaller particles.

If an electron was made up of three smaller, identical particles with charge *q *which are brought in from an infinite distance to the vertices of an equilateral triangle, it would have the arrangement shown in Fig. 1.2.

![7-5-s-q--q3b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/18-electric-fields/18-5-electric-potential/assets/014-7-5-s-q-q3b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Show that the work done in forming an electron consisting of three identical particles, as shown in Fig. 1.2, is:

$ΔW=\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{e^{2}}{3r}$

Where:

- The distance *r* is the radius of an electron which is 2.82 fm
- *e* is the charge of an electron
- $ε_{0}$ is the permittivity of free space
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Length of side of equilateral triangle, *r* = 2.82 fm = 2.82 × 10<sup>-15</sup> m

From data sheet:

- Permittivity of free space, $ε_{0}$ = 8.85 × 10<sup>-12</sup> F m<sup>-1</sup>
- Magnitude of the charge of an electron, *e* = 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C

Determine size of charge of each particle, *q*:

- *q *= $\frac{1}{3}$*e ***[1 mark]**

Work done bringing second electron into the triangle, $\DeltaW_{2}$ :

- Work done, ∆*W* = *q*∆*V*
- Electric potential, *V* = $\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}$
- ∆*V =*$V_{2}-V_{\infty}$* *– where $V_{2}$ is the electric potential at the second vertex due to the existing electron
- $\DeltaW_{2}$= $1 \frac{1}{3} e \times ( \frac{1 \frac{1}{3} e}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \ \epsilon_{0} r} - 0 )$
- $\DeltaW_{2}$ = $\frac{\frac{e^{2}}{9}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the electric potential at the third vertex due to the other two electrons, $V_{3}$:

- $V_{3}$= 2 ×$\frac{q}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$
- $V_{3}$ = $\frac{\frac{2}{3}e}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$ **[1 mark]**

Work done bringing third electron into the triangle, $\DeltaW_{3}$:

- $\DeltaW_{3}$ = *q*($V_{3}-V_{\infty}$)
- $\DeltaW_{3}$ =`1 third e x ( (2 / 3 e)/(4 pi epsilon _ 0 r) - 0 )`
- $\DeltaW_{3}$ =$\frac{\frac{2}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$  **[1 mark]**

Calculate total work done in forming the electron:

- $\DeltaW$ =  $\DeltaW_{2}+\DeltaW_{3}$
- $\DeltaW$ =  $\frac{\frac{1}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}+\frac{\frac{2}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$
- $\DeltaW$ =$\frac{\frac{3}{9}e^{2}}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}r}$
- $\DeltaW$ =$\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{3e^{2}}{9r}$
- $\DeltaW$ =$\frac{1}{4\mathrm{πε}_{0}}\frac{e^{2}}{3r}$  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *To form the electron, we take each of the three charges from infinity and place them in the corners of the triangle.  When the first electron is brought from infinity to its position there is **no work done** as there are **no other charges**. *

> *When the second electron is brought from infinity into its position it has to do work against the repulsive force of the first electron. *

> *When the third electron is brought from infinity into its position it has to do work against the repulsive force of both the first and second electrons.*

- Rest mass of electron, $m_{e}$= 9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg
- Elementary charge, *e* = 1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C
- Speed of light in free space, *c *= 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the kinetic energy of the electrons when they leave the electron gun, $E_{k}$ :

- $E_{k}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$m$( v_{e} )^{2}$
- $E_{k}$ =$\frac{1}{2}$ (9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup>) × (0.1 × 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup>)<sup>2</sup>

Calculate the potential difference between the anode and the cathode, Δ*V*:

  - The work done is equal to the gain in kinetic energy

parts.problemMd:
A healthy debate between two physics students concerns the equations for the energy stored by a capacitor.

A transcript of the debate is given below:** **

Student A: “The energy stored *E *by a capacitor is proportional to the potential difference *V*, because *E* = $\frac{1}{2}$*QV*.”

Student B: “Actually, the energy stored *E *by a capacitor is proportional to the *square* of the potential difference, *V*<sup>2</sup>, because *E *=$\frac{1}{2}$*CV*<sup>2</sup>.”

State and explain whether Student A or Student B is correct regarding the energy stored by a capacitor.

The equation for capacitance is: *C* = $\frac{Q}{V}$
parts.solutionMd:
State which student is correct:

- Student B is correct; **[1 mark]**

Explanation:

- When a capacitor is charging / discharging, *Q* <u>is not constant</u> **[1 mark]**
- Capacitance *C* is constant; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, it cannot be said that *E* ∝ *V ***OR** therefore it is only true that *E* ∝ *V*<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *It’s important to note the distinction between the two equations for energy stored by a capacitor:*

> *E** = *$\frac{1}{2}$*QV** = *$\frac{1}{2}$*CV*<sup>*2*</sup>*. *

> *As the capacitor charges, the potential difference across the capacitor plates **V** increases, such that the energy stored by the capacitor **E** increases. *

> *However, during this process, the charge stored **Q** is **also changing **– i.e., it is not constant. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that **E** ∝ **V** because **Q** is not constant. *

> *Whereas the equation **E** = *$\frac{1}{2}$*CV*<sup>*2*</sup>* shows that **E** ∝ **V*<sup>*2*</sup>* for a **constant capacitance** **C**. Therefore, in this case, **Student B** is correct.*

parts.problemMd: Calculate the change in energy stored in a capacitor of capacitance 20 nF when the potential difference between the plates increases from 75 V to 90 V.
parts.solutionMd:
The change in energy stored in the capacitor is:

List the known quantities:

- Capacitance, *C* = 20 nF = 20 × 10<sup>–9</sup> F
- Initial potential difference, *V*<sub>1</sub> = 75 V
- Final potential difference, *V*<sub>2</sub> = 90 V

Determine the correct energy stored equation:

- $W=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

- $\Delta W = 1 \frac{1}{2} C ( V_{2}^{2} - V_{1}^{2} ) = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times ( 20 \times 10^{- 9} ) \times ( 90^{2} - 75^{2} )$** [1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows an experiment carried out to measure the speed of a steel ball when it has been dropped from rest. When the ball is touching the copper contacts, the 85 µF capacitor charges to a potential difference of 4.8 V. When the ball is released, it falls and leaves the copper contacts thus causing the capacitor to discharge through the 2.4 kΩ resistor. Once the ball has fallen a distance of 0.45 m it splits the thin metal rod causing a break in the circuit and the capacitor stops discharging. Fig. 1.2 shows how the potential difference across the resistor varies during the experiment. (Fig 1.2 shows the pd starting at 4.8 V until T1, then discharging down to 2.6 V.)

Calculate the average current that flows through the resistor as the capacitor discharges.

You may ignore air resistance.
parts.solutionMd:
![o4m9kDZ0_7-6-s-q--q1b-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/19-capacitance/19-2-energy-stored-in-a-capacitor/assets/014-o4m9kdz0-7-6-s-q-q1b-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

List the known quantities:

- Capacitance, *C* = 85 µF = 85 × 10<sup>–6 </sup>F
- Distance the ball falls between *T*<sub>*1*</sub>  and *T*<sub>*2  *</sub>= 0.45 m
- Acceleration of free fall, *g*  = 9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup>

Calculate the charge using the capacitance definition and Fig. 1.2:

- Change in potential difference, Δ*V * = 4.8 – 2.6 = 2.2 V
- Δ*Q* = *C*Δ*V *= (85 × 10<sup>–6</sup>) × 2.2
- *Q* = 1.87 × 10<sup>–4 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Calculate the time taken *t*  for the ball to fall 0.45 m:

- The ball is dropped, so initial vertical speed, *u*  = 0 m s<sup>−1</sup>

  - Use the uniformly accelerated motion equation from the data booklet: $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$
- Substitute the known values: $0.45=0+\frac{1}{2}\times9.81\timest^{2}$

  - Rearrange for *t*
- $t=\sqrt{\frac{2\times0.45}{9.81}}=0.303s$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the average current:

- Recall that current, $I=\frac{ΔQ}{Δt}$

  - The time in which charge flows is $t=0.303=T_{2}-T_{1}$
- $I=\frac{1.87\times10^{-4}}{0.303}=6.2\times10^{-4}A$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

**Extract:**

When the ball is touching the copper contacts, the 85 µF capacitor charges to a potential difference of 4.8 V. When the ball is released, it falls and leaves the copper contacts thus causing the capacitor to discharge through the 2.4 kΩ resistor. Once the ball has fallen a distance of 0.45 m it splits the thin metal rod causing a break in the circuit and the capacitor stops discharging. Fig. 1.2 shows how the potential difference across the resistor varies during the experiment. (Potential difference before discharge = 4.8 V; Potential difference after discharge = 2.6 V)

Calculate the amount of energy transferred through the 2.4 kΩ resistor during the discharging of the capacitor.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Resistance, *R* = 2.4 kΩ = 2.4 × 10<sup>3</sup> Ω
- Capacitance, *C* = 85 µF = 85 × 10<sup>–6 </sup>F

Use Fig. 1.2 to work out *V* before and after discharge:

- Potential difference before discharge = 4.8 V
- Potential difference after discharge = 2.6 V

Calculate the energy transferred before and after:

- Recall the equation for energy stored in a capacitor, $E=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$
- Energy before discharge =$\frac{1}{2}$ × (85 × 10<sup>–6</sup>) × 4.8<sup>2 </sup>= 9.792 × 10<sup>–4 </sup>J **AND** Energy after discharge = $\frac{1}{2}$ × (85 × 10<sup>–6</sup>) × 2.6<sup>2 </sup>= 2.873 × 10<sup>–4 </sup>J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total energy transferred through the resistor:

- $\DeltaE$ = (9.792 × 10<sup>–4</sup>) – (2.873 × 10<sup>–4</sup>) **[1 mark]**
- $\DeltaE$ = 6.919 × 10<sup>–4</sup> = 6.9 × 10<sup>–4</sup> J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Dennis disconnects the circuit and increases the e.m.f. of the power supply by 50%.

He states that by doing this, the charge stored in the capacitor will increase by 50% and the energy stored in the capacitor will increase by 125%.

Justify Dennis’s statement with suitable calculations.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities algebraically:

- The initial potential difference across the capacitor, *V*
- The capacitance of the capacitor = *C*
- The initial charge stored by the capacitor,* Q = CV*
- The initial energy stored by the capacitor, *E = *$\frac{1}{2}$*CV*<sup>2</sup>

Write an expression for the new charge stored *Q’* at the new potential difference *V’*:

- *Q’* = *C × V’*

Write an expression for the new charge stored in terms of the old charge stored, *Q*:

- The new potential difference is 50% greater than the old potential difference, so *V’ *= 1.5V
- *Q’ = C × *(1.5*V*) = 1.5*CV = *1.5Q **[1 mark]**

Conclusion about charge stored:

- Dennis is correct / justified about the increase in charge stored **OR** this is an increase of 50% in charge stored; **[1 mark]**

Write an expression for the new energy stored *E’* at the new potential difference *V’*:

- *E’* = ½ ×*C × *$V'^{2}$* *

Write an expression for the new energy stored in terms of the old potential difference, *V*:

- *E’* = ½ × *C × *(1.5*V*)<sup>2</sup>
- *E’* = ½ × *C × *2.25*V*<sup>2</sup> = 2.25 × ($\frac{1}{2}$*CV*<sup>2</sup>) = 2.25 *E ***[1 mark]**

Conclusion about energy stored:

- Dennis is correct/justified about the increase in energy stored / this is an increase of 125% in energy stored (because it has increased from 100% to 225%); **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The technique used in this question – writing ‘new’ quantities in terms of ‘old’ quantities – is very commonly examined. It is powerful because you can directly see how different quantities change in response to proportional increases/decreases. *

> *Make sure you are comfortable with writing two equations in the form ‘old’ and ‘new’, identifying clearly which quantities have changed and which stay constant. For example, if the capacitance **C** stays constant, but the charge stored **Q** and the potential difference **V** changes, then:*

![7-6-s-q--3c--ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/19-capacitance/19-2-energy-stored-in-a-capacitor/assets/011-7-6-s-q-3c-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

> *New quantities might have risen by some percentage, like 25%, so for example: *

> *V’ = **1.25**V*

![screenshot-2022-08-25-at-4-15-39-pm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/19-capacitance/19-3-discharging-a-capacitor/assets/008-screenshot-2022-08-25-at-4-15-39-pm.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

The time constant of the capacitor is 0.24 ms and the capacitance is 78 × 10<sup>–9</sup> F.

Show that the resistance of resistor *R  *is 3.1 kΩ
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Time constant, *τ  *= 0.24 ms
- Capacitance, *C*  = 78 × 10<sup>–9</sup> F

Convert the time constant from ms to s:

- 1 ms = 1 × 10<sup>–3</sup> s
- 0.24 ms = 0.24 × 10<sup>–3</sup> s **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the time constant equation for the resistance, *R*:

- Recall the time constant equation: *τ* = *RC*
- $R=\frac{τ}{C}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the values into the resistance equation:

- $R=\frac{0.24\times10^{-3}}{78\times10^{-9}}=3100Ω=3.1\mathrm{kΩ}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

**Fig. 1.1**

Calculate the time constant of the circuit shown in Fig. 1.1.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Capacitance, *C* = 400 μF = 400 × 10<sup>–6</sup> F
- Resistance, *R* = 5 kΩ = 5000 Ω

Convert the units for capacitance from μF to F:

- μF = × 10<sup>–6</sup> F
- So, 400 μF = 400 × 10<sup>–6</sup> F **[1 mark]**

Substitute known quantities and calculate the time constant:

- Recall the time constant equation, $τ$ = *RC*
- $τ$ = *RC* = 5000 × (400 × 10<sup>–6</sup>) **[1 mark]**
- $τ$ = 2 s **[1 mark]**

> *Remember to always convert the resistance into Ω and capacitance into F to have the time constant in s.*

**Extract:**

After becoming fully charged, a capacitor C is then discharged via a two-way switch, T, through a resistor R of resistance 5 kΩ. The capacitance of the capacitor when fully charged is 400 μF. This is shown in Fig. 1.1. Fig. 1.1. Calculate the time constant of the circuit shown in Fig. 1.1.

The resistor in Fig. 1.1 is replaced with a different resistor with a resistance ten times greater.

All other components are kept the same.

State and explain the effect this has on the time constant of the circuit shown in Fig. 1.1**.**
parts.solutionMd:
The effect on the time constant of the circuit will be:

- The time constant increases <u>by a factor of ten</u>; **[1 mark]**

Explanation:

- This is because the time constant is (directly) <u>proportional to</u> the resistance; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Being able to spot proportionalities and describe them is a crucial skill for A Level physics. *

> *Since the time constant  *$τ$*= **RC**, where **R**  is the resistance and **C** is the capacitance, then you should be able to see that *$τ$* ∝ **R**, if **C** is kept constant. This is the case in this question: but notice that the question specifies the resistance increases by **a factor of ten.** This is a cue to you to be as **quantitative** (numerical) in your answer as well. The time constant must therefore also increase by the same factor, because they are proportional. *

> *In this instance, simply saying ‘the time constant will increase’ **would not gain credit** as a full explanation. *

parts.solutionMd:

- From Fig 1.1, when p.d.$V=6V$, charge $Q=0.9\times10^{-4}C$

The switch is now moved to position B. Show that the time constant of the discharge circuit is 4.2 s.

The fully charged capacitor in **(a) **stores energy $E$.

Determine the time $t$* *taken for the stored energy to decrease from $E$* *to $\frac{E}{4}$.

$t$* *= ......................................... s
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the time *t*aken for the stored energy to decrease from $E$* *to $\frac{E}{4}$:

List the known quantities:

- Time constant, $τ=4.2s$

Consider the relationship between *E *and *V*:

- Energy stored: $E=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$
- (Since $C$ is constant) $E\proptoV^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Obtain the value of *V *using the relationship:

- $\frac{E_{0}}{4}\propto\frac{V_{0}^{2}}{4}$
- $\sqrt{\frac{V_{0}^{2}}{4}}=\frac{V_{0}}{2}$

Use the capacitor discharge equation for *V*:

- $V=V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}$** [1 mark]**
- $\frac{V_{0}}{2}=V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{4.2}}$
- $\ln ( 1 \frac{1}{2} ) = - \frac{t}{4.2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $t=4.2\times\mathrm{ln}2$
- $t=2.9s$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *You must use the relationship *$E\proptoV^{2}$* because *$E=\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$*. **C **is constant** because this is the **capacitance** of this capacitor. *

State and explain the change, if any, to the time constant of the discharge circuit.
parts.solutionMd:
When a second identical capacitor is connected in series to the first capacitor:

- The total capacitance of the circuit halves; **[1 mark]**
- The time constant also halves;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *For two identical capacitors in series, the total capacitance is equal to half of the value of each one, therefore:*

- *For one capacitor: **C*<sub>*T*</sub>* = **C*
- *For two capacitors (in series): **C*<sub>*T*</sub>* = ½**C*

> *The time constant is given by **τ** = **RC**, therefore:*

- *For one capacitor: **τ** = **RC*
- *For two capacitors (in series): **τ** = ½**RC*

parts.problemMd:
A 590 nF capacitor is charged fully from a 20 V battery. At time *t = *0 the capacitor begins to discharge through a resistor. When *t* = 15 s the energy remaining in the capacitor is one eighth of the energy it stored at 20 V.

Show that the potential difference across the capacitor when *t *= 15 s is around 7 V.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the potential difference across the capacitor:

List the known quantities:

- Initial voltage, $V_{1}$ = 20 V
- Final energy stored, $W_{2} = \frac{1}{8} W_{1}$

Recall the equation for the energy stored in a capacitor:

- $W = \frac{1}{2} C V^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the relation between energy stored and voltage:

- Energy stored:  $W \propto V^{2}$  **or ** $\frac{W_{2}}{W_{1}}$ =`\left(\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}\right)^{2}` **[1 mark]**

Calculate the final voltage $V_{2}$ after *t* = 15 s:

- `\frac{W_{2}}{W_{1}} = \frac{1}{8} = \left(\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}}\right)^{2}`
- $\frac{V_{2}}{V_{1}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{8}}$
- $V_{2}$ =  $\sqrt{\frac{1}{8}} V_{1} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{8}} \times 20 = 5 \sqrt{2}$ = 7.071 = 7.1 V (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

The signal generator and oscilloscope are then connected to a capacitor C and resistor R, which has a resistance of 2.2 kΩ, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

Describe how the waveform displayed on the oscilloscope in Fig. 1.1 could be used to determine the capacitance of the capacitor C.

Where appropriate, include calculations in your response.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the maximum voltage:

- <u>Using the Y-voltage gain</u>, the maximum/initial voltage across the capacitor is 12 V (2 V div<sup>-1</sup> × 6 divisions); **[1 mark]**

Use the time-base to determine the time constant of the capacitor:

- The time constant of the capacitor is the time taken to fall to 37% of its initial voltage
- Therefore, 0.37 × 12 = 4.44 V **[1 mark]**
- <u>Use the time-base</u> (of the oscilloscope) to determine how long the voltage takes to fall to 4.44 V; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the capacitance using the time constant and the resistance of R:

- Divide the time constant *τ*  by the resistance of resistor R (2.2 kΩ) to get the capacitance of the capacitor C (because *τ  = RC *); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Wherever possible in the exam, be as specific and as quantitative as possible; note that you are required to state not only what you need (the initial voltage), but also how you intend to get it (using the Y-voltage gain). This is a useful exam technique to bear in mind. *

> *Similarly, the final mark of this question would not be credited with a vague response like “Use the equation **τ** = **RC** to calculate the capacitance”. *

The signal generator and oscilloscope are then connected to a capacitor C and resistor R, which has a resistance of 2.2 kΩ.

parts.solutionMd:
State the effect of altering the time-base of the oscilloscope:

- Decreasing the time-base will stretch the signal horizontally; **[1 mark]**
- This will increase the <u>resolution</u> of time measurements; **[1 mark]**

State how a greater resolution will affect the uncertainty in the measurement:

- A greater resolution will <u>reduce</u> (percentage) <u>*uncertainty*</u> in measurements of time **AND** this will <u>improve</u> the <u>accuracy</u> of determining the <u>time constan</u>t from the oscilloscope; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Decreasing** the time base means each square represents a smaller period of time. This is like 'zooming in' on the time line. If the time base is 0.5 ms, then the screen shows 5 ms. If the time base is 0.1 ms, the screen shows 1 ms and therefore is a greater **resolution**.*

Pacemakers are devices used to deliver short electrical pulses to a patient who is suffering from a cardiac arrest.

Fig. 1.1 shows a circuit that is used in such a pacemaker.

The capacitor has a capacitance of 20 μF and is connected to a resistor of 220 kΩ. This is connected to a power supply of emf 4.0 kV, but upon changing a two-way switch, it forms a circuit with heart tissue. This has a resistance of 400 Ω.

**Fig. 1.1**

The capacitor is fully charged initially. At $t=0$, the two-way switch connects the capacitor to the heart tissue.

![Blank grid graph with voltage V in kilovolts on the vertical axis from 0.0 to 4.0 and time t in milliseconds on the horizontal axis from 0 to 20](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/19-capacitance/19-3-discharging-a-capacitor/assets/017-blank-grid-graph-with-voltage-v-in-kilovolts-on-.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

parts.solutionMd:
List the known values:

- Resistance in the charging circuit, *R* = 220 kΩ
- Capacitance, *C *= 20 μF
- Heart tissue resistance, $R_{H}$ = 400 Ω
- p.d. of the power supply, $V_{0}$ = 4.0 kV

Calculate the time constant of the discharging circuit:

- $τ$ = *RC*
- $τ$ = (400) × (20 × 10<sup>–6</sup>) = 8 × 10<sup>–3</sup> s = 8 ms **[1 mark]**

Calculate the voltage across the capacitor after two time constants:

- In the first 20 milliseconds of discharging, two time constants will have passed
- After $t=RC$ (= 8 ms), the p.d. across the capacitor will be $\frac{V_{0}}{e}$ or $0.37V_{0}$

  - *V* = 0.37 × 4.0 = 1.48 kV
- After  $t=2RC$ (= 16 ms), the p.d. across the capacitor will be $\frac{V_{0}}{e^{2}}$ or $0.37^{2}V_{0}$

  - *V* = 0.37<sup>2</sup> × 4.0 = 0.55 kV

Sketch the graph:

![Graph of capacitor discharge: voltage in kV falls exponentially from 4.0 at 0 ms to near 0 at 20 ms, with marked points at 0, 8 and 16 ms.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/19-capacitance/19-3-discharging-a-capacitor/assets/018-graph-of-capacitor-discharge-voltage-in-kv-falls.png)

- Passing through (8, 1.48) **AND** (16, 0.55); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**** **

> *It’s useful to know how to calculate the voltage across the charging capacitor in terms of the number of time constants that pass. *

> *In order to do this, you just substitute a multiple of the time constant into the charging equation, e.g., **t =** 2**RC** represents a time of two time-constants:*

$x=x_{0}e^{-\frac{2RC}{RC}}=x_{0}e^{-2}$

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Pacemakers are devices used to deliver short electrical pulses to a patient who is suffering from a cardiac arrest. Fig. 1.1 shows a circuit that is used in such a pacemaker. The capacitor has a capacitance of 20 μF and is connected to a resistor of 220 kΩ. This is connected to a power supply of emf 4.0 kV, but upon changing a two-way switch, it forms a circuit with heart tissue. This has a resistance of 400 Ω.

Show that, when charging from 0 C, the time taken for the charge stored in the capacitor to reach 5.0 mC is approximately 0.3 s.

The equation for the charging of a capacitor is:

$x = x_{0} ( 1 - e^{- \frac{t}{R C}} )$

where $x_{0}$ represents the maximum value of a given quantity.
parts.solutionMd:
List  the known quantities:

- Charge, *Q *= 5.0 mC = 5.0 × 10<sup>–3</sup> C
- Time, *t* = 0.3 s
- Maximum voltage, $V_{0}$= 4 kV = 4000 V
- Capacitance *C *= 20 μF = 20 × 10<sup>–6</sup> F

Calculate the time constant of the charging circuit:

- $τ = R C$
- $\\tau = ( 220 \times 10^{3} ) \times ( 20 \times 10^{- 6} ) = 4.4 \mathrm{s}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum charge:

- The maximum charge $Q_{0} = C V_{0}$
- $Q_{0}$= (20 × 10<sup>–6</sup>) × 4000 = 0.08 C **[1 mark]**

Rearrange charge equation for time, *t*:

- The charge stored on a charging capacitor, *Q*, is given by `Q = Q_{0} \left(1 - e^{- \frac{t}{R C}}\right)`
- $\frac{Q}{Q_{0}} = 1 - e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}$
- $e^{-\frac{t}{RC}} = 1 - \frac{Q}{Q_{0}}$
- $\ln ( e^{- \frac{t}{R C}} ) = \ln ( 1 - \frac{Q}{Q} _{0} )$
- $- \frac{t}{R C} = \ln ( 1 - \frac{Q}{Q} _{0} )$
- $t = - R C \ln ( 1 - \frac{Q}{Q} _{0} )$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute values into equation time *t* equation:

- $t = - 4.4 \times \ln ( 1 - \frac{5.0 \times 10^{- 3} }{0.08} )$ = 0.28 s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Pacemaker manufacturers need efficient ways of measuring how quickly the charge and energy are released by capacitors.

One approach uses the ‘exponential factor’ *σ *, which is a ratio of the energy remaining in a capacitor to its initial energy stored.

Show that the exponential factor *σ* is given by:

$σ=e^{-\frac{2t}{RC}}$
parts.solutionMd:
State equation for the voltage *V* of a discharging capacitor:

- $V=V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}$

Write equations for the initial energy $E_{0}$ and final energy *E *stored in a discharging capacitor:

- Initial energy stored $E_{0}$*=*$\frac{1}{2}$* C*$( V_{0} )^{2}$ **AND**
- Final energy stored *E = *$\frac{1}{2}$*C*(*V*)<sup>2</sup> =$\frac{1}{2}$*C*($V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}$)<sup>2 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Take the ratio of the two equations and simplify fully:

- $\frac{E}{E_{0}}$= $\frac{1 \frac{1}{2} C ( V_{0} e^{- \frac{t}{R C}} )^{2}}{1 \frac{1}{2} C ( V_{0} )^{2}}$

Simplify equations fully:

- $\frac{E}{E_{0}}$= $\frac{1 \frac{1}{2} C ( V_{0} )^{2} e^{- \frac{2 t}{R C}}}{1 \frac{1}{2} C ( V_{0} )^{2}}$  = $e^{-\frac{2t}{RC}}$ **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Remember when raising a power in an exponential expression, the new power is found by **multiplying** the two powers together. E.g  (x*<sup>*a*</sup>*)*<sup>*b*</sup>* = x*<sup>*ab*</sup>* therefore for exponentials, (e*<sup>*x*</sup>*)*<sup>*2*</sup>* = e*<sup>*2x*</sup>*.*

> *As always, remember to show **every** step when answering a 'show that' question.*

parts.solutionMd:
The angle which would result in the largest force being exerted on the conductor is:

- *θ* = 90° **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *The equation to calculate the size of the force, **F**, on the conductor is: *

> *         F** = **BIL** sin**(θ**) *

> *The magnetic flux density of the magnetic field, **B**, current flowing through the conductor, **I**, and the length of the conductor, **L**, are all constants. **θ** is the angle between the conductor and the **B** field. *

> *To achieve the largest value for the force acting on the conductor, **F**, sin** θ** need to be as large as possible. The largest value which sin **θ** can have is 1. *

> *To calculate the size of the angle **θ** you need to find the inverse sine of 1.** *

> *         θ** = sin*<sup>*–1*</sup>*(1) = 90 *

> *This means that when the conductor is at 90° (**perpendicular**) to the **B** field, the force exerted on it will be largest.*

parts.problemMd:
A proton of mass *m* and electric charge *q* enters a region of magnetic field at point P and exits at point Q, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

The speed of the proton at P is *v. *The path followed by the proton is a quarter of a circle.

![q1_magnetic-effects-of-electric-currents_ib-sl-physics-sq-medium](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/001-q1-magnetic-effects-of-electric-currents-ib-sl-p.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State whether the speed *v* is the same, more than, or less than, the speed of the proton at Q. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The speed of the proton is:

- The <u>same</u> (at P and Q); **[1 mark]**

This is because:

- The magnetic force is always at right angles / perpendicular to the velocity; **[1 mark]**

**EITHER**

- The velocity (of the proton) changes only in direction; **[1 mark]**
- The speed / magnitude of the velocity (of the proton) does not change; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force (i.e. the radius of the circular path);
- The radius does not change, so, no work is done (by the magnetic force on the charge); **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the kinetic energy, and hence speed (of the proton) does not change; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *To get full marks in this question you must either consider one of two explanations 1. vectors, or 2. energy*

> *Explanation 1 (vectors) is arguably the easier route as you only need to consider the difference between velocity and speed in circular motion*

> *Explanation 2 (energy) is a little more involved, but thinking in terms of energy might suit the way your brain works better, so go for this one if it makes more sense to you. Here we need to consider the work done on the charge while it is in the magnetic field. We're only interested in the displacement in the **direction** of the force. Since the path of the proton is circular, the force is directed towards the centre of the circle, so a change in displacement would be equivalent to a change in **radius**. Always link this back to the kinetic energy, since the work done is simply equal to the **change** in kinetic energy. If no work is done, then there is no change in kinetic energy i.e. it remains constant.*

$R=\frac{mv}{qB}$

where *B* is the magnetic flux density.
parts.solutionMd:
State the equations for centripetal force and the magnetic force on a moving charge:

- Centripetal force: * *$F=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$
- Force on a moving charge:  $F=qvB\mathrm{sin}θ$

Determine the value of sin *θ*:

- The proton is moving at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field, so *θ* = 90⁰
- So, sin 90° = 1, hence $F=qvB$ **[1 mark]**

Equate the magnetic and centripetal forces:

- Since the magnetic force is the force that keeps the proton moving in a circle, this is equal to its centripetal force
- $F=\frac{mv^{2}}{R}=qvB$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange to make radius *R* the subject and simplify:

- $mv^{2}=RqvB$
- $\frac{mv^{2}}{qvB}=R$
- $\frac{m v^{ \cancel{2} } }{q \cancel{v} B} = R$
- $R=\frac{mv}{qB}$* ***[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *This is a very common derivation that you will be expected to know. *

Fig. 1.1 shows two parallel plates. The magnitude of the electric field between the plates is 2.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> N C<sup>–1</sup> and is directed from the top plate to the bottom plate.

The shaded region represents a region of magnetic field that is perpendicular to the page.

![q3b_magnetic-effects-of-electric-currents_ib-sl-physics-sq-medium](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/004-q3b-magnetic-effects-of-electric-currents-ib-sl-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

An electron enters the region between the plates with a speed of 3.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> m s<sup>–1 </sup>and experiences zero net force as it travels through to the other side.

(i) State the direction of the magnetic field

[1]

(ii) Determine the magnitude of the magnetic field.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) State the direction of the magnetic field:

![q3b-magnetic-effects-of-electric-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-3-force-on-a-moving-charge/assets/005-q3b-magnetic-effects-of-electric-ma.png)

- For the net force to be zero, the magnetic force F<sub>B</sub> must act in the opposite direction to the electric force F<sub>E</sub>
- The negatively charged electron will be attracted to the positively charged (top) plate
- Therefore, the magnetic force will be directed downwards / towards the negative (bottom) plate; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Determine the magnitude of the magnetic field:

List the known quantities:

- Electric field strength, *E* = 2.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> N C<sup>–1</sup>
- Speed of electron, *v *= 3.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>

Recall the equation for the force on a charge in an electric field:

- Electric force: * *$E=\frac{F_{E}}{q}\RightarrowF_{E}=Eq$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the electric force on the electron:

- *F*<sub>E</sub>* *= (2.6 × 10<sup>3</sup>) × (1.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup>)
- *F*<sub>E</sub>* *= 4.16 × 10<sup>–16</sup> N **[1 mark]**
- The magnitude of the magnetic and electric forces are the same, i.e. *F*<sub>B</sub> = *F*<sub>E</sub>

Recall the equation for the force on a moving charge in a magnetic field:

- Magnetic force:  $F_{B}=qvB\mathrm{sin}θ$
- The motion of the electron and the magnetic field are perpendicular, so sin 90° = 1
- Therefore, $F_{B}=qvB$* ***[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation and calculate magnetic flux density, *B*:

- $F_{B}=qvB\RightarrowB=\frac{F_{B}}{qv}$
- $B=\frac{4.16\times10^{-16}}{(1.6\times10^{-19})\times(3.0\times10^{5})}=8.7\times10^{-3}T$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]*** *

> *The tricky part of this question is realising that the quantity given 2.6 × 10*<sup>*3*</sup>* N C*<sup>*–1*</sup>* is the equivalent to *$\frac{F}{q}$* for the electric field. Look first at the units N C*<sup>*–1*</sup>*, so it must be *$\frac{\mathrm{Force}}{\mathrm{Charge}}$*.*

![q1-paper-5-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-4-magnetic-fields-due-to-currents/assets/009-q1-paper-5-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

It is suggested that *E* is related to *x* by the relationship

$E=IZe^{-kx}$

where *I* is the current in coil P, and *k* and *Z* are constants.

Plan a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between *E* and *x*.

Draw a diagram showing the arrangement of your equipment.

Explain how the results could be used to determine values for *k* and *Z*.

In your plan you should include:

•    the procedure to be followed

•    the measurements to be taken

•    the control of variables

•    the analysis of the data

•    any safety precautions to be taken.
parts.solutionMd:
Plan a laboratory experiment to test the relationship between *E* and *x*. Draw a diagram showing the arrangement of your equipment. Explain how the results could be used to determine values for *k* and *Z*.

**Each point from the list can score ****one mark**** up to a ****maximum of 15 marks**** (****but read the guidance below in blue****):**

***Defining the problem:***

- *x *is the independent variable and *E *is the dependent variable **OR**** **vary *x *and measure *E*; **[1 mark]**
- The r.m.s current $I_{rms}$ / peak current $I_{0}$* *in coil P is the <u>control variable;</u> **[1 mark]**

***Methods of data collection:***

- A diagram of the apparatus that includes labels for coils P, Q and distance *x* **AND** coils P and Q supported by a stand; **[1 mark]**

- Circuit diagram 1: an a.c. power supply / signal generator connected to coil P in series with an ammeter **AND**
- Circuit diagram 2: a voltmeter / CRO connected to coil Q; **[1 mark]**

- A method to determine *x *e.g. use a ruler to measure the distance *x *between the coils; **[1 mark]**
- A method to measure *x *from the <u>centre</u> of the two coils e.g. measure the width of each coil and divide by 2, then add to the separation of the coils; **[1 mark]**

***Method of analysis:***

- Plot a graph of ln *E* against x; **[1 mark]**
- The gradient of the graph is −*k*; **[1 mark]**
- The y-intercept = ln *IZ*  **or ** $Z = e^{y} \text{short} \text{dash} i n t e r c e p \frac{t}{I}$; **[1 mark]**

***Additional detail including safety procedures:***

**Final answer:** **Any ****six ****from:**

- Do not touch the <u>hot</u> coil / use gloves to position the <u>hot</u> coil; **[1 mark]**
- Use a large current / a large number of turns / an iron core to produce a large magnetic field / induced e.m.f; **[1 mark]**
- Use a high frequency a.c. to produce a large induced e.m.f; **[1 mark]**
- Keep the number of <u>turns</u> on each coil <u>constant</u> / frequency of the a.c. <u>constant</u>; **[1 mark]**
- A method to check that the current is constant** **e.g. use a variable resistor to keep the ammeter reading constant; **[1 mark]**
- Take repeat measurements of *x *for <u>different</u> parts of the coil <u>and</u> take the average; **[1 mark]**
- A method to position the ruler horizontally to measure *x *as described e.g. use a spirit level; **[1 mark]**
- A method to keep the coils parallel e.g. adjust coil Q until the maximum reading is obtained; **[1 mark]**
- Taking logs of the given equation leads to ln *E* = −*k*x + ln (*IZ*); **[1 mark]**
- This relationship is valid if a straight line is produced when the graph of ln *E* against *x* is plotted; **[1 mark]**

**An example of an answer which would score 15 marks is:**** **

<u>Method</u>

1. Set up the apparatus as shown in the diagram below **[1] [2]**. Use a ruler to measure the horizontal distance *x *between the two coils **[3]**.
2. The distance *x* must be measured from the centre of coil P to the centre of coil Q. This centre can be located by measuring the width of both coils, dividing by 2 and then *x* can be obtained by adding these half widths to the separation of the coils **[4]**. A spirit level should be used with a ruler to ensure *x *is measured horizontally** ****[5]****.**
3. The independent variable is* x *and the dependent variable is *E* **[6]**. The current in coil P, the number of turns on each coil and the frequency of the a.c. must be kept constant throughout **[7]**.
4. For different values of *x*, repeat measurements of *x *should be taken at different points on the coil and then calculate an average **[8]**.
5. Connect coil P to a high frequency a.c. to induce a large e.m.f which will in turn, generate a large magnetic field **[9]**** **and induce a current in coil Q.
6. To ensure the coils are parallel, adjust coil Q until the maximum reading is obtained **[10]**

![em-induction-experiment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-4-magnetic-fields-due-to-currents/assets/010-em-induction-experiment.png)

<u>Analysis:</u>

1. Plot a graph using the mean values of ln *E* against *x ***[11]**
2. Taking logs of the equation $E=IZe^{-kx}$ leads to $\mathrm{ln}E=-kx+\mathrm{ln}IZ$ **[12]**.** **This relationship is valid if a straight line is produced when the graph of ln *E* against *x* is plotted **[13]****.**
3. Comparing this to the equation of a straight line, y = mx + c

  - Gradient = −*k *
  - y-intercept = ln *IZ*
4. Determine a value for *k* using *k* = −gradient and *Z* using $Z = e^{y} \text{short} \text{dash} i n t e r c e p \frac{t}{I}$ **[14]**.

<u>Safety considerations:</u>

- The coils will get very hot, so gloves should be worn during handling **[15]**

**[Total: 15 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
State Faraday's Law

(i) in words

[2]

(ii) as an equation, defining all the quantities.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states:

- The (magnitude of the) induced e.m.f. is (directly) proportional to the rate; **[1 mark]**
- of change of magnetic flux linkage; **[1 mark]** ** **

(ii) Faraday's law is defined by the equation

- $\\epsilon = \frac{\Delta ( N \\Phi )}{\Delta t}$ **[1 mark]**
- Where $ε$ = induced e.m.f., $\Delta ( N \\Phi )$ = change in magnetic flux linkage and $\Deltat$ = time interval of change; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *It’s crucial that you remember an emf is only induced if there is a **change** in magnetic flux linkage. *

> *How quickly this quantity changes (i.e., the **rate **of change of magnetic flux linkage) determines the magnitude of the induced emf. *

parts.problemMd:
Lenz’s law is sometimes combined with Faraday’s law in order to explain electromagnetic effects.

Use the words below to complete the description of Lenz's law

| **attracts ** | **opposes** | **density** |
|---|---|---|
| **direction** | **linkage** | **magnitude** |

The _________ of an induced emf is always set up in a way such that it  ________ the change in magnetic flux ___________ that causes it.
parts.solutionMd:
The correct sentence is:

- The **direction** of an induced emf; **[1 mark]**
- is always set up in a way such that it **opposes**; **[1 mark]**
- the change in magnetic flux **linkage** that causes it; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks] **

> *Stating Lenz’s law in words comes up quite often in examinations, make sure you can describe it in terms of the **direction** of the induced emf*

> *The induced emf is always set up in such a way that the effect is to try and **stop**, or **oppose**, whatever is inducing it. This is a consequence of **conservation of energy** (i.e., electromagnetic energy cannot be created for free!).   *

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(ii) Faraday's law is defined by the equation \$\$\epsilon = \frac{\Delta \left(N \Phi\right)}{\Delta t}\$\$ Where \$\$\epsilon\$\$ = induced e.m.f., \$\$\Delta \left(N \Phi\right)\$\$ = change in magnetic flux linkage and \$\$\Delta t\$\$ = time interval of change

Rewrite the equation you wrote in **(a)(ii)** to include Lenz's law.
parts.solutionMd:
The equation including Lenz's law is:

- $\\epsilon = - \frac{\Delta ( N \\Phi )}{\Delta t}$
- Minus sign included; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *Lenz’s law says the **direction** of the induced emf is set up to oppose the change causing it, which is encapsulated by the negative sign in the equation.*

> *This is similar to vectors, for example, if vector **a** and vector **b** are related by **a** = – **b**, this means they point in opposite directions. In this sense, the vectors ‘**oppose**’ each other, just like the induced emf **ε** opposes the changing flux linkage. *

parts.problemMd:
(i) Define magnetic flux.

[2]

(ii) Write the equation for magnetic flux when the magnetic flux density is **not** perpendicular to the area.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Magnetic flux is defined as:

- The product of (magnetic) flux density *B* and area *A*; **[1 mark]**

parts.solutionMd:

parts.solutionMd:
The correct diagrams are as follows:

(i) If the magnet is held at rest in the coil:

- No deflection shown (arrow still pointing upwards); **[1 mark]**

(ii) If the magnet is moved back out of the coil more quickly than it entered:

- Deflection shown; **[1 mark]**

> *The deflection on the voltmeter is a **measure **of the magnitude of the **induced e.m.f.*

> *If the magnet reverses from the coil, there **is** a change in magnetic flux linkage in the **opposite** direction to that initially observed in **Fig. 1.1b** – therefore the deflection on the voltmeter is in the opposite direction as the current is in the opposite direction.*

> *Notice the question says the magnet is removed **faster** than it entered, therefore, the **rate of change** of magnetic flux linkage is greater which means a larger induced e.m.f. and current (and larger deflection), as required by Faraday’s law.*

parts.problemMd:
A solenoid has a coil C of wire wound tightly about its centre, as shown in Fig. 7.1.

![q7b-paper-4-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-5-electromagnetic-induction/assets/001-q7b-paper-4-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 7.1**

The coil C has 96 turns.

The uniform magnetic flux *Φ*, in Wb, in the solenoid is given by the expression

*Φ* = 6.8 × 10<sup>–6</sup> × *I*

where *I* is the current, in A, in the solenoid.

Calculate the average electromotive force (e.m.f.) induced in coil C when a current of 3.5 A is reversed in the solenoid in a time of 2.4 ms.

e.m.f. = ................................... V
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the average electromotive force (e.m.f.) induced in coil C:

List the known quantities:

- Number of turns in coil C, $N$ = 96
- Magnetic flux, $ϕ$ = 6.8 × 10<sup>−6</sup> × $I$
- Current in the solenoid, $I$ = 3.5 A
- Time interval, $t$ = 2.4 ms = 2.4 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s

Recall the equation for Faraday's Law:

- $ε=N\frac{\Deltaϕ}{\Deltat}$

Consider the phrase "the current is reversed":

- This means the current is first reduced to zero and then increased to the same value in the opposite direction
- So, the flux linkage must be considered twice

Substitute the known quantities into the equation for Faraday's Law:

- $\\epsilon = 96 \times \frac{( 6.8 \times 10^{- 6} ) \times 3.5 \times 2}{2.4 \times 10^{- 3} }$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the e.m.f, $ε$:

- $\\epsilon = 1.904 \mathrm{V} = 1.9 \mathrm{V} ( 2 s. f. )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Look out for "the **current is reversed**" this tells you to **multiply** flux linkage **by 2*

parts.problemMd: Define magnetic flux linkage.
parts.solutionMd:

- The product of magnetic flux; **[1 mark]**

> *Make sure you are clear on the terminology used in this topic. *

> *Magnetic flux density**, *$B$*, is a measure of the strength of a magnetic field at a point (force per unit current, per unit length), with units of Tesla, T.*

> *Magnetic flux**, *$Φ$*, is a measure of the total amount of field passing through a single defined area (*$Φ=BA$*), with units of Weber, Wb.*

A coil is connected to a zero-centred ammeter, as shown in Fig. 1.1. A student drops a magnet so that it falls vertically and completely through the coil.

![7-9-s-q--q1a-fig-1-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-5-electromagnetic-induction/assets/007-7-9-s-q-q1a-fig-1-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

![7-9-s-q--q1a-fig-2-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-5-electromagnetic-induction/assets/008-7-9-s-q-q1a-fig-2-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

With reference to Faraday’s Law and Lenz’s Law, evaluate the student’s explanation as illustrated in Fig. 1.2.
parts.solutionMd:
Recall Faraday’s Law and Lenz’s Law:

- Faraday’s Law states that the induced emf is <u>proportional</u> to the <u>rate</u> of change of magnetic flux linkage **AND**
- Lenz’s law states that the induced emf is set up in such a way that it <u>opposes</u> the change causing it; **[1 mark] **

Comment on the correct application of Faraday’s law:

- The student has correctly indicated an induced emf in the coil; **[1 mark]**

  - This is shown by the ammeter deflection
- The induced emf creates a south pole at the top of the coil / north pole at the bottom of the coil as the magnet approaches it; **[1 mark]**

Comment on the correct application of Lenz’s law:

- The student has correctly indicated a reversal of emf as <u>indicated by a reversed current on the ammeter</u>; **[1 mark]**

Comment on the corrections required using Faraday’s Law:

- The emf induced in the opposite direction should be greater than the initial induced emf **OR**
- The student's reversed deflection on the ammeter should be larger than the initial deflection; **[1 mark]**

Comment on the corrections required using Lenz’s Law:

- (As the magnet passes the centre of the coil) the induced emf should create a <u>south pole</u> at the bottom of the coil / a north pole at the top of the coil as the magnet falls through **OR**
- The direction of current round the coil should reverse once the magnet has passed through (in order to oppose the motion); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *Contexts in which you apply Faraday’s Law and Lenz’s Law tend to have a lot of subtleties and are regularly examined, so make sure you carefully consider what happens at each stage of the magnet’s descent. *

parts.problemMd:
As part of an introductory lesson on electromagnetic induction, a physics teacher plans a series of experiments for her students to carry out.** **

In experiment 1, two metal rings A and B are dropped from the same height between two magnets, as shown in Fig. 1.1. They are identical, apart from a small slit cut in B as shown.

parts.solutionMd:
Apply Faraday’s law:

- Faraday’s law states that in a conductor, an emf is induced proportional to the rate of change of flux (linkage)
- As A and B descend, the flux linkage through both of them changes so an emf is induced in them both; **[1 mark]**
- Because A is a complete ring, the emf in it drives a current; **[1 mark]**

Apply Lenz’s law:

- Len’s law states that the induced emf is set up in a direction so as to oppose the change that caused it
- The emf is induced <u>in the same direction</u> in both A and B **AND** there is an <u>upward force on A</u> due to the induced current inside it; **[1 mark]**

Describe the motion of A and B:

- Both A and B <u>accelerate</u> (downward); **[1 mark]**

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

- But A accelerates at a slower rate / the acceleration of A is less than B; **[1 mark]**
- The resultant force on A is smaller than B; **[1 mark]**
- Forces correctly labelled on a sketch as shown below (implying a smaller resultant force on A); **[1 mark]**

![7-9-s-q--q4a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/20-magnetic-fields/20-5-electromagnetic-induction/assets/018-7-9-s-q-q4a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**[Total: 5 marks]**** **

> *Any question involving a metal conductor in motion through a magnetic field should immediately trigger a reminder to you to state and apply both Faraday’s law and Lenz’s law. *

> *The crucial thing you should remember is that an emf is **always** induced if flux linkage changes, but a current is only driven to flow by that emf if the conductor is part of a **complete circuit. **This question interrogates that very fact: only one ring contains a flowing current, which then results in an upward force on it (the magnetic fields interact), opposing its weight force.*

parts.problemMd:
A generator produces an alternating voltage which can be described by the equation

$V = 150 \sin ( 200 \mathrm{\pi } t )$

where *V* is measured in volts and *t* is in seconds.

For this alternating voltage, determine

(i) the peak voltage,

[1]

(ii) the r.m.s. voltage,

[1]

(iii) the frequency.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Alternating voltage: $V = 150 \sin ( 200 \mathrm{\pi } t )$

(i) Determine the peak voltage:

- Alternating voltage:  $V=V_{0}\mathrm{sin}ωt$
- Hence, peak voltage, $V_{0}$ = 150 V** [1 mark]**

(ii) Determine the r.m.s. voltage:

- r.m.s. voltage:  $V_{rms}=\frac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$
- r.m.s. voltage:  $V_{rms}=\frac{150}{\sqrt{2}}$ = 106 V** [1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 below shows the graph of the voltage against time for a mains supply in the UK. Using Fig. 1.1, draw a line to show the dc voltage that gives the same power as produced by the alternating waveform in the mains supply.
The rms voltage is the equivalent dc voltage that would give the same power. V_rms = V_0/√2 = 320/√2 = 226.27 = 230 V (2 s.f.)

An electric oven is connected to the mains supply from part (a), using a cable with a non-negligible resistance. The cable connects the heating element in the oven to the mains supply.

Explain why the rms voltage across the heating element in the oven will be less than the rms voltage calculated in part (a).
parts.solutionMd:
The rms voltage across the heating element will be less than 230 V because:

- There is a potential difference / voltage across the cable; **[1 mark]**
- The (rms) voltage across the oven is 230 V / the mains <u>minus</u> the voltage across the cable; **[1 mark]** **OR**
- The resistance of the cable lowers the current in the circuit; **[1 mark]**
- The voltage across the oven is lower because of *V = IR */ Ohm’s law; **[1 mark]** **OR**
- The resistance of the cable is in series with the heating element; **[1 mark]**
- The voltage splits in ratio across these resistances; **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *It is easy to get into the habit of ignoring the resistance of wires, but in reality wires have a small resistance. Just like adding a resistor to a circuit would reduce the potential difference across the oven, a wire with resistance does the same.*

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 below shows a horizontal wire, held in tension between fixed points at P and Q. A short section of the wire is positioned between the pole pieces of a permanent magnet, which applies a uniform horizontal magnetic field at right angles to the wire. Wires connected to a circuit at P and Q allow an alternating current to be passed through the wire.

![hq2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/21-alternating-currents/21-1-characteristics-of-alternating-currents/assets/014-hq2.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

(i) Explain why the wire oscillates.

[5]

(ii) The permanent magnet produces a uniform magnetic field of flux density 220 mT over a 55 mm length of the wire. Show that the maximum force on the wire is about 40 mN when there is an alternating current of rms value 2.4 A in it.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Explain why the wire oscillates:

- The wire has a magnetic field; **[1 mark]**
- The wire's magnetic field interacts with the uniform magnetic field; **[1 mark]**
- The current flowing through the wire alternates; **[1 mark]**
- The magnetic field around the wire also alternates; **[1 mark]**
- The force on the wire alternates <u>direction</u>; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Show that the maximum force is around 40 mN:

List the known quantities:

- Uniform field flux density, *B*  = 220 mT = 0.220 T
- Length of wire in field, *L*  = 55 mm = 0.055 m
- rms current, *I*<sub>*rms*</sub>  = 2.4 A

Determine the peak current, *I*<sub>0</sub> :

- $I_{rms}=\frac{I_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$
- $I_{0}=2.4\times\sqrt{2}=3.39A$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum force:

- Maximum force occurs at peak current
- $F_{max}=BI_{0}L=0.220\times3.39\times0.055$
- $F_{max}=0.041N=41\mathrm{mN}$ **[1 mark]**
- This is roughly 40 mN

**[Total: 7 marks]**

When modelling the motion of the wire between P and Q, a student says the wire at the midpoint of P and Q is displaced 2.0 cm from equilibrium as it oscillated, and it moves with an average speed of 0.16 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Write an expression for the current supplied to the wire at time *t *. You may leave a factor of π in your expression.
parts.solutionMd:
Write an expression for current:

List the known quantities:

- Displacement from equilibrium, *x*  = 2.0 cm = 0.020 m
- Average speed, *v*  = 0.16 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Peak current, *I*<sub>0</sub>  = 3.4 A (from (a))

Find the period *T  *of oscillations:

- In one period, the wire moves 2.0 cm 4 times (up, back down, down, back up)
- Distance moved, *d*  = 8.0 cm = 0.080 m
- $T=\frac{d}{v}=\frac{0.080}{0.16}=0.50s$ **[1 mark]**

Convert this to angular frequency:

- $ω=\frac{2π}{T}=\frac{2π}{0.50}=4π\mathrm{rad}s^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Write an expression for current:

- $I = I_{0} \sin ( \\omega t )$
- $I = 3.4 \sin ( 4 \mathrm{\pi } t )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You would also gain the marks if you chose to write your angular frequency as 13 rad s*<sup>*−1*</sup>* .*

parts.solutionMd:
Determine the correct capacitor to use for smoothing the output:

List the known quantities:

- Resistance, *R* = 3.6 k Ω = 3600 Ω
- Time interval between adjacent peaks, *t* = 40 ms = 40 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s (from the graph)
- Capacitor 1, *C*<sub>*1*</sub> = 360 nF = 360 × 10<sup>−9</sup> F
- Capacitor 2, *C*<sub>*2*</sub> = 60 µF = 60 × 10<sup>−6</sup> F

Calculate the time constants for both capacitors:

- Time constant:  $T=RC$
- Capacitor 1:  $T_{1}=3600\times(360\times10^{-9})=1.3\times10^{-3}s$
- Capacitor 2:  $T_{2}=3600\times(60\times10^{-6})=0.216s$

Compare the time constants of the capacitors with the time between peaks:

- The time constant of capacitor 1, *T*<sub>*1*</sub> = 1.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s, is <u>less than</u> the time interval, *t* = 40 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s; **[1 mark]**

- The time constant of capacitor 2, *T*<sub>*2*</sub> = 0.216 s, is much <u>greater than</u> the time interval, *t* = 40 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s; **[1 mark]**
- So, the output will be smoothed significantly:

![11-2-sq-5d-mark-scheme-1_hl-sq-medium](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/21-alternating-currents/21-2-rectification-and-smoothing/assets/017-11-2-sq-5d-mark-scheme-1-hl-sq-medium.png)

parts.solutionMd:
Comparing the effects of each capacitor configuration on the output signal:

- The single capacitor <u>smooths</u> the peaks in the output voltage; **[1 mark]**

parts.solutionMd:
To find the photon energy:

List the known quantities:

- Frequency, *f*  = 8.6 × 10<sup>20</sup> Hz
- Planck constant, *h*  = 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s (from the data page)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Scientists are designing a prototype spaceship, with a mass of 4.9 × 10^6 kg. Once it has left the solar system, it will come to rest relative to Earth. It will then be accelerated by 4 very powerful lasers, which will be aimed at 4 large sails on the spaceship. Each laser emits photons with a wavelength of 2.50 × 10^−12 m.
Momentum of a single photon, p = 2.65 × 10^−22 kg m s^−1

Each laser emits 7.5 × 10<sup>25</sup> photons per second.

(i)

Calculate the total momentum of the photons emitted each second from a single laser.

[1]

(ii)

All photons are absorbed by the sails. Calculate the force applied to the spaceship by all of the lasers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To find the total momentum of radiation each second per laser:

List the known quantities:

- Number of photons per pulse = 7.5 × 10<sup>25</sup>
- Momentum of one photon, *p* = 2.65 × 10<sup>−22</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the momentum of photons every second, *p*<sub>*sec *</sub>:

- $p_{s e c} = ( 2.65 \times 10^{- 22} ) \times ( 7.5 \times 10^{25} )$
- $p_{sec}=19900\mathrm{kg}ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) To find the force applied to the spaceship:

List the known quantities:

- Momentum of photons from one laser each second, *p*<sub>*sec*</sub>* * = 19 900 kg m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Number of lasers = 4

Recall the equation relating force, *F* , time, *t* , and change in momentum, Δ*p* :

- $F=\frac{Δp}{Δt}$

Determine the change in momentum of the photons:

- Each second, the photons from one laser change momentum from 19 900 kg m s<sup>−1</sup> to 0 kg m s<sup>−1</sup>

  - This is because they are absorbed by the sails on the spaceship

Determine total force per second:

- From one laser, $F=\frac{19900}{1.0}=19900N$ **[1 mark]**
- From four lasers, $F_{tot}=4\times19900=79600=80000N$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The key to this question is recalling that **force** is the rate of** change of momentum**. As 19 900 kg m s*<sup>*−1*</sup>* of momentum is lost **every** **second** by the photons, the rate of change of momentum is simply 19 900 N. You must show your understanding of this logic in your answer.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

parts.solutionMd:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of spaceship, *m*  = 4.9 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg
- Force applied by lasers, *F*<sub>*tot*</sub>  = 79 600 N

Use Newton's second law:

- $F_{tot}=ma$
- $a=\frac{79600}{4.9\times10^{6}}=1.62\times10^{-2}ms^{-2}$ **[1 mark]**

Recall and rearrange the equation for uniform acceleration:

- $v=u+at$
- $a=\frac{v-u}{t}$

  - where *v*  is final speed and *u*  is initial speed
- Initial speed is zero
- $v=at$

Find the speed after an hour:

- $v = ( 1.62 \times 10^{- 2} ) \times 3600$ **[1 mark]**
- $v=58ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A heated filament and anode are placed in a vacuum, as shown in Fig 1.1. The anode has a gap through which electrons can pass.

![22-1-m-q3a-sq-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-1-energy-and-momentum-of-a-photon/assets/001-22-1-m-q3a-sq-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig 1.1**

A potential difference of 15 V is applied across the filament and anode.

An electron is then emitted from the heated filament with a speed of 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate its initial kinetic energy in electronvolts.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the kinetic energy in eV:

List the known quantities:

- Electron mass, *m*<sub>*e*</sub>  = 9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg
- Speed of electron, *v*  = 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Elementary charge, *e*  = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C

Calculate the kinetic energy, *E*<sub>*k*</sub> , in joules:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}v^{2}$
- $E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 9.11 \times 10^{- 31} \times ( 1.5 \times 10^{6} )^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{k}=1.02\times10^{-18}J$

Convert this to eV:

- $1 \mathrm{J} = ( \frac{1}{1.60 \times 10^{- 19} } ) \text{eV}$
- $E_{k}=1.02\times10^{-18}J=\frac{1.02\times10^{-18}}{1.60\times10^{-19}}\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{k}=6.4\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *It can be easy to become confused when converting between eV and J. Just remember, you can only either divide or multiply by a factor of 1.60 × 10*<sup>*−19*</sup>*.*

> *Going from J to eV, your value should increase a lot (so divide by the very small number, 1.60 × 10*<sup>*−19*</sup>*).*

> *Going from eV to J, your value should decrease a lot (so multiply by the very small number, 1.60 × 10*<sup>*−19*</sup>*).*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A heated filament and anode are placed in a vacuum, as shown in Fig 1.1. The anode has a gap through which electrons can pass. A potential difference of 15 V is applied across the filament and anode. An electron is then emitted from the heated filament with a speed of 1.5 × 10^6 m s^−1. Calculate its initial kinetic energy in electronvolts.

Calculate the electron's final kinetic energy in joules, as it exits the gap in the anode.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the final kinetic energy in joules:

List the known quantities:

- Initial kinetic energy, *E*<sub>*k,i*</sub>  = 6.4 eV (from part (a))
- Potential difference across filament and anode, *V*  = 15 V
- Elementary charge, *e*  = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C

Determine the work done, *W * by the uniform electric field:

- $W=qV$

  - where *q*  is the charge on the particle and *V*  is the potential across the uniform field
- $W=e\times15V=15\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the final kinetic energy, *E*<sub>*k,f *</sub> in eV:

- $E_{k,f}=E_{k,i}+W$
- $E_{k,f}=6.4+15=21.4\mathrm{eV}$ **[1 mark]**

Convert this energy to joules:

- $1\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}J$
- $E_{k , f} = 21.4 \text{eV} = 21.4 \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{- 19} ) \mathrm{J}$
- $E_{k,f}=3.4\times10^{-18}J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Calculate the electron's final kinetic energy in joules, as it exits the gap in the anode.
E_{k,f} = 3.4 × 10^{−18} J

Calculate the momentum of this electron after it has passed through the hole in the anode.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the momentum of the electron:

List the known quantities:

- Kinetic energy, *E*<sub>*k*</sub>  = 3.4 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J (from part (b))
- Electron mass, *m*<sub>*e*</sub>  = 9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg

Rearrange the equation for kinetic energy to make speed the subject:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}v^{2}$
- $v=\sqrt{\frac{2E_{k}}{m_{e}}}$

Substitute the known quantities:

- $v = \sqrt{ \frac{2 \times ( 3.4 \times 10^{- 18} )}{9.11 \times 10^{- 31} } }$ **[1 mark]**
- $v=2.73\times10^{6}ms^{-1}$

Calculate momentum, *p *:

- $p = m v = ( 9.11 \times 10^{- 31} ) \times ( 2.73 \times 10^{6} )$
- $p=2.49\times10^{-24}\mathrm{kg}ms^{-1}=2.5\times10^{-24}\mathrm{kg}ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

p = mv = (9.11 × 10^−31) × (2.73 × 10^6)
p = 2.49 × 10^−24 kg m s^−1 = 2.5 × 10^−24 kg m s^−1

Calculate the number of 3.62 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz photons required to have an equivalent total momentum to the electron. Give your answer to two significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the number of photons needed:

List the known quantities:

- Momentum of electron, *p*<sub>*e*</sub>  = 2.49 × 10<sup>−24</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup>

- Speed of light, *c*  = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Planck constant, *h*  = 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s

Determine the energy of one photon:

- $E = h f = ( 6.63 \times 10^{- 34} ) \times ( 3.62 \times 10^{14} )$ **[1 mark]**
- $E=2.40\times10^{-19}J$

Determine the momentum of one photon, *p *:

- $p=\frac{E}{c}=\frac{2.4\times10^{-19}}{3.00\times10^{8}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $p=8.0\times10^{-28}\mathrm{kg}ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Find the number *n  *of photons needed to match the electron's momentum:

- $n=\frac{2.49\times10^{-24}}{8.0\times10^{-28}}=3112.5=3100$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Photon energy and photon momentum are related by the equation:

*E*<sup>*2*</sup> = (*pc)*<sup>*2*</sup> + (*mc*<sup>*2*</sup>)<sup>2</sup>

Derive from this equation the equation $p=\frac{h}{λ}$ for calculating the momentum of a photon.
parts.solutionMd:
Consider the mass of a photon, *m*:

- The mass of a photon *m *= 0
- So, *E*<sup>*2*</sup> = (*pc)*<sup>*2 *</sup>
- and *E *= *pc ***[1 mark]**

Substitute the equation for photon energy in terms of wavelength:

- $E=\frac{hc}{λ}$
- $pc=\frac{hc}{λ}$ **[1 mark]**
- So, $p=\frac{h}{λ}$

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

Calculate the velocity of an electron with the same momentum.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Wavelength of photon, *λ* = 400 nm = 400 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m
- Planck's constant, *h *= 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s
- Mass of an electron, *m*<sub>*e*</sub> = 9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg

Calculate the momentum of the photon, *p*:

- $p=\frac{h}{λ}$
- $p=\frac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{400\times10^{-9}}$
- $p=1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

Calculate the velocity of the electron, *v*<sub>*e*</sub>:

- Momentum, *p *= *mv*
- So, $v_{e}=\frac{p}{m_{e}}$
- $v_{e}=\frac{1.66\times10^{-27}}{9.11\times10^{-31}}$

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A photon has a wavelength of 400 nm. Calculate the velocity of an electron with the same momentum.
Wavelength of photon, λ = 400 nm = 400 × 10^−9 m; Planck's constant, h = 6.63 × 10^−34 J s; Mass of an electron, me = 9.11 × 10^−31 kg; velocity of the electron, ve = 1822 m s^−1

parts.solutionMd:

- Speed of light in free space, *c *= 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the kinetic energy of the electron, *E*<sub>*e*</sub>:

- $E_{e}=\frac{1}{2}m_{e}v_{e}^{2}$
- $E_{e} = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times ( 9.11 \times 10^{- 31} ) \times 1822^{2}$
- $E_{e}=1.51\times10^{-24}$ J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the photon energy, *E*<sub>*p*</sub>:

- $E_{p}=\frac{hc}{λ}$
- $E_{p} = \frac{( 6.63 \times 10^{- 34} ) \times ( 3.00 \times 10^{8 )}{( 400 \times 10^{-9} } )}$
- $E_{p}=4.97\times10^{-19}$ J **[1 mark]**

Determine the ratio of photon energy to electron energy, $\frac{E_{p}}{E_{e}}$:

- $\frac{E_{p}}{E_{e}}=\frac{4.97\times10^{-19}}{1.51\times10^{-24}}$
- $\frac{E_{p}}{E_{e}}=329139$** [1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A laser sitting at rest on wheels that are free to move produces 5.00 × 10<sup>27</sup> photons. Each photon has a frequency 3.95 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz.

Calculate the magnitude of the momentum in producing these photons on the laser.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Number of photons, *n *= 5.00 × 10<sup>27</sup>
- Frequency of each photon, *f *= 3.95 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz
- Planck's constant, *h *= 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s
- Speed of light in free-space, *c *= 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Obtain an equation in terms of the momentum of *n *photons:

- $p=n\frac{hf}{c}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into the equation to calculate the momentum of *n *photons:

- $p = ( 5.00 \times 10^{27 ) \times \frac{( 6.63 \times 10^{-34} } ) \times ( 3.95 \times 10^{14} )}{( 3.00 \times 10^{8} )}$
- $p=4.365$ kg m s<sup>−1</sup>

**AND**

- This is equivalent to the backwards momentum of the laser; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> $p=\frac{hf}{c}$* is the equation for the momentum of **one** photon, multiply it by the number of photons to get the total momentum. Momentum is conserved, so the forward momentum of the photons is equal to the backwards momentum of the recoiling laser. This is a closed system, as the laser is free to move.*

parts.problemMd:

Obtain an equation in terms of the momentum of n photons:
- p = n (hf/c)

Where n = number of photons, f = frequency, h = Planck's constant, c = speed of light in free-space.

Show that the equation used for part a) is homogeneous.
parts.solutionMd:
Recall the equation from part a) and the units normally used:

- $p=n\frac{hf}{c}$
- $kgms^{-1}=\frac{Js\timesHz}{ms^{-1}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute for SI base units as J and Hz:

- $k g m s^{- 1} = \frac{( k g m^{2} s^{- 2} ) s \times ( s^{- 1} )}{m s^{- 1} }$
- $kgms^{-1}=\frac{kgm^{2}s^{-2}}{ms^{-1}}$
- $kgms^{-1}=\frac{kgm}{s}=kgms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *It is really important you learn the SI base units and how to test an equation for homogeneity. If you forget these in your exam, however, you can always fall back on standard equations like:*

$\mathrm{work}=\mathrm{force}\times\mathrm{distance}$

$\mathrm{force}=\mathrm{mass}\times\mathrm{acceleration}$

> *And use these to find the SI base units of force and energy.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A laser sitting at rest on wheels that are free to move produces 5.00 × 10^27 photons. Each photon has a frequency 3.95 × 10^14 Hz.

Lasers produce photons of light through a process called stimulated emission. parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A certain metal with a work function of 2.2 eV is selected to create two parallel plates. These are connected in a circuit to a sensitive ammeter and a power source, such that a uniform electric field of 140 N C^–1^ exists between them. Fig. 1.2 shows the two plates, labelled A and B, separated by 25 mm in a vacuum. Electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 255 nm is incident on plate B, such that photoelectrons are emitted from B and move towards A. The ammeter detects a photocurrent in the circuit.

Show that the maximum possible speed of the photoelectrons as they reach plate A is approximately 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Wavelength, *λ *= 255 nm = 255 × 10<sup>–9</sup> m
- Distance between the plates, *d* = 25 mm = 25 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- Electric field strength, *E* = 140 N C<sup>–1</sup>
- Work function,*ϕ* = 2.2 eV = 2.2 × (1.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) = 3.5 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J

From the data sheet:

- Speed of light in a vacuum, *c = *3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Planck’s constant, *h* = 6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup> J s
- Magnitude of the charge of electron, *e* = 1.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup> C
- Electron rest mass, $m_{e}$ = 9.11 × 10<sup>–31</sup> kg

Calculate the energy available from incident light:

- *hf* = *h* × $\frac{c}{λ}$ = (6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup>) × $( \frac{3 \times 10^{8}{255 \times 10^{-9} } } )$ = 7.8 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons released to the surface:

- *hf = ϕ* + $KE_{max}$ so $KE_{max}$ = *hf* – *ϕ*
- $KE_{max}$= (7.8 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) – (3.5 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) = 4.3 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the potential difference between the plates, *V*:

- The uniform electric field strength between parallel plates *E =*$\frac{V}{d}$
- The potential difference *V* = *E × d = *140 × (25 × 10<sup>­-3</sup>) = 3.5 V **[1 mark]**

Calculate the kinetic energy transferred due to the potential difference between the plates:

- The potential difference between the plates, *V* = $\frac{W}{e}$
- The work done on the photoelectrons contributes to their KE, so *W* = *KE* = *e × V*
- *KE* = (1.6 × 10<sup>­–19</sup>) × 3.5 = 5.6 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons reaching plate **A**:

- Total maximum $KE_{total}$  = $KE_{max}$ from incident photons + *KE* transferred from the potential difference
- Total maximum $KE_{total}$ = (4.3 × 10<sup>–19</sup>) + (5.6 × 10<sup>­–19</sup>) = 9.9 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum speed of photoelectrons:

- $KE_{total}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$*m*$( v_{m a x} )^{2}$
- 9.9 × 10<sup>–19  </sup>= $\frac{1}{2}$ × (9.11 × 10<sup>–31</sup>) × $( v_{m a x} )^{2}$
- 19.8 × 10<sup>–19</sup> = (9.11 × 10<sup>–31</sup>) × $( v_{m a x} )^{2}$
- $( v_{m a x} )^{2}$ = 2.17 × 10<sup>12</sup>
- $v_{max}$= $\sqrt{2.17\times10^{12}}$ = 1.474 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>–1 </sup>= 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> m s<sup>–1 </sup>(2 s. f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**** **

> *For the final mark, it doesn’t matter whether you substitute the values in before rearranging (as done in this mark scheme) or rearrange for  *$v_{max}$*before substituting, as long as you get the correct final answer.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A certain metal with a work function of 2.2 eV is selected to create two parallel plates. These are connected in a circuit to a sensitive ammeter and a power source, such that a uniform electric field of 140 N C^–1^ exists between them. Fig. 1.2 shows the two plates, labelled A and B, separated by 25 mm in a vacuum. Electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 255 nm is incident on plate B, such that photoelectrons are emitted from B and move towards A. The ammeter detects a photocurrent in the circuit.

Suggest and explain an experimental change to the circuit, part of which is shown in Fig. 1.2, that would reduce the photocurrent measured.
parts.solutionMd:
Suggest the experimental change:

- The terminals of the power supply should be reversed / make plate A negatively charged and plate B positively charged / reverse the direction of the electric field; **[1 mark]**

Explain the effect of the experimental change on the size of the photocurrent:

- This reversal would mean the photoelectrons would <u>do work against the electric field</u> between the plates / electrons would need to <u>do work to cross the potential difference</u> between the plates; **[1 mark]**
- This would reduce the photocurrent because only photoelectrons with sufficient energy would be able to reach plate A / could cross the potential difference; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *If the direction of the electric field is reversed (by reversing the terminals of the power supply) then there will be a force opposing the motion of every photoelectron emitted from the surface of plate B. Therefore, electrons would need to do work **against **this force; only the most energetic photoelectrons (those nearest the surface of the metal!) would be able to cross the space between the plates. The overall effect would thus be a reduction in the photocurrent.*

![2-4-s-q--q2d-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-2-photoelectric-effect/assets/005-2-4-s-q-q2d-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

parts.solutionMd:
To find the work function:

From data page:

- Speed of light in free space, *c = *3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Planck constant, *h* = 6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup> J s

Use Fig. 1.1 to find the wavelength when $KE_{max}$= 0:

- Photoelectrons are only released to the surface if light is incident at the threshold frequency (or threshold wavelength, $λ_{0}$ )
- $λ_{0}$= 590 nm when the $KE_{max}$= 0 from Fig. 1.1; **[1 mark]**

![2-4-s-q--q3a-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/22-quantum-physics/22-2-photoelectric-effect/assets/007-2-4-s-q-q3a-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

Calculate the work function using the threshold wavelength, $λ_{0}$ :

- *hf* = *ϕ* + $KE_{max}$
- When $KE_{max}$= 0, the work function *ϕ *= *h*$f_{0}$
- *ϕ *= *h*$f_{0}$ = *h × *$\frac{c}{λ_{0}}$ = (6.63 × 10<sup>–34</sup>) × $( \frac{3 \times 10^{8}{590 \times 10^{-9} } } )$ = 3.4 × 10<sup>–19</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the work function in electronvolts, *ϕ*:
