parts.problemMd:
Ultrasound is incident on a boundary between two materials. Some of the ultrasound is reflected at the boundary and the rest is transmitted across the boundary.

The acoustic impedance of air is 4.29 × 10<sup>2</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

The acoustic impedance of coupling gel is 1.48 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

The acoustic impedance of skin is 1.65 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the percentage of the ultrasound which would be transmitted into the skin when incident on

(i) an air−skin boundary,

[2]

(ii) a gel−skin boundary.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Acoustic impedance of air, $Z_{a}$ = 4.29 × 10<sup>2</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>
- Acoustic impedance of coupling gel, $Z_{g}$ = 1.48 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>
- Acoustic impedance of skin, $Z_{s}$ = 1.65 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

(i) Calculate the % transmitted into the skin for the air−skin boundary:

- Intensity reflection equation:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ 1 - Z _ 2 ) ^2 / ( Z _ 1 + Z _ 2 ) ^2`
- `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ s - Z _ a ) ^2 / ( Z _ s + Z _ a ) ^2 = ( 1.65 x 10 ^ 6 - 4.29 x 10 ^2 ) ^2 / ( 1.65 x 10 ^ 6 + 4.29 x 10 ^2 ) ^2`
- Fraction reflected:  $\frac{I_{R}}{I_{0}}$ = 0.99896 **[1 mark]**
- % transmitted = (1 − 0.99896) × 100% = 0.1% **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the % transmitted into the skin for the gel−skin boundary:

- `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ s - Z _ g ) ^2 / ( Z _ s + Z _ g ) ^2 = ( 1.65 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.48 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.65 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.48 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2`
- Fraction reflected:  $\frac{I_{R}}{I_{0}}$ = 2.9499 × 10<sup>–3</sup> **[1 mark]**
- % transmitted = (1 − 2.9499 × 10<sup>–3</sup>) × 100% = 99.7% **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Since the equation has the difference in acoustic impedance **squared**, it doesn't actually matter which boundary you use as **Z*<sub>*1*</sub>* and **Z*<sub>*2*</sub>* , as *$( Z_{2} - Z_{1} )^{2} = ( Z_{1} - Z_{2} )^{2}$*. Therefore, focus on making sure you've put in the correct numbers into your calculator and **squared** them too, as this is easy to forget!*

parts.problemMd:
Most modern ultrasound transducers are made from the piezoelectric material lead zirconate titanate (PZT).

Fig. 1.1 shows the effect on the structure of a crystal of PZT when an alternating potential difference is applied across it.

![24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-crystal-applied-p-d--cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/004-24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-crystal-applied-p.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

(i) Describe what happens at a molecular level when an alternating potential difference is applied across a PZT transducer to generate ultrasound.

You may draw on Fig. 1.1 to help with your answer.

[4]

(ii) Describe the conditions that will enable maximum energy conversion into ultrasound to occur.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) When an alternating potential difference (p.d.) is applied to a PZT transducer:

**Final answer:** **Any ****four**** from:**

- The positive / negative charges are attracted to the negative / positive terminal **OR** charges in the lattice (of the PZT crystal) separate; **[1 mark]**
- The movement of the central positive charge (along the central axis) causes the PZT crystal to deform / change shape / expand and contract; **[1 mark]**
- When the p.d. changes direction, the central positive charge moves in the opposite direction, causing the crystal to deform (in the opposite direction); **[1 mark]**
- The repeated crystal deformations lead to oscillations **OR** demonstrate on diagram e.g. `( 1 ) -> with e x p a n d i n g on top ( 2 ) -> with c o n t r a c t i n g on top ( 1 ) -> with e x p a n d i n g on top ( 3 ) -> with c o n t r a c t i n g on top ( 1 )` **[1 mark]**
- The alternating p.d. causes the crystal to oscillate at the same frequency (as the applied field); **[1 mark]**
- The oscillations are transferred to the surrounding air molecules to produce ultrasound (if frequency >20 000 Hz); **[1 mark]** ![24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/005-24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-ma.png)

(ii) Maximum energy transfer occurs when:

- The frequency of the applied (alternating) p.d. is equal to the <u>natural frequency</u> of the PZT crystal / transducer; **[1 mark]**
- This causes resonance to occur; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *The diagram might look daunting at first, but the key part to notice is the **movement of the central ion** which has a net charge of +4e*

![24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-ma1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/006-24-1-1a-h-24-1-h-piezoelectric-ma1.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

The speed of ultrasound in the eye is 1520 m s<sup>–1</sup> and the speed of ultrasound in the lens is 1670 m s<sup>–1</sup>.

Use Fig. 1.3 to calculate the thickness of

(i) the lens, in mm,

[2]

(ii) the eye, in cm.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the thickness of the eye lens:

List the known quantities:

- Speed of ultrasound in the eye, $c_{eye}$ = 1520 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Speed of ultrasound in the lens, $c_{lens}$ = 1670 m s<sup>–1</sup>

(i) Calculate the thickness of the lens:

![24-1-1c-h-24-1-h-ultrasound-puls-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/010-24-1-1c-h-24-1-h-ultrasound-puls-ma.png)

- (From Fig. 1.3) the wave enters the lens at **L**<sub>**1**</sub> when *t* = 8.5 μs
- (From Fig. 1.3) the wave leaves the lens at  **L**<sub>**2**</sub> when *t* = 14 μs
- Time taken:  Δ*t *= 14 – 8.5 = 5.5 μs

Calculate the thickness of the lens:

- Lens thickness = $\frac{1}{2}c_{lens}\Deltat$ **[1 mark]**
- Lens thickness = $1 \frac{1}{2} \times 1670 \times ( 5.5 \times 10^{- 6} )$
- Lens thickness = 4.59 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m = 4.6 mm **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the thickness of the eye :

- (From Fig. 1.3) the wave enters the eye at A when *t* = 5.5 μs
- (From Fig. 1.3) the wave meets the back of the eye at B when *t* = 31.5 μs
- Time taken from **A** to **L**<sub>**1**</sub>:  Δ*t*<sub>A</sub>* *= 8.5 – 5.5 = 3.0 μs
- Time taken from **L**<sub>**2**</sub> to **B**:  Δ*t*<sub>B</sub>* *= 31.5 – 14 = 17.5 μs

Calculate the distances before and after the lens:

- Distance **A** → **L**<sub>**1**</sub> = $\frac{1}{2}c_{eye}\Deltat_{A}$
- Distance **A** → **L**<sub>**1**</sub> = $1 \frac{1}{2} \times 1520 \times ( 3.0 \times 10^{- 6} ) = 2.28 \times 10^{- 3} \mathrm{m}$ **[1 mark]**
- Distance **L**<sub>**2**</sub> → **B** = $\frac{1}{2}c_{eye}\Deltat_{B}$
- Distance **L**<sub>**2**</sub> → **B** = $1 \frac{1}{2} \times 1520 \times ( 17.5 \times 10^{- 6} ) = 1.33 \times 10^{- 2} \mathrm{m}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the thickness of the eye:

- Eye thickness = distance (**A** → **L**<sub>**1**</sub>) + lens thickness + distance (**L**<sub>**2**</sub> → **B**)
- Eye thickness = 0.23 + 0.46 + 1.33 = 2.02 cm **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Take some time to decipher the graph to make sure you understand it before diving into the calculations*

> *At each boundary between media, some of the energy of the ultrasound pulse is **reflected** back to the transducer and the rest is **transmitted. **The reflected pulses are what give rise to the spikes we see on the graph*

- *The first spike represents the ultrasound entering the cornea at boundary **A*
- *The next two spikes represent the boundaries **L*<sub>*1*</sub>* and **L*<sub>*2*</sub>*, which are the front and rear surfaces of the eye lens*
- *The final spike is where contact is made with the retina at boundary **B**, i.e. the back of the eye*

**Fig. 1.4**

When carrying out the scan, a gel is applied between the transducer and eye to enable 100% transmission of the ultrasound into the eye.

Use the information in Table 1.1 and the graph in Fig. 1.4 to calculate the ratio of the intensity of the reflections from A and B, by the time the pulses come back to the receiver.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **acoustic impedance / kg m**<sup>**–2**</sup>** s**<sup>**–1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| eye | 1.52 × 10<sup>6</sup> |
| eye lens | 1.84 × 10<sup>6</sup> |
| surrounding tissue | 1.69 × 10<sup>6</sup> |
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the ratio of the intensity of the reflections from A and B:

List the known quantities:

- Acoustic impedance of the eye, $Z_{e}$ = 1.52 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>
- Acoustic impedance of the lens, $Z_{l}$ = 1.84 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>
- Acoustic impedance of the surrounding tissue, $Z_{t}$ = 1.69 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg m<sup>–2</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient at each boundary:

- Intensity reflection coefficient:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ 1 - Z _ 2 ) ^2 / ( Z _ 1 + Z _ 2 ) ^2`
- Eye-lens boundary:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.84 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.52 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.84 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.52 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 9.1 x 10 ^ - 3` **[1 mark]**
- Eye-tissue boundary:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.69 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.52 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.69 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.52 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 2.8 x 10 ^ - 3` **[1 mark]**

Determine the total energy lost by reflection between A and B:

- At each boundary, only a small fraction of energy is reflected
- Hence, transmitted energy at B = (0.9909 × 0.9909 × 0.9972) = 0.9791, so 0.021 of that is reflected
- It is reasonable to make the approximation 0.9791 ≈ 1.0
- So the same amount of energy is reflected at both A and B; **[1 mark]**

Determine the energy lost by attenuation:

- The decrease in intensity must be due to the attenuation of the signal only
- Total distance travelled = 2 × eye thickness = 4 cm

![NWtsA8zL_24-1-1d-h-24-1-h-attenuation-of-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/012-nwtsa8zl-24-1-1d-h-24-1-h-attenuation-of-ma.png)

- (From the graph) when depth = 4 cm, the intensity is reduced from 8 to 2, or $I_{0}\rightarrow\frac{I_{0}}{4}$
- Therefore, $\frac{I_{A}}{I_{B}}=4$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *At first, this question looks more complicated than it really is. When you realise that all the energy loss results from attenuation, rather than reflection, it simplifies the question greatly*

> *Remember that attenuation happens in both directions. It is reasonable to assume that attenuation occurs at the same rate in all tissues, so you don't need to determine attenuation in the lens and eye separately*

parts.problemMd:
An ultrasound investigation was used to identify a small volume of an unknown substance in a patient. It is suspected that this substance is either a cyst or a tumour.

During the ultrasound investigation, an ultrasound pulse of frequency 5 MHz is passed through soft tissue and then into the small volume of the unknown substance.

The ratio of the reflected intensity to the incident intensity for the ultrasound pulse reflected at the boundary was found to be 7.54 × 10<sup>−5</sup>.

Table 1.1 shows some information about the density and speed of ultrasound in soft tissue, cysts and tumours.

**Table 1.1**

| **material** | **density / kg m**<sup>**−3**</sup> | **ultrasound velocity / m s**<sup>**−1**</sup> |
|---|---|---|
| soft tissue | 1065 | 1530 |
| cyst | 1020 | 1570 |
| tumour | 990 | 1565 |

(i) Use the information in Table 1.1 to show that the unknown medium is a cyst.

[4]

(ii) A pulse of ultrasound reflected from the front surface of the cyst was detected 27.5 µs later and a pulse from the rear surface was detected 43.2 µs later.

Determine the length of the cyst, in cm, to two significant figures.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the percentage of energy from the ultrasonic transducer that is reflected:

- Acoustic impedance:  $Z=ρc$
- Acoustic impedance of soft tissue:  $Z_{st}=1065\times1530=1.629\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$
- Acoustic impedance of cyst:  $Z_{c}=1020\times1570=1.601\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$
- Acoustic impedance of tumour:  $Z_{t}=990\times1565=1.549\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$ **1 mark for all Z values correct**

Use the intensity reflection coefficient equation:

- Intensity reflection coefficient:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ 1 - Z _ 2 ) ^2 / ( Z _ 1 + Z _ 2 ) ^2`
- Cyst:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.601 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.601 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 7.5 x 10 ^ - 5` **[1 mark]**
- Tumour:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.549 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.549 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 6.3 x 10 ^ - 4` **[1 mark]**

Compare the ratios to the ratio given in the question to identify the medium:

- The intensity reflection coefficient given, $7.54\times10^{-5}$, is closer to the value for a cyst than a tumour **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the unknown medium is a cyst

(ii) Determine the length of the cyst:

List the known quantities:

- Time detected from front of cyst = 27.5 µs
- Time detected from rear of cyst = 43.2 µs
- Speed of ultrasound in cyst, *c* = 1570 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the length of the cyst:

- The difference in times is due to the longer signal passing through the cyst, then reflecting
- Length of cyst:  $d=\frac{1}{2}c\Deltat$
- $d = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 1570 \times ( 43.2 - 27.5 ) \times 10^{- 6}$ **[1 mark]**
- $d=0.01232m=1.2\mathrm{cm}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *The time difference accounts for the time spent while the pulse travels through the cyst, and then back through it as it is reflected. Therefore, during half of this time, the pulse travels the length of the cyst, so we can simply find this length using the speed of the pulse and the time taken.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(ii) A pulse of ultrasound reflected from the front surface of the cyst was detected 27.5 µs later and a pulse from the rear surface was detected 43.2 µs later. Determine the length of the cyst, in cm, to two significant figures. [Answer: Speed of ultrasound in cyst, c = 1570 m s^−1; Length of cyst: d = ½ c Δt = ½ × 1570 × (43.2 − 27.5) × 10^−6 = 0.01232 m = 1.2 cm]

Fig. 1.1 shows a beam of X-rays of energy 20 keV incident normally on some soft tissue which contains the cyst.

The cyst is located 2.1 cm from the surface of the soft tissue.

![24-1-3b-h-24-1-h-x-ray-intensity-cyst-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/24-medical-physics/24-1-production-and-use-of-ultrasound/assets/003-24-1-3b-h-24-1-h-x-ray-intensity-cyst-cie-ial-sq.png)

**Fig. 1.1 **(not to scale)

The attenuation constant of the soft tissue is 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup> for X-rays. The incident intensity of the beam is 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>.

You may assume that the attenuating behaviour of X-rays in matter is the same as that of ultrasound in matter.

The X-ray beam is switched on for a time *t*.

Determine the energy of the X-ray beam incident on the front surface of the cyst each second. State any assumptions you make.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the X-ray energy incident on the cyst each second:

List the known quantities:

- Attenuation constant of soft tissue, $μ$* *= 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Initial intensity of the beam, $I_{0}$ = 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>
- Length of the cyst, $d$ = 0.012 m = 1.2 cm (from **(a)**)
- Distance travelled through the tissue, $x$ = 2.1 cm

Calculate the intensity of the X-ray beam at the cyst:

- Intensity of a beam in tissue:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$
- $I = ( 4.6 \times 10^{3} ) e^{- ( 0.85 \times 2.1 )} = 771.9 \mathrm{W} \mathrm{m}^{- 2}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the cross-sectional area of the front surface of the cyst:

- Cross-sectional area of the cyst:  $A = \mathrm{\pi } r^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } \times ( \frac{0.012}{2} )^{2}$ = 1.13 × 10<sup>–4</sup> m<sup>2</sup> **AND**
- Assumption: the front surface is circular; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the power and energy incident on the cyst:

- Intensity of a wave:  $I=\frac{P}{A}\RightarrowP=IA$
- Incident power:  $P = 771.9 \times ( 1.13 \times 10^{- 4} ) = 0.087 \mathrm{W}$
- Energy transferred each second:  $E=Pt=0.087J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You are not explicitly told the shape of the cyst. With the information, you must **assume** that its width is the same as its length. The fact that the question asks for assumptions is a big hint for this.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(a)(ii) A pulse of ultrasound reflected from the front surface of the cyst was detected 27.5 µs later and a pulse from the rear surface was detected 43.2 µs later. Determine the length of the cyst, in cm. Length of cyst: d = 0.01232 m = 1.2 cm.

(b) Fig. 1.1 shows a beam of X-rays of energy 20 keV incident normally on some soft tissue which contains the cyst. The cyst is located 2.1 cm from the surface of the soft tissue. The attenuation constant of the soft tissue is 0.85 cm^–1 for X-rays. The incident intensity of the beam is 4.6 × 10^3 W m^–2. You may assume that the attenuating behaviour of X-rays in matter is the same as that of ultrasound in matter.

The ratio of the intensities of the emergent X-ray beams X and Y is determined to be

$\frac{I_{Y}}{I_{X}}=0.94$

(i) Determine the attenuation coefficient of the cyst.

[3]

(ii) Describe the quality of the images that would be obtained from the ultrasound and the X-ray scans of the cyst, explaining your answers.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Determine the attenuation coefficient of the cyst:

List the known quantities:

- Attenuation coefficient of soft tissue, $μ$* *= 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Initial intensity of the beam, $I_{0}$ = 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>
- Length of the cyst, $d$ = 0.012 m = 1.2 cm (from **(a)**)
- Distance between the tissue and cyst = 2.1 cm
- Total distance = 4.8 cm

Use the attenuation equation:

- X-ray attenuation:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$
- Final intensity of beam X:  $I_{X} = ( 4.6 \times 10^{3} ) e^{- 0.85 \times 4.8}$
- Final intensity of beam Y:  $I_{Y} = ( 4.6 \times 10^{3} ) [ ( e^{- 0.85 \times 2.1} ) ( e^{- 1.2 \\mu } ) ( e^{- 0.85 \times ( 4.8 - 1.2 - 2.1 )} ) ]$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute into the ratio given in the question:

- Ratio of the emergent intensities:  $\frac{I_{Y}}{I_{X}}=0.94$
- Substitute:  $\frac{( 4.6 \times 10^{3} ) [ ( e^{- 0.85 \times 2.1} ) ( e^{- 1.2 \\mu } ) ( e^{- 0.85 \times ( 4.8 - 1.2 - 2.1 )} ) ]}{( 4.6 \times 10^{3} ) e^{- 0.85 \times 4.8} } = 0.94$ **[1 mark]**
- Simplify:  $e^{0.85 ( 4.8 - 2.1 - 1.5 ) - 1.2 \\mu } = 0.94 \Leftrightarrow e^{1.02 - 1.2 \\mu } = 0.94$
- Take natural logs:  $1.02-1.2μ=\mathrm{ln}0.94\Rightarrowμ=\frac{1.02-\mathrm{ln}0.94}{1.2}$
- Attenuation coefficient of cyst:  $μ$ = 0.90 cm<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) Describe and explain the quality of the images from the two scans:

For the X-ray image...

- The <u>attenuation coefficients</u> (of the cyst and the surrounding tissue) are too similar / have approximately the same value **AND**
- (Hence) no / poor contrast would be obtained between the cyst and surrounding tissue / cyst would not be distinguishable from the surrounding tissue; **[1 mark]**

For the ultrasound image...

- The <u>acoustic impedances</u> (of the cyst and the surrounding tissue) are similar / have approximately the same value **AND**
- (Hence) there will be little reflection so the cyst (boundary) would be poorly imaged; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The expression for the attenuation of beam Y may look intimidating, but all it is saying is that the beam is attenuated by 2.1 cm of tissue, 1.2 cm of cyst and 1.5 cm (4.8 cm − 1.2 cm − 2.1 cm) of more tissue.*

> *We can combine as many attenuations as we like simply by multiplying by another exponential factor. Just make sure to use the appropriate coefficient for each difference material.*

parts.solutionMd:

(ii) Calculate the minimum wavelength of photons in the X-ray beam:

> *Work done on a charge, **W** =** QV **where **Q** is the charge and **V** the potential difference. Since the charge of an electron is **e** this means that **W** = **E** (energy transferred) = **eV**.*

Parallel X-ray beams of intensity $I_{0}$ are incident on the muscle and bone as shown. The emergent beam after passing through muscle alone has an intensity of $I_{m}$ and an intensity of $I_{bm}$ after passing through the bone and the muscle.

(i) Determine, in terms of $I_{0}$, the intensities $I_{m}$ and $I_{bm}$ of the emergent X-rays.

The linear attenuation coefficient of bone is 2.90 cm<sup>−1</sup>

The linear attenuation coefficient of muscle of 0.95 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

[4]

(ii) Suggest why, on an X-ray plate, the contrast between bone and muscle is much greater than the contrast between fat and muscle.

The linear attenuation coefficient of fat is 0.90 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the intensities of the emergent X-rays:

List the known quantities:

- Attenuation coefficient in bone, $μ_{b}$ = 2.90 cm<sup>−1</sup>
- Thickness of bone, $x_{b}$ = 2.0 cm
- Attenuation coefficient in muscle, $μ_{m}$ = 0.95 cm<sup>−1</sup>
- Thickness of muscle, $x_{m}$ = 5.0 cm

Determine the intensity of X-rays transmitted through muscle alone:

- Attenuation of X-rays:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$ **[1 mark]**
- Intensity transmitted through muscle alone:  $I_{m}=I_{0}e^{-μ_{m}x_{m}}$
- $I_{m}=I_{0}e^{-0.95\times5.0}=8.7\times10^{-3}I_{0}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the intensity of X-rays transmitted through muscle and bone:

- Intensity transmitted through bone:  $I_{b}=I_{0}e^{-μ_{b}x_{b}}$
- Intensity transmitted through muscle and bone:  $I_{b m} = I_{0} ( e^{- \mu_{b} x_{b} } ) \times ( e^{- \mu_{m} \Delta x} )$
- Where $\Deltax=x_{m}-x_{b}$ = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 cm
- $I_{b m} = I_{0} ( e^{- 2.90 \times 2.0} ) \times ( e^{- 0.95 \times 3.0} )$ **[1 mark]**
- $I_{bm}=1.8\times10^{-4}I_{0}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) The contrast between bone and muscle is much greater than between fat and muscle because:

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** from:**

- Contrast depends on the <u>difference</u> in attenuation; **[1 mark]**
- The difference between µ of muscle and fat is small (hence poor contrast); **[1 mark]**
- The difference between µ of bone and soft tissue / fat is large (hence good contrast); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *Remember in part (i) when the X-rays travel through the muscle and bone, it is travelling through 2.0 cm of bone but only 5.0 – 2.0 = **3.0 cm** of muscle.*

parts.problemMd:
An ultrasound investigation was used to identify a small volume of an unknown substance in a patient. It is suspected that this substance is either a cyst or a tumour.

During the ultrasound investigation, an ultrasound pulse of frequency 5 MHz is passed through soft tissue and then into the small volume of the unknown substance.

The ratio of the reflected intensity to the incident intensity for the ultrasound pulse reflected at the boundary was found to be 7.54 × 10<sup>−5</sup>.

Table 1.1 shows some information about the density and speed of ultrasound in soft tissue, cysts and tumours.

**Table 1.1**

| **material** | **density / kg m**<sup>**−3**</sup> | **ultrasound velocity / m s**<sup>**−1**</sup> |
|---|---|---|
| soft tissue | 1065 | 1530 |
| cyst | 1020 | 1570 |
| tumour | 990 | 1565 |

(i) Use the information in Table 1.1 to show that the unknown medium is a cyst.

[4]

(ii) A pulse of ultrasound reflected from the front surface of the cyst was detected 27.5 µs later and a pulse from the rear surface was detected 43.2 µs later.

Determine the length of the cyst, in cm.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the percentage of energy from the ultrasonic transducer that is reflected:

- Acoustic impedance:  $Z=ρc$
- Acoustic impedance of soft tissue:  $Z_{st}=1065\times1530=1.629\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$
- Acoustic impedance of cyst:  $Z_{c}=1020\times1570=1.601\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$
- Acoustic impedance of tumour:  $Z_{t}=990\times1565=1.549\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}m^{-2}s^{-1}$ **1 mark for all Z values correct**

Use the intensity reflection coefficient equation:

- Intensity reflection coefficient:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( Z _ 1 - Z _ 2 ) ^2 / ( Z _ 1 + Z _ 2 ) ^2`
- Cyst:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.601 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.601 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 7.5 x 10 ^ - 5` **[1 mark]**
- Tumour:  `I _ R / I _ 0 = ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 - 1.549 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 / ( 1.629 x 10 ^ 6 + 1.549 x 10 ^ 6 ) ^2 = 6.3 x 10 ^ - 4` **[1 mark]**

Compare the ratios to the ratio given in the question to identify the medium:

- `I _ R / I _ 0 = 7.54 x 10 ^ - 5 = 7.5 x 10 ^ - 5 ( 2 s. f. )` **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the unknown medium is a cyst

(ii) Determine the length of the cyst:

List the known quantities:

- Time detected from front of cyst = 27.5 µs
- Time detected from rear of cyst = 43.2 µs
- Speed of ultrasound in cyst, *c* = 1570 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the length of the cyst:

- Distance travelled by ultrasound:  $d=\frac{1}{2}c\Deltat$
- $d = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 1570 \times ( 43.2 - 27.5 ) \times 10^{- 6}$ **[1 mark]**
- $d=0.01232m=1.2\mathrm{cm}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

Determine the energy of the X-ray beam incident on the front surface of the cyst each second. State any assumptions you make.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the X-ray energy incident on the cyst each second:

List the known quantities:

- Attenuation constant of soft tissue, $μ$* *= 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Initial intensity of the beam, $I_{0}$ = 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>
- Length of the cyst, $d$ = 0.012 m = 1.2 cm (from **(a)**)
- Distance travelled through the tissue, $x$ = 2.1 cm

Calculate the intensity of the X-ray beam at the cyst:

- Intensity of a beam in tissue:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$
- $I = ( 4.6 \times 10^{3} ) e^{- ( 0.85 \times 2.1 )} = 771.9 \mathrm{W} \mathrm{m}^{- 2}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the cross-sectional area of the front surface of the cyst:

- Cross-sectional area of the cyst:  $A = \mathrm{\pi } r^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } \times ( \frac{0.012}{2} )^{2}$ = 1.13 × 10<sup>–4</sup> m<sup>2</sup> **AND**
- Assumption: the front surface is circular; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the power and energy incident on the cyst:

- Intensity of a wave:  $I=\frac{P}{A}\RightarrowP=IA$
- Incident power:  $P = 771.9 \times ( 1.13 \times 10^{- 4} ) = 0.087 \mathrm{W}$
- Energy transferred each second:  $E=Pt=0.087J$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

An ultrasound investigation was used to identify a small volume of an unknown substance in a patient. It is suspected that this substance is either a cyst or a tumour.

Table 1.1 shows some information about the density and speed of ultrasound in soft tissue, cysts and tumours: soft tissue density 1065 kg m^-3, ultrasound velocity 1530 m s^-1; cyst density 1020 kg m^-3, ultrasound velocity 1570 m s^-1; tumour density 990 kg m^-3, ultrasound velocity 1565 m s^-1.

The length of the cyst was determined to be d = 0.01232 m = 1.2 cm.

A beam of X-rays of energy 20 keV incident normally on some soft tissue which contains the cyst. The cyst is located 2.1 cm from the surface of the soft tissue. The attenuation constant of the soft tissue is 0.85 cm^-1. The incident intensity of the beam is 4.6 × 10^3 W m^-2.

The ratio of the intensities of the emergent X-ray beams X and Y is determined to be

$\frac{I_{Y}}{I_{X}}=0.94$

(i) Determine the attenuation coefficient of the cyst.

[3]

(ii) Compare the quality of the images that would be obtained from the ultrasound and the X-ray scans of the cyst.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Determine the attenuation coefficient of the cyst:

List the known quantities:

- Attenuation coefficient of soft tissue, $μ$* *= 0.85 cm<sup>–1</sup>
- Initial intensity of the beam, $I_{0}$ = 4.6 × 10<sup>3</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>
- Length of the cyst, $d$ = 0.012 m = 1.2 cm (from **(a)**)
- Distance between the tissue and cyst = 2.1 cm
- Total distance = 4.8 cm

Use the attenuation equation:

- X-ray attenuation:  $I=I_{0}e^{-μx}$
- Final intensity of beam X:  $I_{X} = ( 4.6 \times 10^{3} ) e^{- 0.85 \times 4.8}$
- Final intensity of beam Y:  $I_{Y} = ( 4.6 \times 10^{3} ) [ ( e^{- 0.85 \times 2.1} ) ( e^{- 1.2 \\mu } ) ( e^{- 0.85 \times ( 4.8 - 1.2 - 2.1 )} ) ]$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute into the ratio given in the question:

- Ratio of the emergent intensities:  $\frac{I_{Y}}{I_{X}}=0.94$
- Substitute:  $\frac{( 4.6 \times 10^{3} ) [ ( e^{- 0.85 \times 2.1} ) ( e^{- 1.2 \\mu } ) ( e^{- 0.85 \times ( 4.8 - 1.2 - 2.1 )} ) ]}{( 4.6 \times 10^{3} ) e^{- 0.85 \times 4.8} } = 0.94$ **[1 mark]**
- Simplify:  $e^{0.85 ( 4.8 - 2.1 - 1.5 ) - 1.2 \\mu } = 0.94 \Leftrightarrow e^{1.02 - 1.2 \\mu } = 0.94$
- Takes natural logs:  $1.02-1.2μ=\mathrm{ln}0.94\Rightarrowμ=\frac{1.02-\mathrm{ln}0.94}{1.2}$
- Attenuation coefficient of cyst:  $μ$ = 0.90 cm<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) Compare the quality of the images that would be obtained from the ultrasound and the X-ray scans:

For the X-ray image...

- The attenuation coefficients (of the cyst and the surrounding tissue) are too similar / have approximately the same value **AND**
- (Hence) no / poor contrast would be obtained between the cyst and surrounding tissue / cyst would not be distinguishable from the surrounding tissue; **[1 mark]**

For the ultrasound image...

- The acoustic impedances (of the cyst and the surrounding tissue) are similar / have approximately the same value **AND**
- (Hence) there will be a high % of transmission of the ultrasound / low % of reflection (so) cyst would be difficult to distinguish from the surrounding tissue / poor contrast between cyst and tissue; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.problemMd: State what is meant by the term *tracer* in relation to PET scanning.
parts.solutionMd:
A tracer is:

- A substance containing radioactive nuclei that are introduced into the body (before the PET scan); **[1 mark]**
- And are <u>absorbed</u> by the tissues (being studied); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
State the name of the particles that are emitted

(i) by the tracer,

[1]

(ii) from the body and detected by the detectors during PET scanning.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The particles that are emitted from the tracer are:

- Positrons; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The particles that are emitted from the body and detected by the detectors during PET scanning are:

- Gamma photons; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Explain what is meant by *annihilation* in the context of PET scanning.
parts.solutionMd:
Annihilation is:

- When a particle collides with its (corresponding) antiparticle so all its mass is converted into energy; **[1 mark]**
- (In PET scanning) a positron meets an electron and emits a pair of gamma photons; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd: State the **two** quantities which must be conserved in an annihilation event.
parts.solutionMd:
The quantities conserved in an annihilation event are:

- Mass-energy; **[1 mark]**
- Momentum; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

- A positron is emitted by the radiotracer that interacts with an electron in the **surrounding tissue**; **[1 mark]**
- Producing two γ-rays that move apart at **180°** to each other; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is a radiopharmaceutical used for PET scans. It contains radioactive fluorine-18 (F-18), which decays by positron emission with a half-life of 110 minutes.

In preparation for a scan scheduled for 12:00 p.m., a radiologist prepares a sample of F-18 FDG at 5 a.m. earlier in the day. For this scan, the radiologist determines the optimum activity of fluorine-18 would be 10 mCi when the scan starts at 12:00 p.m.

Determine the activity, in GBq, of the dose of fluorine-18 that the radiologist should prepare at 5 a.m.

1 mCi = 3.7 × 10<sup>7</sup> Bq
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the activity of the dose of fluorine-18 that the radiologist should prepare at 5 a.m.:

List the known quantities:

- Half-life, *t*<sub>1/2</sub> = 110 min
- Time, *t *= 7 hours = 7 × 60 = 420 min
- Optimum activity, *A* = 10 mCi
- 1 mCi = 3.7 × 10<sup>7</sup> Bq

Determine the initial activity of the dose of F-18:

- Exponential decay:  $A=A_{0}e^{-λt}\RightarrowA_{0}=\frac{A}{e^{-λt}}$
- Decay constant:  $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{1/2}}$
- $A_{0}=\frac{A}{e^{-\frac{t\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{1/2}}}}=\frac{10}{e^{-\frac{420\times\mathrm{ln}2}{110}}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $A_{0}=141.05\mathrm{mCi}$ **[1 mark]**

Convert the initial activity to GBq:

- $A_{0} = 141 \times ( 3.7 \times 10^{7} ) = 5.219 \times 10^{9} \text{Bq}$
- $A_{0}=5.2\mathrm{GBq}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The Curie (Ci) was the original unit used to express the decay rate (activity) of a sample of radioactive material. Since 1 Ci is equal to 37 GBq (giga-becquerels), it is a more convenient unit to use, particularly in medical physics where decay rates of common radionuclides are of the order MBq and GBq*

parts.problemMd:

1 mCi = 3.7 × 10^7^ Bq

The patient is scheduled to come in an hour earlier, at 11:00 a.m. to receive their injection of F-18 FDG.

parts.solutionMd:
Determine the time at which the sample of F-18 FDG may be injected into the patient:

List the known quantities:

- Initial activity (at 11 a.m.), $A_{0}$ = 15.3 mCi
- Maximum activity, $A$ = 14 mCi
- Decay constant, $λ$ = 6.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup> min<sup>−1</sup>

Determine the time taken to reach the required activity level:

- Exponential decay:  $A=A_{0}e^{-λt}\Rightarrow\frac{A}{A_{0}}=e^{-λt}$
- $\frac{A}{A} _{0} = e^{- \\lambda t} \Leftrightarrow \ln ( \frac{A}{A} _{0} ) = - \\lambda t$
- `t = - 1 / lambda ln ( A / A _ 0 ) <-> t = (ln ( A _ 0 / A ))/(lambda)`
- $t = \frac{\ln ( \frac{15.3}{14} ) }{6.3 \times 10^{- 3}} = 14.09 \min$ **[1 mark]**
- Earliest time the sample can be injected: 11:15 a.m. **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Technically the earliest time would be 11 am + 14.09 minutes which would be 11:14 am and 5.4 seconds! However, since we wouldn't want a time that precise, a sensible time of 11:15 am is required for the final answer.*

(i) Determine the initial number of F-18 nuclei in the injected sample:

- Activity:  $A=λN\RightarrowN_{0}=\frac{A_{0}}{λ}$
- Initial number of nuclei:  $N_{0} = \frac{14 \times ( 3.7 \times 10^{7 )}{1.05 \times 10^{-4} } }$
- Initial number of nuclei:  $N_{0}=4.93\times10^{12}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the equation relating mass, moles and molar mass:

- Moles of a substance:  $n=\frac{N}{N_{A}}$
- Mass of a substance:  $m=n\timesM_{r}\Rightarrowm=\frac{N_{0}}{N_{A}}\timesM_{r}$
- Mass of F-18:  $m=\frac{4.93\times10^{12}}{6.02\times10^{23}}\times0.018=1.47\times10^{-13}\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**
- Mass of F-18 FDG:  $\frac{1.47\times10^{-13}}{0.099}=1.5\times10^{-12}\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) The fraction of F-18 FDG remaining in the patient's body after 6 hours:

- Exponential decay:  $N=N_{0}e^{-λt}\Rightarrow\frac{N}{N_{0}}=e^{-λt}$
- Fraction of F-18 remaining:  $\frac{N}{N} _{0} = e^{- ( 6.03 \times 10^{- 3} ) \times 6 \times 60}$
- Fraction of F-18 remaining:  $\frac{N}{N_{0}}=0.11$ **[1 mark]**
- Fraction of F-18 FDG remaining:  $\frac{N}{N_{0}}=e^{-λt}=0.11$ (i.e. approximately 11% remains) **[1 mark]**

(iii) The actual fraction would likely be lower than 0.11 because:

- The patient would flush out / excrete the F-18 FDG through bodily functions / biological means; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Both computed tomography (CT) scans and positron emission tomography (PET) scans can produce detailed pictures of the organs and tissues inside the body. Both techniques share many similarities and differences.

In recent years, it has become much more common for doctors to use a PET-CT scan which is a machine able to perform both scans simultaneously. This way, doctors can combine the images from both scans to create an enhanced picture of the tissue or organ being studied.

(i) Describe the major differences between a CT scan and a PET scan.

[4]

(ii) Discuss the benefits and risks of using a PET-CT scanner instead of using either scan separately in medical diagnosis.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The major differences between a CT scan and a PET scan are:

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** pairs from:**

**The materials used:**

- In a CT scan: a contrast dye is injected into the patient and X-rays are passed through the body; **[1 mark]**
- In a PET scan: a radioactive tracer / positron-emitting substance is injected into the patient; **[1 mark]**

**The methods of detecting radiation:**

- In a CT scan: the patient is surrounded by (an array of) X-ray detectors which analyse the intensity of X-rays after passing through the patient; **[1 mark]**
- In a PET scan: the patient is surrounded by (a ring of) gamma detectors which analyse the difference in time of arrival of the two gamma photons created by the annihilation of a positron (from the tracer) and electron (from the patient); **[1 mark]**

**The images they produce / information they provide:**

- CT scans produce: a detailed three-dimensional image made up of many images / slices of a region at different angles (so it can be rotated), can be used for hard tissues (bones) and soft tissues (heart, brain etc); **[1 mark]**
- PET scans produce: real-time (three-dimensional) images of metabolic / cellular activity in a region of the body, particularly useful for detecting tumours and diagnosing neurological conditions; **[1 mark]**

**The amount of radiation present in the patient after the scan:**

- In a CT scan: no radiation remains in the body; **[1 mark]**
- In a PET scan: a small amount of radiation remains in the body for a short time; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The benefits and risks of using a PET-CT scanner are:

Benefits:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

- Together the scans provide more accurate diagnoses than the two scans performed separately; **[1 mark]**
- One scan can fill in the gaps that the other scan might not pick up e.g. cell / metabolic activity from PET not seen on CT; **[1 mark]**
- Both scans can be performed at the same time, limiting the time spent in hospital / scanners; **[1 mark]**

Risks:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

- Both use ionising radiation which can damage the patient's cells, so using both carries double the exposure and risk; **[1 mark]**
- Both require injections of substances which may cause adverse side effects; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Table 1.1 shows some information about two radionuclides commonly used in PET scanning.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **Fluorine 18** | **Oxygen 15** |
|---|---|---|
| half-life | 109.8 min | 122 s |
| maximum positron energy / MeV | 0.63 | 1.73 |
| % of decays that occur by β<sup>+</sup> | 97% | 100% |

Under certain conditions, a gamma photon may be converted into an electron and a positron.

Deduce, with suitable calculations, if the decay of one or both radionuclides in Table 1.1 can result in both the annihilation and the creation of electron-positron pairs.
parts.solutionMd:
Deduce whether the annihilation and the creation of electron-positron pairs can occur:

List the known quantities:

- Maximum kinetic energy of β<sup>+</sup> from Fl-18 = 0.63 MeV
- Maximum kinetic energy of β<sup>+</sup> from O-15 = 1.73 MeV
- Rest mass of an electron, *m*<sub>*e*</sub> = 9.11 × 10<sup>−31</sup> kg
- Speed of light, *c* = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the rest mass-energy of an electron-positron pair:

- Minimum possible photon energy:  $E_{min}=2m_{e}c^{2}$
- $E_{m i n} = 2 \times ( 9.11 \times 10^{- 31} ) \times ( 3.00 \times 10^{8 )^{2} = 1.64 \times 10^{-13} } \mathrm{J}$
- Convert to MeV:  $E_{min}=\frac{1.64\times10^{-13}}{1.60\times10^{-19}}=1.02\mathrm{MeV}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the minimum possible energy of the annihilation photons:

- Min energy of one photon = $\frac{1}{2}\times1.02=0.51\mathrm{MeV}$
- (When O-15 / F-18 decay they) both emit a positron which annihilates with a nearby electron to produce two photons each with a minimum energy of 0.51 MeV; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum possible energy of the annihilation photons from fluorine-18 decay:

- Maximum possible photon energy:  $E_{max}=2m_{e}c^{2}+KE_{max}$
- Max energy available:  $E_{max}=1.02+0.63=1.65\mathrm{MeV}$
- Max energy of one photon = $\frac{1}{2}\times1.65=0.83\mathrm{MeV}$
- 0.83 MeV < 1.02 MeV (therefore) photon (from Fl-18) does <u>not</u> have enough energy to create an electron-positron pair; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum possible energy of the annihilation photons from oxygen-15 decay:

- Max energy available:  $E_{max}=1.02+1.73=2.75\mathrm{MeV}$
- Max energy of one photon = $\frac{1}{2}\times2.75=1.38\mathrm{MeV}$
- 1.38 MeV > 1.02 MeV (therefore) photon (from O-15) has enough energy to create an electron-positron pair; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Table 1.1 shows some information about two radionuclides commonly used in PET scanning. Table 1.1: Fluorine 18 / Oxygen 15. half-life: 109.8 min / 122 s. maximum positron energy / MeV: 0.63 / 1.73. % of decays that occur by β^+^: 97% / 100%.

In practice, it is observed that the majority of gamma photons emitted have an energy of 511 keV and travel at exactly 180° to each other, regardless of the initial energy of the positron.

When fluorine-18 is used as a tracer, a very small proportion of the gamma photons have energies greater than 511 keV and do not travel at exactly 180° to each other.

When oxygen-15 is used as a tracer, a slightly larger proportion of the gamma photons have energies greater than 511 keV and do not travel at exactly 180° to each other.

(i) Explain these observations.

[6]

(ii) Suggest a potential issue in the detection of the gamma rays if the majority of photons possessed energies greater than 511 keV.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Explain the observations of energy and momentum in detected gamma photons:

**Observation 1:** The majority of gamma photons have an energy of 511 keV and travel at exactly 180° to each other because...

- The majority of positrons dissipate all of their kinetic energy (before annihilation); **[1 mark]**
- By interacting with matter / atoms in the tissue of the patient; **[1 mark]**

**Observation 2: **With Fl-18, a very small proportion of the gamma photons have energies greater than 511 keV and do not travel at exactly 180° to each other because...

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** from:**

- Emitted positrons (from fluorine-18) have non-zero kinetic energy (up to 0.63 MeV); **[1 mark]**
- Some of the positrons / electrons may not come to a complete rest (before annihilation); **[1 mark]**
- (Hence) the annihilation photons may have different energies / momenta; **[1 mark]**
- In order to conserve momentum, the photons may have different components of velocity (hence they would not move in exactly opposite directions); **[1 mark]**

**Observation 3:** With O-15, a slightly larger proportion of the gamma photons have energies greater than 511 keV and do not travel at exactly 180° to each other because...

- Emitted positrons (from oxygen-15) can have <u>higher kinetic energies</u> than the positrons from fluorine-18; **[1 mark]**
- Hence, expected that a slightly larger proportion of these positrons would not come to a complete rest **OR** more positrons are expected to have non-zero energy / momentum when they annihilate; **[1 mark]**

(ii) If the majority of photons possessed energies greater than 511 keV:

**Final answer:** **Any ****two**** from:**

- Many (photon pairs) would not travel in exactly opposite directions; **[1 mark]**
- This could make it harder to locate the exact position of the annihilation event; **[1 mark]**
- This could affect the overall image quality / resolution; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 8 marks]**

> *You don't need to know the exact mechanisms by which positrons (or electrons) dissipate energy, you just need to be aware that they **lose energy** when they **interact with matter** as you have seen in various topics, such as in the photoelectric effect and the production of X-rays*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Table 1.1 shows some information about two radionuclides commonly used in PET scanning. For Fluorine 18: half-life = 109.8 min; maximum positron energy = 0.63 MeV; % of decays that occur by β+ = 97%. For Oxygen 15: half-life = 122 s; maximum positron energy = 1.73 MeV; % of decays that occur by β+ = 100%.

A tracer contains radioactive fluorine-18 and has an initial activity of 450 MBq. A typical PET scan using fluorine-18 takes 30 minutes.

Determine the number of photons produced during a PET scan using fluorine-18. Assume that all photons produced in annihilation events are detected by the detector.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the number of photons produced during a PET scan using fluorine-18:

List the known quantities:

- Half-life, *t*<sub>1/2 </sub>= 109.8 min
- % of decays that occur by β<sup>+</sup> emission = 97%
- Initial activity, *A*<sub>0</sub> = 450 MBq = 450 × 10<sup>6</sup> Bq
- Time, *t* = 30 min

Determine the decay constant of fluorine-18:

- Decay constant:  $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{1/2}}$
- $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{1/2}}=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{109.8\times60}=1.052\times10^{-4}s^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the initial number of fluorine-18 nuclei in the tracer:

- Activity:  $A=λN\RightarrowN=\frac{A}{λ}$
- Initial number of nuclei:  $N_{0}=\frac{A_{0}}{λ}=\frac{450\times10^{6}}{1.052\times10^{-4}}=4.277\times10^{12}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the number of nuclei remaining after 30 minutes:

- Radioactive decay:  $N=N_{0}e^{-λt}\RightarrowN=N_{0}e^{-\frac{t\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{1/2}}}$
- Remaining number of nuclei:  $N = ( 4.277 \times 10^{12 ) \times e^{-} \frac{30 \times \ln 2}{109.8}} = 3.539 \times 10^{12}$
- Number of positrons emitted = $0.97 ( N_{0} - N ) = 0.97 ( 4.277 \times 10^{12} - 3.539 \times 10^{12} ) = 7.158 \times 10^{11}$**[1 mark]**

Determine the number of photons emitted:

- Each positron-electron annihilation corresponds to the production of two photons
- Therefore, number of photons = 2 × number of positrons emitted
- Number of photons produced: $\DeltaN$ = 2 × (7.158 × 10<sup>11</sup>)
- Number of photons produced = 1.43 × 10<sup>12</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Make sure to multiply the number of nuclei remaining by 0.97! This is because 97% of the decays of fluorine-18 are beta-plus, or positron, decay and positrons are the only type of decay we are interested in *

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Table 1.1 shows some information about two radionuclides commonly used in PET scanning. Table 1.1: Fluorine 18 half-life 109.8 min, Oxygen 15 half-life 122 s; maximum positron energy / MeV: Fluorine 18 = 0.63, Oxygen 15 = 1.73; % of decays that occur by β+: Fluorine 18 = 97%, Oxygen 15 = 100%.

A tracer contains radioactive fluorine-18 and has an initial activity of 450 MBq. A typical PET scan using fluorine-18 takes 30 minutes. A typical PET scan using oxygen-15 takes 6 minutes.

Determine the initial activity of oxygen-15 required to produce the same number of photons as the scan using fluorine-18.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the initial activity of oxygen-15 required:

List the known quantities:

- Half life of O-15, *t*<sub>1/2 </sub>= 122 s
- Number of photons = 1.68 × 10<sup>12</sup> (from **(c)**)
- Number of positrons emitted, *N* = 8.4 × 10<sup>11</sup>
- % of decays that occur by β<sup>+</sup> emission = 100%
- Time, *t* = 6 min = 6 × 60 = 360 s

Determine the decay constant of oxygen-15:

- Decay constant:  $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{1/2}}$
- $λ=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{t_{1/2}}=\frac{\mathrm{ln}2}{122}=5.682\times10^{-3}s^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the initial number of oxygen-15 nuclei in the tracer:

- Radioactive decay:  $N=N_{0}e^{-λt}\RightarrowN_{0}=\frac{N}{e^{^{-λt}}}$
- Initial number of nuclei:  $N_{0} = \frac{8.4 \times 10^{11}{e^{- ( 5.682 \times 10^{-3} } ) \times 360} }$
- Initial number of nuclei:  $N_{0}=6.50\times10^{12}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the initial activity of oxygen-15 required:

- Activity:  $A=λN$
- $A_{0} = \\lambda N_{0} = ( 5.682 \times 10^{- 3} ) \times ( 6.50 \times 10^{12} )$
- $A_{0}=3.7\times10^{10}\mathrm{Bq}=37\mathrm{GBq}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

Explain how a standard candle can be used to measure astronomical distances.
parts.solutionMd:
A standard candle can be used to measure astronomical distances by:

**EITHER**

- Measuring the standard candle's flux / brightness / intensity on Earth; **[1 mark]**
- Using the inverse square law (of flux) to calculate distance; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Using $F=\frac{L}{4πd^{2}}$; **[1 mark]**
- Where *F* = flux / brightness / intensity (of standard candle), *L* = luminosity, *d* = distance (to standard candle); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A standard candle in a distant galaxy is found to have a luminosity of 2.0 × 10<sup>36</sup> W and a radiant flux intensity on Earth of 2.59 × 10<sup>–15</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>.

Show that the distance of the galaxy from the Earth is about 8 × 10<sup>24</sup> m.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the distance of the galaxy from the Earth is about 8 × 10<sup>24</sup> m:

List the known quantities:

- Radiant flux on Earth, *F* = 2.59 × 10<sup>–15</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup>
- Luminosity, *L* = 2.0 × 10<sup>36</sup> W

Calculate the distance to the galaxy using the inverse square law:

- Inverse square law of flux:  $F=\frac{L}{4πd^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $d=\sqrt{\frac{L}{4πF}}$
- $d = \sqrt{ \frac{2.0 \times 10^{36}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 2.59 \times 10^{-15} } )} } = 7.84 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{m}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the distance of the Cepheid from the Earth:

List the known quantities:

- Luminosity of the Sun, $L_{Sun}$ = 3.8 × 10<sup>26</sup> W

Determine the luminosity from the graph:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Recently, astronomers have observed a type 1a supernova called Encore in a distant galaxy. Measurements of the light from Encore revealed that the galaxy is 10 billion light-years away.

Light from supernova Encore is collected using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The JWST detects a peak power reading of 5.3 × 10<sup>−16</sup> W. Theory predicts that this reading corresponds to Encore's peak luminosity of 2.4 × 10<sup>36</sup> W.

1 ly = 9.46 × 10<sup>15</sup> m

(i) Calculate the peak radiant flux intensity at the JWST.

[3]

(ii) Show that the collecting area of the JWST is 25 m<sup>2</sup>.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Distance from Earth, $d$ = 10 billion light-years = 10 × 10<sup>9</sup> ly
- Peak luminosity of supernova, $L$ = 2.4 × 10<sup>36</sup> W
- Peak power (measured by JWST), $P$ = 5.3 × 10<sup>−16</sup> W
- 1 ly = 9.46 × 10<sup>15</sup> m

(i) Calculate the peak radiant flux intensity at the JWST:

Convert the distance from light-years to metres:

- Distance:  $d$ = (10 × 10<sup>9</sup>) × (9.46 × 10<sup>15</sup>) = 9.46 × 10<sup>25</sup> m **[1 mark]**

Use the inverse square law of flux to calculate the peak intensity:

- Inverse square law of flux:  $F=\frac{L}{4πd^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Substitute:  $F = \frac{2.4 \times 10^{36} }{4 \mathrm{\pi } ( 9.46 \times 10^{25} )^{2}}$
- Peak radiant flux intensity:  $F$ = 2.13 × 10<sup>−17</sup> W m<sup>−2</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) Show that the collecting area of the JWST is 25 m<sup>2</sup>:

- Intensity equation:  $F=\frac{P}{A}\RightarrowA=\frac{P}{F}$
- Substitute:  $A=\frac{5.3\times10^{-16}}{2.13\times10^{-17}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Collecting area: $A$ = 24.9 = 25 m<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Solar panels consisting of combinations of photovoltaic cells use energy in the radiation received from the Sun to generate electricity.

An advertisement for solar panels claims that the intensity of radiation from the Sun incident at the top of the Earth’s atmosphere is more than 2 kW m<sup>−2</sup>.

Assess the validity of this claim.

Use the following data:

- radius of Sun = 6.96 × 10<sup>8</sup> m
- surface temperature of Sun = 5790 K
- distance from Sun to Earth = 1.50 × 10<sup>11</sup> m
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the radiant flux intensity at the top of the Earth's atmosphere:

List the known quantities:

- Radius of Sun, *r* = 6.96 × 10<sup>8</sup> m
- Surface temperature of Sun, *T *= 5790 K
- Distance from Sun to Earth, *d *= 1.50 × 10<sup>11</sup> m
- Stefan-Boltzmann constant, σ = 5.67 × 10<sup>−8 </sup>W m<sup>−2</sup> K<sup>−4</sup>

Calculate the luminosity of the Sun:

- Stefan-Boltzmann law:  $L=4πr^{2}σT^{4}$
- $L = ( 5.67 \times 10^{- 8} ) \times 4 \pi \times ( 6.96 \times 10^{8} )^{2} \times ( 5790 )^{4}$
- $L=3.879\times10^{26}W$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the radiant flux intensity:

- Flux intensity:  $F=\frac{L}{4πd^{2}}$
- $F = \frac{3.879 \times 10^{26 }{4 \pi \times ( 1.50 \times 10^{11} )^{2}} = 1371.92 \mathrm{W} \mathrm{m}^{-2} }$ **[1 mark]**
- $F=1.37\mathrm{kW}m^{-2}$ **[1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- 1.37 kW m<sup>–2</sup> < 2 kW m<sup>–2</sup> so the claim is false; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *'Assess the validity of this claim' normally means 'check this claim is correct'*

> *You can do this by calculating the value for the intensity, and then seeing how that value compares with the value they have mentioned*

> *You must **always** write a conclusion statement stating whether the claim is valid or not **and why*

> *This is best done quantitatively i.e. using numbers (X < Y so Y is not valid)*

A space probe is sent on a mission from Earth to Mars.

Power for the space probe is provided by solar panels that collect radiant energy from the Sun. The solar panels have a total area of 31 m<sup>2</sup> and are directly facing the Sun throughout the journey. The efficiency of the solar panels is 30%.

The mean orbital radius of Mars about the Sun is 2.3 × 10<sup>11</sup> m.

Compare the power available to the probe when it leaves Earth's atmosphere to the power available on its arrival at Mars.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the power available to the probe at Earth and Mars and compare:

List the known quantities:

- Radiant flux intensity at Earth, $F$ = 1370 W m<sup>−2</sup> (from **(a)**)
- Surface area of solar panels, *A* = 31 m<sup>2</sup>
- Efficiency of solar panels = 30% = 0.3
- Distance from Sun to Earth, $d_{E}$ = 1.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> m
- Distance from Sun to Mars, $d_{M}$ = 2.3 × 10<sup>11</sup> m

Determine the power available to the probe at Earth:

- Power:  $P=FA$
- The panels have an efficiency of 30%, so
- Total power available (at Earth):  $P_{E}$ = 0.3 × 1370 × 31 = 12 740 W **[1 mark]**

Determine the power available to the probe at Mars:

- Radiant flux intensity:  $F=\frac{L}{4πd^{2}}$
- Since $F\propto\frac{1}{d^{2}}$ and $P\proptoF\RightarrowP\propto\frac{1}{d^{2}}$
- Ratio:  `P _ M / P _ E = ( d _ E / d _ M ) ^2 <-> P _ M = P _ E x ( d _ E / d _ M ) ^2`
- Total power available (at Mars):  $P_{M} = 12 740 \times ( \frac{1.5 \times 10^{11} }{2.3 \times 10^{11} } )^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- Total power available (at Mars):  $P_{M}$ = 5420 W **[1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- The power available to the probe at Mars is 5420 W compared to 12 740 W at Earth, this is a decrease of 42.5%; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the area of solar panels required to reach Neptune:

List the known quantities:

- Distance from Sun to Earth = $d_{E}$
- Distance from Sun to Neptune, $d_{M}=30d_{E}$
- Required power at Neptune, $P$ = 5420 W (from **(b)**)

Determine the radiant flux intensity at Neptune:

- Radiant flux intensity:  $F=\frac{L}{4πd^{2}}$
- Ratio:  `F _ N / F _ E = ( d _ E / d _ N ) ^2 <-> F _ N = F _ E x ( d _ E / d _ N ) ^2`
- Radiant flux intensity at Neptune:  $F_{N} = 1370 \times ( \frac{d_{E} }{30 d_{E} } )^{2} = 1370 \times ( \frac{1}{30} )^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Comment on the viability of the mission:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

- The mass of the solar panels would make the launch (from Earth) difficult; **[1 mark]**
- A different energy source (e.g. nuclear power) would be more efficient / compact; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

radius = .................................... m [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Show that the surface temperature of the star in **(a)** is approximately 6700 K. Explain your reasoning:

List the known quantities:

- Peak wavelength emitted by the Sun, $λ_{Sun}$ = 500 nm = 500 × 10<sup>−9 </sup>m
- Surface temperature of Sun, $T_{Sun}$ = 5800 K
- Peak wavelength emitted by the star, $λ_{max}$ = 430 nm = 430 × 10<sup>−9 </sup>m

Use Wien's displacement law to calculate the temperature $T_{star}$:

- $λ_{max}\propto\frac{1}{T}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{λ_{Sun}}{λ_{star}}=\frac{T_{star}}{T_{Sun}}$
- $T_{star}=5800\times\frac{500}{430}$
- $T_{s t a r} = 6740 \mathrm{K} = 6700 \mathrm{K} ( 2 s. f. )$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Use the information in **(a)** and **(b)(i)** to determine the radius of the star:

List the known quantities:

- Luminosity, $L$ = 4.8 × 10<sup>29</sup> W
- Temperature, $T$ = 6700 K
- Stefan-Boltzmann Law: $L=4πσr^{2}T^{4}$
- Stefan-Boltzmann Constant, $σ$ = 5.67 × 10<sup>−8</sup> W m<sup>−2</sup> K<sup>−4</sup>

Use the Stefan-Boltzmann Law:

- $L=4πσr^{2}T^{4}$
- $r^{2}=\frac{L}{4πσT^{4}}$
- $r = \sqrt{ \frac{( 4.8 \times 10^{29 )}{4 \pi \times ( 5.67 \times 10^{-8} } ) \times 6700^{4} } }$ **[1 mark]**
- $r = 1.83 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{m} = 1.8 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{m} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *You need to use your **GCSE maths** skills to remember how to find the **constant of proportionality** for two quantities that are **directly proportional*

Fig. 1.2 shows the rate of emission from two of the stars, Sadr and Aljanah, plotted against wavelength. From the graph: Sadr peak wavelength = 400 nm AND Aljanah peak wavelength = 650 nm.

parts.solutionMd:
Determine the surface temperature of Sadr:

List the known quantities:

- Surface temperature of Aljanah, $T_{A}$ = 4700 K

Use the graph to determine the peak wavelengths:

![peak-wavelength-wien-graph-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/25-astronomy-and-cosmology/25-2-stellar-radii/assets/008-peak-wavelength-wien-graph-ma.png)

Use Wien's law to determine the surface temperature of Sadr:

- Wien's law:  $T\propto\frac{1}{λ_{max}}$
- Therefore, $\frac{T_{S}}{T_{A}}=\frac{λ_{A}}{λ_{S}}$
- $T_{S}=T_{A}\times\frac{λ_{A}}{λ_{S}}=4700\times\frac{650}{400}$ **[1 mark]**
- $T_{S}$ = 7600 K **[1 mark]**

> *You must be confident in turning proportionalities into equations.*

> *Therefore, *$T_{S}λ_{S}=T_{A}λ_{A}\Rightarrow\frac{T_{S}}{T_{A}}=\frac{λ_{A}}{λ_{S}}$*.*

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the ratio of the luminosities of stars A and B:

List the known quantities:

- Surface temperature of star A, $T_{A}$ = 25 000 K
- Surface temperature of star B, $T_{B}$ = 4300 K
- Ratio of radii = $\frac{r_{B}}{r_{A}}=1.1\times10^{5}$

Use the Stefan-Boltzmann law to determine the ratio of the luminosities:

- Stefan-Boltzmann law:  $L=4πr^{2}σT^{4}$
- Ratio:  `L _ B / L _ A = (r _ B ^2 T _ B ^ 4)/(r _ A ^2 T _ A ^ 4) = ( r _ B / r _ A ) ^2 x (T _ B ^ 4 )/(T _ A ^ 4)` **[1 mark]**
- `L _ B / L _ A = (( 1.1 x 10 ^ 5 ) ^2 x ( 4300 ) ^ 4)/(( 25 000 ) ^ 4)` **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{L_{B}}{L_{A}}=1.059\times10^{7}=1.1\times10^{7}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In the equation *$L=4πr^{2}σT^{4}$*, 4πσ is a **constant**. Therefore, *$\frac{L}{r^{2}T^{4}}=4πσ=constant$*.  *

parts.problemMd:
In recent years, astronomers have discovered sources of fast radio bursts (FRBs) in other galaxies. Studies suggest that these sources may be a type of standard candle.

An FRB source emits intense bursts of radio waves, each burst lasting for a fraction of a second. The closest FRB source is in a massive spiral galaxy 4.60 × 10<sup>24 </sup>m from the Earth. A detector of area 1.00 × 10<sup>−4 </sup>m<sup>2</sup> on the surface of the Earth received bursts of radio waves. In one burst, 9.40 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J of energy was received in a time of 1.15 ms.

(i) Show that the luminosity of the source is about 2 × 10<sup>35 </sup>W.

[4]

(ii) When FRB sources were first discovered, some observers suggested that the bursts might be extraterrestrial communications.

Suggest why this is unlikely.

luminosity of the Sun = 3.8 × 10<sup>26 </sup>W

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Show that the luminosity of the source is about 2 × 10<sup>35 </sup>W:

List the known quantities:

- Distance from Earth, $d$ = 4.60 × 10<sup>24 </sup>m
- Area of detector, $A$ = 1.00 × 10<sup>−4 </sup>m<sup>2</sup>
- Energy of burst, $E$ = 9.40 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J
- Time of burst, $t$ = 1.15 ms = 1.15 × 10<sup>-3 </sup>s

Determine the power of the burst of radio waves:

- Power:  $P=\frac{E}{t}=\frac{9.40\times10^{-23}}{1.15\times10^{-3}}=8.17\times10^{-20}W$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the intensity of the burst:

- Intensity:  $F=\frac{P}{A}=\frac{8.17\times10^{-20}}{1.00\times10^{-4}}=8.17\times10^{-16}Wm^{-2}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the inverse square law of flux equation to find luminosity:

- Inverse square law of flux:  $F=\frac{L}{4πd^{2}}$
- $L = 4 \mathrm{\pi } d^{2} F = 4 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 4.60 \times 10^{24 )^{2} \times ( 8.17 \times 10^{-16} } )$ **[1 mark]**
- $L=2.17\times10^{35}=2.2\times10^{35}W$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
In 2017, an ultra-cool star in our galaxy Trappist-1 was discovered with at least five of its own orbiting planets.

Astronomers have studied it extensively to determine if there is a possibility of finding life on some of the planets orbiting Trappist-1.

Table 1.1 below shows some data.

**Table 1.1 **

|   | **Trappist-1** | **Sun** |
|---|---|---|
| **Luminosity *****L / L***<sub>**☉**</sub> | 5.26 × 10<sup>−4</sup> | 1 |
| **Surface temperature *****T / T***<sub>**☉**</sub> | 0.4 | 1 |
| **Radius of star / *****R***<sub>**☉**</sub> | *R* | 1 |
| **Distance between Earth and Sun / m** | − | 1.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> |
| **Distance between planets and Trappist-1 / m** | 1.6 × 10<sup>9</sup> to 9.0 × 10<sup>9</sup> | − |

The temperature *T,* in K, of a planet, its distance *d* from the star and the luminosity *L* of the star are related by the expression

$\frac{T^{4}d^{2}}{L}=419\times10^{3}$

(i) Show that the radius *R* of Trappist-1 is smaller than the radius of the Sun.

[2]

(ii) The average temperature of the Earth is about 290 K.

Using data from Table 1.1, comment on the possibility of life existing on some of the planets orbiting Trappist-1.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Show that the radius *R* of T-1 is smaller than the radius of the Sun

List the known quantities:

- Luminosity of T-1, *L* = (5.26 × 10<sup>−4</sup>)*L*<sub>☉</sub>
- Surface temperature of T-1, *T* = 0.4*T*<sub>☉</sub>
- Radius of T-1 = *R*

Use the Stefan-Boltzmann law to determine the radius of T-1:

- Stefan-Boltzmann law:  $L=4πr^{2}σT^{4}\RightarrowR=\sqrt{\frac{L}{4πσT^{4}}}$
- Radius of the Sun:  `R _ ☉ = sqrt( (L _ ☉)/(4 pi sigma ( T _ ☉ ) ^ 4) )`
- Radius of T-1:  `R = sqrt( (( 5.26 x 10 ^ - 4 ) L _ ☉)/(4 pi sigma ( 0.4 T _ ☉ ) ^ 4) )`
- Radius of T-1:  `R = sqrt( (5.26 x 10 ^ - 4 )/(0.4 ^ 4) ) x R _ ☉ = 0.14 R _ ☉` **[1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- 0.14 < 1, therefore, the radius of T-1 is smaller than the radius of the Sun; **[1 mark]**

Determine the luminosity of T-1:

- (From question):  $\frac{T^{4}d^{2}}{L}=419\times10^{3}\RightarrowL=\frac{T^{4}d^{2}}{419\times10^{3}}$

- Luminosity of T-1:  *L* = (5.26 × 10<sup>−4</sup>) × (3.8 × 10<sup>26</sup>) = 2.0 × 10<sup>23</sup> W **[1 mark]**

Determine the range of temperatures of planets around T-1:

- $\frac{T^{4} d^{2}}{L} = 419 \times 10^{3} \Leftrightarrow T = \sqrt[4]{ \frac{L \times ( 419 \times 10^{3} )}{d^{2}} }$
- Inner-most planet temperature:  $T_{m i n} = \sqrt[4]{ \frac{( 419 \times 10^{3} ) \times ( 2.0 \times 10^{23} )}{( 9.0 \times 10^{9} )^{2}} } = 179 \mathrm{K}$

- $T_{min}=180K$  **AND ** $T_{max}=430K$ **[1 mark]**

Write a conclusion:

- With temperatures ranging from 179 to 425 K it is very <u>likely</u> that life could exist on a planet around Trappist-1; **[1 mark]**

**Final answer:** **And max ****one**** from:**

- The planets orbit closer to Trappist-1; **[1 mark]**
- It is possible for the temperature on the planets to be similar to Earth; **[1 mark]**

name: Hubble’s Law & the Big Bang Theory

parts.problemMd: State Hubble's law.
parts.solutionMd:
Hubble's law states:

**EITHER**

- The (recessional) speed of a galaxy is (directly) proportional to its distance from the Earth; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- $H_{0}=\frac{v}{d}$, where *v* = speed of recession of galaxy (from observer), *d *= distance of galaxy (away from observer); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:

Explain how the Hubble constant can be used to determine an age for the universe.
parts.solutionMd:
The Hubble constant can be used to determine an age for the universe from:

- $H_{0}=\frac{v}{d}$, the Hubble constant $H_{0}$ has units of s<sup>−1</sup>
- (Therefore) the age of the universe = $\frac{1}{H_{0}}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *Notice *$\frac{1}{H_{0}}$* will have units of **s** (seconds) which can then be converted into years for the age of the universe.*

parts.problemMd:

The Hubble constant can be used to determine an age for the universe from: H_0 = v/d, the Hubble constant H_0 has units of s^−1. (Therefore) the age of the universe = 1/H_0

The Hubble constant is estimated to be 2.2 × 10<sup>–18</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the age of the Universe in years.

1 year = 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the age of the universe in years.

List the known quantities:

- The Hubble constant, $H_{0}$ = 2.2 × 10<sup>–18</sup> s<sup>–1</sup>
- 1 year = 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s

Substitute the values into the age of the universe equation:

- Age of the universe = $\frac{1}{H_{0}}$
- Age of the universe = $\frac{1}{2.2\times10^{-18}}=4.54\times10^{17}s$ **[1 mark]**

Convert the age from seconds into years:

- Age of the universe = $\frac{4.54\times10^{17}}{3.15\times10^{7}}$ **[1 mark]**
- Age of the universe = $1.4\times10^{10}\mathrm{years}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The age of the universe will always come out as around 14 billion years (14 × 10*<sup>*9*</sup>* years), so if your answer in the exam is ever wildly off from this you know that something has gone wrong in your calculation (most likely some powers or putting numbers in your calculator incorrectly!). *

> *You can also remember this value from the intro theme tune to 'The Big Bang Theory' American sitcom:*

> *'**Our whole universe was in a hot, dense state** **Then nearly fourteen billion years ago expansion started, wait**'*

parts.solutionMd:
The main ideas of the Big Bang theory are:

- The Universe started with an explosion / Big Bang; **[1 mark]**
- All matter and energy was concentrated at a (single) point; **[1 mark]**
- The explosion caused the universe to expand** **from this (single) point; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Explain why the redshift of galaxies is considered to be evidence for the Big Bang theory.
parts.solutionMd:
The redshift of galaxies is considered to be evidence for the Big Bang theory because:

- If the Universe is expanding, then it must have been closer together in the past; **[1 mark]**
- The expansion of the Universe can be extrapolated back to its point of origin (known as the Big Bang); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *If the Universe is expanding at a measurable rate, then it makes sense that if we were able to rewind this expansion we would find a point in time where the Universe existed at a single point in time and space (called a singularity). This is the point at which the Big Bang is thought to have occurred. By doing this, scientists have been able to estimate the age of the Universe to be about 13.7 billion years old.*

parts.problemMd:
An astronomer observes that light from a galaxy has been shifted towards the blue end of an emission spectrum.

State and explain what can be deduced about the motion of the galaxy from this observation.
parts.solutionMd:
Blueshift means that:

- The galaxy is moving <u>towards</u> the observer; **[1 mark]**

This is because:

- Blueshift is a decrease in the observed wavelength of light (emitted from incoming stars and galaxies) **OR**
- The light from distant galaxies has a shorter wavelength than the same light observed on Earth; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The change in the wavelength of the observed light can tell us about the motion of the galaxy relative to the Earth*

- *If it is moving **away** from the Earth, the wave will spread out, hence the **wavelength will increase** and appear more **red** (hence the term 'red shift')*
- *If it is moving **towards **the Earth, the wave will bunch together, hence the **wavelength will decrease** and appear more** blue** (hence the term 'blue shift')*

As the universe expands, the wavelength of the detected radiation at a time *t* is larger than it was at a time* t*<sub>0</sub> in the past by a factor of

$\frac{R}{R_{0}}=1+z$

This expression represents the expansion rate of the universe.

Where* R* represents the separation of two galaxies at time *t*, *R*<sub>0</sub> represents the value of *R* at the time *t*<sub>0</sub> the radiation was emitted, and *z* represents the redshift, which is given by

$z\approx\frac{\Deltaλ}{λ}\approx\frac{v}{c}$

(i) Using the scale factor, or otherwise, determine, in years, the approximate age of the universe at the instant when the detected light from the distant galaxy in** (a) **was emitted.

parts.solutionMd:
(i) Determine the age of the universe when the light from the distant galaxy was emitted:

List the known quantities from **(a)**:

- Emitted wavelength, *λ* = 454 nm
- Change in wavelength, Δ*λ* = 26 nm
- Hubble constant, *H*<sub>0</sub> = 2.6 × 10<sup>−18</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the value of redshift for the galaxy:

- Redshift:  $z\approx\frac{\Deltaλ}{λ}=\frac{26}{454}=0.057$ **[1 mark]**

Use the expression to determine the expansion rate of the universe:

- Expansion rate:  $\frac{R}{R_{0}}=1+z=1+0.057=1.057$
- Expansion rate:  $\frac{R}{R_{0}}=\frac{t}{t_{0}}=1.057$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the age of the universe:

- Age of the universe (now):  $t=\frac{1}{H_{0}}$
- $t=\frac{1}{2.6\times10^{-18}}=3.85\times10^{17}s$
- $t=\frac{3.85\times10^{17}}{60\times60\times24\times365}=12.2\times10^{9}\mathrm{years}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the age of the universe when the light was emitted:

- Age of the universe (then):  $\frac{t}{t_{0}}=1.057\Rightarrowt_{0}=\frac{t}{1.057}$
- $t_{0}=\frac{12.2\times10^{9}}{1.057}=11.5\times10^{9}\mathrm{years}$ **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the universe was 11.5 billion years old when the light was emitted

(ii) The assumption made in the calculation is:

- The rate of expansion (of the universe) is uniform / constant / non-accelerated **OR** *H*<sub>0</sub> is constant over time; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The alternative method you could use is to consider how far the light has travelled in light years and subtract this from the age of the universe, this is because *

- *1 light year = the **distance** travelled by light in one year*
- *1 light year = speed of light (m s*<sup>*−1*</sup>*) × time (seconds in 1 year) *
- *1 light year = (3 × 10*<sup>*8*</sup>*) × (60 × 60 × 24 × 365)*

> *Although you are not required to know anything about light years for your exam, using your knowledge of light in this way can help to further your understanding of the topic of cosmology and the vast distances involved*

> *This means the light was emitted **0.7 billion years** ago*

> *At this time, the universe was (12.2 − 0.7) = **11.5 billion years old*

Star B has the larger orbital r, hence it is the faster star, v_B = 5.34 × 10^7 m s^−1.

The orbital period of the binary system about the common centre of mass is 21 days.

Show that the orbital radius of star B is about twice the orbital radius of star A.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the orbital radius of star B is about twice the orbital radius of star A:

List the known values:

- Period of system, *T* = 21 days = 21 × (60 × 60 × 24) = 1.81 × 10<sup>6</sup> s
- Velocity of star A, *v*<sub>A</sub> = 2.59 × 10<sup>7</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup> (from **(b)**)
- Velocity of star B, *v*<sub>B</sub> = 5.34 × 10<sup>7</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup> (from **(b)**)

Determine the orbital radius of star A:

- $r_{A} = \frac{( 2.59 \times 10^{7} ) ( 1.81 \times 10^{6} )}{2 \mathrm{\pi } } = 7.46 \times 10^{12} \mathrm{m}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the orbital radius of star B:

parts.problemMd:
Newton assumed that the universe was infinite, uniform and static. The Big Bang model suggests space and time originated at one point around 14 billion years ago. At this time the temperature was very high.

In 1965, Penzias and Wilson discovered cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation with a wavelength of around 1 mm.

Determine the current temperature of the CMB.

Surface temperature of the Sun = 5800 K

Peak wavelength emission of the Sun = 500 nm
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the current temperature of the CMB:

List the known quantities:

- Surface temperature of the Sun, $T_{Sun}$ = 5800 K
- Peak wavelength emission of the Sun, $λ_{Sun}$ = 500 nm
- Peak wavelength emission of the CMB, $λ_{CMB}$ = 1 mm

Use Wien's law to determine the temperature of the CMB:

- Wien's law:  $T\propto\frac{1}{λ_{max}}$
- Therefore, $\frac{T_{CMB}}{T_{Sun}}=\frac{λ_{Sun}}{λ_{CMB}}\RightarrowT_{CMB}=T_{Sun}\times\frac{λ_{Sun}}{λ_{CMB}}$
- $T_{CMB}=5800\times\frac{500\times10^{-9}}{1\times10^{-3}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $T_{CMB}=2.9K$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

This radiation was first emitted around 300 000 years after the Big Bang, during a stage of the universe's history called the 'era of recombination'.

At this stage, the radiation was in the visible region of the spectrum and had a temperature of around 3000 K.

Determine the factor by which the universe has expanded since the universe was at a temperature of 3000 K.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the factor by which the universe has expanded:

- List the known quantities:

  - Initial temperature, $T_{then}$ = 3000 K
  - Final temperature, $T_{now}$ = 2.9 K (from **(a)**)

Use the relationship between energy and temperature for a photon:

- Energy-temperature relation for photons:  $E\proptoT$
- $\frac{energyofphotonsat3K}{energyofphotonsat3000K}=\frac{kT_{now}}{kT_{then}}=\frac{2.9}{3000}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{energyofphotonsat3K}{energyofphotonsat3000K}=0.00097$ **[1 mark]**

Use the equation for photon energy

- Photon energy:  $E=\frac{hc}{λ}\Rightarrowλ\propto\frac{1}{E}$
- $\frac{λofphotonsat3K}{λofphotonsat3000K}=\frac{1}{0.00097}=1030$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember, redshift tells us the **factor of expansion** of the universe at different points in time/space, so in a question like this, you need to think about the relationships you know to try and get a ratio in terms of *$\frac{\Deltaλ}{λ}$

> *Since the difference in wavelengths between these temperatures is so large, *$\Deltaλ\approxλofphotonsat3K$

parts.problemMd: Estimate the speed of an apple as it hits the ground after falling from a tree.
parts.solutionMd:
Estimate the speed of an apple as it hits the ground after falling from a tree:

- Height of apple on a tree, *h* ≈ 5 m **[1 mark]**

*Acceptable range for h = 2 to 20 m*

Use energy conservation to estimate the speed:

- Change in GPE = Gain in KE
- $mgh=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- $v^{2}=2gh\Rightarrowv=\sqrt{2gh}$
- $v\approx\sqrt{2\times9.81\times5}$

*Acceptable range for v = 6 to 20 m* s<sup>−1</sup>

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Estimate the number of kilowatt-hours used by a lightbulb if switched on for a whole day.
parts.solutionMd:
Estimate the number of kilowatt-hours used by a lightbulb if switched on for a whole day:

- Power output of a lightbulb ≈ 70 W **[1 mark]**

*Acceptable range for power = 20 to 100 W*

Convert from W to kWh in 24 hours:

- $P=\frac{E}{t}\RightarrowE=Pt$
- Kilowatt-hours is a unit of energy, so $E ( k W h ) = \frac{P ( W ) \times t ( h r )}{1000}$
- $E ( k W h ) \approx \frac{70 \times 24}{1000}$
- *E*(kWh) ≈ 1.68 ≈ 1.7 kWh per day **[1 mark]**

*Acceptable range for E(kWh) = 0.5 to 2.4 kWh*

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Estimate the density, in g cm<sup>−3</sup>, of the head of an adult person.

- Radius of a head, *r* ≈ 10 cm **[1 mark]**

*Acceptable range for radius = 7 to 12 cm*

- Mass of a head, *m* ≈ 5 kg = 5000 g **[1 mark]**

*Acceptable range for mass = 1 to 10 kg (1000 to 10 000 g)*

Use the equation for volume of a sphere with the density equation:

- Volume of an adult's head ≈ volume of a sphere
- Volume of a sphere:  $V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$
- Density:  $ρ=\frac{m}{V}=\frac{m}{\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}}$
- `rho = (5000)/(4 / 3 pi x ( 10 ) ^3)` **[1 mark]**
- $ρ$ = 1.194 = 1.2 g cm<sup>−3</sup> **[1 mark]**

*Acceptable range for density = 0.1 to 7.0 g cm*<sup>*−3*</sup>

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *When asked a question, such as this, where you likely have no reference to make a reasonable estimate for something, like the mass of a person's head, think about reasonable approximations you could make*

> *For example, if the mass of an adult person is about 70 kg, you could make a reasonable assumption that their head might make up about 10% of this mass, which would be 7 kg*

> *It's important that you communicate this in your answer so the examiner can see your lines of thought, and even if you are outside of the acceptable range, you could still earn extra marks for method and reasoning*

parts.problemMd:

- Circumference of Earth = 2π* *× (6.4 × 10<sup>6</sup>) = 4 × 10<sup>7</sup> m **[1 mark]**

Calculate how many people would be needed:

- Number of people ≈ $\frac{circumferenceofEarth}{armspan}$
- Number of people ≈ $\frac{4\times10^{7}}{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- Number of people ≈ 2 × 10<sup>7</sup> **[1 mark]**

*Acceptable range for number of people estimate = 1.3 × 10*<sup>*7*</sup>* to 4 × 10*<sup>*7*</sup>

> *If you have approximated the arm span of a person to a different value than 2 m, that's ok, as long as it is a **reasonable** approximation. You may have said, 1.5 m or somewhere in between, and that's ok. You would still get the marks. But, if you approximated it to 5 m, this is **not** a reasonable estimation and you would not get the first mark. However, you would still get the other two marks if your calculations were correct, no matter what number you used.*

> *Questions that ask you to **estimate** may not always contain an unknown value that you need to approximate, like arm span in this question. They may just use inexact values such as the diameter of the Earth, or the mass of a proton as 1 atomic mass unit. Don't let this throw you, the calculation is just the same as it would be if you were using exact values. If you do approximate something, like the hand span, just remember to use the 'approximately equal to' sign ≈*

parts.problemMd:
