parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A man with a mass of 65 kg stands in an elevator. The elevator initially accelerates uniformly for 1.8 s followed by a period of a constant velocity of 2.5 m s^–1^ and then a final uniform deceleration for 1.8 s.

Suggest and explain during the deceleration period, which direction of elevator travel would make the man feel

(i) lighter

[2]

(ii) heavier

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The man would feel lighter when:

- (The elevator is) decelerating while travelling <u>upwards</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Since the reaction force (on him) / *R* is smaller / lower; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The man would feel heavier when:

- (The elevator is) decelerating while travelling <u>downwards</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Since the reaction force (on him) / *R* is larger / higher; **[1 mark]**

** ****[Total: 4 marks]**

> *This question shows why it’s important that you state the forces and acceleration in parts (a) and (b) the correct way around.*

> *The key idea here is that deceleration is **always in the opposite direction to motion.*

> *Hence, ‘decelerating while travelling upwards’ means a resultant force acts **downwards**.*

> *The man feels lighter because the reaction force is smaller (imagine if the reaction force was reduced to zero, the man would suddenly float off the surface of the lift and experience ‘weightlessness’!)*

> *Similarly, ‘decelerating while travelling downwards’ means a resultant force acts **upwards**. The man feels heavier because the reaction force is larger (it sometimes feels like the floor is pushing itself harder into your feet, making you feel ‘heavy’)*

> *The fact that the man no longer feels the normal force on the elevator is an important point in this question.*

> *The feeling of a person’s weight actually comes from what they are standing on (Earth, an elevator, weighing scales) pushing up on that person with the same force as their weight downwards.*

> *You don’t ‘feel’ your weight downwards on a pair of weighing scales, the scales push upwards on you with a force equal to your weight.*

- Mass of C:  $m_{C}=\frac{27.7}{9.81}=2.8\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

Three boxes A, B, and C are connected using an inextensible rope of negligible mass, as shown in Fig. 1.1. parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the acceleration of block C:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of B, $m_{B}$ = 2.4 kg
- Mass of C, $m_{C}$ = 2.8 kg (from **(c)**)
- Weight of C, $m_{C}g$ = 27.7 N (from **(c)**)
- Frictional force on B, $F_{B}$ = 6.4 N (from **(b)**)
- New tension in BC = $T$

Determine the new resultant forces on B and C:

- Resultant force on B:  $T-m_{B}g\mathrm{sin}35^{\circ}-F_{B}=m_{B}a$ **[Eq. 1]  ****[1 mark]**
- Resultant force on C:  $m_{C}g-T=m_{C}a$ **[Eq. 2]  ****[1 mark]**

Add [Eq. 1] and [Eq. 2] together and rearrange for *a*:

- $T-m_{B}g\mathrm{sin}35^{\circ}-F_{B}+m_{C}g-T=m_{B}a+m_{C}a$
- $m_{C} g - m_{B} g \sin 35^{\circ} - F_{B} = ( m_{B} + m_{C} ) a$
- $a=\frac{m_{C}g-m_{B}g\mathrm{sin}35^{\circ}-F_{B}}{m_{B}+m_{C}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known quantities and calculate:

- $a = \frac{27.7 - ( 2.4 \times 9.81 \times \sin 35^{\circ} ) - 6.4}{2.4 + 2.8}$
- $a$ = 1.499 = 1.5 m s<sup>−2</sup> **[1 mark]**

> *There is a change in the tension in the rope between B and C because the forces acting on block B have changed. *

parts.problemMd:
A rock climber of mass 80 kg slips after attaching a bolt firmly onto a piece of rock that they are climbing as shown in Fig. 1.1.

At the lowest point of the climber's fall, the length of the rope between the harness and the bolt is 24 m. The climber comes to rest and all the energy from the fall has been absorbed by the rope.

The rope has an unstretched length of 19 m and a stiffness of 560 N m<sup>–1</sup>.

![qu-4b-figure-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-1-momentum-and-newtons-laws-of-motion/assets/010-qu-4b-figure-1.jpg)

**Fig. 1.1**

Assume that the extension of the rope is proportional to its tension and the mass of the rope and the effects of air resistance are negligible.

Calculate

(i) the resultant force acting on the climber when he reaches the lowest point in the fall.

[3]

(ii) the extension of the rope when the climber’s acceleration is zero.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass of the climber, $m$ = 80 kg
- Stretched length of rope = 24 m
- Unstretched length of rope, $L$ = 19 m
- Stiffness of rope, $k$ = 560 N m<sup>–1</sup>

(i) Calculate the resultant force acting on the climber when he reaches the lowest point in the fall:

- The lowest point is when the rope reaches its maximum extension
- $\Deltax_{max}$ = stretched length – unstretched length = 24 – 19 = 5 m **[1 mark]**

Determine the resultant force on the climber:

- Resultant = $F-W$ where $F=k\Deltax$ (Hooke's law) and $W=mg$ (weight)
- Resultant = $k\Deltax_{max}-mg$
- Resultant = (560 × 5) – (80 × 9.81) **[1 mark]**
- Resultant = 2015.2 = 2020 N **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the extension of the rope when the climber’s acceleration is zero:

- When acceleration = 0:  $F=W$
- So, $mg=k\Deltax_{min}\Rightarrow\Deltax_{min}=\frac{mg}{k}$
- $\Deltax_{min}=\frac{80\times9.81}{560}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\Deltax_{min}$ = 1.4 m **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *It's useful to consider the free-body force diagrams of the climber at the different stages of his fall*

> *At the highest point (before falling):*

- *The forces acting on the climber are his weight and the reaction force which are balanced*
- *Hence *$R-mg=0$

> *Between the highest point and **L**:*

- *The climber freefalls under gravity, only his weight acts (as air resistance/drag is ignored)*

> *Between **L** and Δ**x*<sub>*max*</sub>*:*

- *The rope begins to stretch, and we are assuming extension is proportional to tension, so the restoring force is equal to Hooke's law*
- *Hence the resultant force is *$k\Deltax_{max}-mg=ma$
- $\Deltax_{max}$* is the point where the climber comes to rest*

> *Between Δ**x*<sub>*max*</sub>* and Δ**x*<sub>*min*</sub>*:*

- *The extension decreases as the resultant force/acceleration decrease to zero*
- $\Deltax_{min}$* is the point where the climber comes to rest again and the forces acting on him are balanced again*
- *Hence *$k\Deltax_{min}-mg=0$

![rock-climber-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-1-momentum-and-newtons-laws-of-motion/assets/011-rock-climber-ma.png)

Hemp is one of the strongest fibres with a very high tensile strength and is extremely rigid. Hemp ropes were the first to be used for ship rigging which adjusted the position of the sails and supported the masts.

parts.solutionMd:
Determine the average resultant forces exerted by the hemp and nylon ropes:

List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m* = 80 kg
- Initial speed, *u* = 19.3 m s<sup>−1</sup> (from **(b)**)
- Final speed, *v* = 0
- Time for nylon, $\Deltat_{nylon}$ = 0.664 s
- Time for hemp, $\Deltat_{hemp}$ = 0.035 s

Use impulse to determine the average resultant force exerted:

- Impulse:  $F\Deltat=\Deltap\RightarrowF=\frac{m\Deltav}{\Deltat}$
- Nylon:  $\DeltaF_{nylon}=\frac{80\times19.3}{0.664}$ = 2325 N **[1 mark]**
- Hemp:  $\DeltaF_{hemp}=\frac{80\times19.3}{0.035}$ = 44 114 N **[1 mark]**

Determine the ratio of the forces:

- $\frac{\DeltaF_{hemp}}{\DeltaF_{nylon}}=\frac{44114}{2325}=18.97$ **[1 mark]**
- Hence, the average resultant force exerted by hemp rope is about 20 times larger than that of the nylon rope

**[Total: 3 marks]**

Determine the percentage of the original gravitational potential energy of the ball that remains when it reaches its maximum height after bouncing five times.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Initial velocity, *u *= 22.5 m s<sup>−1 </sup>
- Mass, *m *=  0.15 kg
- Final velocity, *v *= 12.8 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the initial *E*<sub>*k i*</sub>  and final kinetic *E*<sub>*k f*</sub>  energy upon impact:

- Recall: Kinetic energy, *E*<sub>*k*</sub> = $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- *E*<sub>*k i*</sub>  = $\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\times0.15\times22.5^{2}=37.97J$
- *E*<sub>*k f*</sub>*  *= $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\times0.15\times12.8^{2}=12.29J$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the fractional change of kinetic energy after each impact:

- $\frac{E_{kf}}{E_{ki}}=\frac{12.29}{37.97}=0.32$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the percentage change after five bounces:

- $0.32^{5} \times 100 = 0.336 \%$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *When the ball falls, it converts its gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy. Therefore, its fractional change in kinetic energy is equal to its fractional change in gravitational potential energy, as energy needs to be conserved by transferring from one store to the other. In this calculation we are ignoring heating effects.*

parts.solutionMd:
State the principle of conservation of momentum:

Consider whether any external forces act in the explosion:

Consider the momentum before the explosion:

Consider the momentum after the explosion:

- So for momentum to be conserved:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A stationary uranium nucleus decays by emitting an α particle and thorium nucleus.

Assume that all of the energy released in the emission process is transferred as kinetic energy to the α particle and the recoiling nucleus and is equal to 6.55 MeV.

Calculate the kinetic energy of the Thorium nucleus and α particle in MeV.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Total energy released, *E *= 6.55 MeV
- Mass of Thorium nucleus, *M*<sub>*th*</sub>  = 228 *u  *(from part (a))
- Mass of alpha particle, *M*<sub>*α*</sub>  = 4 *u  *(from part (a))
- Unified atomic mass unit, *u *= 1.661 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg = 931.5 MeV

Apply the conservation of momentum to the explosion and obtain an expression for the velocity of the Thoriun nucleus, *v*<sub>*th*</sub>* *:

- *p*<sub>*th*</sub> = *p*<sub>*α*</sub> therefore *M*<sub>*th*</sub>*v*<sub>*th*</sub> = *M*<sub>α</sub>*v*<sub>α </sub> **OR** 0 = *p*<sub>*α *</sub> − *p*<sub>*th*</sub> so 0 = *M*<sub>α</sub>*v*<sub>α </sub>− *M*<sub>*th*</sub>*v*<sub>*th*</sub>
- So, *v*<sub>*th*</sub> = $\frac{M_{α}v_{α}}{M_{th}}$

Combine the equations, using *v*<sub>*th*</sub> from above, for kinetic energy of alpha-particle, *E*<sub>*k*</sub>* *<sub>*α*</sub>*  *and kinetic energy of a thorium particle *E*<sub>*k th *</sub>to obtain a ratio for kinetic energy:

- Recall: $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- $E_{kα}=\frac{1}{2}M_{α}(v_{α})^{2}$ **AND**** ** $E_{kth}=\frac{1}{2}M_{th}(v_{th})^{2}$

- $E_{k} t h = 1 \text{half} M_{t} h ( \frac{M_{ \alpha } v_{ \alpha }}{M_{t} h} ) ^{2}$

- $E_{kth}=\frac{E_{kα}(M_{α})}{M_{th}}$
- Therefore, the ratio for kinetic energy: $\frac{E_{kth}}{E_{kα}}=\frac{M_{α}}{M_{th}}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the ratio of the masses and obtain an expression for *E*<sub>*k th*</sub>:

- $\frac{E_{kth}}{E_{kα}}=\frac{4u}{228u}=\frac{1}{57}$
- $E_{kth}=\frac{E_{kα}}{57}$ **[1 mark]** **   **

Calculate the kinetic energy of the Thorium nucleus  and α particle:

- $E_{kth}+E_{kα}=E$
- $\frac{E_{kα}}{57}+E_{kα}=6.55\mathrm{MeV}$
- Therefore  $\frac{58}{57}E_{kα}=6.55\mathrm{MeV}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{kα}=\frac{57}{58}\times6.55=6.44$
- Rearrange the equation to calculate *E*<sub>*k*</sub>* *<sub>*th*</sub>:

  - *E*<sub>*k*</sub>* *<sub>*th *</sub>= *E *− *E*<sub>*k*</sub>* *<sub>*α*</sub> = 6.55 − 6.44 = 0.11 MeV **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A stationary uranium nucleus decays by emitting an α particle and thorium nucleus. Discuss how the principle of conservation of momentum applies in this explosion. Mass of Thorium nucleus, M_th = 228 u; Mass of alpha particle, M_α = 4 u.
Assume that all of the energy released in the emission process is transferred as kinetic energy to the α particle and the recoiling nucleus and is equal to 6.55 MeV. Calculate the kinetic energy of the Thorium nucleus and α particle in MeV. E_k th = 0.11 MeV; E_k α = 6.44 MeV.

parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Kinetic energy of Thorium nucleus, *E*<sub>*k*</sub>* *<sub>*th*</sub> = 0.11 MeV (from part (b))
- Kinetic energy of α particle, *E*<sub>*k*</sub>* *<sub>*α*</sub> = 6.44 MeV (from part (b))
- Mass of Thorium nucleus, *M*<sub>*th*</sub> = 228 *u *(from part (a))
- Mass of α particle, *M*<sub>*α*</sub> = 4 *u *(from part (a))
- Unified atomic mass unit, *u *= 1.661 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg = 931.5 MeV

**Method 1: Calculate the momentum of each nucleus**

Calculate the momentum of the Thorium nucleus:

- $E_{kth}=\frac{1}{2}M_{th}(v_{th})^{2}$
- Rearrange to obtain *v*<sub>*th*</sub>:

  - $v_{th}=\sqrt{\frac{2E_{kth}}{M_{th}}}$
- Convert *M*<sub>*th*</sub> into MeV:

  - *M*<sub>*th*</sub> = 228 *u *= 228 × 931.5 MeV = 212 382 MeV
- Substitute *M*<sub>*th*</sub> into the equation for *v*<sub>*th*</sub>:

  - $v_{th}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times0.11}{212382}}$ = 1.02 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m s<sup>−1 </sup>
- Convert *M*<sub>*th *</sub>into kg:

  - *M*<sub>*th*</sub> = 228 *u *= 228 × (1.661 × 10<sup>−27</sup>) = 3.787 × 10<sup>−25</sup> kg
  - *p*<sub>*th*</sub> = *M*<sub>*th*</sub>v<sub>th</sub> = (3.787 × 10<sup>−25</sup>) × (1.02 × 10<sup>−3</sup>) = 3.9 × 10<sup>−28</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

Calculate the momentum of the α particle:

- $E_{kα}=\frac{1}{2}M_{α}(v_{α})^{2}$
- Rearrange to obtain *v*<sub>*α*</sub>:

  - $v_{α}=\sqrt{\frac{2E_{kα}}{M_{α}}}$
- Convert *M*<sub>*α*</sub> into MeV:

  - *M*<sub>*α*</sub> = 4 *u *= 4 × 931.5 MeV = 3726 MeV
- Substitute *M*<sub>*α*</sub> into the equation for *v*<sub>*α*</sub>:

  - $v_{α}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times6.44}{3726}}$ = 58.9 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m s<sup>−1 </sup>
- Convert *M*<sub>*th *</sub>into kg:

  - *M*<sub>*α*</sub> = 4 *u *= 4 × (1.661 × 10<sup>−27</sup>) = 6.644 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg
  - *p*<sub>*α*</sub> = *M*<sub>*α*</sub>v<sub>*α*</sub> = (6.644 × 10<sup>−27</sup>) × (58.9 × 10<sup>−3</sup>) = 3.9 × 10<sup>−28</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- The Uranium nucleus is stationary, so the momentum before the decay = 0
- Both the Thorium nucleus and α particle have the same momentum (but in opposite directions) **AND**
- (Therefore) the momentum after the decay is also 0 / is conserved; **[1 mark]**

**Method 2: Show that the ratio of the momentum of each nucleus equals 1**

Determine the equation for the ratio of the momentum of Thorium and the α particle:

- Ratio of momentum = $\frac{M_{th}v_{th}}{M_{α}v_{α}}$
- $E_{kth}=\frac{1}{2}M_{th}(v_{th})^{2}$
- Rearrange to obtain *v*<sub>*th*</sub>:

  - $v_{th}=\sqrt{\frac{2E_{kth}}{M_{th}}}$
- $E_{kα}=\frac{1}{2}M_{α}(v_{α})^{2}$
- Rearrange to obtain *v*<sub>*α*</sub>:

  - $v_{α}=\sqrt{\frac{2E_{kα}}{M_{α}}}$
- Substitute for the velocities of Uranium and α particle into the ratio of momentum:

  - $\frac{M_{th}\sqrt{\frac{2E_{kth}}{M_{th}}}}{M_{α}\sqrt{\frac{2E_{kα}}{M_{α}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2M_{th}E_{kth}}{2M_{α}E_{kα}}}=\sqrt{\frac{M_{th}E_{kth}}{M_{α}E_{kα}}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known values into the ratio of velocities:

- $\sqrt{\frac{228u\times0.11MeV}{4u\times6.44MeV}}=\sqrt{\frac{228\times0.11}{4\times6.44}}$ = 0.9867 = 1 **[1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- Since the Uranium nucleus is stationary, the momentum before the decay = 0
- Both the Thorium nucleus and α particle have the same momentum (in opposite directions) so their ratios are equal to 1 **AND**
- (Therefore) the momentum after the decay is also 0 / is conserved; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Units are important in this question. You can either convert the mass in atomic units (u) to MeV or kg, as long as they are the same unit on the numerator and denominator of the fraction. When using the momentum equation **p** = **mv** the mass must be converted into kg from MeV or J so the final units for moments are kg m s*<sup>*–1*</sup>*.*

> * *

> *A small algebra trick to combine a variable outside a square root and inside a square root:*

- $m=\sqrt{m^{2}}$
- *Therefore, *$m \sqrt{ \frac{2 E_{k} }{m} } = \sqrt{ \frac{m^{2} 2 E_{k} }{m} } = \sqrt{ \frac{m^{ \cancel{2} } 2 E_{k} }{ \cancel{m} } } = \sqrt{m 2 E_{k} }$

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the magnitude of the resistive force:

List the known quantities:

- Weight, *W* = *mg* = 250 × 9.81

parts.problemMd:
Strongman competitions involve competitors performing various challenges where they have to produce very high forces.

In one particular event, a competitor must drag a cement block across a rough floor, using a rope.

When an object is moving, the frictional force is proportional to the normal reaction force of the object.

In the first round of the competition, the competitor must drag a 200 kg block across the rough surface. In the second round, they must drag a new 280 kg block across the same surface. The force exerted by the competitor in round 2 is 1650 N.

Calculate the difference in the frictional forces between the first and second rounds, when the blocks are in motion.

You may assume the block moves with constant speed and air resistance can be ignored.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage increase of force between rounds:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of block in round 1, *m*<sub>*1*</sub>  = 200 kg
- Mass of block in round 2, *m*<sub>*2*</sub>  = 280 kg
- Frictional force in round 2, *F*<sub>*2*</sub>  = 1650 N
- Frictional force ∝ normal reaction force
- Acceleration of free fall, *g*  = 9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup> (from data page)

Calculate the normal reaction force, *R*<sub>*1*</sub> , *R*<sub>*2*</sub> , of each block:

- The block is not accelerating vertically, so vertical forces are balanced

  - *R  = W = mg*
- $R_{1}=W_{1}=m_{1}g=200\times9.81=1962N$ **AND**
- $R_{2}=W_{2}=m_{2}g=280\times9.81=2747N$ **[1 mark]**

Compare the frictional forces, *F* , of blocks 1 and 2:

- $F\proptoR$
- $\frac{F_{2}}{F_{1}}=\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}}=\frac{2747}{1962}=1.40$ **[1 mark]**

Determine frictional force from round 1:

- $\frac{F_{2}}{F_{1}}=1.40\rightarrowF_{1}=\frac{F_{2}}{1.40}$
- $F_{1}=\frac{1650}{1.40}=1179N$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the difference:

- $F_{2}-F_{1}=1650-1179=470N$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *At A level, the concept of proportionality comes up frequently.*

> *You may quickly realise that the mass being 1.4× larger means that weight, reaction force and therefore friction is also 1.4× greater. But you must make this thought process known to your examiner, so write it all down. *

> *You may also have reached a similar answer by finding a constant of proportionality i.e. **F = kR  **where **k**  is the constant of proportionality and using this to calculate the difference.*

Determine the new mass when the trucks are stuck together:

Since the final momentum is positive, this implies the trolleys are moving in the same direction as trolley **X** at the beginning. *

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A trolley X with mass of 400 g is moving on a track with a velocity of 1.2 m s^−1^ towards a stationary trolley Y with mass of 800 g. Trolley X collides with trolley Y and subsequently, they stick together.

(i) Calculate the velocity of the two trucks after the collision: Velocity after: v = 0.48/1.2 = 0.4 m s^−1^

Explain why the collision cannot be described as elastic.
parts.solutionMd:
The collision is not elastic because:

- The final velocity / kinetic energy is <u>less</u> after the collision **OR**
- The relative speed of separation is <u>less than</u> the relative speed of approach; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *If you're not sure how to calculate the relative speeds, it is simply:*

- *The relative speed of approach:  *$( u_{X} - u_{Y} ) = ( 1.2 - 0 ) = 1.2 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{- 1}$
- *The relative speed of separation:  *$v_{XY}=0.4ms^{-1}$

> *It's useful to note that when two objects stick together after a collision, they can **never** be elastic*

> *In fact when two objects stick together, it is said to be “perfectly” inelastic, because, in this scenario, the maximum amount of kinetic energy is dissipated.*

> *You can think of this as the remaining energy wasted as heat or sound. If there was a collision of two cars where one drives into a stationary one, you would hear the sound of the collision.*

parts.problemMd: State the difference between an elastic and an inelastic collision.
parts.solutionMd:
The difference between an elastic and an inelastic collision is:

- In an elastic collision, the total kinetic energy is conserved **OR** relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation; **[1 mark]**
- In an inelastic collision, kinetic energy is not conserved / is lost **OR** relative speed of approach > relative speed of separation; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the momentum of the ball at the start, before it hits the wall:

List the known quantities:

- Velocity, *v* = 35 m s<sup>−1</sup>

State the equation for momentum and calculate:

- Momentum: $p=mv$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A ball collides with a wall at a velocity of 35 m s^−1^ and rebounds with velocity *v*. The ball has a mass of 0.025 kg. The motion of the ball is shown in Fig. 1.1. Calculate the momentum of the ball at the start, before it hits the wall: Momentum: p = m v = 0.025 × 35 = 0.875 = 0.88 kg m s^−1^

The collision is perfectly elastic.

Determine

(i) the rebound velocity of the ball

[1]

(ii) the magnitude of the change in momentum of the ball.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m* = 0.025 kg
- Initial momentum = 0.875 kg m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Initial velocity = 35 m s<sup>−1</sup>

(i) Determine the rebound velocity of the ball:

- For a perfectly elastic collision:  relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation
- Hence, rebound (final) velocity:  *v* = –35 m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) Determine the change in momentum of the ball:

- Change in momentum:  Momentum after − momentum before
- Change in momentum:  Δ*p* = -mv - mv = -2mv
- Change in momentum:  Δ*p* = (0.025 × –35) − (0.025 × 35) **OR** 2 × 0.875 **[1 mark]**
- Magnitude of the change in momentum:  Δ*p* = 1.75 = 1.8 kg m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The question demonstrates the importance of direction. Since momentum is a vector quantity, the direction influences the sign on the value.*

> *The **magnitude **of the change in momentum means don't worry about the signs, the final answer should just be the **size**. However, the negative or positive signs are important to get to this stage!*

> *If momentum was a scalar, you would say the 'change in momentum' was zero, as the magnitude of the momentum before and after didn't change. However, the fact that the momentum acts in the opposite direction afterwards means the magnitude of the total momentum is **twice** that of the momenta before and after the collision.*

> *This very fact has crucial implications in the real world, such as in gas laws, where it can be used to explain why gas pressure exists*

parts.problemMd:
A ball X of mass 140 g travelling at constant velocity *v* collides head-on with a stationary ball Y of mass 620 g, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![3-2-1a-m-3-2-ball-x-y-conservation-of-momentum-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/044-3-2-1a-m-3-2-ball-x-y-conservation-of-momentum-c.png)

After the collision, ball X comes to a stop. Ball Y moves off in the same initial direction as X with a velocity of 0.8 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Determine the velocity *v* of ball X before the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the velocity *v *of ball X before the collision:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of X = 140 g
- Mass of Y = 620 g
- Velocity of X before the collision = *v*
- Velocity of X after the collision = 0
- Velocity of Y before the collision = 0
- Velocity of Y after the collision = 0.8 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Use conservation of momentum to write an expression for *v*:

- Momentum before collision:  $m_{X}v_{X}+m_{Y}v_{Y}=140v+0$
- Momentum after collision:  $m_{X} v_{X} + m_{Y} v_{Y} = 0 + ( 620 \times 0.8 )$
- Conservation of momentum:  Momentum before collision = Momentum after collision
- Conservation of momentum:  $140v=620\times0.8$ **[1 mark]**
- Rearrange:  $v=\frac{620\times0.8}{140}$ **[1 mark]**
- $v$ = 3.543 = 3.5 m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A ball X of mass 140 g travelling at constant velocity v collides head-on with a stationary ball Y of mass 620 g. After the collision, ball X comes to a stop. Ball Y moves off in the same initial direction as X with a velocity of 0.8 m s^−1. [Determined in (a): velocity v of ball X before the collision = 3.5 m s^−1]

(i) Show that the collision in **(a)** is inelastic.

[3]

(ii) Explain why the collision in **(a)** is inelastic.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Show that the collision in **(a)** is inelastic:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of X = 140 g = 0.14 kg
- Mass of Y = 620 g = 0.62 kg
- Velocity of X before the collision = 3.5 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Velocity of X after the collision = 0
- Velocity of Y before the collision = 0
- Velocity of Y after the collision = 0.8 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Determine the kinetic energy before and after the collision:

- KE before = $1 \frac{1}{2} m_{X} v_{X}^{2} + 1 \frac{1}{2} m_{Y} v_{Y}^{2} = ( 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 0.14 \times 3.5^{2} ) + 0$
- KE before = 0.8575 = 0.86 J **[1 mark]**
- KE after = $1 \frac{1}{2} m_{X} v_{X}^{2} + 1 \frac{1}{2} m_{Y} v_{Y}^{2} = 0 + ( 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 0.62 \times 0.8^{2} )$
- KE after = 0.1984 = 0.20 J **[1 mark]**

Write a concluding sentence:

- The kinetic energy after the collision is <u>less</u> than the kinetic energy before the collision, hence it is an inelastic collision; **[1 mark]**

(ii) The collision is inelastic because:

- Some of X's (kinetic) energy has been transferred to other forms of energy (such as heat and sound); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The balls are replaced by an aluminium sphere of mass 2.7 kg and a steel sphere of 7.9 kg as shown in Fig. 1.2.

The aluminium sphere has an initial velocity of 10.0 m s<sup>–1</sup> when it collides with the stationary steel sphere. Immediately after the collision, the velocity of the steel sphere is 5.1 m s<sup>–1</sup>.

![3-2-1c-m-3-2-metal-spheres-conservation-of-momentum-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/045-3-2-1c-m-3-2-metal-spheres-conservation-of-momen.png)

Calculate the velocity *v* of the aluminium sphere immediately after the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the velocity of the aluminium sphere immediately after the collision:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of aluminium sphere, $m_{Al}$ = 2.7 kg
- Mass of steel sphere, $m_{S}$ = 7.9 kg
- Initial velocity of aluminium sphere, $u_{Al}$ = 10.0 m s<sup>–1 </sup>
- Initial velocity of steel sphere, $u_{S}$ = 0
- Final velocity of aluminium sphere = $v$
- Final velocity of steel sphere, $v_{S}$ = 5.1 m s<sup>–1 </sup>

Use conservation of momentum to write an expression for *v*:

- Momentum before collision:  $m_{A l} u_{A l} + m_{S} u_{S} = ( 2.7 \times 10 ) + 0$ **AND**
- Momentum after collision:  $m_{A l} v_{A l} + m_{S} v_{S} = ( 2.7 \times v ) + ( 7.9 \times 5.1 )$**[1 mark]**
- Conservation of momentum:  Momentum before collision = Momentum after collision
- $( 2.7 \times 10 ) = 2.7 v + ( 7.9 \times 5.1 ) \Leftrightarrow v = \frac{27 - ( 7.9 \times 5.1 )}{2.7}$ **[1 mark]**
- $v$ = −4.922 = −4.9 m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The negative sign is necessary for the final answer*

  - *This tells us that the aluminium sphere **changes** direction*
- *Remember to show your working - the first mark is for **substitution**, not just stating the equation!*

parts.problemMd:
Two identical blocks A and B each of mass 400 g are travelling towards each other along a straight line through their centre, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![3-2-2a-m-3-2-momentum-blocks-same-speed-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/042-3-2-2a-m-3-2-momentum-blocks-same-speed-cie-ial-.png)

Both blocks are moving at a speed of 0.36 m s<sup>–1</sup> relative to the surface.

As a result of the collision, the blocks reverse their direction of motion and travel at the same speed as each other. During the collision, 33% of the kinetic energy of the blocks is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy.

(i) State the total momentum of the blocks before the collision.

[1]

(ii) State and explain whether the collision is elastic or inelastic.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The total momentum of the blocks before the collision is:

- Total momentum = *mu* + *mu* = (400 × 0.36) + (400 × −0.36)
- Total momentum = 0 **[1 mark]**

(ii) The collision is:

- Inelastic; **[1 mark]**

Because:

- 33% of the kinetic energy is lost as heat **OR **in elastic collisions, 100% of kinetic energy is conserved; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Most scenarios where two objects collide and then move in opposite directions are commonly elastic. However, there is information given in the question that suggests that this isn’t the case for this scenario.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two identical blocks A and B each of mass 400 g are travelling towards each other along a straight line through their centre. Both blocks are moving at a speed of 0.36 m s^–1^ relative to the surface. As a result of the collision, the blocks reverse their direction of motion and travel at the same speed as each other. During the collision, 33% of the kinetic energy of the blocks is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy.

Calculate the final speed of the blocks.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the final speed of the blocks:

List the known quantities:

- Energy lost = 33% = 0.33  $\Leftrightarrow E_{k ( 2 )} = 0.67 \times E_{k ( 1 )}$
- Initial speed of each block, *u* = 0.36 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Final speed of each block = *v*

Write an expression for the ratio of the initial and final kinetic energies:

- Kinetic energy:  $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\RightarrowE_{k}\proptov^{2}$
- Initial kinetic energy:  $E_{k ( 1 )} \propto u^{2}$
- Final kinetic energy:  $E_{k ( 2 )} \propto v^{2}$
- `E _ k ( 1 ) end _ / E _ k ( 2 ) end _ = u ^2 / v ^2` **[1 mark]**

Determine the final speed of the blocks, *v*:

- $\frac{E_{k ( 1 )} }{0.67 \times E_{k ( 1 )} } = \frac{0.36^{2}}{v^{2}} \Leftrightarrow v^{2} = 0.36^{2} \times 0.67$
- $v=0.36\times\sqrt{0.67}$ **[1 mark]**
- $v$ = 0.2947 = 0.29 m s<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two identical blocks A and B each of mass 400 g are travelling towards each other along a straight line through their centre. Both blocks are moving at a speed of 0.36 m s^–1 relative to the surface. As a result of the collision, the blocks reverse their direction of motion and travel at the same speed as each other. During the collision, 33% of the kinetic energy of the blocks is transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy.
Calculate the final speed of the blocks: v = 0.2947 = 0.29 m s^–1

The duration of the collision between the blocks is 750 ms.

Determine the average force exerted by one block on the other.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the average force exerted by one block on the other:

List the known quantities:

- Initial speed of both blocks, *u *= 0.36 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Final speed of both blocks, *v* = 0.29 m s<sup>–1</sup> (from **(b)**)
- Mass of each block, *m* = 400 g = 0.4 kg
- Time during the collision, Δ*t* = 750 ms = 750 × 10<sup>–3</sup> s

Calculate the change in velocity, Δ*v*

- Δ*v* = *v* –* u* = 0.36 – (–0.29) = 0.65 m s<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

Calculate the average force, *F*:

- Momentum: $p=mv$* *
- Force:  $F=\frac{\Deltap}{\Deltat}=\frac{m\Deltav}{\Deltat}$
- $F=\frac{0.4\times0.65}{750\times10^{-3}}$ **[1 mark]**
- *F* = 0.35 N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *A common mistake in this question is calculating the change in velocity Δ**v** as 0.36 – 0.29 = 0.07 m s*<sup>*–1*</sup>

> *This is incorrect as it is not treating velocity as a **vector** which has both magnitude and direction*

> *Make sure to consider just one of the blocks, and be clear on which direction you are taking as the positive direction:*

![3-2-momentum-blocks-same-speed-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/043-3-2-momentum-blocks-same-speed-ma.png)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two identical blocks A and B each of mass 400 g are travelling towards each other along a straight line through their centre, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

The same blocks are investigated with different initial speeds. Block A is launched towards B at a speed of 0.6 m s<sup>−1</sup> and B is launched towards A at a speed of 0.4 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Once the blocks collide, they stick together and move as one after the collision.

Determine the speed of the combined blocks after the collision and state the direction.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the speed and direction of the combined blocks after the collision:

List the known quantities:

- Initial velocity of block A, *v*<sub>*A*</sub> = 0.6 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Initial velocity of block B, *v*<sub>*B*</sub> = −0.4 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Mass of block A, *m*<sub>*A*</sub> = 400 g = 0.4 kg
- Mass of block B, *m*<sub>*B*</sub> = 400 g = 0.4 kg

Use conservation of linear momentum:

- Conservation of momentum:  Total momentum before the collision = Total momentum after the collision
- Conservation of momentum:*  *$m_{A} v_{A} + m_{B} v_{B} = ( m_{A} + m_{B} ) v$* ***[1 mark]**
- Rearrange:*  *$v = \frac{m_{A} v_{A} + m_{B} v_{B} }{m_{A} + m_{B} } \Leftrightarrow v = \frac{m ( v_{A} + v_{B} )}{2 m}$
- $v=\frac{0.4(0.6-0.4)}{2\times0.4}$ **[1 mark]**
- $v$ = 0.1 m s<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

State the final speed and direction:

- Speed after the collision = 0.1 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Direction = same as initial direction of A;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A fast-moving asteroid B collides with a slower-moving asteroid A as shown in Fig. 1.1. Asteroid B becomes embedded within asteroid A as shown.

![3-2-3a-m-3-2-linear-momentum-asteroid-collision-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/051-3-2-3a-m-3-2-linear-momentum-asteroid-collision-.png)

Before the collision, asteroid A had a velocity of 3.61 km s<sup>−1</sup> and a momentum of 2.00 × 10<sup>17</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup>.

(i) State the principle of conservation of linear momentum.

[2]

(ii) Show that the mass of asteroid A was about 5.5 × 10<sup>13</sup> kg.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The principle of conservation of linear momentum states that:

- The momentum <u>of a system</u> remains constant **OR** total momentum before (a collision) = total momentum after (a collision); **[1 mark]**
- Provided that there are no external / resultant forces acting; **[1 mark]** ** **

(ii) Show that the mass of asteroid A was about 5.5 × 10<sup>13</sup> kg:

List the known quantities:

- Velocity of A, *m*<sub>*A*</sub> = 3.61 km s<sup>−1</sup> = 3.61 × 10<sup>3</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Momentum of A, *p*<sub>*A*</sub> = 2.00 × 10<sup>17</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup>

Determine the mass of A:

- $p=mv$ **[1 mark]**
- $m=\frac{p}{v}$
- $m_{A}=\frac{2.00\times10^{17}}{3.61\times10^{3}}$ = 5.54 × 10<sup>13</sup> kg **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *It's very common for students to miss the second marking point from their definitions of conservation of momentum - make sure you learn both parts!*

> *Remember to use the unrounded calculated value for the mass of asteroid A*

> *You should always work with more sig figs than you need during your calculation and then round at the end to avoid a cumulative rounding error*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A fast-moving asteroid B collides with a slower-moving asteroid A as shown in Fig. 1.1. Asteroid B becomes embedded within asteroid A as shown.

Before the collision, asteroid A had a velocity of 3.61 km s^−1^ and a momentum of 2.00 × 10^17^ kg m s^−1^.

(ii) Show that the mass of asteroid A was about 5.5 × 10^13^ kg. (m_A = 5.54 × 10^13 kg)

Calculate the combined velocity, in km s<sup>−1</sup>, of the asteroids after the collision.

mass of asteroid B = 6.40 × 10<sup>12</sup> kg

velocity of asteroid B before the collision = 14.0 km s<sup>−1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the combined velocity of the asteroids after the collision:

- Initial velocity of asteroid A, $u_{A}$ = 3.61 × 10<sup>3</sup> m s<sup>−1 </sup>
- Momentum of asteroid A,$p_{A}$ = 2.00 × 10<sup>17</sup> kg m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Mass of asteroid B, $m_{B}$ = 6.40 × 10<sup>12</sup> kg
- Initial velocity of asteroid B, $u_{B}$ = 14.0 km s<sup>−1</sup> = 14.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> m s<sup>−1 </sup>

Apply conservation of momentum:

- After the collision, asteroid B is absorbed by asteroid A, so the asteroids have a combined mass of $m_{A}+m_{B}$
- $p_{before}=p_{after}$
- $p_{A + m_{B} u_{B} = ( m_{A} + m_{B} } ) v$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange and calculate the combined velocity $v$:

- $v=\frac{p_{A}+m_{B}u_{B}}{m_{AB}}$

- $v = \frac{( 2.00 \times 10^{17} ) + [ ( 6.40 \times 10^{12} ) \times ( 14.0 \times 10^{3} ) ] }{( 5.54 \times 10^{13} ) + ( 6.40 \times 10^{12} )}$ **[1 mark]**
- $v$ = 4686 = 4.69 km s<sup>−1</sup> (3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(a)(ii) Show that the mass of asteroid A was about 5.5 × 10^13 kg: Velocity of A = 3.61 km s^−1 = 3.61 × 10^3 m s^−1; Momentum of A = 2.00 × 10^17 kg m s^−1; m_A = (2.00 × 10^17)/(3.61 × 10^3) = 5.54 × 10^13 kg.

A short time later, the combined asteroid AB collides with a stationary asteroid C. Immediately following the collision, the asteroids are deflected by the angles shown in Fig. 1.2.

![Asteroid AB travels at 2.6 kilometres per second at an 8-degree angle to the initial direction of AB, and asteroid C travels at 6.5 kilometres per second at a 10-degree angle to the initial direction of AB.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/052-asteroid-ab-travels-at-2-6-kilometres-per-second.png)

Show that the mass of asteroid C is about 2.0 × 10<sup>13</sup> kg.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the mass of asteroid C is about 2.0 × 10<sup>13</sup> kg:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of asteroid AB, *m*<sub>AB</sub> = (6.4 × 10<sup>12</sup>) + (5.54 × 10<sup>13</sup>) = 6.18 × 10<sup>13</sup> kg
- Mass of asteroid C = *m*<sub>C</sub>
- Initial velocity of asteroid AB, *u*<sub>AB</sub> = 4.69 km s<sup>–1</sup> (from (b))
- Final velocity of asteroid AB, *v*<sub>AB</sub> = 2.6 km s<sup>–1</sup>
- Final velocity of asteroid C, *v*<sub>C</sub> = 6.5 km s<sup>–1</sup>
- Angle between AB and the horizontal, *θ*<sub>AB</sub> = 8°
- Angle between C and the horizontal, *θ*<sub>C</sub> = 10°

Calculate the initial momentum of the system:

- $p_{i}=m_{AB}v_{AB}$
- $p_{i} = ( 6.18 \times 10^{13} ) \times ( 4.69 \times 10^{3} )$
- $p_{i}$ = 2.896 × 10<sup>17</sup> kg m s<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

Calculate the final momentum of the system:

- $p_{f}=m_{AB}v_{AB}\mathrm{cos}θ_{AB}+m_{C}v_{C}\mathrm{cos}θ_{C}$
- $p_{f} = [ ( 6.18 \times 10^{13} ) \times ( 2.6 \times 10^{3} ) \times \cos 8^{\circ} ] + [ m_{C} \times ( 6.5 \times 10^{3} ) \times \cos 10^{\circ} ]$
- $p_{f} = ( 1.607 \times 10^{17} ) \cos 8^{\circ} + m_{C} ( 6.5 \times 10^{3} ) \cos 10^{\circ}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the conservation of momentum to calculate the mass of asteroid C:

- Total initial momentum = total final momentum, or $p_{i}=p_{f}$
- $2.896 \times 10^{17} = ( 1.607 \times 10^{17} ) \cos 8^{\circ} + m_{C} ( 6.5 \times 10^{3} ) \cos 10^{\circ}$
- $m_{C} = \frac{( 2.896 \times 10^{17} ) - ( 1.607 \times 10^{17} ) \cos 8^{\circ}}{( 6.5 \times 10^{3} ) \cos 10^{\circ}}$ = 2.04 × 10<sup>13</sup> kg **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Make sure you get lots of practice with momentum conservation in 2D scenarios; the extra step of resolving vector components can trip up many students!*

> *We only need to consider the **horizontal components** of the velocities of the asteroids:*

![Asteroid AB has a horizontal velocity of2.6 times 10 to the power of 3 times cos 8, and asteroid C has a horizontal velocity of 6.5 times 10 to the power of 3 times cos 10. ](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/053-asteroid-ab-has-a-horizontal-velocity-of2-6-time.png)

Initial velocity of asteroid AB, u_AB = 4.69 km s^−1.

parts.solutionMd:
Determine if the collision in **(c)** is elastic or inelastic:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of asteroid AB, *m*<sub>AB</sub> = (6.4 × 10<sup>12</sup>) + (5.54 × 10<sup>13</sup>) = 6.18 × 10<sup>13</sup> kg
- Mass of asteroid C, *m*<sub>C</sub> = 2.04 × 10<sup>13</sup> kg (from (c))
- Initial velocity of asteroid AB, *u*<sub>AB</sub> = 4.69 km s<sup>–1</sup> (from (b))
- Final velocity of asteroid AB, *v*<sub>AB</sub> = 2.6 km s<sup>–1</sup>
- Final velocity of asteroid C, *v*<sub>C</sub> = 6.5 km s<sup>–1</sup>

Calculate the initial kinetic energy of the system:

- $\mathrm{KE}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}m_{AB}u_{AB}^{2}$
- $KE_{i} = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times ( 6.18 \times 10^{13} ) \times ( 4.69 \times 10^{3} )^{2}$
- $\mathrm{KE}_{i}$ = 6.8 × 10<sup>20</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the final kinetic energy of the system:

- $\mathrm{KE}_{f}=\frac{1}{2}m_{AB}v_{AB}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}m_{C}v_{C}^{2}$
- $KE_{f} = [ 1 \frac{1}{2} \times ( 6.18 \times 10^{13} ) \times ( 2.6 \times 10^{3} )^{2} ] + [ 1 \frac{1}{2} \times ( 2.04 \times 10^{13} ) \times ( 6.5 \times 10^{3} )^{2} ]$
- $\mathrm{KE}_{f}$ = 6.4 × 10<sup>20</sup> J **[1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- An inelastic collision is one where kinetic energy is not conserved
- Since $\mathrm{KE}_{i}>\mathrm{KE}_{f}$, energy has dissipated, so the collision is inelastic; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Ball X has a mass of 50 g and is supported by a long string, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![cie-ial-3-2-q4a-conservation-of-momentum-ball-and-wall](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/046-cie-ial-3-2-q4a-conservation-of-momentum-ball-an.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The ball is pulled back and released. The ball collides normally with a flat surface at a velocity of 4.5 m s<sup>−1</sup> and rebounds elastically.

The positive direction is horizontal and to the right.

Determine the total change in momentum of ball X.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the total change in momentum of the ball:

In an elastic collision:

- KE before = KE after
- Therefore, initial velocity = final velocity (= 4.5 m s<sup>−1</sup>) **[1 mark]**

The change in momentum is:

- Momentum before = $mv$
- Momentum after = $-mv$
- Change in momentum:  $\Delta p = ( - m v ) - m v = - 2 m v$
- Change in momentum:  $\Deltap$ = -2 × (50 × 10<sup>−3</sup>) × 4.5 = -0.45 kg m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

**Extract:**

Ball X is hung next to ball Y which is supported by a string of the same length, as shown in Fig. 1.2.

**Fig. 1.2**

Ball Y has a mass of 125 g.

The balls are each pulled back and pushed towards each other. When the balls collide, the strings are vertical. The balls rebound in opposite directions.

The velocities of X and Y just before and just after the collision are shown in Fig. 1.2.

Use the conservation of linear momentum to determine the rebound velocity $v$ of Y.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the conservation of linear momentum to determine the rebound velocity of Y.

List the known quantities:

- Mass of X, $m_{X}$ = 50 g
- Mass of Y, $m_{Y}$ = 125 g
- Initial velocity of X, $u_{X}$ = 4.5 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Final velocity of X, $v_{X}$ = −2.8 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Initial velocity of Y, $u_{Y}$ = −2.2 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Final velocity of Y, $v_{Y}=v$

The momenta before and after the collision:

- Momentum before = $m_{X}u_{X}+m_{Y}u_{Y}$
- Momentum before = (50 × 4.5) + (125 × −2.2) **[1 mark]**
- Momentum after = $m_{X}v_{X}+m_{Y}v_{Y}$
- Momentum after = (50 × −2.8) + (125 × $v$) **[1 mark]**

Conservation of linear momentum:

- Momentum before = momentum after:  $m_{X}u_{X}+m_{Y}u_{Y}=m_{X}v_{X}+m_{Y}v_{Y}$
- (50 × 4.5) + (125 × −2.2) = (50 × −2.8) + (125 × $v$)
- 225 − 275 = −140 + 125$v$$\Rightarrow125v=90$
- Rebound velocity of Y:  $v=\frac{90}{125}=0.72=0.7ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In this question, you do not need to convert the mass of the balls to kg. Both balls have their mass in grams and when divided in g or kg the ratio will be the same. *

- Initial velocity of Y, $u_{Y}$ = −2.2 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Final velocity of Y, $v_{Y}$ = 0.7 m s<sup>−1</sup> (from (b))

An elastic collision is...

Write a conclusion:

  - Relative speed of approach: $u_{X}-u_{Y}$ = 4.5 − (−2.2) = 6.7 m s<sup>−1</sup>

parts.solutionMd:
Use Newton’s laws to explain why the magnitude of the change in momentum of each ball is the same

Newton's third law states...

- When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other
- Therefore, the force on X is equal (in magnitude) and opposite (in direction) to the force on Y; **[1 mark]**

Newton's second law states...

- The resultant force on an object is equal to the rate of change of momentum (i.e. Δp/Δt) of the object, and it acts in the same direction, or F = Δp/Δt
- Therefore, the force (on X & Y) is equal to / proportional to the rate of change of momentum; **[1 mark]**

The change in momentum of X & Y is the same because...

- The time of collision is the same for both balls (hence change in momentum is the same); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The bullet has a momentum of 9.8 kg m s<sup>−1</sup> just before it hits a target.

It takes 4.5 ms for the bullet to be stopped by the target.

Calculate the average force needed to stop the bullet.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the average force needed to stop the bullet

List the known quantities:

- Momentum of bullet before hitting target, *p*<sub>*s*</sub> = 9.8 kg m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Time taken for bullet to stop, Δ*t* = 4.5 ms = 4.5 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s

Determine the change in momentum Δp as the bullet is stopped by target:

- The bullet comes to rest, therefore final momentum = 0
- Change in momentum:  Δ*p* = 9.8 kg m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

Calculate the average force *F* needed to stop the bullet:

- Force & momentum:  $F=\frac{\Deltap}{\Deltat}$
- Average force:  $F=\frac{9.8}{4.5\times10^{-3}}$  **[1 mark]**
- Average force:  $F = 2177.8 = 2200 \mathrm{N} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**** **

> *Calculations like this one are usually given what examiners call 'error carried forward' (you will see it written 'ecf' in mark schemes).*

> *This means that, for example, if you forgot to convert ms to s (using 4.5 s rather than 0.0045) then you could still get the other three marks, as long as your final answer was 2200 N.*

> *However, if you did get this then your 'sanity check' at the end should have seen you looking at this number and realising it must be wrong, since it suggests that being shot by a rifle feels similar to having someone pat you lightly on the back!*

Two spheres, A and B, are moving in a straight line on a smooth horizontal surface. Sphere A has a mass of 0.30 kg and a velocity of 5.0 m s<sup>−1</sup>. Sphere B has a mass of 0.20 kg and a velocity of 2.0 m s<sup>−1</sup>. Both spheres move in the same direction, as shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Two spheres move to the right before and after a collision. Before: sphere A has mass 0.30 kilograms and velocity 5 metres per second; sphere B has mass 0.20 kilograms and velocity 2 m/s metres per second. After: A has velocity 2.6 metres per second and B has velocity v.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/033-two-spheres-move-to-the-right-before-and-after-a.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Sphere A collides with sphere B. After the collision, sphere A continues to move in the same direction with a velocity of 2.6 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

(i) Calculate the velocity $v$ of sphere B after the collision.

[2]

(ii) By calculation of kinetic energies, state and explain whether the collision of the spheres is inelastic or perfectly elastic.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the velocity $v$ of sphere B after the collision:

- List the known quantities:

  - Mass of A, $m_{A}$ = 0.30 kg
  - Mass of B, $m_{B}$ = 0.20 kg
  - Initial velocity of A, $u_{A}$ = 5.0 m s<sup>−1</sup>
  - Initial velocity of B, $u_{B}$ = 2.0 m s<sup>−1</sup>
  - Final velocity of A, $v_{A}$ = 2.6 m s<sup>−1</sup>
  - Final velocity of B, $v_{B}$ = $v$
- Determine the momentum of the spheres before and after the collision

$p=mv$

Total momentum before = $m_{A}u_{A}+m_{B}u_{B}$

Total momentum before = $( 0.30 \times 5.0 ) + ( 0.20 \times 2.0 )$

Total momentum after = $m_{A}v_{A}+m_{B}v_{B}$

Total momentum after = $( 0.30 \times 2.6 ) + ( 0.20 \times v )$ **[1 mark]**

- Apply conservation of momentum and calculate $v$:

Total momentum before = total momentum after

$( 0.30 \times 5.0 ) + ( 0.20 \times 2.0 ) = ( 0.30 \times 2.6 ) + ( 0.20 \times v )$

$v = \frac{( 0.30 \times 5.0 ) + ( 0.20 \times 2.0 ) - ( 0.30 \times 2.6 )}{0.20}$

$v=$ $5.6ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) To determine whether the collision of the spheres is inelastic or perfectly elastic:

- Calculate the initial kinetic energy of the spheres

$E_{K}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$

initial $E_{K} = ( 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 0.30 \times 5.0^{2} ) + ( 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 0.20 \times 2.0^{2} )$

initial $E_{K}=4.15J$

- Calculate the final kinetic energy of the spheres

final $E_{K} = ( 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 0.30 \times 2.6^{2} ) + ( 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 0.20 \times 5.6^{2} )$

final $E_{K}=4.15J$ **[1 mark]**

- Write a concluding statement

**Since initial **$E_{K}$** = final **$E_{K}$**, the collision is ****elastic** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for either value of initial $E_{K}$**OR** final $E_{K}$ correct
> 
> 1 mark for the values of initial $E_{K}$ and final $E_{K}$ both correct **AND** evidence that the collision is inelastic

- Vertical momentum of B:  $p_{B}=\frac{1}{2}M\times3.6v\mathrm{cos}θ$ **[1 mark]**
- Vertical momentum of C:  $p_{C}=\frac{5}{2}M\times0.6v$ **[1 mark]**

Apply conservation of momentum in the vertical direction:

- Conservation of momentum:  total momentum before = total momentum after

  - Total momentum before = 0
  - Total momentum after = $p_{A}+p_{B}-p_{C}$

- $p_{A}+p_{B}-p_{C}=0$
- $p_{A}+p_{B}=p_{C}$
- $\frac{3}{2}M\times1.2v\mathrm{cos}θ+\frac{1}{2}M\times3.6v\mathrm{cos}θ=\frac{5}{2}M\times0.6v$ **[1 mark]**

Simplify and calculate $θ$:

- $( \frac{3}{2} \times 1.2 + 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 3.6 ) \cos \\theta = \frac{5}{2} \times 0.6$
- $\mathrm{cos}θ=\frac{1.5}{3.6}$
- $θ$ = 65.38 = 65° **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Another stationary firework explodes into four fragments which travel in different directions in a horizontal plane.

Fig. 1.2 shows the velocity and mass of each fragment.

**Fig. 1.2**

Apply the principle of conservation of momentum to determine

(i) the velocity $v_{2}$

[2]

(ii) the mass $m_{3}$

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Fragment (1): mass $m_{1}$ = 20 g, velocity $v_{1}$ = 260 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Fragment (2): mass $m_{2}$ = 12 g, velocity = $v_{2}$
- Fragment (3): mass = $m_{3}$, velocity $v_{3}$ = 200 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Fragment (4): mass $m_{4}$ = 32 g, velocity $v_{4}$ = 300 m s<sup>−1</sup>

(i) Determine the velocity of fragment (2):

- Momentum of (4):  $p_{4}=m_{4}v_{4}=32\times300$
- Momentum of (2):  $p_{2}=m_{2}v_{2}=12\timesv_{2}$

Apply conservation of momentum:

- Conservation of momentum (taking $p_{2}$ as the positive direction):  $0=p_{2}-p_{4}\Rightarrowp_{2}=p_{4}$
- $12\timesv_{2}=32\times300$ **[1 mark]**
- $v_{2}=\frac{32\times300}{12}=800ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Determine the mass of fragment (3):

- Momentum of (1):  $p_{1}=m_{1}v_{1}=20\times260$
- Momentum of (3):  $p_{3}=m_{3}v_{3}=m_{3}\times200$

Apply conservation of momentum:

- Conservation of momentum (taking $p_{1}$ as the positive direction):  $0=p_{1}-p_{3}\Rightarrowp_{1}=p_{3}$

- $20\times260=m_{3}\times200$ **[1 mark]**
- $m_{3}=\frac{20\times260}{200}=26g$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *This kind of explosion question can look daunting at first, but taking some time to understand what is going on reveals the problem can be simplified by isolating the fragments and focusing on each line of action one at a time*

> *Since the fragments all move at 90° to one another, you can consider the directions independently, similar to taking 'horizontal' and 'vertical' components in other vector problems. Once you realise this, then you can see that the fragments on the same line have **equal momenta*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A stationary firework explodes into three different fragments that move in a horizontal plane. Fig. 1.1. shows the masses and velocities of the fragments A, B and C in terms of M and v. Fragment A: mass = 3/2 M, velocity = 1.2v. Fragment C: mass = 5/2 M, velocity = 0.6v. From part (a), the speed of fragment B is vB = 3.6v (mass = 1/2 M).

From part (b), the angle θ = 65°.

Another stationary firework explodes into four fragments which travel in different directions in a horizontal plane. Fig. 1.2 shows the velocity and mass of each fragment. Fragment (1): mass = 20 g, velocity = 260 m s^−1; Fragment (2): mass = 12 g, velocity = 800 m s^−1; Fragment (3): mass = 26 g, velocity = 200 m s^−1; Fragment (4): mass = 32 g, velocity = 300 m s^−1.

Both fireworks have the same initial mass and release the same amount of kinetic energy.

Calculate

(i) the value of *M*

[1]

(ii) the magnitude of *v*.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Fragment (A):  mass = $\frac{3}{2}M$, velocity = $1.2v$
- Fragment (B):  mass = $\frac{1}{2}M$, velocity = $3.6v$
- Fragment (C):  mass = $\frac{5}{2}M$, velocity = $0.6v$
- Fragment (1):  mass = 20 g, velocity = 260 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Fragment (2):  mass = 12 g, velocity = 800 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Fragment (3):  mass = 26 g, velocity = 200 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Fragment (4):  mass = 32 g, velocity = 300 m s<sup>−1</sup>

(i) Calculate the value of *M*:

- Sum of the masses (from **(b)**) = $\frac{3}{2}M+\frac{1}{2}M+\frac{5}{2}M=\frac{9}{2}M$
- Sum of the masses (from **(c)**) = 20 + 12 + 26 + 32 = 90 g
- Therefore, $\frac{9}{2}M=90g\RightarrowM=\frac{90}{4.5}=20g$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the magnitude of *v*:

Total kinetic energy of fragments A, B and C:

- $E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} M v^{2} [ ( \frac{3}{2} \times 1.2^{2} ) + ( 1 \frac{1}{2} \times 3.6^{2} ) + ( \frac{5}{2} \times 0.6^{2} ) ]$
- $E_{k}=4.77Mv^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Total kinetic energy of fragments 1, 2, 3 and 4:

- $E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} [ ( 0.020 \times 260^{2} ) + ( 0.012 \times 800^{2} ) + ( 0.026 \times 200^{2} ) + ( 0.032 \times 300^{2} ) ]$
- $E_{k}=6476J$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the value of v:

- Total KE:  $4.77Mv^{2}=6476$
- $v=\sqrt{\frac{6476}{4.77\times0.020}}$
- $v=261=260ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The key is in the question:*

- *both fireworks have the **same initial mass*

> *This means the total mass of fragments A, B and C is equal to the total mass of fragments 1, 2, 3 and 4*

- *both fireworks release the **same amount of kinetic energy*

> *This means the total KE of fragments A, B and C is equal to the total KE of fragments 1, 2, 3 and 4*

> *To get the total KE of fragments A, B and C, start by writing the kinetic energy of each in terms of M and v and then simplify:*

$E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} ( \frac{3}{2} M \times ( 1.2 v )^{2} ) + 1 \frac{1}{2} ( 1 \frac{1}{2} M \times ( 3.6 v )^{2} ) + 1 \frac{1}{2} ( \frac{5}{2} M \times ( 0.6 v )^{2} )$

$E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} M v^{2} [ ( \frac{3}{2} \times ( 1.2 )^{2} ) + ( 1 \frac{1}{2} \times ( 3.6 )^{2} ) + ( \frac{5}{2} \times ( 0.6 )^{2} ) ]$

$E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} M v^{2} \times ( 9.54 ) = 4.77 M v^{2}$

parts.problemMd:
A pellet of mass 2.7 g is fired into a stationary block of mass 540 g suspended from a rigid support as shown in Fig. 1.1.

The pellet becomes completely embedded in the block. The block can swing freely at the end of a light inextensible string of length 1.5 m measured from the pivot to the centre of the block.

![qu-5b-figure-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/048-qu-5b-figure-2.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The centre of mass of the block rises by a height *h* at an angle of 35° to the vertical.

Determine the velocity of the pellet and the block immediately after the pellet is embedded.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the velocity of the pellet and the block immediately after the pellet is embedded:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of pellet = 2.7 g
- Mass of block<sub> </sub>= 540 g
- Combined mass, $M$ = 540 + 2.7 = 542.7 g
- Angle between string and vertical, *θ *= 35°
- Length of string, *L *= 1.5 m

Calculate the change in height, *h*:

![qu-5b-mark-scheme](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/049-qu-5b-mark-scheme.png)

- From the diagram: $L=L\mathrm{cos}θ+h\Rightarrowh=L-L\mathrm{cos}θ$
- $h=1.5-1.5\mathrm{cos}35^{\circ}=0.271m$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the initial speed of the block and the pellet:

- From conservation of energy:  Initial KE = final GPE
- Initial KE = $\frac{1}{2}Mu^{2}$ **AND** final GPE = $Mgh$ **[1 mark]**
- Equate and rearrange:  $\frac{1}{2}Mu^{2}=Mgh\Rightarrowu=\sqrt{2gh}$
- Substitute:  $u=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.271}$ **[1 mark]**
- Initial speed of pellet and block:  $u$ = 2.306 = 2.3 m s<sup>−1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *This type of question is known as a ‘ballistic pendulum’ and the marks are given for the method, as well as the final answer, so make sure you set out your working clearly!*

> *The ‘initial kinetic energy’ is treated as when the pellet first strikes and completely embeds itself in the block. Therefore, the mass is always the **sum** of the mass of the pellet and block. *

> *You can see that when you equate KE and GPE algebraically, the mass term cancels, so if you're confident doing this, it will definitely save you some time when doing the calculation step!*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A pellet of mass 2.7 g is fired into a stationary block of mass 540 g suspended from a rigid support as shown in Fig. 1.1. The pellet becomes completely embedded in the block. The block can swing freely at the end of a light inextensible string of length 1.5 m measured from the pivot to the centre of the block. The centre of mass of the block rises by a height h at an angle of 35° to the vertical. Determine the velocity of the pellet and the block immediately after the pellet is embedded.
Initial speed of pellet and block: u = 2.306 = 2.3 m s^−1 (from (a))

Calculate the velocity of the pellet just before it strikes the block.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the velocity of the pellet just before it strikes the block:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of the pellet, $m_{p}$ = 2.7 g = 0.0027 kg
- Mass of the block, $m_{b}$ = 540 g = 0.540 kg
- Combined mass, $M$ = 542.7 g = 0.5427 kg
- Initial velocity of pellet and block, $u$ = 2.306 m s<sup>−1</sup> (from **(a)**)

Apply the principle of conservation of momentum:

- Total momentum lost by pellet = total momentum gained by pellet and block
- Total momentum lost by pellet = $m_{p}v_{p}$
- Total momentum gained by pellet and block = $( m_{p} + m_{b} ) u = M u$
- $m_{p} v_{p} = ( m_{p} + m_{b} ) u \Leftrightarrow m_{p} v_{p} = M u$ **[1 mark]**
- $v_{p}=\frac{Mu}{m_{p}}=\frac{0.5427\times2.306}{0.0027}$ **[1 mark]**
- $v_{p}$ = 463.506 = 464 m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A popular demonstration of the conservation of momentum and conservation of energy is Newton’s cradle. It features several identical polished steel balls hung in a straight line in contact with each other, as shown in Fig. 1.2.

If one ball is pulled back and allowed to strike the line, one ball is released from the other end whilst the rest are stationary. If two are pulled out, two are released on the other end and so forth.

![qu-5a-figure-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/050-qu-5a-figure-1.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Explain why swinging one ball from the left will not release two balls on the right.

Assume that the demonstration takes place in a vacuum.
parts.solutionMd:
Swinging one ball from the left will not release two balls on the right because:

- This would violate the conservation of energy / energy will not be conserved; **OR**
- It is an inelastic collision but should be elastic (in a vacuum); **[1 mark]**

Apply conservation of momentum:

- Conservation of momentum:  total momentum before = total momentum after
- Total momentum before = *mu*
- Total momentum after = 2*mv*
- Conservation of momentum:  $mu=2mv\Rightarrowv=\frac{u}{2}$* ***[1 mark]**
- Therefore, conservation of momentum is not violated if the final speed of the two balls is <u>halved</u>; **[1 mark]**

Apply conservation of energy:

- In a vacuum, there is no energy lost to the surroundings
- Hence, elastic collision:  total kinetic energy before = total kinetic energy after
- Total kinetic energy before = $\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}$
- Total kinetic energy after = $1 \frac{1}{2} ( 2 m ) ( \frac{u}{2} )^{2} = 1 \frac{1}{4} m u^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, conservation of energy is violated as half the kinetic energy is lost; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A body of mass $M$ and moving with velocity $V$ explodes into three equal fragments each of mass $\frac{M}{3}$, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![3-2-3a-h-momentum-explosion-equal-fragments-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/3-dynamics/3-3-linear-momentum-and-its-conservation/assets/041-3-2-3a-h-momentum-explosion-equal-fragments-cie-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Fragment 2 continues to move along the horizontal plane with velocity $v_{2}$, while fragments 1 and 3 move off at an angle of 60° to the horizontal with velocities $v_{1}$ and $v_{3}$ respectively, as shown.

By applying the principle of conservation of momentum in the vertical plane, show that  $v_{1}=v_{3}$
parts.solutionMd:
Show that $v_{1}=v_{3}$ by considering momentum in the vertical plane:

- Vertical plane:  total momentum before = 0
- Vertical plane:  total momentum after = $( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{1} \sin 60^{\circ} - ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{3} \sin 60^{\circ}$ **[1 mark]**

Apply conservation of momentum:

- Conservation of momentum:  total momentum before = total momentum after
- $0 = ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{1} \sin 60^{\circ} - ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{3} \sin 60^{\circ}$
- Simplify:  $( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{1} \sin 60^{\circ} = ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{3} \sin 60^{\circ} \Leftrightarrow v_{1} = v_{3}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A body of mass \$\$M\$\$ and moving with velocity \$\$V\$\$ explodes into three equal fragments each of mass \$\$\frac{M}{3}\$\$, as shown in Fig. 1.1. Fragment 2 continues to move along the horizontal plane with velocity \$\$v_{2}\$\$, while fragments 1 and 3 move off at an angle of 60° to the horizontal with velocities \$\$v_{1}\$\$ and \$\$v_{3}\$\$ respectively, as shown. By applying the principle of conservation of momentum in the vertical plane, show that \$\$v_{1} = v_{3}\$\$

By applying conservation of momentum in the horizontal plane, show that  $3 V = ( v_{1} + v_{2} )$
parts.solutionMd:
Show that $3 V = ( v_{1} + v_{2} )$ by considering momentum in the horizontal plane:

- Horizontal plane:  total momentum before = $MV$
- Horizontal plane:  total momentum after = $( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{1} \cos 60^{\circ} + ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{2} + ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{3} \cos 60^{\circ}$ **[1 mark]**

Apply conservation of momentum:

- Conservation of momentum:  total momentum before = total momentum after
- $M V = ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{1} \cos 60^{\circ} + ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{2} + ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{3} \cos 60^{\circ}$
- Substitute $v_{1}=v_{3}$ in:  $M V = 2 \times ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{1} \cos 60^{\circ} + ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- Simplify:  $V = 2 \times ( 1 \frac{1}{3} ) v_{1} \cos 60^{\circ} + ( 1 \frac{1}{3} ) v_{2} \Leftrightarrow 3 V = ( v_{1} + v_{2} )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The full worked solution is shown below:*

$M V = ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{1} \cos 60^{\circ} + ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{2} + ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{3} \cos 60^{\circ}$

$V = 2 \times ( 1 \frac{1}{3} ) v_{1} \cos 60^{\circ} + ( 1 \frac{1}{3} ) v_{2}$

A body of mass \$\$M\$\$ and moving with velocity \$\$V\$\$ explodes into three equal fragments each of mass \$\$\frac{M}{3}\$\$, as shown in Fig. 1.1. parts.solutionMd:
Express velocities $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ in terms of $V$:

- Kinetic energy of mass *M*:  $KE_{i}=\frac{1}{2}MV^{2}$
- Kinetic energy of fragment 1:  $K E_{1} = 1 \frac{1}{2} ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{1}^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the expressions into the ratio:

- $\frac{KE_{1}}{KE_{i}}=\frac{4}{3}\RightarrowKE_{1}=\frac{4}{3}KE_{i}$
- $1 \frac{1}{2} ( \frac{M}{3} ) v_{1}^{2} = \frac{4}{3} ( 1 \frac{1}{2} M V^{2} )$ **[1 mark]**

Simplify to determine the velocity of fragment 1:

- $\frac{1}{3}v_{1}^{2}=\frac{4}{3}V^{2}\Rightarrowv_{1}^{2}=4V^{2}$
- Velocity of fragment 1:  $v_{1}=2V$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the velocity of fragment 2:

- $3V=v_{1}+v_{2}\Rightarrowv_{2}=3V-2V$
- Velocity of fragment 2:  $v_{2}=V$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
In the 1st century CE Greek-Egyptian engineer Hero of Alexandria described a simple steam engine, which was at least 100 years old when he wrote about it.

Now commonly called a Hero's engine, the machine is a steam turbine which can be made to rotate by boiling water in a sealed vessel beneath it. Two pipes channel the steam produced through nozzles which project outwards.

Fig. 1.1. shows Hero's engine in operation.

![4-1-3a-h-heros-engine-alamy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-1-turning-effects-of-forces/assets/031-4-1-3a-h-heros-engine-alamy.png)

**Fig. 1.1.**

Explain why the vessel rotates around its axis

i) by referring to energy stores and transfers.

[3]

ii) by referring to forces, naming any relevant laws.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
Explain why the vessel rotates around its axis:

i) by referring to energy stores and transfers:

**Final answer:** **Any ****three ****from:**

- Chemical energy store converted to thermal energy store as the fire burns; **[1 mark]**
- The water boils (undergoing) vaporisation / turns to steam; **[1 mark]**
- <u>Nozzles</u> create jets of <u>steam</u> which are <u>perpendicular</u> to the line between them; **[1 mark]**
- Thermal energy store transfers to kinetic energy; **[1 mark]**

ii) by referring to forces, naming any relevant laws:

**Final answer:** **Any ****three ****from:**

- The vessel exerts a force on the steam to eject it; **[1 mark]**
- According to Newton's third law, the steam exerts an equal and opposite reaction force on the nozzle / vessel; **[1 mark]**
- There is an unbalanced force on the vessel; **[1 mark]**
- According to Newton's second law / F = ma, the vessel accelerates; **[1 mark]**
- A force applied at a distance from the pivot produces torque; **[1 mark]**
- Two forces applied at equal distances from the pivot produce a <u>couple</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Torque (of a couple) = <u>one</u> of the forces × distance between the nozzles / force; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

A team of decorators set up a raised bench to allow them to reach the ceiling.

The bench consists of a plank which is resting in a horizontal position on two supports **B** and **C**. The plank is modelled as a uniform rod **AD** of length 2.7 m and mass 15 kg. The supports at **B** and **C** are 0.4 m from each end of the plank, as shown in Fig 1.1.

![4-1-1a-m-moments-decorators](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/046-4-1-1a-m-moments-decorators.png)

**Fig 1.1**

Two decorators, Ruby and Luke, stand on the plank. Luke has a mass of 85 kg and stands in the middle of the plank.

Ruby has a mass of 72 kg and stands at end **A**.

The plank remains horizontal and in equilibrium. The decorators can be modelled as point masses.

Calculate:

(i) The magnitude of the normal reaction force at **B**.

[3]

(ii) The magnitude of the normal reaction force at **C**.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass of Ruby, *M*<sub>R </sub>= 72 kg
- Mass of Luke, *M*<sub>L</sub> = 85 kg
- Mass of the plank, *M*<sub>P</sub> = 15 kg
- Length of plank, AD = 2.7 m
- Acceleration due to gravity, *g* = 9.81 m s<sup>–2</sup>

Sketch a simplified diagram showing measurements and point masses:

![screenshot-2023-03-09-at-09-21-34](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/047-screenshot-2023-03-09-at-09-21-34.png)

(i) Calculate the magnitude of the normal reaction force at **B**

Apply the principle of moments to take moments about point **C**:

- sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments
- $( R_{B} \times 1.9 ) = ( W_{R} \times ( 2.7 - 0.4 ) ) + ( W_{P} + W_{L} ) \times 0.95$ **[1 mark]**
- $R_{B} = \frac{( 72 g \times 2.3 ) + ( 100 g \times 0.95 )}{1.9}$ **[1 mark]**
- $R_{B} = 1346 = 1300 \mathrm{N} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the magnitude of the normal reaction force at **C**

Equate vertical forces:

- Since the plank is in equilibrium, the sum of upwards forces upwards = sum of forces downwards /** **$ΣF_{up}=ΣF_{down}$/** **$R_{B}+R_{C}=W_{R}+W_{L}+W_{P}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate normal reaction force at **C**:

- $R_{C} = ( W_{R} + W_{L} + W_{P} ) - R_{B}$
- $R_{C} = ( 72 g + 85 g + 15 g ) - 1346$ **[1 mark]**
- $R_{C} = 341 = 340 \mathrm{N} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *It's very common for students to think that creating their own diagrams is a waste of time since 'it doesn't get any marks'. *

> *It's true that the diagram isn't marked by the examiner directly, **but **it allows you to get the correct answer quickly, meaning you not only get these marks, but have **time** to answer the rest of the paper too!*

> *For part (ii) you may have decided to take moments again. Any correct method that gets a correct answer will score full marks in the exam. *

> *If you chose this method, your calculation should look like:*

- *Apply the principle of moments to take moments about point **B**:*

  - *sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments*
  - $( W_{P} + W_{L} ) \times 0.95 = ( R_{C} \times 1.9 ) + ( W_{R} \times 0.4 )$* [1 mark]*
  - $R_{C} = \frac{( 100 g \times 0.95 ) - ( 72 g \times 0.4 ) }{1.9}$* [1 mark]*
  - $R_{C} = 342 = 340 \mathrm{N} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$* [1 mark]*

parts.problemMd:
A pole **PR **has a length 6.0 m and a weight *W* N. The pole is held in a horizontal position in equilibrium by two vertical ropes attached to the pole as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![4-1-3a-m-pole-with-vertical-ropes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/038-4-1-3a-m-pole-with-vertical-ropes.png)

**Fig. 1.1.**

A load of weight 10 N is attached to the rod at **R**.

The tension in the rope attached at **Q** is six times as large as the tension in the rope attached at **P**.

The pole is uniform and the ropes are light inextensible strings.

Calculate the value of *W*.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the value of *W*

Write an expression for *T*<sub>P</sub> in terms of *T*<sub>Q</sub> :

- $T_{Q}=6T_{P}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the value of *W* by setting up simultaneous equations:

Apply the principle of moments around **P**:

![screenshot-2023-03-13-at-12-36-07](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/039-screenshot-2023-03-13-at-12-36-07.png)

- sum of the clockwise moments = sum of the anti-clockwise moments
- $3 W + ( 10 \times 6 ) = ( 4.1 \times 6 T_{P} )$
- $3W+60=24.6T_{P}$
- $T_{P}=\frac{3W+60}{24.6}$ *(equation 1)*** [1 mark] **

Apply the principle of moments around **Q**:

Sketch a diagram showing measurements and forces:

![screenshot-2023-03-13-at-12-29-02](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/040-screenshot-2023-03-13-at-12-29-02.png)

- sum of the clockwise moments = sum of the anti-clockwise moments
- $( 10 \times 1.9 ) + 4.1 T_{P} = 1.1 W$
- $4.1T_{P}=1.1W-19$
- $T_{P}=\frac{1.1W-19}{4.1}$ *(equation 2)*** [1 mark]**

Combine *equations 1* and* 2* to find *W*:

- $\frac{3W+60}{24.6}=T_{P}=\frac{1.1W-19}{4.1}$ **[1 mark]**
- $4.1 \times ( 3 W + 60 ) = 24.6 \times ( 1.1 W - 19 )$
- $12.3W+246=27.06W-467.4$
- $( 27.06 - 12.3 ) W = 246 + 467.4 \rightarrow 14.76 W = 713.4$
- $W = 48 \mathrm{N} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Without a clear sketch showing all the distances and forces, you have a **much** smaller chance of setting up the correct simultaneous equations, especially with the different distances. It also helps clearly see which forces are clockwise or anticlockwise depending on where you take moments from. *

> *Although the sketch doesn't earn marks directly, it is good practice for getting the calculation right.*

parts.problemMd:
A uniform plank of wood of mass 40 kg and length 5.0 m is used by a boy to help him cross a ditch.

In the ditch is a rock, which is used to support the plank horizontally 1.1 m from one end, as shown in Fig. 1.1. The other end of the plank is supported by the bank.** **

![4-2-s-q--q3b-medium-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/043-4-2-s-q-q3b-medium-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the vertical supporting force from the rock:

- The weight of 40 × *g* occurs at the centre of the (uniform) plank so *d* = ½ × 5.0
- Moment of plank from the bank = *mg* × *d*
- Moment of plank from the bank = (40 × *g*) × (½ × 5.0)
- Moment of plank from the bank = 40 × 9.81 × 2.5 = 981 N m **[1 mark]**

This moment is balanced by the reaction force from the rock

- Moment of plank from the rock = *F* × (5.0 – 1.1)
- Moment of plank from the rock = *F* × 3.9 **[1 mark]**

- Vertical force from rock:  $F=\frac{981}{3.9}$ = 251.5 = 250 N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

A uniform plank of wood of mass 40 kg and length 5.0 m is used by a boy to help him cross a ditch. In the ditch is a rock, which is used to support the plank horizontally 1.1 m from one end, as shown in Fig. 1.1. The other end of the plank is supported by the bank.

parts.solutionMd:
Determine whether the boy can walk to the far end of the plank without it tipping:

- (At the point of tipping) there is no (reaction) force from the bank; **[1 mark]** *This point must be in words, not implied from a calculation*
- So, moments on the RHS of the rock must be lower than moments on the LHS

**Supporting calculation 1:**

- Taking moments about the rock to show RHS < LHS; **[1 mark]**
- 540 N m < 550 N m, therefore, plank will not tilt; **[1 mark]** *Example of calculation:*

  - LHS = (2.5 – 1.1) × 40 × *g *= 56 × 9.81 = 549.36 = 550 N m
  - RHS = 1.1 × 50 × *g *= 55 × 9.81 = 539.6 = 540 N m

**OR   Supporting calculation 2:**

- Showing a moment calculation that gives the maximum boy’s weight / mass that can be supported on the far edge of the plank (500 N / 51 kg) **[1 mark]**
- 50 kg < 51 kg, therefore, plank will not tilt; **[1 mark]** *Example of calculation:*

  - Maximum weight = $\frac{40\times9.81\times1.4}{1.1}$ = 499 = 500 N (or 51 kg)

**OR   Supporting calculation 3:**

- Showing a moment calculation that gives the maximum distance the boy can be from the rock without tipping (1.12 m) **[1 mark]**
- 1.1 m < 1.12 m, therefore, plank will not tilt; **[1 mark]** *Example of calculation:*

  - Maximum distance = $\frac{40\times1.4}{50}$ = 1.12 m

**[Total: 3 marks]**

Calculate the minimum vertical force *T* required to start raising the front of the ship. Assume the ship pivots about point **P**.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the minimum vertical force *T*:

- Total clockwise moments (tension in rope) about P = *T *× 15
- Total anticlockwise moments (weight of the ship) about P = *W* × 6.0

![4-1-s-q--q5b-medium-cie-a-level-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/065-4-1-s-q-q5b-medium-cie-a-level-ma.png)

Use the principle of moments to find tension *T*:

- Total clockwise moments = Total anticlockwise moments
- *T *× 15 = (4.6 × 10<sup>4</sup>) × 6.0 **[1 mark]**
- $T = \frac{( 4.6 \times 10^{4} ) \times 6.0}{15}$ = 1.8 × 10<sup>4</sup> N **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
