Calculate the minimum vertical force *T* required to start raising the front of the ship. Assume the ship pivots about point **P**.
T = 1.8 × 10^4 N

Calculate the minimum force *F* that must be exerted to start to raise the front of the ship.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the minimum force *F*:

- Perpendicular component of *T *= *T* cos (21°) **[1 mark]**

The front of the ship will raise when...

- Total clockwise moments (pulling force *F*) > Total anticlockwise moments (perpendicular component of *T*)
- *F* × 7.5 > *T* cos (21°) × 3.0

![2BJMfWDd_4-1-s-q--q5c-medium-cie-a-level-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/066-2bjmfwdd-4-1-s-q-q5c-medium-cie-a-level-ma.png)

The minimum force required to raise the ship is...

- Total clockwise moments = Total anticlockwise moments
- *F* × 7.5 = *T* cos (21°) × 3.0 **[1 mark]**
- $F = \frac{( 1.8 \times 10^{4} ) \cos 21^{\circ} \times 3.0}{7.5}$* *= 6722 = 6700 N (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**** **

*Allow F = 7100 N if 1.9 × 10*<sup>*4*</sup>* used*** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

The beam's weight of 50 newtons acts at its centre and a cube of density 2800 kilograms per cubic metre hangs at 0.8 m from A.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/034-a-horizontal-beam-ab-of-length-2-40-metres-the-l.png)

**Fig. 2.1** (not to scale)

A cube of side length 0.075 m is suspended from the beam at a distance of 0.80 m from A. The cube is made from a material of density 2800 kg m<sup>−3</sup>.

The beam is in equilibrium. Assume that the hinge is frictionless.

(i) Show that the weight of the cube is about 12 N.

[2]

(ii) By taking moments about A, calculate the tension $T$ in the wire.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To show that the weight of the cube is about 12 N:

- List the known quantities

  - Side length of the cube, $l$ = 0.075 m
  - Density of the cube, $ρ$ = 2800 kg m<sup>−3</sup>
  - Acceleration of free fall, $g$ = 9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup>
- Calculate the volume of the cube:

$V=l^{3}$

$V=0.075^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

- Use the density equation to calculate the weight of the cube:

$ρ=\frac{m}{V}$

$W=mg=ρVg$

$W=2800\times0.075^{3}\times9.81$

$W=11.58...$

$W=$$12N$** **(2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

(ii) To calculate the tension $T$ in the wire:

- Identify the moments acting about A

Anticlockwise moment = $T\times2.40$

Clockwise moments = $( 50 \times 1.20 ) + ( 11.58 \times 0.80 )$ **[1 mark]**

- Apply the principle of moments and calculate $T$:

Since the beam is in equilibrium, anticlockwise moments = clockwise moments

$T \times 2.40 = ( 50 \times 1.20 ) + ( 11.58 \times 0.80 )$

$T = \frac{( 50 \times 1.20 ) + ( 11.58 \times 0.80 )}{2.40}$

$T=28.86...$

$T=$ $29N$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for $( T \times 2.40 )$ **OR**  $( 50 \times 1.20 )$ **OR**  $( 11.58 \times 0.80 )$
> 
> 1 mark for the correct application of the principle of moments to calculate $T$

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The dimensions of an older, 'Routemaster' bus are: Height = 4.38 m; Width = 2.44 m; Mass = 7.47 tons
Determine the height above the ground of the centre of mass of the bus when it is empty and normally parked: h = 1.22 × tan(50) = 1.5 m

To be considered safe to use on the road the bus must be safe when carrying passengers.

To test this the top deck is weighted with iron blocks or sandbags to the equivalent of 60 passengers, while the lower deck is left empty.

The average passenger is assumed to have a mass of 65 kg and their centres of mass can be considered to act at a height of 3.28 m above the road.

1 ton = 1000 kg

For this safety test

(i) Calculate the new height of the centre of mass of the bus above the road.

[2]

(ii) Suggest why the test is done with the top deck weighted to capacity and the bottom deck left empty.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the new height of the centre of mass of the bus:

Determine the total mass of the 'passengers' and the empty bus:

- Mass of 'passengers', $m_{p}=65\mathrm{kg}\times60\mathrm{passengers}=3900\mathrm{kg}$
- Mass of empty bus, $m_{b}=7.47\mathrm{tons}\times1000\mathrm{kg}=7470\mathrm{kg}$

Model the bus as a horizontal rod and take moments:

**Method 1: take moments around the new centre of mass and calculate:**

![screenshot-2023-03-27-at-08-43-34](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/069-screenshot-2023-03-27-at-08-43-34.png)

Set up simultaneous equations for *x* and *y*:

- In equilibrium, $7470g\timesx=3900g\timesy\rightarrow7470x=3900y$ (*equation 1*)
- Taking distance measurements, $1.5+x+y=3.28\rightarrowy=1.78-x$ (*equation 2*)

Substitute *equation 2* into *equation 1* and calculate:

- $7470x=3900y$
- $7470 x = 3900 \times ( 1.78 - x )$
- $7470x+3900x=6942$
- $x=0.61m$ **[1 mark]**

Add distances together to find the height of C above the road:

- new height, $h=1.5+0.61=2.11m$ **[1 mark]**

**Method 2: take moments about the road, assuming a combined mass, and calculate:**

![screenshot-2023-03-27-at-08-47-54](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/070-screenshot-2023-03-27-at-08-47-54.png)

Apply the principle of moments around **R**::

- In equilibrium, $( 7470 g \times 1.5 ) + ( 3900 g \times 3.28 ) = ( 7470 g + 3900 g ) \times X$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate:

- $( 11 205 \cancel{g} ) + ( 12 792 \cancel{g} ) = ( 11 370 \cancel{g} ) \times X$
- $X=2.11m$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Suggest why the test is done with the top deck weighted to capacity and the bottom deck left empty:

- This moves the centre of mass to the highest position / makes the bus the least stable it could be; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The dimensions of an older, 'Routemaster' bus are: Height = 4.38 m; Width = 2.44 m; Mass = 7.47 tons. Buses are tested for stability using a tilting platform; the angle the bus makes with the horizontal is gradually increased until the bus begins to topple.

To be considered safe the bus must be safe when carrying passengers. To test this the top deck is weighted to the equivalent of 60 passengers, while the lower deck is left empty. The average passenger is assumed to have a mass of 65 kg and their centres of mass act at a height of 3.28 m above the road. The new height of the centre of mass of the bus above the road = 2.11 m.

To pass the safety test the bus must be able to tilt to 28° when loaded as in part (c).

(i) Deduce whether the bus has passed the safety test.

[2]

(ii) The safety testers imagine that the bus had 60 passengers upstairs, no passengers downstairs and that **all **the passengers on the top deck stood up simultaneously. This would shift their centres of mass by a mean distance of 40 cm higher.

Explain whether this will make the bus fail its safety test.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Deduce whether the bus has passed the safety test:

Set up a triangle to calculate the angle using trigonometry:

![screenshot-2023-03-27-at-08-54-48](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/071-screenshot-2023-03-27-at-08-54-48.png)

- Angle inside triangle, $\\theta = \tan ^{- 1} ( \frac{2.11}{1.22} ) = 60^{\circ}$
- Angle between bus and road, $θ_{R}=90-60=30^{\circ}$ **[1 mark]**

Draw a conclusion:

- The bus <u>tilted to more than 28°</u> without tipping so <u>yes</u> it does pass the safety test; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Explain whether all the passengers upstairs standing will make the bus fail its safety test.:

Calculate new angle between bus and road by moving the centre of mass 40 cm higher:

- $\\theta = \tan ^{- 1} ( \frac{2.11 + 0.4}{1.22} ) = 64^{\circ}$
- New angle between bus and road, $θ_{R}=90-64=26^{\circ}$

Draw a conclusion:

- The bus <u>tilts to less than 28°</u> without tipping so <u>yes</u> it will fail the safety test; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *For the final part of the question you could have recalculated the new centre of mass due to the passengers standing up. However, for only one mark, there is probably a quicker way.*

> *By simply moving the centre of mass up by the full 40 cm (which is the maximum it could possibly shift) we still find that the bus fails the safety test, so the question has been answered without the need for further calculation.*

parts.problemMd:
A bench consists of a plank which is resting in a horizontal position on two supports B and C. The plank is modelled as a uniform rod AD of length 2.7 m and mass 20 kg. The supports at B and C are 0.5 m from each end of the plank, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![4-2-s-q--q3a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/054-4-2-s-q-q3a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Two animals sit on the plank. The rabbit has a mass of 2.5 kg and sits in the middle of the plank and the quail has a mass of 4.3 kg and sits at the end A. The plank remains horizontal and in equilibrium. The animals can be modelled as point masses.

Calculate:

(i) The magnitude of the normal reaction force at B

[2]

(ii) The magnitude of the normal reaction force at C

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass of rabbit, $m_{R}$= 2.5 kg
- Mass of quail, $m_{Q}$= 4.3 kg
- Mass of the plank, $m_{P}$= 20 kg
- Acceleration due to gravity, *g* = 9.81 m s<sup>–2</sup>

![4-2-s-q--q3a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/055-4-2-s-q-q3a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

(i) The magnitude of the normal reaction force at B

Take moments about point C:

- Principle of moments: Sum of anti–clockwise moments = sum of clockwise moments about a pivot
- Anti­–clockwise moments about C = ($( W_{Q} \times d_{Q} )$+ ( $W_{R}+W_{P}$ ) × $d_{P}$) where $d_{C}$ and $d_{P}$ are perpendicular distances from the pivot to the weight of the quail and the plank, respectively
- Clockwise moment about C = $R_{B}$× $d_{B}$

Calculate the normal reaction force at B, $R_{B}$:

- (4.3*g* × (2.7 – 0.5)) + ((2.5*g + *20*g*) × (0.85) = $R_{B}$× (0.85 + 0.85) **[1 mark]**
- 9.46*g* + 19.125*g* = $R_{B}$× 1.7
- $R_{B}$= $\frac{9.46g+19.125g}{1.7}$= 16.81*g* = 16.81 × 9.81 = 164.9 = 165 N **[1 mark]**

(ii) The magnitude of the normal reaction force at C

Equate vertical forces:

- Since the plank is in equilibrium, all the forces upwards = all forces downwards
- Forces upwards =$R_{B}$+ $R_{c}$
- Forces downwards = $W_{Q}$+ $W_{R}$ +$W_{P}$

Calculate normal reaction force at C, $R_{c}$:

- 16.81*g *+$R_{c}$ = 4.3*g* + 2.5*g *+ 20*g *= 26.8*g ***[1 mark]**
- $R_{c}$= 26.8*g* – 16.81*g* = 9.99*g* = 9.99 × 9.81 = 98.00 = 98 N (2 s. f.) **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

> *This question gives the masses of the animals instead of their weight. Whether you multiply by **g** to get the weight during the calculation or at the end is up to you. In some instances where there are a lot of calculations, it is easier to only multiply by **g **(to calculate their weight) at the very end to avoid numerical errors. *

> *Students often forget about the fact that the vertically upwards forces must also equal the vertically downwards forces for a system to be in equilibrium too. Therefore, you do not need to take moments again for part (ii).*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A bench consists of a plank which is resting in a horizontal position on two supports B and C. The plank is modelled as a uniform rod AD of length 2.7 m and mass 20 kg. The supports at B and C are 0.5 m from each end of the plank, as shown in Fig. 1.1. Two animals sit on the plank. The rabbit has a mass of 2.5 kg and sits in the middle of the plank and the quail has a mass of 4.3 kg and sits at the end A. The plank remains horizontal and in equilibrium. The animals can be modelled as point masses.

Whilst the quail stays at point A the rabbit now moves along the plank to point X.

Given that the plank remains horizontal and in equilibrium, and that the magnitude of the normal reaction force at B is now twice the magnitude of the normal reaction force at C, calculate the distance BX.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass of rabbit, $m_{R}$= 2.5 kg
- Mass of quail, $m_{Q}$= 4.3 kg
- Mass of the plank, $m_{P}$= 20 kg
- Acceleration due to gravity, *g* = 9.81 m s<sup>–2</sup>

![4-2-s-q--q3b-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/056-4-2-s-q-q3b-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

Equate vertical forces:

- Since the plank is in equilibrium, all the forces upwards = all forces downwards
- Forces upwards = $R_{B}$+ $R_{c}$= 2$R_{c}$+ $R_{c}$= 3$R_{c}$
- Forces downwards = $W_{Q}$+ $W_{R}$+ $W_{P}$

Calculate normal reaction force at C, $R_{c}$:

- 3$R_{c}$= 4.3*g* + 2.5*g *+ 20*g *= 26.8*g ***[1 mark]**
- $R_{c}$= $\frac{26.8g}{3}$= 8.933*g* (= 87.636 N) **[1 mark]**

Take moments about** **B:

- Anti–clockwise moments about B = ( $W_{Q}\timesd_{Q}$) + ( $R_{c}\timesd_{c}$ )
- Clockwise moments about B = ($W_{P}\timesd_{P}$ ) + ($W_{R}\timesd_{R}$)

Calculate distance BX, $d_{R}$:

- (4.3*g* × 0.5) + (8.933*g *× (0.85 + 0.85) = (20*g *× 0.85) + (2.5*g *× $d_{R}$) **[1 mark]**
- 2.15*g* + 15.1861*g* = 17*g* + (2.5*g *×$d_{R}$)
- $d_{R}$= BX** **= $\frac{2.15g+15.1861g-17g}{2.5g}$ = 0.13 m **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

> *Labelling all the forces and distances on the diagram in your exam is essential for moments questions. This helps calculate any missing distances. *

> *Whenever any point moves in a moments question, the reaction forces upwards will also change. Therefore, *$R_{c}$* and *$R_{B}$* are not the same as in part (a) for this part (b). *

> *The point where the pivot is taken from doesn’t actually matter (because the Principle of Moments will always be true, about any pivot), so you will still get the same final answer. However, since we do not know in this question (it is different to part (a)), then if we take moments about B then we do not need to worry about this force. The key is to take moments about a point where you don’t know the value of the force: this way, the unknown force will not appear in your moments equations (since **d** will be 0).*

parts.problemMd:
A pole PR has a length 4 m and a weight *W* newton. The pole is held in a horizontal position in equilibrium by two vertical ropes attached to the pole at the points P and R where PR = 4 m, as shown in Fig. 1.2.

![M7bW4f~v_4-2-s-q--q3c-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/057-m7bw4f-v-4-2-s-q-q3c-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

A load of weight 17 N is attached to the rod at R. The pole is uniform and the ropes are light inextensible strings.

Given that the tension in the rope attached to the pole at Q is seven times the tension in the rope attached to the pole at P, calculate the value of *W*.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Weight of load, *F* = 17 N
- Distance PR = 4 m
- Distance QR = 4 − 2.4 = 1.6 m
- $T_{Q}=7T_{P}$

![r5MDu_r3_4-2-s-q--q3c-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/058-r5mdu-r3-4-2-s-q-q3c-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

Equate vertical forces:

- Since the plank is in equilibrium, all the forces upwards = all forces downwards
- Forces upwards: $T_{P}$+ $T_{Q}$ = $T_{P}$ + 7$T_{P}$= 8$T_{P}$
- Forces downwards: *W* + *F*
- 8$T_{P}$= *W* + *F* = *W* + 17 **[1 mark]**

Determine the equation for the tension in the rope at P, $T_{P}$:

- Taking moments about point Q
- Anti­–clockwise moment about Q = (*W* × $d_{W}$ ) where $d_{W}$ is the distance of the weight *W* from Q
- Clockwise moments about Q = ($T_{P}$× $d_{P}$) + (*F *× $d_{F}$) where $d_{P}$ and $d_{F}$ are the distance of P and the force from the load *F* from Q respectively
- (*W* × (2.4 – 2)) = ($T_{P}$× 2.4) + (17 × 1.6)
- 0.4*W* = 2.4$T_{P}$+ 27.2 **[1 mark]**

Calculate the weight of the pole, *W*:

- 8$T_{P}$ = *W* + 17 and 0.4*W* = 2.4$T_{P}$+ 27.2
- $T_{P}$ = $\frac{W}{8}$+ 2.125
- 0.4*W* = 2.4($\frac{W}{8}$+ 2.125) + 27.2 = 0.3*W* + 5.1 + 27.2 ** [1 mark]**
- 0.1*W* = 32.3
- *W* = 323 N **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

> *Look out for simultaneous equations! This is where you can set up the same number of unique equations as there are unknown variables. In this question, there are two equations with two unknowns (**W** and *$T_{P}$*). *

> *If you’d like to refresh your maths skills on this topic, then check out the Save My Exams GCSE Maths revision notes on ‘Linear Simultaneous Equations’.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A pole PR has a length 4 m and a weight *W* newton. The pole is held in a horizontal position in equilibrium by two vertical ropes attached to the pole at the points P and R where PR = 4 m, as shown in Fig. 1.2. A load of weight 17 N is attached to the rod at R. The pole is uniform and the ropes are light inextensible strings. Given that the tension in the rope attached to the pole at Q is seven times the tension in the rope attached to the pole at P, calculate the value of *W*. [W = 323 N]

Q is now moved to a point further along the pole until the length QR is 0.8 m, as shown in Fig. 1.3. The pole still remains in equilibrium. The load of 17 N is now moved to a point *x*  metres from P. The beam remains in equilibrium in a horizontal position.

![4-2-s-q--q3d-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/059-4-2-s-q-q3d-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

Fig. 1.3

The rope at Q will break if its tension exceeds 212 N. The rope at P cannot break.

Find the range of possible positions on the beam where the load can be attached without the rope at Q breaking.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Weight of load, *F* = 17 N
- Distance PR = 4 m
- Distance QR = 0.8 m
- Distance PQ = 3.2 m
- Weight of the pole, *W* = 323 N (from part c)
- Max $T_{Q}$ = 212 N

![4-2-s-q--q3d-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-2-equilibrium-of-forces/assets/060-4-2-s-q-q3d-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

Determine equation for tension at Q, $T_{P}$:

- Take moments about P
- Anti­–clockwise moment about P =$T_{Q}$ × $d_{Q}$  where $d_{Q}$ is the distance of Q from P
- Clockwise moments about P = (*F* × $d_{F}$) + (*W *× $d_{W}$) where $d_{F}$ and $d_{W}$ are the distance of the force *F* and the weight *W* from P respectively
- $T_{Q}$ × 3.2 = 17*x *+ (323 × 2) **[1 mark]**
- 3.2 $T_{Q}$= 17*x *+ 646
- $T_{Q}$= 5.31*x* + 202 **[1 mark]**

Calculate the range of values for *x*:

- $T_{Q}$< 212 therefore, 5.31*x* + 202 < 212
- *x *< 1.88
- 0 < *x *< 1.88 m **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**** **

> *When you are asked for a ‘range’ of values, there is likely to be inequality. These are equations with the ‘less than’ (<) or ‘more than’ (>) symbols, and they can be rearranged exactly like regular equations. Just remember if you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the direction of the inequality sign switches! *

> *The details of the rearranging for the inequality are shown below:*

> *5.31**x** + 202 < 212*

> *Subtract 202 from both sides:*

> *5.31**x** < 10*

> *Divide both sides by 5.31:*

> *x** < 1.88 *

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(i) The equation for density is: ρ = m/V where ρ = density, m = mass and V = volume.

(ii) The equation for pressure is: P = F/A where P = pressure, F = force and A = area.

Fig. 1.1 shows a measuring cylinder containing a liquid with depth *h* and cross-sectional area *A.*

Using the equations you stated in (b) and (c), show that pressure at a point in the liquid is $\DeltaP=ρg\Deltah$

![4-2-1d-e-density-pressure](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-3-density-and-pressure/assets/034-4-2-1d-e-density-pressure.png)

**Fig. 1.1.**
parts.solutionMd:
Show that in a liquid the pressure at the depth h is found using $\DeltaP=ρg\Deltah$:

Write out all the equations which will be needed:

- Pressure:  $P=\frac{F}{A}$ *(equation 1)*
- At the depth *h,* the force is the **weight** of liquid at *h*:  $W=mg$ *(equation 2)*
- Density:  $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$ *(equation 3)*
- Volume of a cylinder, $V=Ah$ *(equation 4)*

Substitute *equation 3* into *equation 1* to get a new term for the weight:

- $W=ρVg$ **[1 mark]**

Replace the term *V* with the expression in *equation 4*:

- $W=ρAhg$ *(equation 5)*

Substitute equation 5 into equation 1 and cancel to complete the derivation:

- $P = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{\\rho \cancel{ \cancel{ \cancel{A} } } h g}{ \cancel{A} }$  **[1 mark]**
- $ΔP=ρgΔh$

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *When doing a derivation it's helpful to write down any relevant equations before you start.*

> *Also keep the equation you are deriving in front of you, so that you can see when you are getting close.*

> *Finally, practice!*

parts.problemMd:
The Galileo thermometer was invented in the 17th century and it is still popular today. The thermometer consists of a column of liquid containing roughly spherical, weighted, glass bulbs, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![4-2-3a-m-4-2-galileo-thermometer-cie-ial-sq](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-3-density-and-pressure/assets/030-4-2-3a-m-4-2-galileo-thermometer-cie-ial-sq.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The spheres move up or down in the column as the temperature changes.

At a certain temperature, one of the spheres begins to fall through the liquid at an increasing** **speed.

(i) State the property of the liquid that causes the spheres to move up or down as the temperature changes.

[1]

(ii) The sphere has a radius of 1.2 cm and once settled, it displaces a total mass of 7.3 g of the liquid.

Calculate the value of the property of the liquid named in **(a)(i)**.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The property of the liquid that changes with temperature is:

- Density; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the density of the liquid:

List the known quantities:

- Radius, *r* = 1.2 cm = 1.2 × 10<sup>–2</sup> m
- Mass of liquid displaced, *m* = 7.3 g = 7.3 × 10<sup>–3</sup> kg

Determine the volume of the sphere

- Volume of a sphere:  $V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$
- $V = \frac{4}{3} \mathrm{\pi } ( 1.2 \times 10^{- 2} )^{3}$ = 7.24 × 10<sup>–6</sup> m<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

Determine the density of the liquid:

- Density:  $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$
- $ρ=\frac{7.3\times10^{-3}}{7.24\times10^{-6}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $ρ$ = 1008.5 = 1010 kg m<sup>–3</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The basic principle of a Galileo thermometer is that the liquid in the column will become denser if the room temperature drops and less dense if the room temperature rises.*

> *As a result, the spheres, which have a fixed density, will float or sink depending on the temperature of the room:*

- *An object will **float** if it is **less dense** than the fluid i.e. the spheres will float when the **temperature is low*
- *An object will **sink** if it is **denser **than the fluid it is placed in i.e. the spheres will sink when the **temperature is high*

![galileo-thermo-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-3-density-and-pressure/assets/031-galileo-thermo-ma.png)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The sphere has a radius of 1.2 cm and once settled, it displaces a total mass of 7.3 g of the liquid.

Show that the upthrust on the sphere is about 0.07 N.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the upthrust on the sphere is about 0.07 N:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of liquid displaced, *m* = 7.3 g = 7.3 × 10<sup>–3</sup> kg
- Acceleration of free fall, *g* = 9.81 m s<sup>–2 </sup>

Calculate the upthrust:

- Upthrust = Weight of liquid displaced; **[1 mark]**
- Upthrust = *mg *= (7.3 × 10<sup>–3</sup>) × 9.81 = 7.16 × 10<sup>–2</sup> = 0.072 = 0.07 N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

The spheres in the column are identical but have different masses due to the counterweight attached to them.

parts.problemMd:
A submarine below the surface of the sea is stationary in a region where the density of the seawater is 1.03 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>.

The submarine has a volume of 5.83 × 10<sup>3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>.

Calculate the upthrust exerted on the submarine by the seawater.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the upthrust exerted on the submarine by the seawater:

List the known quantities:

- Volume of submarine, $V$ = 5.83 × 10<sup>3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>
- Density of seawater, $ρ$ = 1.03 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>
- Acceleration of free fall, *g* = 9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup>

Use Archimedes' principle equation to calculate upthrust:

- Upthrust:  $U=ρgV$ **[1 mark]**
- Upthrust:  $U = ( 1.03 \times 10^{3} ) \times 9.81 \times ( 5.83 \times 10^{3} )$
- Upthrust:  $U$ = 5.89 × 10<sup>7 </sup>N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A submarine below the surface of the sea is stationary in a region where the density of the seawater is 1.03 × 10^3 kg m^−3. The submarine has a volume of 5.83 × 10^3 m^3. Calculate the upthrust exerted on the submarine by the seawater. Upthrust: U = ρgV = (1.03 × 10^3) × 9.81 × (5.83 × 10^3) = 5.89 × 10^7 N

Explain why the mass of the submarine must be 6.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg.
parts.solutionMd:
The mass of the submarine must be 6.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg because:

- Weight (of the submarine) is equal to the upthrust; **[1 mark]**

Use a calculation to justify a mass of 6.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg:

**EITHER**

- Using weight:  $W=mg\Rightarrowm=\frac{W}{g}$
- Mass:  $m=\frac{5.89\times10^{7}}{9.81}$ = 6.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Using density:  $ρ=\frac{m}{V}\Rightarrowm=ρV$
- $m = ( 1.03 \times 10^{3} ) \times ( 5.83 \times 10^{3} )$** **= 6.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A submarine below the surface of the sea is stationary in a region where the density of the seawater is 1.03 × 10^3 kg m^−3. The submarine has a volume of 5.83 × 10^3 m^3.
Explain why the mass of the submarine must be 6.0 × 10^6 kg. (Weight of the submarine is equal to the upthrust.)

The submarine moves into a region of the sea where the water is less salty, and the density of the water reduces to 1.01 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup> .

Explain what would happen to the submarine as it moves into this region of lower density seawater.
parts.solutionMd:
As the submarine moves into a region of lower-density seawater:

- The upthrust (of the water on the submarine) will be <u>less</u> than the weight (of the submarine); **[1 mark]**
- Hence, a resultant force will act downwards on the submarine; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the submarine will (begin to) <u>sink</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A submarine below the surface of the sea is stationary in a region where the density of the seawater is 1.03 × 10^3 kg m^−3. The submarine has a volume of 5.83 × 10^3 m^3. [Upthrust = 5.89 × 10^7 N]
The submarine moves into a region of the sea where the water is less salty, and the density of the water reduces to 1.01 × 10^3 kg m^−3.

The submarine alters its weight by pumping water in or out of its internal tanks.

Determine the mass of water that the submarine should pump, in or out of its tanks, to maintain its depth below the surface of the sea.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the required change in mass of water needed to maintain its depth:

List the known quantities:

- Density of new water,$ρ$ = 1.01 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>
- Volume of submarine, $V$ = 5.83 × 10<sup>3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>
- Initial upthrust = 5.89 × 10<sup>7 </sup>N
- Acceleration of free fall, *g* = 9.81 m s<sup>−2</sup>

Calculate the new upthrust:

- Upthrust:  $U=ρgV$
- Upthrust:  $U = ( 1.01 \times 10^{3} ) \times 9.81 \times ( 5.83 \times 10^{3} ) = 5.78 \times 10^{7} \mathrm{N}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the net downward force to calculate the required mass to be lost:

- Resultant force:  $F = ( 5.89 \times 10^{7} ) - ( 5.78 \times 10^{7} ) = 1.14 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{N}$
- Required change in mass:  $m=\frac{W}{g}=\frac{1.14\times10^{6}}{9.81}=1.17\times10^{5}\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A hollow brass cylinder with closed ends is floating on the surface of the water.

The cylinder has a length of 4.0 cm and an external diameter of 2.1 cm as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![q15-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-3-density-and-pressure/assets/041-q15-wph11-01-jan-2022-edexcel-int-as-a-level-phy.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

63% of the volume of the cylinder is submerged. The cylinder contains negligible weight of air.

Explain why the brass cylinder floats.
parts.solutionMd:
The brass cylinder floats because:

**EITHER**

- There is an upthrust which is equal to the weight of water displaced; **[1 mark]**
- The upthrust is equal to the weight of the cylinder (when it’s partially submerged); **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- The (overall) density (of the cylinder) is less than the density of the water; **[1 mark]**
- The weight of water displaced is equal to the weight of the cylinder; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A hollow brass cylinder with closed ends is floating on the surface of the water. The cylinder has a length of 4.0 cm and an external diameter of 2.1 cm as shown in Fig. 1.1. 63% of the volume of the cylinder is submerged. The cylinder contains negligible weight of air.

The density of water is 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>.

Show that the mass of the cylinder is about 9 × 10<sup>−3</sup> kg.
parts.solutionMd:
Show that the mass of the cylinder is about 9 × 10<sup>−3</sup> kg:

List the known quantities:

- Diameter of cylinder = 2.1 cm = 2.1 × 10<sup>−2</sup> m
- Length of cylinder, $l$ = 4.0 cm = 4.0 × 10<sup>−2</sup> m
- Percentage of cylinder submerged = 63%
- Density of water = 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>

Determine the volume of the brass cylinder that is submerged:

- Volume of brass cylinder:  $V = π r^{2} l$
- $V = \mathrm{\pi } \times ( \frac{2.1 \times 10^{- 2} }{2} )^{2} \times ( 4.0 \times 10^{- 2} ) = 1.39 \times 10^{- 5} \mathrm{m}^{3}$ **[1 mark]**
- Volume that is submerged: $V_{s u b} = 0.63 \times ( 1.39 \times 10^{- 5} ) = 8.76 \times 10^{- 6} \mathrm{m}^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the mass of the cylinder:

- Mass of cylinder = mass of water displaced
- $ρ = \frac{m}{V} \Rightarrow m = ρ V$
- Mass of cylinder:  `m = \left(1 \times 10^{3}\right) \times \left(8 . 76 \times 10^{- 6}\right)` = 8.76 × 10<sup>−3</sup> kg **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A hollow brass cylinder with closed ends is floating on the surface of the water. The cylinder has a length of 4.0 cm and an external diameter of 2.1 cm. 63% of the volume of the cylinder is submerged. The cylinder contains negligible weight of air.

The density of water is 1.0 × 10^3 kg m^−3. The mass of the cylinder is about 9 × 10^−3 kg (8.76 × 10^−3 kg). Volume of brass cylinder V = π r^2 l = π × (2.1 × 10^−2 / 2)^2 × (4.0 × 10^−2) = 1.39 × 10^−5 m^3. Volume submerged = 0.63 × 1.39 × 10^−5 = 8.76 × 10^−6 m^3.

Deduce whether an identical hollow cylinder made of gold would also float.

Assume that the volume of gold is the same as the volume of brass.

- Density of gold = 19.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>
- Density of brass = 8.7 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
Deduce whether an identical hollow cylinder made of gold would also float:

List the known quantities:

- Density of gold = 19.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>
- Density of brass = 8.7 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>

Determine the equivalent volume of gold:

- Volume of gold = volume of brass
- Volume of brass that floats:  $V=\frac{m}{ρ}=\frac{8.76\times10^{-3}}{8.7\times10^{3}}$
- Equivalent volume of gold:  $V=1.01\times10^{-6}m^{3}$** [1 mark]**

Calculate the volume of water required to float the gold cylinder:

- Mass of gold cylinder:  $m=ρV$
- Mass of gold cylinder:  $m = ( 19.3 \times 10^{3} ) \times ( 1.01 \times 10^{- 6} ) = 0.0194 \text{kg}$ **[1 mark]**
- Minimum volume of water required to float cylinder:  $V=\frac{m}{ρ}$
- $V=\frac{0.0194}{1.00\times10^{3}}=1.94\times10^{-5}m^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

State a conclusion backed up by calculated values:

Minimum volume of water required to float cylinder = $1.94\times10^{-5}m^{3}$

Volume of gold cylinder = $1.39\times10^{-5}m^{3}$

- $1.94\times10^{-5}m^{3}>1.39\times10^{-5}m^{3}$, therefore the gold cylinder would sink; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

Maximum mass (or weight) of water that could be displaced = 0.014 kg (0.14 N)

Mass of the gold cylinder (or weight) = 0.019 kg (0.19 N)

- 0.019 kg  > 0.014 kg **or** 0.19 N > 0.14 N, therefore the gold cylinder would sink; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The Cartesian Diver is a popular science project which can be used to demonstrate physical concepts.

A 'diver' is made by bending a loop of drinking straw into a U-shape and then weighting it with modelling clay.

A large plastic bottle is filled with water, leaving a small volume of air at the top.

The diver is carefully added, so that some water enters it but the straw remains floating upright due to trapped air.

Finally the lid is tightly screwed back onto the bottle, making a sealed container.

The completed Cartesian Diver and the construction of the diver are shown in Fig. 1.1.

![4-2-1a-h-cartesian-diver-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-3-density-and-pressure/assets/023-4-2-1a-h-cartesian-diver-1.png)

**Fig. 1.1.**

When the sides of the bottle are squeezed and released in response the 'diver' moves up and down rapidly as illustrated by Fig. 1.2.

![4-2-1a-h--cartesian-diver-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-3-density-and-pressure/assets/024-4-2-1a-h-cartesian-diver-2.png)

**Fig. 1.2.**

Discuss the physics of the Cartesian Diver when the sides of the bottle are squeezed.

(i) Explain the observed motion of the 'diver'.

[5]

(ii) Predict which direction the diver moves in when the sides of the bottle are squeezed.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
Discuss the physics of the Cartesian Diver when the sides of the bottle are squeezed:

(i) Explain the observed motion of the 'diver':

**Final answer:** **Any ****five ****from:**

- The trapped air in the <u>bottle</u> compresses; **[1 mark]**
- Because gas is compressible (but water is not); **[1 mark]**
- The air pressure in the <u>bottle</u> increases; **[1 mark]**
- This increases the pressure everywhere; **[1 mark]**
- The bottle is a sealed unit / closed system; **[1 mark]**
- So, (the Increased pressure) compresses the air bubble in the diver; **[1 mark]**
- The density of the diver increases so it sinks; **[1 mark]**
- The volume of water displaced by the diver decreases; **[1 mark]**
- This reduces the upthrust on the diver; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Predict which direction the diver moves in when the sides of the bottle are squeezed:

- Downwards / sinks; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
To prevent the overloading and sinking of ships markings, known as load lines, are required on ships hulls since the Middle Ages.

As the ship is loaded it sinks lower in the water. Once the load line meets the waterline, the ship is deemed to be fully loaded.

In 1876 Samuel Plimsoll refined the load line to reflect the needs of increasingly international trading routes. Today the 'Plimsoll line' has markings to show safe loading levels in fresh, saltwater, and warm and cold temperatures.

The Plimsoll line markings on ships today are shown in Fig. 1.1. The expected labels, their meanings and indications of temperature are written below.

![4-2-2a-h-plimsoll-line-buoyancy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-3-density-and-pressure/assets/038-4-2-2a-h-plimsoll-line-buoyancy.png)

**Fig. 1.1.**

Explain why the ships sit lower in the water when they are fully loaded.
parts.solutionMd:
Explain why the ships sit lower in the water when they are fully loaded:

- (In equilibrium the) upthrust equals the weight of the ship (and its load); **[1 mark]**
- Upthrust is (defined as / calculated from the) weight of displaced water; **[1 mark]**
- When weight increases, required upthrust increases;** [1 mark]**
- More water has to be displaced; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
In a simple classroom demonstration of the principle behind the Plimsoll Line, a teacher places an egg in a beaker of distilled water at close to 0°C.

The egg sinks to the bottom of the beaker as shown in Fig. 1.2.

![4-2-2c-h-egg-in-water-buoyancy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-3-density-and-pressure/assets/040-4-2-2c-h-egg-in-water-buoyancy.png)

**Fig. 1.2.**

Suggest and comment on the likely next steps in this demonstration.
parts.solutionMd:
Suggest and comment on the likely next steps in this demonstration:

**Steps must be in this order:**

- Add salt / sugar to make water more dense **AND **the egg will move upwards; **[1 mark]** **THEN**
- (After the egg has risen) heat the water to make it less dense **AND **the egg will move downwards / sink; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *This question is harder than it looks!*

> *The egg starts sitting on the bottom of the beaker. For the classroom demonstration to work the students must see something happen. In other words, the egg must first move upwards. Only then it can be made to move back down.*

> *Starting with a step which would make the egg sink wouldn't work because observers wouldn't see anything happening.*

> *Since the water is already ice cold only one method can be used to increase density. And you can't take the salt back out once it is dissolved, so the only way to reduce density is to heat the water.*

parts.problemMd:
Hot air balloons consist of an envelope with an open mouth through which air can be heated using a burner. The air inside becomes much hotter than its surroundings. Lifted by this method, the balloon can carry a large amount of weight across very long distances.

A very large capacity balloon, as shown in Fig. 1.1. can carry 25-30 people.

![4-2-3a--h-hot-air-balloon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-3-density-and-pressure/assets/035-4-2-3a-h-hot-air-balloon.png)

**Fig. 1.1.**

The envelope has a diameter at its widest point of of 32 m when it is filled with air. The total mass of the balloon, air, equipment and passengers is 20 900 kg. When the air temperature is 15 °C the density of the air outside the balloon is 1.225 kg m<sup>−3</sup>.

When the air inside the envelope is hot enough, the balloon is released.

(i) Calculate the resultant upwards force on the balloon.

[3]

(ii) Calculate the initial upwards acceleration of the balloon.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
When the air inside the envelope is hot enough, the balloon is released:

(i) Calculate the resultant upwards force on the balloon:

Determine the volume of the fully inflated balloon:

- $V = \frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3} = \frac{4}{3} \pi ( \frac{d}{2} )^{3} = \frac{4}{3} \pi \times 16^{3} = 17 157 \mathrm{m}^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

Use a sketch to identify the forces:

![hot air balloon MA](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/4-forces-density-and-pressure/4-3-density-and-pressure/assets/036-hot-air-balloon-ma.png)

Calculate upthrust:

- $U=ρVg=1.225\times17157\times9.81=206177N$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate weight and subtract from upthrust to find the resultant force:

- $W=mg=20900\times9.81=205029N$ **[1 mark]**
- $R=U-W=206177-205029=1148N$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the initial upwards acceleration of the balloon:

Apply Newton's Second Law:

- $F=ma$
- $a=\frac{R}{m}=\frac{1148}{20900}=0.055ms^{-2}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:
State whether the child or the adult is more efficient at moving the suitcase, explaining your reasoning:

- The child is more efficient: **[1 mark]**

> 
> Both exert 20 N over 2.5 m = 50 J total input each.
> 
> The child pushes horizontally on a smooth floor, so all 50 J is useful (efficiency = 100%). The adult pulls at 70°, so only F cos70 × s = 17 J is useful horizontal work (efficiency = 17/50 = 34%).

> Therefore, the child is more efficient.

Calculate the rate of work done moving the bag:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of the bag, *m* = 64 kg
- Time, *t* = 0.1 minutes = 0.1 × 60 = 6 s

Determine the work done against gravity:

![5-1-pythagoras-work-done-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/5-work-energy-and-power/5-1-energy-conservation/assets/018-5-1-pythagoras-work-done-ma.png)

- Vertical height lifted:  $\Delta h = \sqrt{( 2.25 )^{2} - ( 1.25 )^{2}} = 1.871 \mathrm{m}$ **[1 mark]**
- Work done against gravity (GPE):  $W=mg\Deltah$
- $W=64\times9.81\times1.871=1175J$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the rate of work done using the power equation:

- Rate of work done (power):  $P=\frac{E}{t}=\frac{1175}{6}$
- $P=196=200W$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Notice that the question asks for the 'rate of doing work' which is the definition of power, hence the final unit being the watt (W). The units W and J s*<sup>*−1*</sup>* are equivalent, so you can use either.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A crane is used to lift the bag from the ground onto the loading area of a truck. The mass of the bag is 64 kg. The crane takes 0.1 minutes to lift the bag from the ground to the loading area of the truck. Calculate the rate of work done by the crane when moving the bag.
Mark scheme: Vertical height lifted: Δh = √((2.25)² − (1.25)²) = 1.871 m. Work done against gravity (GPE): W = mgΔh = 64 × 9.81 × 1.871 = 1175 J. Rate of work done (power): P = E/t = 1175/6 = 196 = 200 W (2 s.f.).

The crane is powered using an electric motor. The efficiency of the crane is 74 %.

The crane is used to load approximately 400 bags with an average mass of 60 kg each day.

(i) Calculate the power used by the crane's motor to lift the bag in part (c).

[1]

(ii) The typical working efficiency of a crane is 80%.

Explain how the difference in efficiency may affect the number of bags the crane can lift in a day.

[3]

(iii) Suggest **one** change which could increase the efficiency of the motor and explain how it would achieve this.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the power used by the crane's motor to lift the bag in part (c):

List the known quantities:

- Efficiency = 74% = 0.74
- Useful power = 200 W (from **(c)**)

Calculate the total power used by the motor to lift the bag:

- $efficiency=\frac{usefulpower}{totalpower}\Rightarrowtotalpower=\frac{usefulpower}{efficiency}$
- $totalpower=\frac{200}{0.74}=270W$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) The difference in efficiency would affect the number of bags the crane can lift because:

**Final answer:** **Any ****three ****from:**

- More energy is needed for the same work done; **[1 mark]**
- At 80% efficiency, the motor would need 120 J less per bag; **[1 mark]**
- Total energy difference: 120 J × 400 bags = 48 000 J; **[1 mark]**
- (This is significant because) this is the equivalent of 44 bags per day; **[1 mark]**

(iii) A change which would increase the efficiency of the motor:

**EITHER**

- Lubricate / oil any moving parts; **[1 mark]**
- This would reduce (energy) losses due to friction / heat; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Tighten / secure / fasten any parts which move / rattle; **[1 mark]**
- This would reduce (energy) losses due to sound / kinetic energy; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *In part (ii), the full calculation is as follows:*

- *Energy required per 60 kg bag = **mg**Δ**h** = 60 × 9.81 × 1.871 = 1100 J*
- *At 74% efficiency, it uses 270 × 6 = 1620 J*
- *At 80% efficiency, it would use (200/0.80) × 6 = 1500 J*
- *Energy difference = 1620 − 1500 = 120 J per bag*

- *After lifting 400 bags, this equates to a total energy difference of 120 × 400 = 48 000 J wasted per day*
- *Which is equivalent to (48 000/1100) ≈ 44 bags per day*

> *This means a motor with 80% efficiency could lift 44 more bags per day than a motor working at 74% efficiency.*

> *In part (iii) you are asked to increase the efficiency of the motor, not the process. Responses to do with changing the height of the loading platform won't affect the running of the motor.*

> *To answer a question like this one, where you probably don't know and are having to infer the answers, first think where energy losses could happen. Mostly concentrate on thermal, kinetic and sound energy. Then think how this would happen, and finally how to address the problem.*

**Extract:**

The foot of the hill is 20 m lower than the cyclist's starting point and the cyclist reaches a top speed of 12 m s^−1^ before they start to brake at the foot of the hill. (i) change in gravitational potential energy = 18 000 J; (ii) kinetic energy gained by the cyclist = 6600 J. Total mass of cyclist and bicycle m = 92 kg.

The cyclist buys a set of tyres which claim to 'increase efficiency by 30% compared to your old tyres'.

The cyclist tests out the new tyres by riding down the same hill. With the new tyres, the cyclist achieves a top speed of 14 m s<sup>−1</sup> at the bottom of the hill.

Deduce whether the claim is correct or incorrect.
parts.solutionMd:
Deduce whether the claim that the new tyres *'increase efficiency by 30% compared to your old tyres' *is correct or incorrect:

List the known quantities:

- KE with old tyres = 6600 J
- Change in GPE = 18 000 J
- Top speed with new tyres, *v*<sub>*new*</sub> = 14 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Determine the efficiency of the old and new tyres:

- Efficiency = $\frac{usefulenergyout}{totalenergyin}$ **[1 mark]**
- In this case, the useful energy is the final kinetic energy, and the total energy is the initial GPE
- Efficiency = $\frac{finalKE}{initialGPE}$ **[1 mark]**
- Efficiency of old tyres = $\frac{6600}{18000}=0.367$
- Efficiency of new tyres = $\frac{\frac{1}{2}\times92\times14^{2}}{18000}=0.501$

Determine the % increase in efficiency:

- Ratio of efficiencies:  $\frac{eff_{new}}{eff_{old}}=\frac{0.501}{0.367}=1.37$ **OR** $\frac{eff_{old}}{eff_{new}}=0.73$ **[1 mark]**
- % increase = 1.37 = 37% **OR** (100 − 73)% = 37%
- % increase = 37% **[1 mark]**

Write a concluding sentence:

- The claim of a 30% increase is correct as the new tyres lead to a 37% increase in efficiency (compared to the old tyres); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Note that a 30 % increase does not mean adding 30 % to the original number, it means increasing the original number by 30 % of itself. *

> *To make this question a lot easier, you can use the fact that efficiency is directly proportional to the kinetic energy gained, as this is the sole useful energy output we are interested in. As a result, you can simply plug in the squares of the velocities to get a ratio which is exactly the same as the ratio of the efficiencies, but you don't have to go to the trouble of calculating the new KE or old and new efficiencies. A much more efficient approach!*

- *The initial GPE and the mass of the cyclist stay the same, so: *$efficiency\proptofinalKE\proptov^{2}$* *
- *% increase = *$( \frac{e f f_{n e w} }{e f f_{o l d} } - 1 )$* **OR** *$( \frac{K E_{n e w} }{K E_{o l d} } - 1 )$* **OR** *`( v _ n e w end _ ^2 / v _ o l d end _ ^2 - 1 )`* *
- *% increase = *$( \frac{14^{2}}{12^{2}} - 1 ) \times 100 \% = 36 \%$* *

parts.problemMd:
It has been predicted that in the future, large offshore wind turbines may have a power output ten times that of the largest ones currently in use. These turbines could have a blade length of 50 m or more. A turbine such as this is shown in Fig. 1.1 below.

![4-6-s-q--q1a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/5-work-energy-and-power/5-1-energy-conservation/assets/024-4-6-s-q-q1a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Calculate the power this turbine can produce, at a wind speed of 15 m s<sup>–1</sup> assuming that it is 100% efficient.

Give your answer in MW.

The density of air is 1.2 kg m<sup>–3</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the power of the turbine:

List the known quantities:

- Blade length,* r* = 50 m
- Wind speed, *v* = 15 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Density of air, $ρ$= 1.2 kg m<sup>–3</sup>

Determine an equation for the power of one turbine:

- Power, *P* =$\frac{Energy}{time}$
- The type of energy that the turbine converts is the <u>kinetic energy</u>,$E_{k}$
- *P* =$\frac{E_{k}}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

  - Power is the kinetic energy <u>per second</u>

Determine an equation for the kinetic energy per unit volume of air transferred from the wind to the turbine:

- Kinetic energy for a certain mass, $E_{k}$= $\frac{1}{2}$*mv*<sup>*2*</sup>
- Density, *ρ* =$\frac{m}{V}$ therefore, *m* = *ρV*
- Kinetic energy per unit volume of air from the wind, $E_{k}$=  $\frac{1}{2}$ *ρv*<sup>*2 *</sup>**[1 mark]**

Determine an equation for the kinetic energy for the volume of air the turbine sweeps through in one second:

- The volume can be modelled as a cylinder of air passing through the turbine each second, with the turbines sweeping out an area *A* and wind speed *v*
- Therefore, *V* = *vA*
- Kinetic energy per second,$E_{k}$= $\frac{1}{2}$ *ρv*<sup>*2*</sup>* × vA* = $\frac{1}{2}$ *ρv*<sup>3</sup>*A  ***[1 mark]**

Calculate the area swept by the blade, *A *in one second and use this to determine the power:

- The shape of the area that the blades sweep out is a circle
- *A* =$\mathrm{πr}^{2}$ where *r* is the blade length
- Therefore*, P* = $E_{k}$= $\frac{1}{2}$ *ρv*<sup>3</sup>π*r*<sup>2</sup>
- *P* = $\frac{1}{2}$ × 1.2 × (15)<sup>3</sup> × π × (50)<sup>2 </sup>**[1 mark]**
- *P *= 15.904 × 10<sup>6</sup> W = 16 MW **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 5 marks]**** **

> *The key point to understand in this question is that the power is the kinetic energy **per second**. In other words, if we calculate the kinetic energy for 1 second, this is equal to the power. *

> *Calculating the volume of air that the blades sweep through can be difficult to visualise. The volume of a cylinder **V** = **A** × *$l$* where **A** is the cross–sectional area (the circle =*$\mathrm{πr}^{2}$* ) and *$l$* **is the longer side of the cylinder. In this case, we are calculating the volume **per second**, therefore we can use the speed **v **for this side instead of *$l$*. *

> *This may be clearer through looking at the units. **A** has units m*<sup>*2*</sup>* and **v** units m s*<sup>*–1*</sup>* therefore **V** has the units m*<sup>*3*</sup>* s*<sup>*–1*</sup>* i.e. the volume per second.*

![4-6-s-q--q1a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/5-work-energy-and-power/5-1-energy-conservation/assets/025-4-6-s-q-q1a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

It has been predicted that in the future, large offshore wind turbines may have a power output ten times that of the largest ones currently in use. These turbines could have a blade length of 50 m or more. Calculate the power this turbine can produce, at a wind speed of 15 m s^–1^ assuming that it is 100% efficient. The density of air is 1.2 kg m^–3^. Answer: P = 15.904 × 10^6 W = 16 MW.

A factory uses 14 100 kWh of electricity per year.

Determine the number of factories that the wind turbine from part (a) can power for 1 year.

Assume that the wind is blowing onto the wind turbine at 15 m s<sup>−1</sup> on average, for 24 hours every day, 365 days a year.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Power of wind turbine, *P*<sub>*W*</sub> = 16 MW = 16 × 10<sup>6</sup> W (from part a)
- Energy use per year per factory, *E*<sub>*F*</sub> =14 100 kWh = 14.1×10<sup>3</sup> kWh
- Time = 1 year = 365 days

Calculate the total energy produced by one wind turbine in one year, *E*<sub>*W*</sub>:

- When the wind blows at 15 ms<sup>-1</sup>, *P*<sub>*W*</sub> = 16 × 10<sup>6</sup> W
- Which is 16 × 10<sup>6</sup> J s<sup>−1</sup>
- In one year, the turbine operates for 60 × 60 × 24 × 365 = 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s **[1 mark]**
- Therefore the energy it generates in one year is

  - *E*<sub>*W *</sub>= (16 × 10<sup>6</sup> J s<sup>−1</sup>) × (3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s) = 5.04 × 10<sup>14</sup> J** [1 mark]**

Convert the energy required per factory in one year to J:

- Energy required per factory, *E*<sub>*F*</sub> = 14 100 kWh = 14.1 × 10<sup>6</sup> Wh
- Convert Wh to Ws

  - (14.1 × 10<sup>6</sup>) × (60 × 60) = 5.076 × 10<sup>10 </sup>Ws
- $P=\frac{E}{t}$ therefore, $E=Pt$

  - Therefore, 1 J = 1 Ws
  - Hence, *E*<sub>*F *</sub>= 5.076 × 10<sup>10 </sup>Ws = 5.076 × 10<sup>10 </sup>J **[1 mark]**

Calculate the number of factories that can be powered by the wind turbine, *N*:

- Number of factories = $\frac{\mathrm{Energy} \mathrm{generated} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{one} \mathrm{wind} \mathrm{turbine} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{one} \mathrm{year}}{\mathrm{Energy} \mathrm{required} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{one} \mathrm{factory} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{one} \mathrm{year}}$
- *N *=$\frac{E_{W}}{E_{F}}$ = $\frac{5.04\times10^{14}}{5.076\times10^{10}}$ = 9900 (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *You may think that it is not possible for one wind turbine to power 9900 factories for a year but actually these turbines are much bigger than current turbines and offshore the wind is blowing more quickly meaning more power is generated. The radius of the wind turbine is 50 m, this is the length of an Olympic sized swimming pool. *

> *Don’t be put off by the unit ‘kWh’ (kilo–watt hour). This is just a unit of energy equal to 1 kW (1000 W) of power sustained for 1 hour.*

> *If you correctly used a power of 15.9 MW from part (a), you also would have gained an answer that rounds to 9900 and full marks. The final answer is given to 2 s.f. because the input values from part (a) were to 2 s.f.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Calculate the power this turbine can produce, at a wind speed of 15 m s^–1^ assuming that it is 100% efficient. Give your answer in MW. The density of air is 1.2 kg m^–3^. [Answer: P = 15.904 × 10^6 W = 16 MW]

A German physicist Albert Betz concluded in 1919 that no wind turbine can convert more than 59.3 % of the kinetic energy of the wind into mechanical energy turning the rotor, which then becomes electrical energy. This is known as the Betz limit.

The coefficient of power, $C_{p}$ of a wind turbine is a measure of how efficiently the wind turbine converts the energy in the wind into electricity. A good wind turbine has a $C_{p}$ that reaches 70 % of the Betz limit.

Assuming the wind turbine in part (a) is considered a good turbine, calculate its revised power output.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Power output from turbine, *P* = 16 MW = 16 × 10<sup>6</sup> W (from part a)
- Betz limit = 59.3 %

Calculate the coefficient of power, $C_{p}$:

- 0.70 × 59.3 % = 41.51 % **[1 mark]**

Calculate revised power output:

- Power output =$C_{p}$ × *P* = 0.4151 × (16 × 10<sup>6</sup>) = 6.6 MW **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 2 marks]**** **

> *The Betz limit seems like a very low value of energy conservation. Since wind turbines work by slowing down passing wind, if a wind turbine was 100% efficient, then all of the wind would have to stop completely upon contact with the turbine. We know this is not the case because the wind then travels behind it. *

> *In order to stop the wind completely, the air wouldn't move out of the way to the back of the turbine, which would prevent further air from coming in, causing the turbine to stop spinning. However, it would not be generating electricity if it stopped spinning! Other facts such as friction between the parts will also reduce efficiency.*

parts.problemMd:
A cyclist rides along a road up an incline at a steady speed of 5.0 m s<sup>–1</sup>. The mass of the rider and bicycle is 70 kg and the bicycle travels 27 m along the road for every 2.0 m gained in height. Neglect energy loss due to frictional forces.

Calculate the power developed by the cyclist in riding up the slope.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Speed, *v* = 5.0 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Mass, *m* = 70 kg
- Distance, *s* = 27 m for every 2.0 m gained in height

![4-6-s-q--q2a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/5-work-energy-and-power/5-1-energy-conservation/assets/030-4-6-s-q-q2a-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

Determine an equation for the force on the cyclist, *F*:

- The only force on the cyclist is their weight pulling them down the slope
- *F* = *W* sin*θ *= *mg* sin*θ*

  - *W* is the weight of the rider and bicycle

Calculate sin*θ*:

- sin*θ* = $\frac{opposite}{hypotenuse}$= $\frac{2.0}{27}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in values to calculate the force, *F*:

- *F* = 70 × 9.81 ×$\frac{2.0}{27}$ = 50.87 N **[1 mark]**

Calculate the power, *P*:

- *P* = *Fv* = 50.87 × 5.0 = 254.35 = 250 W (2 s. f.) **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**** **

> *The power is developed by the cyclist as it moves against the resistive force of gravity. In other words, the cyclist must do work **against** the force of gravity to travel up the incline (this is sometimes known as ‘negative’ work). The force is the **component** of the weight that acts **along** the incline, since **P** = **Fv** is derived from **W** = **Fs** where **W** is the work done, **F** is the force and **s** is the distance moved in the direction of the force. *

> *P** = **Fv** is very commonly misused. It can only be used if the object is moving at **constant** velocity (which is the case in this question) and the force must be in the direction **parallel** to the distance moved. Therefore, the most common way students lose marks in this question is by not resolving components of the weight.*

> *You could also have gotten to the same answer by using the work done against the gravitational force (weight) per unit time. This method would also gain full marks.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A cyclist rides along a road up an incline at a steady speed of 5.0 m s^–1^. The mass of the rider and bicycle is 70 kg and the bicycle travels 27 m along the road for every 2.0 m gained in height. Neglect energy loss due to frictional forces. Calculate the power developed by the cyclist in riding up the slope. P = Fv = 50.87 × 5.0 = 254.35 = 250 W (2 s. f.)

The cyclist now travels along a steeper incline at an angle of 6.5º to the horizontal.

Calculate the power output required from the cyclist on this new plane and discuss

how this value differs from that in part (a).

Assume the cyclist maintains the same speed along the road.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Speed, *v* = 5.0 m s<sup>–1</sup>
- Mass, *m* = 70 kg
- Angle of incline, *θ* = 6.5º

Write an equation with power *P* and work done *W*:

- The work done by cyclist equals their gravitational potential energy gained
- $\DeltaE_{p}=mg\Deltah$
- Power, *P* =$\frac{W}{t}$ =$\frac{mg\Deltah}{t}$

Calculate height, *h*:

- Sin*θ *= $\frac{opposite}{hypotenuse}$=$\frac{\Deltah}{5.0}$
- Δ*h* = 5.0 sin*θ* = 5.0 sin(6.5) **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the values:

- Since power is the change in energy per unit **time**, we can substitute time as 1 second
- *P* = $\frac{70 \times 9.81 \times 5.0 \times \sin ( 6.5 )}{1}$= 390 W **[1 mark]**

Discussion:

- The power output on the steeper incline is <u>higher</u>; **[1 mark]**
- This is because the cyclist has to do more <u>work</u> against gravity; **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *This question might look a little confusing as to why we would use the distance of the hypotenuse in m s*<sup>*–1*</sup>* (the velocity). This is because we want the unit of power to be in J s*<sup>*–1*</sup>* (W) or N m s*<sup>*–1*</sup>*, which means we don’t just want the distance but the distance **each second**. This might make more sense when looking at the units: *

> *P **= *$\frac{mg\Deltah}{t}$* = *$\frac{[ k g ] [ N k g^{- 1} ] [ m ]}{s}$*=*$\frac{[ N ] [ m ]}{[ s ]}$

> *Therefore, *$\frac{m}{s}$* or m s*<sup>*–1*</sup>* must come from the velocity (which has units m s*<sup>*–1*</sup>*)*

> *Since the angle of incline has now changed for this question, make sure **not** to use the value of Δ**h** given in part (a), since this has now changed!*

![4-6-s-q--q2b-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/5-work-energy-and-power/5-1-energy-conservation/assets/031-4-6-s-q-q2b-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

The cyclist now travels along a steeper incline at an angle of 6.5º to the horizontal. Assume the cyclist maintains the same speed along the road.

The cyclist stops pedalling and the bicycle freewheels up the incline for a short time.

Considering the energy transfers, calculate the distance travelled along the slope from when the cyclist stops pedalling to where the bicycle comes to rest.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m* = 70 kg
- Angle of incline, *θ* = 6.5º

Determine the energy transfers:

- The initial kinetic energy of the cyclist is transferred to the gain in gravitational potential energy

Calculate the initial kinetic energy, $E_{k}$:

- Therefore, the gain in GPE, $\DeltaE_{p}$ is also 875 J; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the height the cyclist has travelled, *h*:

- $\DeltaE_{p}=mg\Deltah$
- $\Deltah=\frac{\DeltaE_{p}}{mg}$ = $\frac{875}{70\times9.81}$= 1.27 m **[1 mark]**

Calculate displacement, *s*:

![4-6-s-q--q2c-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/5-work-energy-and-power/5-1-energy-conservation/assets/032-4-6-s-q-q2c-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

- sin*θ *=$\frac{opposite}{hypotenuse}$ =$\frac{h}{s}$
- *s* =$\frac{h}{sinθ}$ =$\frac{1.27}{s i n ( 6.5 )}$ = 11 m **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

When an object is accelerated from rest, energy is stored. Name the energy store and state the reason for it. Answer: Kinetic energy is stored when a force is applied (and makes an object accelerate); Work is done by the force (and energy is transferred to the object).

State the equation for kinetic energy, defining all the units mentioned: E_k = 1/2 m v^2, where E_k = kinetic energy, m = mass, v = velocity.

Referring to your answer to part (a), derive the expression for kinetic energy stated in part (b).
parts.solutionMd:
Referring to your answer to part (a), derive the expression for kinetic energy stated in part (b):

- Energy transferred = work done **OR** $W_{d}=F\timess$ (by definition) **[1 mark]**
- Newton's Second Law:  $F=ma$ **[1 mark]**
- Using the SUVAT equation:  $v^{2}=u^{2}+2as$, if *u* = 0 then $a=\frac{v^{2}}{2s}$** [1 mark]**
- Substitute into $F=ma\RightarrowF=m\times\frac{v^{2}}{2s}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{mv^{2}}{s}$** [1 mark]**
- Substitute into $W_{d}=F\timess\RightarrowW_{d}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{mv^{2}}{s}\timess=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ ** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *This derivation is longer than the one for gravitational potential energy and must be learned more carefully. Since these are the Easy questions we have been quite generous with our marks. In the exam this would be worth two or three marks.*

Determine the energy transferred by the water falling through the turbines:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Pumped hydroelectric systems store large bodies of water behind a dam. When electricity is needed in the grid, the dam is lifted, allowing water to flow from the upper reservoir. One such power station, known as the Cruachan power station, is shown in Fig. 1.1. This facility has been producing hydroelectric power since 1965. The vertical distance between the base of the upper reservoir and the turbine is 396 m. This arrangement allows Cruachan power station to produce a power output of 0.62 GW with an efficiency of 76%. Determine the energy transferred by the water each second in order to achieve this power output. [Mark scheme: Total power input = 0.62/0.76 = 0.82 GW; Energy transferred each second = 0.82 GJ or 8.2 × 10^8 J]

Water is made to flow out of the upper reservoir through connecting pipes at a rate of 200 m<sup>3</sup> per second. The density of water is 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>.

(i) Use this flow rate to determine the energy transferred by the water each second.

[4]

(ii) Explain why this value is **not **consistent with the energy transfer rate calculated in **(a)**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:

- Therefore, the depth of the upper reservoir = (22 × 2) = 44 m **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Anaisha launches a pebble vertically upwards using a sling shot. The speed of the pebble as it leaves the sling shot is 28 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate the height that the pebble gains.

Assume that air resistance is negligible.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the height that the pebble reaches:

List the known quantities:

- Initial speed, *v*<sub>*i*</sub> = 28 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Gravitational field strength, *g* = 9.81 N kg<sup>−1</sup>

Combine the equations for kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy:

- Recall the equations

  - $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ and $\DeltaE_{p}=mg\Deltah$
- The energy in the system is conserved, therefore:

  - $E_{ki}+E_{pi}=E_{kf}+E_{pf}$
  - $\frac{1}{2}mv_{i}^{2}+mgh_{i}=\frac{1}{2}mv_{f}^{2}+mgh_{f}$

- Define initial height of pebble, *h*<sub>*i*</sub> = 0 and final velocity of pebble, *v*<sub>*f*</sub> = 0 at the top of its trajectory
- Therefore, $\frac{1}{2}mv_{i}^{2}=mgh_{f}$  and mass cancels out leaving $\frac{1}{2}v_{i}^{2}=gh_{f}$
- Hence, $h_{f}=\frac{v_{i}^{2}}{2g}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known values to calculate the final height:

- $h_{f} = \frac{ 28^{2}}{2 \times 9.81} = 40 \mathrm{m} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *An approach equating loss of energy from the kinetic store with gain in energy in the gravitational potential store produces the exact same result as the method above. It is just a rearrangement of the second line of maths.*

> *We can define the initial height of the pebble as 0 m, as we only care about the **change** in height. Realising that a projectile has a vertical speed of zero (at the turning point) is crucial for questions like this.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The mass of the pebble is 300 g.

Anaisha notices a basket hanging by a string from a tree. The basket has a mass of 280 g and the length of the string is 85 cm. Anaisha uses her slingshot to fire the pebble horizontally, which lands in the basket. The basket then swings out to an angle of 45°.

Calculate the speed of the pebble as she fired it.

Assume that air resistance is negligible and that there is no breeze.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the speed of the pebble:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of basket, *m*<sub>b</sub> = 280 g = 0.28 kg
- Mass of pebble, *m*<sub>p</sub> = 300 g = 0.30 kg
- Length of string, $l$ = 85 cm = 0.85 m
- Angle of swing, *θ* =  45°

Determine an expression for the initial velocity of the pebble:

- The collision is inelastic, therefore momentum is conserved

  - $p_{before}=p_{after}$
  - $m_{p}v_{pi}+m_{b}v_{bi}=m_{p}v_{pf}+m_{b}v_{bf}$
- Since there is no breeze we can assume that the initial velocity of the basket is zero

  - $m_{p}v_{pi}=m_{p}v_{pf}+m_{b}v_{bf}$
- Rearranging for the initial velocity of the pebble

  - $v_{p i} = v_{b + p} ( \frac{m_{b} + m_{p} }{m_{p} } )$ **[1 mark]**
  - Where $v_{b+p}$ is the velocity of the pebble in the basket as it begins to swing

Determine $v_{b+p}$, labelled as $v_{b+pi}$ below, from an analysis starting when the pebble enters the basket:

- During the swing, the energy of the pebble-basket system is constant

  - $E_{ki}+E_{pi}=E_{kf}+E_{pf}$
  - $1 \frac{1}{2} ( m_{p + m_{b} ) v_{b} + p i}^{2} + ( m_{p + m_{b} ) g h_{i} = 1 \frac{1}{2} ( m_{p} + m_{b} ) v_{b} + p f}^{2} + ( m_{p} + m_{b} ) g h_{f}$
  - Rearrange,  rewriting *h*<sub>*f*</sub>* * − *h*<sub>*i*</sub>  as Δ*h*  and $v_{b+pf}$ is zero at the top of the swing
  - Hence, $1 \frac{1}{2} ( m_{p + m_{b} ) v_{p} + b i}^{2} = ( m_{p} + m_{b} ) g \Delta h$
- The total masses cancel out

  - $\frac{1}{2}v_{p+bi}^{2}=gΔh$
  - $v_{p+bi}=\sqrt{2gΔh}$ **[1 mark]**
- The height of the swing is

  - `capital delta h = l - l cos theta = l ( 1 - cos theta )`
  - `capital delta h = 0.85 ( 1 - cos ( 45 ) ) = 0.249 m` **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, $v_{p+bi}=\sqrt{2\times9.81\times0.249}=2.21ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the initial speed of the pebble:

- $v_{p i} = v_{b + p i} ( \frac{m_{b} + m_{p} }{m_{p} } ) = 2.21 ( \frac{0.28 + 0.30}{0.30} ) = 4.3 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{- 1} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *This is complex multi-step problem that takes some thinking about. It can be helpful to sketch out a diagram so that you can see visually what is going on in the scenario, and which variables you can infer from the situation. This will help you to navigate your way to the answer.*

![pebble-basket-ma](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/5-work-energy-and-power/5-2-gravitational-potential-energy-and-kinetic-energy/assets/028-pebble-basket-ma.png)

parts.problemMd:
In a theme park ride, a cage containing passengers falls freely a distance of $x$* *m from **A** to **B** and travels in a circular arc of radius 25 m from **B** to **C**.

Brakes are applied at **C** after which the cage with its passengers travels 70 m along an upward sloping ramp and comes to rest at **D**. The track, together with relevant distances, is shown in Fig. 1.2. **CD** makes an angle of *θ *with the horizontal.

![4-6-s-q--q4b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/5-work-energy-and-power/5-2-gravitational-potential-energy-and-kinetic-energy/assets/023-4-6-s-q-q4b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

alt: For a passenger of mass 70 kg, the force keeping them in circular motion at **C** is 5.4 kN.

The force required for circular motion on a passenger of mass 70 kg at **C** is 5.4 kN.

parts.solutionMd:
To calculate height $x$.

List the known quantities:

- Mass of passenger, *m* = 70 kg
- Height dropped by passenger = $x$
- Radius of circular motion, *r* = 25 m
- Force required for circular motion, *F* = 5.4 kN = 5.4 × 10<sup>3</sup> N

Calculate the velocity at **C**, *v*:

- Recall the equation for centripetal force, $F=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$
- *v* =$\sqrt{\frac{Fr}{m}}$
- *v* = $\sqrt{ \frac{( 5.4 \times 10^{3} ) \times 25}{70} }$= 43.92 m s<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Consider energy changes between point **A** and **C**:

- The gravitational potential energy at **A** is converted to kinetic energy at point **C**

  - Vertical distance from **A **to **C **is *h*
- $\frac{1}{2}$*mv*<sup>*2*</sup> = *mgh ***[1 mark]**

Rearrange for *h* and substitute in values:

- Mass cancels out, leaving $\frac{1}{2}v^{2}=gh$
- Rearranging for h gives $h=\frac{v^{2}}{2g}$
- $h=x+25m$  therefore  $x+25=\frac{v^{2}}{2g}$
- $x$ = $\frac{v^{2}}{2g}$– 25
- $x$ = $\frac{( 43.92 )^{2}}{2 \times 9.81}$– 25 = 73 m **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**** *** *

- Resistive force by brakes, *F* = 4.8 kN = 4.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> N
- Horizontal distance between **C** and **D**, *s* = 70 m
- Height from **A** to **C **= *h*
- Height from **A** to **B**, $x$ = 73 m (from part b)

Calculate height *h*:

- *h* = $x$ + 25 = 73 + 25 = 98 m

Consider energy changes between **A** and **D**:

- Gravitational potential energy lost from **A** to **C** = Work done against resistive force from **C** to **D** + gravitational potential energy gained from **C** to **D**
- $\Delta E_{p ( A t o C )}$= *Fs* + $\Delta E_{p ( C t o D )}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange equation for sin *θ*:

- $\DeltaE_{p(CtoD)}$= $\DeltaE_{p(AtoC)}$– *Fs*
- $\DeltaE_{p(CtoD)}$*= mgs* sin*θ*
- *mgs* sin*θ *= *mgh* – *Fs*
- sin*θ = *$\frac{mgh-Fs}{mgs}$**[1 mark]**

Substitute in values and calculate *θ:*

- *θ *= $\sin ^{- 1} ( \frac{( 720 \times 9.81 \times 98 ) - ( 4.8 \times 10^{3} ) \times 70}{720 \times 9.81 \times 70} )$**[1 mark]**
- *θ *= 46º **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

> *This question can be done by substituting values and calculating *$\Delta E_{p ( A t o C )}$*, **Fs **and separately *$\Delta E_{p ( C t o D )}$*and then rearranging for **θ, **both methods will still achieve full marks. *

> *Remember that **h** in the gravitational potential energy **mgh** is always the **vertical **height that the object falls from / gains. In this case, it is **s** sin**θ**. This is seen using trigonometry: *

A block of mass 0.40 kg slides in a straight line with a constant speed of 0.30 m s<sup>–1</sup> along a horizontal surface, as shown in Fig. 3.1.
