**Fig. 3.1**

Assume that there are no resistive forces opposing the motion of the block.

The block hits a spring and decelerates. The speed of the block becomes zero when the compression of the spring is 8.0 cm.

(i) Calculate the initial kinetic energy of the block.

kinetic energy = ....................................................... J [2]

(ii) The variation of the compression x of the spring with the force F applied to the spring is shown in Fig. 3.2.

![q3b-ii-paper-2-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-1-stress-and-strain/assets/028-q3b-ii-paper-2-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 3.2**

Assume that the elastic potential energy of the spring when its compression is 8.0 cm is equal to the initial kinetic energy of the block.

Use your answer in **(b)(i)** to calculate the maximum force *F*<sub>max</sub> exerted on the spring by the block.

*F*<sub>max</sub> = ...................................................... N [2]

(iii) Calculate the maximum deceleration of the block.

deceleration = ................................................. m s<sup>–2</sup> [2]

(iv) State and explain whether the block is in equilibrium:

- before it hits the spring

........................................................................................................

- when its speed becomes zero.

........................................................................................................

[2]

(v) The block is now replaced by another block of the same mass. Frictional forces affect the motion of this block so that it has a speed of 0.25 m s<sup>–1</sup> when it makes contact with the spring.

A short time later, the block has a speed of 0.15 m s<sup>–1</sup> as it loses contact with the spring and moves back along its original path.

Calculate the magnitude of the change in momentum of the block.

change in momentum = .................................................... N s [2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass of block, $m$ = 0.40 kg
- Velocity of block, $v$ = 0.30 m s<sup>−1</sup>

(i) Calculate the initial kinetic energy of the block:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}\times0.4\times0.3^{2}$
- $E_{k}=0.018J$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the maximum force *F*<sub>max</sub> exerted on the spring by the block:

From the graph when $F=F_{max}$:

- Compression, $x$ = 8.0 cm = 8 × 10<sup>−2</sup> m

Equate the elastic potential $E_{p}$ and  $E_{k}$ of the block and rearrange for $F_{max}$:

- $E_{k = E_{p} = 1 \frac{1}{2} ( F_{m} a x} ) x$
- $0.018 = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times F_{m a x} \times ( 8 \times 10^{- 2} )$ ** [1 mark]**
- $F_{m a x} = \frac{0.018 \times 2}{( 8 \times 10^{- 2} )}$
- $F_{max}=0.45N$** [1 mark]**

(iii) Calculate the maximum deceleration of the block:

- $F=ma$ **[1 mark]**
- $a=\frac{F_{max}}{m}$
- $a=\frac{0.45}{0.40}$
- $a = 1.125 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{- 2} = 1.1 \mathrm{m} \mathrm{s}^{- 2} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

(iv) Consider whether the block is in equilibrium during the following:

Before it hits the spring:

- The velocity is constant / the resultant force is zero, so the block is in equilibrium; **[1 mark]**

When its speed becomes zero:

- There is deceleration / the resultant force is not zero, so the block is <u>not</u> in equilibrium; **[1 mark]**

(v) Calculate the magnitude of the change in momentum of the block:

List the known quantities:

- Initial velocity of block, $u$ = 0.25 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Final velocity of block, $v$ = −0.15 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate the change in momentum:

- $p=mv$ **or** $mu=0.40\times0.25$ **or** $mv=0.40\times0.15$ **[1 mark]**
- $\Deltaρ$ = momentum before − momentum after
- $\Delta \\rho = m u - m v = m ( u - v )$
- $\Delta \\rho = 0.4 \times ( 0.25 - ( - 0.15 ) )$
- $\Deltaρ=0.16Ns$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 10 marks]**

- *In part (v) "moves back along its original path" tells you that the block's **direction** is **opposite*

  - *So, the **velocity** is **negative*

parts.problemMd:
Nichrome is a common alloy used to make coins and heating elements in electrical appliances. It consists of 80% by volume of nickel and 20% by volume of chromium.

Determine the mass of nickel and the mass of chromium required to make a wire of nichrome of volume 0.50 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>.

Density of nickel = 8.9 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>

Density of chromium = 7.1 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg m<sup>−3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the mass of nickel and the mass of chromium required to make a wire of nichrome of volume 0.50 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>

Determine how much of the total volume will consist of each metal:

- Volume of nickel = 80% × total volume
- Volume of nickel = $0.8\times(0.50\times10^{-3})=4.0\times10^{--4}m^{3}$
- Volume of chromium = 20% × total volume
- Volume of chromium = $0.2\times(0.50\times10^{-3})=1.0\times10^{--4}m^{3}$

Use the equation for density to find the mass required:

- $m=ρ\timesv$
- Mass of nickel, $m_{n} = \rho_{n} \times v_{n} = ( 8.9 \times 10^{3} ) \times ( 4.0 \times 10^{- 4} ) = 3.56$
- Mass of nickel, $m_{n} = 3.6 \text{kg} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**
- Mass of chromium, $m_{c} = \rho_{c} \times v_{c} = ( 7.1 \times 10^{3} ) \times ( 1.0 \times 10^{- 4} ) = 0.71$

parts.problemMd:
Two different cables with spring constants *k*<sub>1</sub> and *k*<sub>*2*</sub> are connected in series.

Starting from Hooke's law, show that the combined spring constant, *K* of the two springs is given by the equation $K=\frac{k_{1}k_{2}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Consider the situation and obtain equations in terms of the force applied, *F*:

- Two springs connected in series provide a longer, flimsier spring
- When a force is applied to the combined spring the same force is applied evenly to each individual spring
- The springs have different spring constants so the extension they undergo is different
- Hence when *x*<sub>1</sub> is the extension for spring *k*<sub>1</sub> and *x*<sub>2</sub> is the extension of spring *k*<sub>2</sub>:

  - *F *= *K*(*x*<sub>*1*</sub> + *x*<sub>*2*</sub>) (Equation 1) **AND**
  - *F *= *k*<sub>1</sub>*x*<sub>1 </sub>(Equation 2) **AND**
  - *F *= *k*<sub>2</sub>*x*<sub>*2 *</sub>(Equation 3) **[1 mark]**

Combine equations 2 and 3 to make *x*<sub>*1*</sub> the subject:

- *k*<sub>1</sub>*x*<sub>1</sub> = *k*<sub>2</sub>*x*<sub>*2*</sub>
- $x_{1}=\frac{k_{2}x_{2}}{k_{1}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute for *x*<sub>*1*</sub> in equation 1:

- $F = K ( ( \frac{k_{2} x_{2} }{k_{1} } ) + x_{2} )$
- $F = K ( \frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}} + 1 ) x_{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Combine this equation with equation 3 and rearrange to make *K *the subject:

- $k_{2} x_{2} = K ( \frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}} + 1 ) x_{2}$
- $k_{2} = K ( \frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}} + 1 )$
- $\frac{k_{2}}{ ( \frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}} + 1 ) } = K$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Take your time and work through this type of question slowly thinking about the force applied when two wires are in series. You won't get marks for it because the question asks you **to show **but you will need to check you have completed the question correctly by rearranging this final equation for **K **as follows:*

![file-000-12](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-1-stress-and-strain/assets/019-file-000-12.png)

As part of a quality check, a manufacturer of dog leads selects a sample of the wires used for the leads to a tensile test.

The sample of wires used is 3.0 m long and is of constant circular cross–section of diameter 0.92 mm. Hooke’s law is obeyed up to the point when the wire has been extended by 20 mm at a tensile stress of 4.6 × 10<sup>8</sup> Pa.

The maximum load the wire can support before breaking is 350 N at an extension of 12 cm.

![6-1-q2a-h-sq-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-1-stress-and-strain/assets/029-6-1-q2a-h-sq-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Sketch a graph on Fig. 1.1** **to show how you expect the tensile stress to vary with strain and mark the values of stress with corresponding strain at the limit of Hooke's law and the breaking point.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Original length, *L* = 3.0 m
- Diameter, *d* = 0.92 mm = 0.92 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- Tensile stress = 4.6 × 10<sup>8 </sup>Pa
- Extension for Hooke’s law limit = 20 mm = 0.02 m
- Breaking force, *F* = 350 N
- Breaking extension = 12 cm = 0.12 m

Calculate cross-sectional area, *A:*

- *A* = π*r*<sup>*2*</sup> = $\frac{\mathrm{πd}^{2}}{4}$ = $\frac{ \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 0.92 \times 10^{- 3} )^{2}}{4}$
- *A* = 6.65 × 10<sup>–7</sup> m<sup>2</sup>

Calculate the breaking stress:

- Breaking stress = $\frac{breakingforce}{area}$ = $\frac{350}{6.65\times10^{-7}}$
- Breaking stress = 5.26 × 10<sup>8</sup> Pa **[1 mark]**

Calculate the breaking strain:

- Breaking strain = $\frac{Breakingextension}{L}$ = $\frac{0.12}{3}$ = 0.040 = 40 × 10<sup>−3</sup> **[1 mark] **

Calculate the tensile strain:

- Tensile strain = $\frac{ExtensionforHooke'slawlimit}{L}$ = $\frac{0.02}{3}$ = 0.0067 = 6.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup> **[1 mark] **

A graph that would score 3 marks should look like:

![img-1154](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-1-stress-and-strain/assets/030-img-1154.jpeg)

- The graph line is a straight section up to the Hooke’s law limit and is curved in the tensile section of the graph; **[1 mark]**
- Point at tensile stress and tensile strain (6.7 × 10<sup>−3</sup>, 4.6 × 10<sup>8</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Point at breaking stress and breaking strain (40, 5.26 × 10<sup>8</sup>); **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 6 marks]**** **

> *There are a few clues in the question as to the shape of this graph. ‘Hooke’s law is obeyed up to the point’ means that the stress–strain curve will only be a straight diagonal line up to a point. Beyond this point, if it doesn’t obey Hooke’s Law this means the line starts to curve (i.e., The material starts to plastically deform). The 'maximum load before breaking' implies that at this stress–strain point, this graph will end. Therefore, the two points to calculate on the graph are the stress­–strain at the end of the Hooke’s law section, and the final stress–strain before the wire breaks. *

> *Remember to label your axes appropriately, including all the units and any powers of 10 (e.g., × 10*<sup>*8*</sup>*).*

parts.problemMd:
Calculate the force needed to extend a piece of 3.0 m leather dog leash with a radius of 2.3 mm to change its surface area by 4.1 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m<sup>2</sup>. Assume that the cross–sectional area is kept constant throughout the extension.

Young Modulus of leather = 0.05 GPa.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Original length, *L* = 3.0 m
- Change in surface area = 4.1 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m<sup>2</sup>
- Radius, *r*  = 2.3 mm = 2.3 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- Young Modulus of leather = 0.05 GPa = 0.05 × 10<sup>9</sup> Pa

Determine the equation for extension Δ*L* from the change in surface area, ΔSA:

- Surface area of a cylinder = 2π*r L* + 2π*r*<sup>*2*</sup>
- ΔSA = (2π*r*$L_{2}$*­*+ 2π*r*<sup>*2*</sup>) – (2π*r­*$L_{1}$+ 2π*r*<sup>*2*</sup>)
- ΔSA = 2π*r *(­$L_{2}-L_{1}$) = 2π*r*Δ*L*
- Δ*L*  = $\frac{\Delta\mathrm{SA}}{2\mathrm{πr}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute into Young Modulus equation:

- Young Modulus = $\frac{FL}{A\DeltaL}$ = $\frac{FL}{A\times\frac{\Delta\mathrm{SA}}{2πr}}$
- Cross-sectional area, *A* = π*r*<sup>*2*</sup>
- Young Modulus =$\frac{FL}{\mathrm{πr}^{2}\times\frac{\Delta\mathrm{SA}}{2\mathrm{πr}}}$ = $\frac{FL}{r\times\frac{\Delta\mathrm{SA}}{2}}$ = $\frac{2FL}{r\times\DeltaSA}$  **[1 mark]**

Calculate force, *F*:

- *F* = $\frac{Youngmodulus\timesr\times\DeltaSA}{2L}$
- *F* = $\frac{( 0.05 \times 10^{9 ) \times ( 2.3 \times 10^{-3} } ) \times ( 4.1 \times 10^{- 3} )}{2 \times 3.0}$ **[1 mark]**
- *F *= 78.58 = 79 N **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *If you forget the formula for areas and volumes for 3D shapes, don’t panic! Just take time to figure them out from your GCSE Maths knowledge. For example: the curved surface area of the cylinder = 2π**rh **where **r** is the radius and **h** is the height of the cylinder. *

> *The total surface area of a cylinder includes the areas of the two circular cross–sectionals on either side. To determine the surface area of any 3D shape, add up the area of all its faces. This is shown for the cylinder below:*

![4-8-s-q--q3c-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-1-stress-and-strain/assets/031-4-8-s-q-q3c-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

> *Notice that the length of the shorter side of the rectangle that makes up the curved part of the cylinder is the circumference of a circle. The total surface area is therefore:*

> *2π**r L** + π**r*<sup>*2*</sup>* + π**r*<sup>*2*</sup>* = 2π**r L** + 2π**r*<sup>*2*</sup>

To prevent the walls of old buildings collapsing a metal rod is often used to tie opposite walls together, as shown in Fig. 1.2 below.

![4-8-s-q--q5a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-1-stress-and-strain/assets/032-4-8-s-q-q5a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

In one case a steel tie rod of diameter 15 mm is used. When the nuts are tightened, the rod extends by 6 %. The Young Modulus of steel is 2.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> Pa.

Calculate the force exerted on the walls by the rod.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Diameter, *d* = 15 mm = 15 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- Young Modulus of steel = 2.5 × 10<sup>11</sup>Pa
- Extension of rod = 6 %

Calculate the strain:

- Strain = $\frac{\DeltaL}{L}$ = 6 % = 0.06 **[1 mark]**

Calculate the cross-sectional area, *A*:

- *A* = π*r*<sup>*2*</sup> = $\frac{\mathrm{πd}^{2}}{4}$
- *A* = $\frac{ \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 15 \times 10^{- 3} )^{2}}{4}$ = 1.77 × 10<sup>–4</sup> m<sup>2 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Calculate the stress:

- Young Modulus = $\frac{stress}{strain}$ therefore, Stress = Strain × Young Modulus
- Stress = 0.06 × (2.5 × 10<sup>11</sup>) = 1.50 × 10<sup>10</sup> Pa **[1 mark]**

Calculate force, *F*:

- Stress = $\frac{F}{A}$ therefore, *F* = Stress × *A*
- *F* = (1.50 × 10<sup>10</sup>) × (1.77 × 10<sup>–4</sup>)
- *F* = 2.66 × 10<sup>6</sup> N = 2.66 MN **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

> *If the rod extends by 6 % that means the **ratio** of it extension to the original length is equal to 6 % or 0.06. You can check this by putting in some numbers:*

> *For example:*

- *If **L** = 5 m, therefore **L** + Δ**L** = 5 × 1.06 = 5.3 (increased by 6 %)*
- *Strain = *$\frac{\DeltaL}{L}$* = *$\frac{5.3-5}{5}$* = 0.06*

> *This force is the force exerted **on** the rod **by** the walls, but according to Newton's third law, this is equal in size to the force exerted **by** the rod **on** the walls.*

parts.problemMd:
Another identical spring is loaded with weights.

It has an extension of 8.0 cm and stores 24 J of elastic potential energy.

Calculate the spring constant of this spring.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the spring constant of the spring:

List the known quantities:

- Extension, $x$ = 8.0 cm = 0.08 m
- Elastic potential energy, $E_{P}$ = 24 J

Recall the equation for elastic potential energy:

- $E_{P}=\frac{1}{2}kx^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange for *k* :

- $k=\frac{2E_{P}}{x^{2}}=\frac{2\times24}{0.08^{2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $k=7500Nm^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The relationship between applied force and change in length of the springs was measured for a range of values of force. The results are plotted on the graph in Fig. 1.3.

Derive the formula for the elastic potential energy stored by the spring from the graph of force against extension.
parts.solutionMd:
Derive the formula for the elastic potential energy stored by the spring from the graph of force against extension:

*Work done*

- The work done on / by the spring to stretch or compress it is equal to the elastic potential energy stored in the spring; **[1 mark]**
- Work done, $ΔW=F\timesd$ (by definition)
- *d*, distance moved in the direction of the force = Δ*x*, (the compression or extension)

* Area under the force-compression graph*

- Therefore, the area under the graph represents the work done / energy required to compress / extend the spring; **[1 mark]**
- Area under graph = area of a right-angle triangle = ½ × base height =  ½ × Δ*x × F ***[1 mark]**
- Which is the same as elastic potential energy $E_{p}=\frac{1}{2}Fx$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd: The aluminium alloy wire has a diameter of 1.2 mm. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the wire when it shows an extension of 7.5 cm under a total stress of 190 MPa.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the wire:

List the known quantities:

- Stress, σ = 190 MPa = 190 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa
- Extension, *x* = 7.5 cm = 0.075 m
- Diameter of the wire, *d* = 1.2 mm = 1.2 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m

Calculate the cross-sectional area of the wire, *A*:

- $A=πr^{2}$
- $A = \pi ( \frac{1.2 \times 10^{- 3} }{2} )^{2}$
- $A=1.13\times10^{-6}m^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the force, *F *applied to the wire:

- Stress, $σ=\frac{F}{A}$ $\rightarrow$ $F=σA$
- $F = ( 190 \times 10^{6 ) \times ( 1.13 \times 10^{-6} } )$
- $F=214.7N$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the elastic potential energy, *E*<sub>*p*</sub> stored in the wire:

- $E_{p}=\frac{1}{2}Fx$
- $E_{p}=\frac{1}{2}\times214.7\times0.075$
- $E_{p}=8.05J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A steel bar is 40 mm long and has cross-sectional area 4.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>.

The bar is compressed using a vice so that the length is reduced by 0.20 mm.

The Young Modulus of steel = 2.1 × 10<sup>11</sup> Pa.

Calculate the compressive force exerted on the bar.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the compressive force exerted on the bar:

List the known quantities:

- Cross-sectional area of bar, $A$ = 4.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>
- Length of bar, $x$ = 40 mm
- Compression of bar, $\Deltax$ = 0.20 mm
- Young-Modulus, $E$ = 2.1 × 10<sup>11</sup> Pa

Use the full equation for the Young Modulus:

- $E=\frac{F}{A}\times\frac{x}{Δx}$

Rearrange to make *F* the subject and calculate:

- $F = \frac{E \times A \times \Delta x}{x} = \frac{( 2.1 \times 10^{11 ) \times ( 4.5 \times 10^{-4} } ) \times 0.2}{40}$ **[1 mark]**
- $F=472500$ N

Write the answer to two sig figs and include the unit:

- $F=4.7\times10^{5}N$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A light spring of length 2.2 cm is hung from a fixed point. An object of weight 4.0 N is hung from the other end of the spring. Fig. 1.1 shows the length of the spring when the object is in equilibrium.

![4-7-s-q--q2a-fig-1-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-2-elastic-and-plastic-behaviour/assets/041-4-7-s-q-q2a-fig-1-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The object is then pulled vertically downwards and is no longer in its equilibrium position. This is shown in Fig. 1.2.

![4-7-s-q--q2a-fig-2-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-2-elastic-and-plastic-behaviour/assets/042-4-7-s-q-q2a-fig-2-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

The change in elastic potential energy Δ*E*  between the spring in Fig. 1.1 and Fig. 1.2 is 0.30 J.

Calculate the length of the spring in Fig. 1.2.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Change in elastic potential energy, Δ*E* = 0.30 J
- Force, *F* = 4.0 N
- Extension of spring in Fig. 1.1, $\Deltax_{a}$= 10.5 cm – 2.2 cm = 8.3 cm = 0.083 m
- Original length, *L* = 2.2 cm = 0.022 m

Calculate the spring constant of the spring, *k*:

- Hooke’s law: *F* = *k *Δx
- *k * = $\frac{F}{\Deltax}$ = $\frac{4.0}{0.083}$ = 48.19 = 48 N m<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]**

Determine the equation for the change in elastic potential energy, Δ*E*:

- Elastic potential energy, *E*  = $\frac{1}{2}$× *k *× (Δ*x*)<sup>2</sup>

  - It is the same spring, so both scenarios have the same value of *k*
- Δ*E*  = $\frac{1}{2}$*k *(($\Deltax_{b}$)<sup>2</sup> – ($\Deltax_{a}$)<sup>2</sup>) **[1 mark]**

  - Where $\Deltax_{a}$ is the extension of the spring in Fig. 1.1 and $\Deltax_{b}$ is the extension in Fig. 1.2

Rearrange the equation for the extension in Fig. 1.2, $\Deltax_{b}$:

- $\Deltax_{b}$= $\sqrt{ \frac{2 \Delta E}{k} + ( \Delta x_{a} )^{2}}$
- $\Deltax_{b}$= $\sqrt{ \frac{2 \times 0.30}{48} + ( 0.083 )^{2}}$ = 0.139 = 0.14 m **[1 mark]**

Calculate length of the spring:

- Length = *L* + $\Deltax_{b}$ = 0.022 + 0.14 = 0.162 m (16.2 cm) **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**** **

> *Remember to convert to **metres** from **centimetres** for all the extension and lengths. This is because the change in elastic potential energy, **E** is measured in **Joules (J)**. The SI base unit for Joules is **N m**. Therefore, the calculation will not work if you keep all your values in cm!*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A light spring of length 2.2 cm is hung from a fixed point. An object of weight 4.0 N is hung from the other end of the spring. The object is then pulled vertically downwards and is no longer in its equilibrium position (Fig. 1.2). The change in elastic potential energy ΔE between the spring in Fig. 1.1 and Fig. 1.2 is 0.30 J. Spring constant k = 48 N m^–1; Extension Δx_b = 0.139 m; Weight W = 4.0 N.

The object is released from its position shown in Fig. 1.2.

Calculate its initial acceleration.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Spring constant, *k* = 48 N m<sup>–1</sup> (from part a)
- Extension, $\Deltax_{b}$= 0.139 m (from part a)
- Weight, *W* = 4.0 N

Calculate the mass, *m*:

- *W* = *mg*
- *m* = $\frac{W}{g}=\frac{4.0}{9.81}=0.408$ kg **[1 mark]**

Calculate the resultant force, *F* on the object:

- Downwards force, $F_{d}$ = *W* = 4.0 N
- Upwards force, $F_{u}$= $k$$\Deltax_{b}$= 48 × 0.139 = 6.672 N
- Resultant force = $F_{u}-F_{d}$ = 6.672 – 4.0 = 2.672 N **[1 mark]**

Calculate acceleration, *a*:

- Resultant force, *F* = *ma*
- $a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{2.672}{0.408}=6.55$ m s<sup>–2 </sup>**[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**** **

> *It is important to understand the direction of forces to understand this question. There isn’t just the weight force pushing the spring downwards, but since the spring has been stretched when released it will go back to its equilibrium position. This is the upwards force, therefore the resultant force is upwards.*

parts.problemMd:
An adventure experience is shown in Fig. 1.1 below.

![4-7-s-q--q4a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-2-elastic-and-plastic-behaviour/assets/054-4-7-s-q-q4a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The rider is strapped into a rigid harness attached to one end of an elastic rope AB. The rider and the rope behave in the same way as a mass–spring system.

The rope has an unstretched length of 23 m. When stretched, the rope obeys Hooke’s law. The rider and harness have a total mass of 65 kg.

The rider is initially held at rest at ground level. The lower end of rope B is attached to the rigid harness at a point which is 3.1 m above the ground, so the harness doesn’t injure the rider by being too close. The top end of the rope, A, is adjusted so the rope becomes unstretched when the rider is at the highest point of the ride. The rider is released and moves upwards, reaching a maximum height when the rope is at its unstretched (natural) length. The rider then oscillates vertically.

The height of point A above the ground is 51 m.

Calculate the spring constant of the rope neglecting air resistance and ignoring the mass of the rope in this question.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Unstretched length, *L* = 23 m
- Height of** **B above the ground, *x* = 3.1 m
- Mass of rider and harness, *m* = 65 kg
- Height of** **A above the ground, *h* = 51 m

Calculate the extension, Δ*L*:

- Since the rider is at their maximum height when the rope is unstretched, this means Δ*L* is the amplitude of the oscillations of the rider
- *h* = *x* + Δ*x + *Δ*x + L*
- *2*Δ*L *= *h – x – L *= 51 – 3.1 – 23 = 24.9
- Δ*L* = $\frac{24.9}{2}=12.45$ m **[1 mark]*** *

Compared forces on the rider in equilibrium:

- When the rider eventually comes to rest, suspended above the ground, their force downwards (weight) will equal the force upwards from Hooke’s law
- So, *mg* = *k*Δ*x ***[1 mark]**

Calculate the spring constant, *k*:

- $k=\frac{mg}{\Deltax}=\frac{65\times9.81}{12.45}=51.22$ N m<sup>–1 </sup>
- $k = 51 \mathrm{N} \mathrm{m}^{- 1} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$<sup> </sup>**[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**** **

> *Although the calculations for this question are not necessarily difficult, the setup of the question requires some thinking. Drawing a free-body diagram can help visualise which forces and distances are required here. The important part is that **A** is adjusted so that the rope is unstretched when the rider reaches the maximum amplitude of their oscillation (i.e. the rope doesn’t go completely slack and continue upwards from the force, and instead is still vertically downwards, just unstretched). *

> *This means that the combination of the initial height above the ground (**x**) the maximum (Δ**L**) and minimum amplitude (Δ**L**) of the oscillation (which is the extension of the rope due to the rider) **and** the unstretched length of the rope (**L**) all make up the distance from the ground to point A (**h**).*

![92cf5d8f-bb72-418a-a831-8f97960b7405](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-2-elastic-and-plastic-behaviour/assets/055-92cf5d8f-bb72-418a-a831-8f97960b7405.jpeg)

> *The second half of the diagram shows the movement of the rider from the start to its final position at equilibrium (the rider and the harness is represented by the circle as a point mass. Art is not my strong point). In practice, the rider’s oscillations will become smaller and smaller till they reach equilibrium and at rest. This is where their weight downwards is equal to the force upwards due to Hooke’s law.*

parts.problemMd:
A different ride consists of a 15 m length of rope, stretched into a ‘V’ shape PQR on a frame, as shown in Fig 1.2. The frame is 16 m wide and the rider stands in the middle at position R. The ends of the elastic rope are fixed to the frame at the point P and Q.

![6-2-q2b-h-sq-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/6-deformation-of-solids/6-2-elastic-and-plastic-behaviour/assets/056-6-2-q2b-h-sq-cie-ial-physics.png)

The rider is attached to the midpoint of the elastic rope at** **R. The Young Modulus of the rope is 1920 Pa, and the cross-sectional area of the rope is 1 m<sup>2</sup>.

Calculate the elastic potential energy of the elastic rope in the initial position shown in the diagram.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Young Modulus = 1920 N
- Unstretched length of rope, *L* = 15 m

Calculate the extension of the rope:

- The final length of the rope is 2 × PR (or 2 × RQ)
- PR = $\sqrt{8^{2}+15^{2}}$ = 17 m
- Final length = 2 × 17 = 34 m
- Extension, *x *= 34 – *L* = 34 – 15 = 19 m **[1 mark]**

Calculate the spring constant, *k*:

- Young Modulus =$\frac{FL}{Ax}$
- From Hooke’s Law: *F* = *kx*
- Young Modulus =* *$kx\times\frac{L}{\Deltax}=kL$* ***[1 mark]**
- $k=\frac{Youngmodulus}{L}=\frac{1920}{15}=128$ N m<sup>–1 </sup>**[1 mark]*** *

Calculate the elastic potential energy, *E*:

- *E* = $\frac{1}{2}$*k *(Δ*x*)<sup>2</sup> = $\frac{1}{2}$ × 128 × (19)<sup>2</sup> = 23104 = 23 000 J (23 kJ) **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Circular water waves are produced by vibrating dippers at points P and Q, as illustrated in Fig. 4.1.

![q4b-paper-2-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/7-waves/7-1-progressive-waves/assets/025-q4b-paper-2-specimen-2022-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 4.1** (not to scale)

The waves from P alone have the same amplitude at point R as the waves from Q alone. Distance PR is 44 cm and distance QR is 29 cm.

The dippers vibrate in phase with a period of 1.5 s to produce waves of speed 4.0 cm s<sup>–1</sup>.

(i) Calculate the wavelength of the waves.

wavelength = .................................................... cm [2]

(ii) Calculate the path difference at point R of the waves from P and Q.

Give your answer in terms of the wavelength λ of the waves.

path difference = ....................................................... λ [1]

(iii) Describe the motion, if any, of the water particles at point R.

Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Wave speed, $v$ = 4.0 cm s<sup>–1</sup>
- Time period, $T=\frac{1}{f}$ = 1.5 s
- Distance PR = 44 cm
- Distance QR = 29 cm

i) Use the wave equation to determine wavelength, $λ$:

- $v=fλ$
- $λ=\frac{v}{f}$ **[1 mark]**
- $λ$ = 4.0 × 1.5 = 6.0 cm **[1 mark]**

ii) Calculate the path difference at point R of the waves from P and Q:

- The difference between distances PR and QR = 44 − 29 = 15 cm
- Number of wavelengths in 15 cm = $\frac{15}{6}=\frac{5}{2}$ = 2.5
- Path difference = 2.5$λ$ or $\frac{5}{2}λ$ **[1 mark]** ** **

iii) Describe the motion, if any, of the water particles at point R:

- The path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths **OR **the waves have a phase difference of 180°; **[1 mark]**
- (This results in destructive interference, hence) the particles are at rest / have no motion; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Spotting that *$λ=\frac{v}{f}=v\times\frac{1}{f}=v\timesT$* can save you some time in part (i)*
- *Remember to state **path difference** as a **multiple of wavelength** for part (ii)*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 represents a progressive wave travelling from left to right on a stretched string. The frequency of the wave is 30 Hz.

Describe how the vertical displacement of point **X** on the string varies in the next period.
parts.solutionMd:
To describe how the vertical displacement of point **X** on the string varies in the next period:

First  $\frac{1}{4}$  cycle:

- Displacement of X will be **positive** (or ‘**up’**) to a maximum positive displacement; **[1 mark]**

Next  $\frac{1}{2}$  cycle:

- **Downwards** to equilibrium position ($\frac{1}{4}$ cycle) **and **maximum negative displacement ( $\frac{1}{4}$ cycle); **[1 mark]**

Last  $\frac{1}{4}$  cycle:

- **Upwards** to equilibrium position / zero displacement; **[1 mark]**

*If the motion of X is 180 degrees out of phase with the one shown then a maximum of two marks can be gained (i.e. X initially moving downwards)*

*Accept 0.008 s for  *$\frac{1}{4}$* cycle and 0.017 for *$\frac{1}{2}$* cycle*

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Visualising the subsequent motion of a point on the wave is tricky. The wave is travelling to the right hand side, so it's subsequent motion will be the wave motion drawn **behind** it. *

parts.problemMd:

Fig. 1.1 represents a progressive wave travelling from left to right on a stretched string. The frequency of the wave is 30 Hz.

Determine the phase difference between the current position of **X** and the position of **X** 0.0825 s later.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Frequency, *f *= 30 Hz (From part (a))

To determine the phase difference between the current position of **X** and the position of **X** 0.0825 s later:

Calculate the time period of 1 wave cycle:

- 1 period = $\frac{1}{f}$= $\frac{1}{30}$ = 0.033 s

Determine the number of wave cycles in 0.0825 s:

- 0.0825 s is $\frac{0.0825}{0.033}$= 2.5 complete cycles **[1 mark]**

Determine the phase difference over 2.5 cycles:

- The phase difference of 1 cycle = 360 °
- So, the phase difference of ½ cycle = 180°
- (Therefore, there is a) phase difference of 180° / $π$ radians / anti-phase (between the two positions of **X**) **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Remember that a phase difference of 360 degrees is a complete 1 wavelength cycle, so there is actually no phase difference. *

parts.problemMd:
While a microphone is connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope, a student strikes a tuning fork nearby. The sound wave produced by the tuning fork is displayed as a trace on the screen.

Fig. 1.2 shows the resulting trace. The time-base and gain are given on the screen.

![3-1-s-q--q1b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/7-waves/7-1-progressive-waves/assets/015-3-1-s-q-q1b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Use Fig. 1.2** **to calculate the wavelength of the sound wave produced.

(The speed of sound is approximately 330 m s<sup>–1</sup>).
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Wave speed, *v* = 330 m s<sup>–1</sup>

Determine the time period of the oscilloscope trace using the time-base:

- The time-base on the X-axis is set to a scale of 400 μs / div
- Therefore, each division represents 400 × 10<sup>–6</sup> s
- One time period is 4 divisions (shown below); **[1 mark]**

![3-1-s-q--q1b-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/7-waves/7-1-progressive-waves/assets/016-3-1-s-q-q1b-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

- Therefore, time period (one full cycle), *T *= 4 × (400 × 10<sup>–6</sup>) = 1.6 × 10<sup>–3</sup> s **[1 mark] **

Calculate the frequency of the wave:

- *f* = $\frac{1}{T}$
- *f* = $\frac{1}{1.6\times10^{-3}}$= 625 Hz **[1 mark] **

Use the wave speed equation to calculate the wavelength of the sound wave:

- *v = fλ*
- 330 = 625 × *λ*
- *λ* =$\frac{330}{625}$ = 0.53 m **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
A cathode-ray oscilloscope (C.R.O.) is used to trace the ultrasound pulses sent from the boat and the reflected pulses returning to the boat. The C.R.O. trace is shown in Fig. 1.2.

![sl-sq-4-2-hard-q3b-trace-of-ultrasound-pulses](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/7-waves/7-1-progressive-waves/assets/024-sl-sq-4-2-hard-q3b-trace-of-ultrasound-pulses.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

The ultrasound travels through water at 1452 m s<sup>−1</sup>, and the wavelength of the pulse is 0.023 m.

For the ultrasound pulses:

(i) Calculate the frequency

[1]

(ii) Calculate the distance to the sea bed

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) For the ultrasound pulses, calculate the frequency, *f:*

List the known quantities:

- Speed of ultrasound wave in water, *v* = 1452 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Wavelength of ultrasound pulse, *λ *= 0.023 m

Using the wave speed equation:

- $v=fλ\rightarrowf=\frac{v}{λ}$
- $f=\frac{1452}{0.023}$ = 63130 Hz **[1 mark]**

(ii) For the ultrasound pulses, calculate the distance to the sea bed:

From the graph determine the time taken for the pulse to reach the sea bed:

- The tall pulses are those sent from the boat, the small pulses are those reflected from the sea floor
- The time between the tall emitted pulse and the smaller echo is two divisions of the axis

  - Each division of the axis is 0.10 s
  - Therefore, the time between sending and receiving the pulses is 0.20 s
- However, the pulse travels from the boat to the sea bed and back in this time

  - Therefore, the time taken to reach the sea bed is 0.10 s
  - *t* = 0.10 s **[1 mark]**
- $v=\frac{d}{t}$

  - Therefore, *d* = *vt*
  - *d = *1452 × 0.10 = 145.2 m **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Ultrasound is used to measure the depth of oceans, seas and lakes. Fig. 1.1 shows a pulse of ultrasound being emitted from the boat, travelling down to the sea bed and being reflected back to the boat.

A cathode-ray oscilloscope (C.R.O.) is used to trace the ultrasound pulses sent from the boat and the reflected pulses returning to the boat. The C.R.O. trace is shown in Fig. 1.2. The ultrasound travels through water at 1452 m s^−1^, and the wavelength of the pulse is 0.023 m.

The boat moves out to an area where the sea is deeper.

(i) State and explain two changes that would occur on the cathode-ray oscilloscope trace. You may include diagrams in your answer.

[4]

(ii) When the sea is over 450 m deep, the pulses must be transmitted less frequently. Explain why this is the case.

parts.solutionMd:
(i) State and explain two changes that would occur on the cathode-ray oscilloscope trace:

**Change 1**

State change 1:

- The <u>horizontal separation</u> between the transmitted pulse and the reflected pulse will <u>increase;</u> **[1 mark]**

Explain change 1:

- The sea is deeper so the <u>distance</u> travelled by the pulses <u>increases</u>, and will therefore <u>take longer</u> to reach the sea bed, (and longer to return); **[1 mark]**

**Change 2**

State change 2:

- The <u>amplitude</u> of the <u>reflected pulses</u> will be <u>smaller / decrease</u>; **[1 mark]**

Explain change 2:

- Some of the <u>energy is absorbed by</u> the surrounding <u>water</u>. Since they have to travel through a <u>greater depth</u> of water, <u>more energy will be lost;</u> **[1 mark]**

(ii) When the sea is over 450 m deep, the pulses must be transmitted less frequently. Explain why this is the case

Calculate the time taken between the transmission and detection of each pulse at 450 m:

- $t=\frac{d}{v}=\frac{450\times2}{1452}$ = 0.6 s** [1 mark]**

Explain why this means the pulses must be transmitted less frequently:

- The cathode-ray oscilloscope trace shows that the pulses are transmitted <u>every 0.6 s</u>; **[1 mark]**
- <u>At a depth of 450 m</u>, the reflected pulses would coincide with / arrive at the same time as the transmitted pulses;** [1 mark]**
- <u>At greater depths</u>, the reflected pulses would be detected after subsequent / the next pulses have been transmitted; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A scientist is conducting an experiment on bees. Fig 1.1 shows the set up monitoring equipment near a hive, including a microphone which picks up the buzz from individual bees flying past. A single bee flies at a constant speed in a straight line past the microphone, and the frequency of the buzz is detected.

The speed of the bee is 8.9 m s<sup>−1</sup>. The maximum frequency of sound recorded by the microphone is 271 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

(i) Calculate the frequency of sound produced by the bee.

[2]

(ii) Determine the minimum frequency recorded by the microphone.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Speed of the bee, *u*<sub>s</sub>* *= 8.9 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Maximum frequency of sound, *f*<sub>max</sub><sub>* *</sub>= 271 Hz
- Speed of sound in air, *v* = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>

From the formula page:

- $f_{0} = f_{S} \frac{v}{( v \pm u_{s} )}$

(i) To determine the frequency of sound produced by the bee, *f*<sub>*S*</sub>:

State the conditions for maximum frequency of sound:

- The maximum frequency is found when the bee is moving towards the microphone
- Therefore, the equation becomes $f_{0} = f_{S} \frac{v}{( v - u_{s} )}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation and substitute in values to find* f*:

- $f_{0}(v-u_{s})=f_{S}v$
- $f_{S}=\frac{f_{0}(v-u_{s})}{v}$
- $f_{S}=\frac{271\times(340-8.9)}{340}=264\mathrm{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) To determine the minimum frequency of sound recorded by the microphone, *f*<sub>min</sub>:

State the conditions for minimum frequency of sound:

- The minimum frequency is found when the bee is moving away from the microphone
- Therefore, the equation becomes $f_{0} = f_{S} ( \frac{v}{v + u_{s} } )$  **[1 mark]**

Calculate minimum *f*<sub>*S*</sub>*:*

- $f_{0} = 264 \times ( \frac{340}{340 + 8.9} ) = 257 \text{Hz}$  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The approximation equation, *$\frac{Δλ}{λ}=\frac{v}{c}$*, cannot be used as the speed of sound is too similar in magnitude to the speed of the bee.*

- Speed of sound in air, *v* = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>

From the formula page:

- $f_{0} = f_{S} \frac{v}{( v \pm v_{s} )}$

Calculate the frequency heard by the observer, *f*<sub>*0*</sub>*:*

- A source moving <u>towards</u> a stationary observer has a denominator $(v-v_{s})$
- Therefore, the equation becomes $f_{0} = f_{S} \frac{v}{( v - v_{s} )}$
- $f_{0} = 650 \times ( \frac{340}{340 - 13.4} )$ = 677 Hz **[1 mark]**

Determine the change in frequency, Δ*f*:

- $\Deltaf=f_{0}-f_{S}=677-650=27\mathrm{Hz}$  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *This is a straightforward question, with a twist that you're being asked for the change in frequency, Δ**f **not just the observed frequency, **f*<sub>*0*</sub>*.** This means an extra step is required to calculate Δ**f**.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

An ambulance siren emits two pure sounds. The lower of the two sounds has a frequency of 650 Hz. It is travelling towards a stationary observer at 13.4 m s^−1^. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s^−1^.

Calculate the change in frequency, Δf, between the source frequency and that heard by the observer. (From part (a): observed frequency f0 = 677 Hz, Δf = 27 Hz)

The ratio between the two frequencies emitted by the ambulance is 0.722.

(i) Determine the second frequency as heard by the observer.

[4]

(ii) Explain the effect a change in speed of the ambulance will have on the ratio between the two observed frequencies.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Lower frequency emitted sound, *f*<sub>*S*</sub>* *<sub>1</sub> = 650 Hz (from part (a))
- Lower frequency observed sound, *f*<sub>*0 *</sub><sub>1</sub><sub>* *</sub>= 677 Hz (from part (a))
- Higher frequency emitted sound = *f*<sub>*S 2*</sub>
- Higher frequency observed sound *= f*<sub>*O 2*</sub>
- Speed of sound, *v* = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Speed of ambulance, *v*<sub>s</sub> = 13.4 m s<sup>−1</sup>

(i) Describe the relationship between the ratio of observed frequencies and the ratio of emitted frequencies:

- The ratio between the two emitted frequencies is the same as the ratio between the two frequencies as heard by the observer; **[1 mark]**

Determine the higher frequency of emitted sound, *f*<sub>*S*</sub>* *<sub>2</sub>:

- $\frac{f_{S1}}{f_{S2}}=0.722$
- $f_{S1}=0.722\timesf_{S2}$
- $f_{S2}=\frac{f_{S1}}{0.722}=\frac{650}{0.722}=900$ Hz **[1 mark]**

Determine the higher frequency of observed sound, *f*<sub>O 2</sub>

- $f_{O 2} = f_{s 2} \frac{v}{( v - v_{s} )} = 900 \times \frac{340}{( 340 - 13.4 )}$ **[1 mark]**
- $f_{O2}=937\mathrm{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) The effect of a change in the speed of the ambulance on the observed frequencies:

- If the ambulance is moving faster the observed frequencies will both be higher **OR**
- If the ambulance is moving slower the observed frequencies will both be lower; **[1 mark]**

- However, the ratio between them will remain at 0.722; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *In part (ii) the key is to recognise that whilst speed will change the pitch of the observed frequencies, the ratio between them does not change. This is because both emitted frequencies are multiplied by the same factor, *$( \frac{v}{v - v_{s} } )$*.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The speed of sound in air is 340 m s^−1^.

As the ambulance approaches a red light at which a number of cars are stopped, it changes its siren to a single monotone sound which the car drivers observe as 700 Hz. The ambulance slows further to 5.3 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Observed wavelength can be calculated using the following equation:

$lambda_{0} = lambda_{S} ( 1 \pm v_\frac{{s}}{v} )$

Calculate the wavelength of sound emitted by the ambulance.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Frequency of observed sound, *f*<sub>*0*</sub>* *= 700 Hz
- Speed of the ambulance, *v*<sub>*s*</sub> = 5.3 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Speed of sound, *v* = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>

Calculate wavelength of the observed sound:

- $v=fλ$
- $λ_{0}=\frac{v}{f_{0}}=\frac{340}{700}$= 0.486 m **[1 mark]**

State the conditions for calculating the observed wavelength from a source moving away from the observer:

- When a source is moving towards the observer, the operator in the brackets will be '−'
- Therefore, the equation $lambda_{o} = lambda_{S} ( 1 - v_\frac{{s}}{v} )$ is used; **[1 mark]**

Substitute in values and calculate the wavelength, *λ *of sound emitted by the ambulance:

- $lambda_{o} = lambda_{s} ( 1 - v_\frac{{s}}{v} )$
- $lambda_{S} = \frac{lambda_{o}}{ ( 1 - v_\frac{{s}}{v} ) } = \frac{0.486}{ ( 1 - \frac{5.3}{340} ) }$ **[1 mark]**

- Therefore, *λ *= 0.494 m **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Make sure you know which operators to use with each equation: it is dependent on whether it is the source is moving or the observer, and on whether the motion is towards or away from each other.*

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows a stationary wave source, R, emitting a sound wave. The source produces waves with a constant frequency. The distance between each successive wavefront is equal to the wavelength of the waves produced by R.

![7-3-m-q3a-sq-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/7-waves/7-3-doppler-effect-for-sound-waves/assets/005-7-3-m-q3a-sq-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The speed of sound in air is *v*.

Sketch three successive wavefronts produced when the source is moving to the right at a speed of 0.75*v*.
parts.solutionMd:
A sketch which would obtain 2 marks is:

![9-5-doppler-hl-saqs-medium-q4a-ms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/7-waves/7-3-doppler-effect-for-sound-waves/assets/006-9-5-doppler-hl-saqs-medium-q4a-ms.png)

- The time between the emission of each wavefront from the source = time period, *T*

  - $\mathrm{time} \mathrm{period} \mathrm{of}a\mathrm{wave},T=\frac{1}{\mathrm{wave} \mathrm{frequency},f}$
- The distance travelled by each wavefront is given by $s=vt$
- If *t* = *T*, then:

  - $s=vT=\frac{v}{f}$
- Since $v=f\timesλ$

  - $\frac{v}{f}=λ=s$
- Therefore, the distance travelled by the wavefront in one time period, *T* = *λ* **[1 mark]**

- The source is moving at 0.75v. Therefore, at the same time, the source has moved 0.75*λ*

  - This is one and a half a square on the diagram
  - Therefore, for each successive wavefront the centre of the circle will be half a square further on;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *To construct the diagram, it is easiest to think about where the source will have moved to in a unit time, i.e. 0.75**v** each time. This means the wavefront which has travelled the furthest (largest diameter) will be centred on 0.75**λ** from point R (1.5 squares). The next wavefront at 1.5**λ **(3 squares) and the final one at 2.25**λ** (4.5 squares).*

parts.problemMd:
A train is travelling at 45 m s<sup>−1</sup> and blows a whistle at a frequency of 750 Hz. A person is waiting at a level crossing for the train to pass. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Calculate the frequency observed by the person:

(i) In still air.

[1]

(ii) When the wind is blowing at 10 m s<sup>−1</sup> towards the train and away from the person.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Speed of the train, $v_{s}$= 45 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Frequency of the source, $f$ = 750 Hz
- Speed of sound, $v$ = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Wind speed = 10 m s<sup>−1</sup>

(i) Substitute in values and calculate the observed frequency in still air:

- Recall the Doppler Equation: $f_{0} = f_{s} ( \frac{v}{v \pm v_{s} } )$
- The source is moving towards the observer, therefore the operator in the denominator is −
- $f_{0} = 750 ( \frac{340}{340 - 45} ) = 864 \text{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) To calculate the frequency observed when the wind is blowing at 10 m s<sup>−1</sup> towards the train and away from the person:

Determine the speed of sound in the wind:

- Sound travelling from the train to the observer moves against the wind, reducing its effective speed
- New speed of sound = 340 − 10 = 330 m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

Substitute in known values and calculate the observed frequency:

- $f_{0} = 750 ( \frac{330}{330 - 45} ) = 868 \text{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *"A person is waiting at a level crossing for the train to pass". This tells us that the train is travelling towards the observer. *

> *Remember that velocity is a vector, so the wind is travelling in the opposite direction to the train, so it will be **negative**.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A train is travelling at 45 m s^−1^ and blows a whistle at a frequency of 750 Hz. A person is waiting at a level crossing for the train to pass. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^−1^.

After the train passes the level crossing, it slows down as it approaches a tunnel. Wind is funnelled down the tunnel towards the train reaching a velocity of 27 m s<sup>−1</sup>. The observer at the level crossing hears the whistle at a frequency of 729 Hz.

Calculate the new speed of the train.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Speed of the wind = 27 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Observed frequency, $f_{0}$= 729 Hz
- Frequency of the whistle, $f_{s}$ = 750 Hz (from part (a))
- Speed of sound, $v$ = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup> (from part (a))

Calculate the new speed of sound taking the wind into effect:

- $v_{new}=340-27=313$ m s<sup>−1</sup> **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the Doppler equation to make $v_{s}$ the subject:

- Recall the Doppler equation: $f_{0} = f_{s} ( \frac{v}{v \pm v_{s} } )$
- The train is moving away from the observer, and so the operator is +
- $\frac{f_{0}}{f_{s}v}=\frac{1}{v+v_{s}}$
- $v+v_{s}=\frac{f_{s}v}{f_{0}}$
- $v_{s}=\frac{f_{s}v}{f_{0}}-v$

Substitute in known quantities and calculate $u_{s}$:

- $v_{s}=\frac{750\times313}{729}-313=9.02ms^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Read the question carefully. The wind is blowing towards the train (i.e. against the direction of sound travel from train to observer), so it reduces the effective speed of sound. This is why the effective speed of sound is 313 m s⁻¹. Note the difference between the frequency emitted by the whistle and the frequency heard by the observer and don't mix them up!*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A train is travelling at 45 m s^−1^ and blows a whistle at a frequency of 750 Hz. A person is waiting at a level crossing for the train to pass. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^−1^.

After exiting the tunnel, the train stops at a station. The observer from part (a) is now walking to the platform to catch the train at a speed of 1.5 m s<sup>−1</sup>. The human ear can distinguish between frequency differences of around 3.6 Hz.

The Doppler equation for a moving observer is:

$f_{o} = f_{s} ( \frac{v \pm v_{o} }{v} )$

Show that the change in frequency of the train's whistle, as heard by the walking observer, can be considered negligible.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Frequency of the whistle, $f$ = 750 Hz (from part (a))
- Speed of the observer $v_{o}$= 1.5 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Speed of sound in air, $v$ = 340 m (from part (a))
- Resolution of human hearing = 3.6 Hz

From the question:

- $f_{o} = f_{s} ( \frac{v \pm v_{o} }{v} )$

Calculate $f_{0}$:

- $f_{0} = 750 ( \frac{340 + 1.5}{340} ) = 753.3 \text{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

Explain why this frequency change is negligible:

- The resolution of human hearing is around 3.6 Hz

  - Therefore any change in frequency less than this will be undetectable
- The change in frequency heard by the moving observer in this case is 753.3 − 750 = 3.3 Hz

  - This is less than 3.6 Hz
  - Therefore the frequency change can be considered negligible; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Here the walker is moving in the same direction as the train was moving in parts a) and b) towards the platform. It can be helpful to sketch a diagram showing the train journey across the crossing, through the tunnel and to the platform, as there is a lot in each question part.*

> *The observer is moving towards the stationary source so in the equation the numerator is **v + v*<sub>*o*</sub>*, and their velocities are added together.*

> *It is important to recognise also that the person is moving too slowly to observe a change in the frequency of the sound. *

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A train is travelling at 45 m s^−1^ and blows a whistle at a frequency of 750 Hz. A person is waiting at a level crossing for the train to pass. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m s^−1^.

Once the train has left the station, it travels down a line with two tracks. Another train is approaching on the opposite track with a speed of 7.6 m s<sup>−1</sup>. The speed of the departing train is 83% of the speed of the second train.

When both the observer and source are moving, the following equation can be used to determine the new frequency:

$f_{o} = f_{s} ( \frac{v + v_{o} }{v - v_{s} } )$

Calculate the frequency of this same whistle as observed by a passenger on the approaching train as a percentage of $f_{s}$.
parts.solutionMd:

- Speed of approaching train, $v_{o}$= 7.6 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Frequency of the whistle, $f$ = 750 Hz (from part (a))
- Speed of sound, $v$ = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup> (from part (a))

From the question:

- $f_{o} = f_{s} ( \frac{v + v_{o} }{v - v_{s} } )$

Substitute in values and calculate $f_{0}$:

- $f_{0} = 750 \times ( \frac{340 + 7.6}{340 - 6.31} ) = 781 \text{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine $f_{0}$ as a percentage of $f_{s}$:

- $\frac{781}{750} = 1.04 = 104 \%$ of $f$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A racing car is travelling at 300 km h<sup>−1</sup> on a race track.

![e9p28~EB_9-5-ib-hl-sqs-hard-q2a-question](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/7-waves/7-3-doppler-effect-for-sound-waves/assets/004-e9p28-eb-9-5-ib-hl-sqs-hard-q2a-question.png)

The stationary observer hears a frequency of sound of 1550 Hz from the exhaust as the car approaches them (position 1). You can assume the speed of sound to be 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>.

Determine the frequency of sound heard by:

(i) A stationary observer standing next to the track as the car passes (position 2) .

[1]

(ii) A stationary observer standing next to the track behind the current position of the car (position 3).

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Speed of the car, $v_{s}$= 300 km h<sup>−1</sup>
- Frequency of sound heard by the stationary observer in front of the car, $f_{o}$ = 1550 Hz
- Speed of sound in air, $v$ = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup>

(i) To determine the frequency of the sound heard by a stationary observer as the car passes:

Note the relationship between $f_{s}$ and $f_{0}$ in this situation:

- At that instant, the radial component of the car’s velocity is zero, so there is no Doppler shift

  - Therefore, the frequency heard by the observer will be equal to that emitted by the car exhaust, $f_{s}$

Convert 300 km h<sup>−1</sup> to m s<sup>−1</sup>:

- 1 km h<sup>−1</sup> = $\frac{1000}{3600}$m s<sup>−1</sup>
- 300 km h<sup>−1</sup> = $\frac{1000}{3600}\times300=83.3$ m s<sup>−1</sup>

Substitute in known values to the Doppler equation and calculate $f$:

- Recall the Doppler equation: $f_{0} = f_{s} ( \frac{v}{v \pm v_{s} } )$
- The car is moving towards the original observer and so the denominator is −
- $1550 = f_{s} ( \frac{340}{340 - 83.3} )$
- $f_{s}=\frac{1550\times256.7}{340}=1170\mathrm{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) To determine the frequency heard by the stationary observer as the car moves away:

Substitute in known values and calculate $f_{0}$:

- The car is moving away from the observer so the denominator is +
- $f_{0} = 1170 ( \frac{340}{340 + 83.3} ) = 940 \text{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A racing car is travelling at 300 km h^−1^ on a race track. The stationary observer hears a frequency of sound of 1550 Hz from the exhaust as the car approaches them (position 1). You can assume the speed of sound to be 340 m s^−1^. Speed of the car, v_s = 300 km h^−1^; Frequency of sound heard by the stationary observer in front of the car, f_o = 1550 Hz; Speed of sound in air, v = 340 m s^−1^. Convert 300 km h^−1^ to m s^−1^: 300 km h^−1^ = 83.3 m s^−1^. Using the Doppler equation f_0 = f_s(v/(v ± v_s)): 1550 = f_s(340/(340 − 83.3)), f_s = 1170 Hz (frequency emitted by the car at 300 km h^−1^).

The car from part (a) opens its Drag Reduction System (DRS) increasing its top speed by 10 km h<sup>−1</sup>. It then overtakes another car which is travelling at 300 km h<sup>−1</sup>.

The equation which can be used when both source and observer are moving is:

$f_{o} = f_{s} ( \frac{v \pm v_{o} }{v \pm v_{s} } )$

The frequency of the sound emitted by the car exhaust is directly proportional to the speed. When the maximum frequency is observed then $v\pmv_{o}$ and $v\pmv_{s}$ are both at their minimum.

Calculate the maximum and minimum frequency of sound heard from the faster car, as heard by the driver of the car being overtaken during this manoeuvre.
parts.solutionMd:
State the known quantities:

- Speed of observer, $v_{o}$= 300 km h<sup>−1</sup> = 83.3 m s<sup>−1</sup> (from part (a))
- Maximum speed of source, $v_{smax}$= 310 km h<sup>−1</sup> = 86.1 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Frequency emitted by a car at 300 km h<sup>−1</sup>, $f_{o}$= 1170 Hz (from part (a))
- Speed of sound in air, *v* = 340 m s<sup>−1</sup> (from part (a))

From the question:

- $f_{0} = f_{s} ( \frac{v \pm v_{o} }{v \pm v_{s} } )$

Calculate $f_{s}$ when the source and observer are stationary:

- Frequency is directly proportional to the speed
- Rearrange $f_{0} = f_{s} ( \frac{v \pm v_{o} }{v \pm v_{s} } )$ and make *v *= 0 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Therefore, $f_{s} = 1170 \times ( \frac{86.1}{83.3} ) = 1209 \text{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the nature of the operators when the observed frequency is at a maximum:

- Maximum frequency is observed when the faster car is catching the slower car
- When the source is moving towards the observer, the operators will be consistent with the denominators when only one is moving
- The source is moving towards the observer: **AND**

  - $v-v_{s}$ in the denominator
- The observer is moving away from the source (or at least trying to!)

  - $v-v_{o}$ in the numerator; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the maximum frequency:

- $f_{0} = f_{s} ( \frac{v - v_{o} }{v - v_{s} } ) = 1209 \times ( \frac{340 - 83.3}{340 - 86.1} ) = 1222 \text{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the nature of the operators when the observed frequency is at a minimum:

- Minimum frequency is observed when the faster car is pulling away from the slower car
- When the source is moving away from the observer, the operators will be consistent with the denominators when only one is moving.
- The source is moving away from the observer: **AND**

  - $v+v_{s}$ in the denominator
- The observer is moving towards the source (or at least trying to!)

  - $v+v_{o}$ in the numerator; **[1 mark]**

Calculate the minimum frequency:

$f_{o} = f_{s} ( \frac{v + v_{o} }{v + v_{s} } ) = 1209 \times ( \frac{340 + 83.3}{340 + 86.1} ) = 1201 \text{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Here the overtaking car is the source and the car being overtaken the observer. To determine the operators in the equation for maximum frequency (when the faster car is behind), consider that the source is driving towards the observer, and the observer is driving away from the source, only more slowly.*

- *This gives *$v-v_{o}$* in the numerator and *
- $v-v_{s}$* in the denominator*

parts.problemMd:
A different scientist uses a speed gun to observe the speed of the car in part c). The car has a speed of 11.7 m s<sup>−1</sup>. The speed gun emits microwaves of wavelength 20 cm and measures the change in frequency between the emitted and received microwaves which is calculated using the equation:

$\Deltaf=\frac{2fv}{c}$

Where:

- *f *is the frequency of the emitted microwaves
- *v *is the speed of the approaching car
- *c *is the speed of the microwaves through the air

Calculate the frequency of the microwaves received by the speed gun. Give your answer as accurately as required.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Speed of car, $v_{car}$ = 11.7 m s<sup>−1</sup>
- Wavelength of microwaves, $λ$ = 20 cm = 0.20 m
- Speed of light in free space, $c$* = *3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>

Determine the frequency of the emitted microwaves, $f$:

- Recall the wave equation: $v=fλ$
- $f=\frac{v}{λ}$
- $f=\frac{3.00\times10^{8}}{0.2}$
- $f=1.5\times10^{9}\mathrm{Hz}$  **OR** 1.5 GHz **[1 mark]**

Calculate the change in frequency, $\Deltaf$ detected by the gun:

- From the question: $\Deltaf=\frac{2fv}{c}$
- $\Deltaf=\frac{2\times58.5\times11.7}{3.00\times10^{8}}$
- $\Deltaf=117\mathrm{Hz}$  **[1 mark]**

Calculate the frequency detected by the gun, $f_{d}$:

- $\Deltaf=f_{d}-f$
- $f_{d}=\Deltaf+f$
- $f_{d}=117+1.5\times10^{9}$
- $f_{d}=1500000117\mathrm{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The change in frequency is really small, so don't let that confuse you. You must give your answer fully to show that the detected frequency is different to the emitted frequency. *

parts.problemMd:
A satellite passing Neptune communicates with Earth using a microwave transmitter with an output power of 24.0 W and wavelength 78 900 µm.

The satellite's controller is located on Earth, at a distance of 4.40 × 10<sup>12 </sup>m when the signal is transmitted.

For this communication

(i) Calculate the time taken for the signal to be detected by the controller.

[1]

(ii) Calculate the energy of a microwave photon.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the time taken for the signal to be detected by the controller:

List the known quantities:

- Distance from satellite to controller, *s* = 4.40 × 10<sup>12 </sup>m
- Speed of light in free space, *c* = 3.00 × 10<sup>8 </sup>m s<sup>−1</sup> (from the data page)

Using the speed equation, calculate time taken:

- $v=\frac{d}{t}\rightarrowt=\frac{d}{v}$
- $t=\frac{4.40\times10^{12}}{3.00\times10^{8}}$ = 1.47 × 10<sup>4</sup> s** [1 mark]  **

(ii) Calculate the energy of a microwave photon:

List the known quantities:

- Wavelength of microwave, *λ* = 78 900 µm
- Planck constant, *h* = 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s (from the data page)

Combine the photon energy and wave speed equations to give a formula for energy using wavelength:

- Wave speed, $v=fλ$ and photon energy, $E=hf$
- $E=\frac{hc}{λ}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known values to calculate the energy of a microwave photon:

- $E = \frac{( 6.63 \times 10^{- 34} ) \times ( 3.00 \times 10^{8 )}{78900 \times 10^{-6} } }$ = 2.52 × 10<sup>−24</sup> J (3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A satellite passing Neptune communicates with Earth using a microwave transmitter with an output power of 24.0 W and wavelength 78 900 µm. The satellite's controller is located on Earth, at a distance of 4.40 × 10^12 m when the signal is transmitted.

(ii) Calculate the energy of a microwave photon: E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10^−34 × 3.00 × 10^8)/(78900 × 10^−6) = 2.52 × 10^−24 J (3 s.f.)

The controller dish aerial has an effective area of 258 m<sup>2</sup>.

For the communication from part (b)

(i) Determine the power received by the controller dish aerial. You may assume that the power transmitted by the satellite radiates uniformly in all directions.

[2]

(ii) The actual power received by the controller dish aerial is 1.4 × 10<sup>−15</sup> W. Suggest why this is different to the calculated power received.

[2]

(iii) Calculate the rate at which microwave photons arrive at the controller dish aerial.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Determine the power received by the controller dish aerial:

List the known quantities:

- Output power of satellite = 24.0 W (from part (b))
- Distance from satellite to controller = 4.40 × 10<sup>12</sup> m
- Area of controller dish aerial = 258 m<sup>2</sup>

Devise a formula for the amount of power reaching the controller dish:

- Surface area of a sphere, $A=4πr^{2}$
- Since the power transmitted by the satellite is assumed to radiate uniformly in all directions
- $P=\frac{\mathrm{Output} \mathrm{power}}{4πr^{2}}\times\mathrm{area} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{controller} \mathrm{dish}$** [1 mark]**

Substitute the known values to calculate the power reaching the controller dish:

- $P = \frac{24.0}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 4.40 \times 10^{12} )^{2}} \times 258$ = 2.55 × 10<sup>−23</sup> W (3 s.f.)** [1 mark]**

(ii) The actual power received by the controller dish aerial is 1.4 × 10<sup>−15</sup> W. Suggest why this is different to the calculated power received:

- The calculation <u>assumed that power is radiated uniformly in all directions</u>, but (in reality) the signal emitted by the satellite is directed to Earth (by a dish); **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the calculated power received is less than the actual power received because <u>less power is lost</u> (radiating in different directions); **[1 mark]**

(iii) Calculate the rate at which the microwave photons actually arrive at the controller dish aerial:

List the known quantities:

- Energy of a microwave photon, *E* = 2.52 × 10<sup>−24 </sup>J (from part (b))

Devise a formula for the rate of photon detection:

- $\mathrm{Rate} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{photon} \mathrm{detection}=\frac{\mathrm{Power} \mathrm{received}}{\mathrm{Energy} \mathrm{of}a\mathrm{microwave} \mathrm{photon}}$**[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate the rate of photon detection:

- $\mathrm{Rate} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{photon} \mathrm{detection}=\frac{1.4\times10^{-15}}{2.52\times10^{-24}}$ = 5.6 × 10<sup>8 </sup>s<sup>-1</sup> (2 s.f.)** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *This question is synoptic; it draws on content from multiple topics, as exam questions frequently do. If you need some help with the maths, it is covered in more detail in the *[*Luminosity & Radiant Flux*](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/physics/cie/25/revision-notes/25-astronomy-and-cosmology/25-1-standard-candles/luminosity-and-radiant-flux/)* Revision Note.*

parts.solutionMd:

List the known quantities:

Determine the intensity of the polarised light, $I_{1}$ incident on analyser B:

parts.solutionMd:
To determine the intensity of the light leaving analyser B:

List the known quantities:

- Intensity of incident light, $I_{0}$ = 64 W m<sup>−2 </sup>
- Intensity of polarised light, $I_{1}$ = 32 W m<sup>−2 </sup>(from part (b))

parts.problemMd:
Plane-polarised electromagnetic waves are incident on an aerial positioned to give a maximum response.

High winds cause the aerial to rotate anti-clockwise about the plane of the incident wave until it makes an angle of 40° to the plane of wave oscillation.

Calculate the percentage reduction in the amplitude of the signal received by the aerial following the high winds.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Change in direction of the aerial = 40°

Find an expression linking the initial and final amplitude of the waves following polarisation:

- Malus's law: $I=I_{0}\mathrm{cos}^{2}θ$
- Since $I\proptoA^{2}$:

  - $\frac{I}{I} _{0} = ( \frac{A}{A} _{0} )^{2} = \cos ^{2} \\theta$
  - $\frac{A}{A_{0}}=\mathrm{cos}θ$
- Therefore, $A=A_{0}\mathrm{cos}θ$ **[1 mark]**

Find an expression for the percentage reduction:

- $A=A_{0}\mathrm{cos}40$
- Percentage reduction = $\frac{initial \text{amplitude} - \text{final} amplitude}{initial amplitude} \times 100 \%$
- Percentage reduction = $\frac{A_{0} - A_{0} \cos 40}{A_{0} } \times 100 \%$ **[1 mark]**

Evaluate to find percentage reduction:

- $\frac{A_{0} - A_{0} \cos 40}{A_{0} } \times 100 \% = ( 1 - \cos 40 ) \times 100 \% = 23.4 \%$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The high winds cause permanent damage to the aerial. After the aerial is repaired, it remains at an angle of 15° to the plane of wave oscillation and is found to oscillate with an amplitude of 54.0 μm. The intensity of the electromagnetic waves received at this angle is measured to be 0.056 mW m<sup>-2</sup>.

When the aerial is positioned to give a maximum response, it is found to oscillate with an amplitude of 55.9 μm.

Determine the intensity of the incident electromagnetic waves.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Maximum vibration amplitude, $A_{0}$ = 55.9 μm, when $θ=0^{\circ}$
- Measured vibration amplitude, $A$ = 54.0 μm, when $θ=15^{\circ}$
- $A=A_{0}\mathrm{cos}θ$
- $I\proptoA^{2}$

Determine the ratio between the intensities:

- The maximum response is achieved when the aerial is perfectly aligned with the plane of wave oscillation, where $θ=0^{\circ}$ and $I=I_{0}$
- Since intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude:

  - $I_{0}\proptoA_{0}^{2}$
  - $\frac{I}{I} _{0} = ( \frac{A}{A} _{0} )^{2}$
- $\frac{I}{I} _{0} = ( \frac{54.0}{55.9} )^{2} = 0.933$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the incident intensity of the waves:

- $I_{0}=\frac{I}{0.933}$
- $I_{0}=\frac{0.056}{0.933}=0.060\mathrm{mW}m^{-2}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Generally speaking, it’s really good practice to specify angles of rotation in polaroid filter questions. For example, if the intensity of light transmitted behind two polaroid filters is 100% when the two filters are aligned at an angle **θ**, then the light intensity will fall to 0% when this angle is (**θ **+ 90*<sup>*º*</sup>*) and then back up to 100% at (**θ **+ 180*<sup>*º*</sup>*) and back to 0% at (**θ **+ 270*<sup>*º*</sup>*) and then finally back to 100% at (**θ **+ 360*<sup>*º*</sup>*) – yes really, this much detail! You will usually secure full credit for specific descriptions through a full rotation.*

> *However, in this question, it is sufficient to refer to ‘some angle **θ**’ because you are only required to determine if the light is polarised or not. A full description of the effects on the intensity of transmitted light through a full rotation is not required.*

parts.problemMd: Explain the difference between energy transfers in progressive waves and stationary waves.
parts.solutionMd:
The difference between progressive waves and stationary waves are:

- In a progressive wave, energy is transferred along the wave (without transferring the medium);** [1 mark]**
- In a stationary wave, energy is <u>stored</u> / not transferred; **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *In a stationary wave, energy oscillates between kinetic and potential forms within loops but is not transferred along the medium*

parts.problemMd:
Describe the phase difference between two points on

(i) a progressive transverse wave

[1]

(ii) a stationary wave.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) On a progressive transverse wave:

- Two adjacent points vibrate with different phases; **[1 mark]**

(ii) On a stationary wave:

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

- All points between two adjacent nodes vibrate in phase; **[1 mark]**
- If separated by an even number of nodes, two adjacent points vibrate in phase; **[1 mark]**
- If separated by an odd number of nodes, two adjacent points vibrate out of phase; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**** **

> *On **both **progressive and stationary waves, the phase of a particle constantly changes as it vibrates up or down through its cycle*

> *On a **progressive **wave, the phase difference between two points is constantly changing*

- *This phase difference can be described by *$\frac{2πd}{λ}$*, where *$d$* is the distance between the two points*
- *This expression does **not **apply to stationary waves*

> *On a **stationary **wave, two points are either completely in phase or completely out of phase:*

- *When two points are on either side of a node, they are out of phase (phase difference = π)*
- *When two points have none or a factor of two nodes (i.e. 2 nodes, 4 nodes) in between them, they are in phase (phase difference = 0)*

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
Sound waves, like waves on a string, can produce stationary waves inside air columns.

A physics technician demonstrates how sound can set up stationary waves using a tall tube of cross-sectional area 4.0 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m<sup>2</sup> and a loudspeaker connected to a signal generator, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![3-2-s-q--q2a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/8-superposition/8-1-stationary-waves/assets/037-3-2-s-q-q2a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The signal generator is switched on so that sound waves enter the tube. He slowly pours water into the tube and the sound gradually increases in volume, reaching a first maximum at a particular instant. Immediately after the volume begins to decrease.

Water continues to be added until the volume rises again, reaching a second and final maximum after a further 3.2 × 10<sup>–3 </sup>m<sup>3</sup> of water is poured in.

Determine the wavelength of the sound waves.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Cross-sectional area of the tube = 4.0 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m<sup>2</sup>
- Volume of water between two sound maxima = 3.2 × 10<sup>–3 </sup>m<sup>3</sup>

Calculate the length of the water column between the first and second maxima of sound:

- $length=\frac{volume}{area}$
- Therefore, the length of the water column between the first maxima and second maxima = $\frac{3.2\times10^{-3}}{4.0\times10^{-3}}$= 0.8 m **[1mark]**

Calculate the wavelength:

- The length of the water column corresponds to $\frac{1}{2}$*λ*
- Therefore $\frac{1}{2}$*λ *= 0.8 m
- *λ = *0.8 × 2 = 1.6 m **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**** **

> *The first maxima of sound is heard when some water is already inside the tube. This is sketched below:*

![3-2-s-q--q2a-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/8-superposition/8-1-stationary-waves/assets/038-3-2-s-q-q2a-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Sound waves, like waves on a string, can produce stationary waves inside air columns. A physics technician demonstrates how sound can set up stationary waves using a tall tube of cross-sectional area 4.0 × 10^–3 m^2 and a loudspeaker connected to a signal generator. The signal generator is switched on so that sound waves enter the tube. He slowly pours water into the tube and the sound gradually increases in volume, reaching a first maximum at a particular instant.
