parts.problemMd:
Two coherent sources, A and B, which are in phase with each other, emit microwaves of wavelength 40.0 mm.

A detector is placed at the point P where it is 0.93 m from A and 1.19 m from B, as shown in Fig. 1.1. The centre axis is normal and a bisector to the straight line joining A and B.** **

![3-3-s-q--q2a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/8-superposition/8-3-interference/assets/013-3-3-s-q-q2a-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Deduce whether the detected signal at P is a maximum or minimum.
parts.solutionMd:
Deduce whether the detected signal at P is a maximum or minimum:

- Path difference BP – AP = 1.19 – 0.93 = 0.26 m **[1 mark]**
- Number of wavelengths: * *$n=\frac{pathdifference}{wavelength}=\frac{0.26}{40\times10^{-3}}$ = 6.5 **[1 mark]**

Explain the magnitude of the signal at** **P in terms of the phase difference:

- Constructive interference occurs when path difference = $nλ$
- Destructive interference occurs when path difference = $( n + 1 \frac{1}{2} ) \\lambda$

- Since path difference = 6.5λ, microwaves arrive at** **P with a phase difference of 180° (π rad) and interfere destructively
- Therefore, the magnitude of the signal at P is a <u>minimum</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Path difference, in terms of the number of wavelengths, is super popular among examiners – because it links so well with phase difference. And let’s face it: ‘path difference’ and ‘phase difference’ sound very similar – so lots of students are likely to mix them up! *

> *You should practice looking out for the length of a path or ray of light in questions to do with interference – if more than one length is given, you’ll likely need the path difference between them. Then you should always think about that path difference in terms of a multiple of wavelengths. *

> *A subtle point to bear in mind is that this question specifies whether the two sources A and B are coherent and in phase with each other. This means any phase difference is only due to a path difference – i.e., a difference in the distance travelled by each source of waves.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two coherent sources, A and B, which are in phase with each other, emit microwaves of wavelength 40.0 mm. A detector is placed at the point P where it is 0.93 m from A and 1.19 m from B, as shown in Fig. 1.1. The centre axis is normal and a bisector to the straight line joining A and B. Deduce whether the detected signal at P is a maximum or minimum. [Answer: Path difference BP – AP = 1.19 – 0.93 = 0.26 m = 6.5λ, so the signal at P is a minimum. O is on the bisector where AO = BO, path difference = 0 m, so O is a maximum.]

The amplitude of the waves emitted from source B is twice that of the waves emitted from source A.

Calculate the ratio of the intensity at** **P to the intensity at O.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the ratio of the intensity at P to the intensity at O:

List the known quantities:

- Amplitude of waves from source A =* A*
- Amplitude of waves from source B = 2*A*

Determine the amplitude at O:

- The path difference between AO and BO is zero
- Therefore, the amplitude at O is a maximum; **[1 mark]**

Write an expression for the ratio of the intensity at P to the intensity at O in terms of amplitude:

- Intensity:  $I\proptoA^{2}$
- Hence, the ratio:  $\frac{i n t e n s i t y a t P}{i n t e n s i t y a t O} = ( \frac{a m p l i t u d e a t P}{a m p l i t u d e a t O} )^{2}$
- The resultant amplitude at P is a minimum = 2*A – A*
- The resultant amplitude at O is a maximum = 2*A *+ *A*
- Therefore, $( \frac{a m p l i t u d e a t P}{a m p l i t u d e a t O} )^{2} = ( \frac{2 A - A}{2 A + A} )^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Simplify the expression to determine the ratio:

- $\frac{i n t e n s i t y a t P}{i n t e n s i t y a t O} = ( \frac{2 A - A}{2 A + A} )^{2}$= $( \frac{A}{3 A} )^{2}$ = $( 1 \frac{1}{3} )^{2}$= $\frac{1}{9}$
- $\frac{intensityatP}{intensityatO}$ = 0.11 **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *To see why the resultant amplitude at O is given by 2**A** + **A**, remember that this question specifies the centre axis is a bisector to the line joining A and B: in other words, AO and BO are the same length. This means the path difference is 0 m, and therefore waves from A arrive in phase with waves from B; point O has a maximum (resultant) amplitude.*

![3-3-s-q--q2a-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/8-superposition/8-3-interference/assets/014-3-3-s-q-q2a-answer-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

> *Since** **O is a position of maximum resultant amplitude, by the principle of superposition, this is the result of the sum of the two amplitudes which meet: in this case, 2**A** + **A**. *

> *Similarly, the resultant amplitude is minimised at P by 2**A** – **A**.*

Students in a laboratory have created the following set-up shown in Fig 1.1. Parallel rays of monochromatic light from two adjacent slits A and B of wavelength *λ* are incident normally on a diffraction grating with a slit separation *d.*

![9-3-ib-hl-hsq2a-q](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/8-superposition/8-4-the-diffraction-grating/assets/017-9-3-ib-hl-hsq2a-q.png)

parts.solutionMd:
Consider the path difference in terms of wavelength, *λ* when bright fringes are created:

- Constructive interference between two parallel rays of light from two adjacent slits A and B results in bright fringes of light known as maxima; **[1 mark]**
- AC is the path difference between the two parallel rays of light; **[1 mark]**
- Constructive interference occurs when the path difference between the two rays is a whole number of wavelengths

  - Therefore, AC =* nλ, *where *n *is an integer and corresponds to the order of maxima; **[1 mark]**

Consider the path difference in terms of trigonometry:

- Using trigonometry:

  - $sinθ=\frac{AC}{AB}$
  - So, AC = *d *× sin*θ ***[1 mark]**

Equate the two expressions for path difference, AC:

- Therefore the equation to calculate the angle of diffraction, *θ* of each order of maxima *n *is:

  - *nλ *= *d*sin*θ *as required; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:

- The gradient of a straight line, $\frac{\Deltay}{\Deltax}$
- Therefore, $\frac{\Delta\mathrm{sin}θ}{\Deltan}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}θ}{n}$ **[1 mark]**

Consider the gradient of the graph in terms of the diffraction grating equation:

- Δ*n *= 5
- So, gradient = $\frac{0.39}{5}$ = 0.078** [1 mark]**

- Gradient = $\frac{λ}{d}$ so $d=\frac{λ}{Gradient}$
- $d=\frac{499\times10^{-9}}{0.078}$
- *d *= 6.40 × 10<sup>−6</sup> m **[1 mark]**

![Diagram showing wave diffraction through a grating. parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Monochromatic light is incident normally on a diffraction grating.

A diffraction pattern forms on a screen.

The light has a wavelength of 630 nm. The diffraction grating has 4.50 × 10<sup>2</sup> lines per millimetre.

Determine the total number of gaps between orders, formed on the screen.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the total number ofgaps between orders, formed  on the screen:

- List the known quantities:

  - Wavelength, $λ$ = 630 nm = 630 × 10<sup>-9</sup> m
  - Number of lines*, *$N$ = 4.50 × 10<sup>2</sup> lines mm<sup>-1</sup>

- Recall the diffraction grating equation:

$d\mathrm{sin}θ=nλ$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the separation $d$ of the lines in the grating in metres:

$N=\frac{4.50\times10^{2}}{10^{-3}}=4.50\times10^{5}\mathrm{lines}m^{-1}$

$d=\frac{1}{N}=\frac{1}{4.50\times10^{5}}$

$d=2.22\times10^{-6}m$ **[1 mark]**

- Determine the highest diffraction order $n$ produced on the screen:

The highest possible order is at $θ=90^{\circ}$ **OR** $\mathrm{sin}θ=1$

$d\mathrm{sin}90^{\circ}=nλ$

$n=\frac{d}{λ}$ **[1 mark]**

$n=\frac{2.22\times10^{-6}}{630\times10^{-9}}$

$n=3.52...$

The highest order produced is $n=3$

- Determine the total number of gaps formed on the screen:

Total number of gaps = 2 × 3

Total number of gaps = **6** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for stating the diffraction grating equation $d\mathrm{sin}θ=nλ$
> 
> 1 mark for $d=\frac{1}{4.50\times10^{5}}$ **OR** $d=2.22\times10^{-6}m$
> 
> 1 mark for $d\mathrm{sin}90^{\circ}=nλ$ **OR** $d=nλ$ **OR**  $n=\frac{d}{λ}$
> 
> 1 mark for the total number of gaps = $2n$ **AND** given as an integer

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember to always round your calculated value of $n$ down rather than up. This is because $n$ indicates the total number of visible maxima.
> 
> In a diffraction pattern, there is one gap between each pair of adjacent maxima. In this case, there are three diffraction maxima on either side of the central maximum, and therefore 6 gaps between these as visible on the screen.

parts.solutionMd:

From the formulae page:

parts.solutionMd:

Refer to the existence of free electrons in copper:

Describe the effect of the potential difference:

- The potential difference produces an <u>electric field</u> (in the wire); **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
The diameter of a wire XY varies linearly with distance along the wire as shown in Fig. 6.1.

![A cylindrical conductor with current I flowing from left to right. Diameter at point X is 2d, narrowing to d at point Y. Drift speed at X is indicated as Vx.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-1-electric-current/assets/008-a-cylindrical-conductor-with-current-i-flowing-f.png)

**Fig. 6.1**

There is a current $I$ in the wire. At end X of the wire, the diameter is $2d$ and the average drift speed of the free electrons is $v_{X}$. At end Y of the wire, the diameter is $d$.

On Fig. 6.2, sketch a graph to show the variation of the average drift speed with position along the wire between X and Y.

![Grid graph with x-axis labelled "position along wire" from X to Y, and y-axis labelled "average drift speed" with increments vx to 4vx.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-1-electric-current/assets/009-grid-graph-with-x-axis-labelled-position-along-w.png)

**Fig. 6.2**
parts.solutionMd:
Sketch a graph to show the variation of the average drift speed with position along the wire:

- Determine the relationship between drift speed and wire diameter

Cross-sectional area of wire: $A = \mathrm{\pi } r^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } ( \frac{d}{2} )^{2}$

At X: $A = \mathrm{\pi } ( \frac{2 d}{2} )^{2} = \mathrm{\pi } d^{2}$

At Y: $A = \mathrm{\pi } ( \frac{d}{2} )^{2} = \frac{ \mathrm{\pi } d^{2}}{4}$

Drift speed: $I=Anvq$

$v=\frac{I}{Anq}$

Since $I$, $n$, and $q$ are constant $v\propto\frac{1}{A}$

$\frac{v_{Y}}{v_{X}}=\frac{d^{2}}{\frac{d^{2}}{4}}=4$

Therefore $v_{Y}=4v_{X}$

- Sketch a line on the graph:

![Graph of average drift speed versus position along a wire, showing a curve with increasing positive gradient from vx at X to 4vx at Y.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-1-electric-current/assets/010-graph-of-average-drift-speed-versus-position-alo.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a line drawn between (X, $v_{X}$) and (Y, $4v_{X}$)
> 
> 1 mark for a line drawn with an increasing magnitude of gradient

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since diameter $d$ varies linearly, area $A$ varies as $d^{2}$, so $v\propto\frac{1}{d^{2}}$. This means the variation of $v$ with $d$ is a non-linear increase. Hence, the gradient increases towards Y.

parts.problemMd:

[1]

(ii) Write one **joule** in terms of units of **potential difference** and **electric charge**

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The equation which relates electric charge and potential difference is:

- $\mathrm{potential} \mathrm{difference}=\frac{\mathrm{work} \mathrm{done}}{\mathrm{charge}}$ **[1 mark] **

(ii) Write one joule in equivalent units:

- *W* = *VQ, *where *W* is the energy transferred (or work done)
- Therefore, [*W*] = [*V*][*Q*]** [1 mark]**
- So, one joule J = volt × coulomb **OR** V C **[1 mark] **

parts.problemMd:
A lamp is powered by a 3.0 V cell.

Calculate the work done on the lamp by a single electron in this circuit.
parts.solutionMd:
To find work done by a single electron:

List the known quantities:

- Potential difference, *V*  = 3.0 V

From the data page:

- Elementary charge, *e*  = 1.60 × 10<sup>−19</sup> C

Recall the equation for potential difference:

- $V=\frac{W}{Q}$

Rearrange for work done and substitute the known quantities:

- Here, *Q*  is the charge on an electron
- $W = Q V = ( 1.60 \times 10^{- 19} ) \times 3.0$ **[1 mark]**
- $W=4.8\times10^{-19}J$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A lamp is powered by a 3.0 V cell. Calculate the work done on the lamp by a single electron in this circuit.
Work done by an electron with one cell, W = 4.8 × 10^−19 J

Three more identical 3.0 V cells are added in series to the circuit.

Calculate the new work done per electron.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the new work done:

List the known quantities:

- Number of 3.0 V cell in total = 4
- Work done by an electron with one cell, *W*  = 4.8 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J (from part (c))

Find the factor by which potential difference has increased:

- Potential difference was 3.0 V
- New potential difference is 3.0 × 4 = 12 V **[1 mark]**
- Potential difference has increased by a factor of 4

Find the new work done per electron:

- Potential difference is directly proportional to work

  - $W=QV$
  - Therefore, $W\proptoV$
- If p.d. has increased by a factor of 4, so has work done per electron
- New work done = 4 × 4.8 × 10<sup>−19</sup> = 1.920...× 10<sup>−18</sup>
- New work done = 1.9 × 10<sup>−18</sup> J (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *This method uses proportionality, but you could have equally just found the new potential difference of 12 V and put it back into the potential difference equation. Notice how the answer is still given to two significant figures, as per the given quantities.*

![9-2-m-q2a-sq-heaters-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-2-potential-difference-and-power/assets/009-9-2-m-q2a-sq-heaters-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Determine the most efficient heater.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the power of each heater:

- From the data booklet: *P *= *IV*
- Heater A: *P*<sub>*A*</sub> = 17 × 90 = 1530 W **AND**
- Heater B: *P*<sub>*B*</sub> = 8.0 × 220 = 1760 W **AND**
- Heater C: *P*<sub>*C*</sub> = 6.5 × 240 = 1560 W **[1 mark]**

Determine the efficiency of each heater:

- Recall the equation for efficiency, *E *= $\frac{\mathrm{useful} \mathrm{power} \mathrm{out}}{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{power} \mathrm{in}}$
- *E*<sub>*A*</sub> = $\frac{1500}{1530}=0.98$ **AND**
- *E*<sub>*B*</sub> = $\frac{1500}{1760}=0.85$ **AND**
- *E*<sub>*C*</sub>* = *$\frac{1500}{1560}=0.96$* ***[1 mark]**

Clarify the most efficient heater:

- Heater A is the most efficient heater; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Don't let the efficiency confuse you. The power output is 1500 W because the heaters are all rated to provide an output power of 1500 W. The input power is the power obtained from the input current and potential difference. *

> *The marks can be awarded for efficiencies given as decimals or percentages.*

parts.solutionMd:
Show that the resistivity of the metal is 6.67 × 10<sup>–7 </sup>Ω m

List the known quantities:

- Resistance, *R* = 6.1 Ω
- Diameter, *d* = 0.44 mm* *= 0.44 × 10<sup>–3</sup> m
- Length, *l* = 1390 mm = 1.39 m

Determine the equation for the resistivity, *ρ*:

- $R = \frac{ρl}{A} \Rightarrow ρ = \frac{RA}{l}$**[1 mark]**

Substitute in the values:

- `rho = (6.1 x ( 1.52 x 10 ^ - 7 ))/(1.39) = 6.67 x 10 ^ - 7 capital omega m` **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

| **Metal** | **Resistivity / Ω m** |

| Copper | 1.7 × 10<sup>–8</sup> |

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the cross-sectional area of the metal wire:

The photograph shows a statue of Buddha in Sri Lanka, which is protected by a lightning conductor.

![q5-nov-2020-9ph0-03-edexcel-as-a-level-phy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/9-electricity/9-3-resistance-and-resistivity/assets/068-q5-nov-2020-9ph0-03-edexcel-as-a-level-phy.png)

During a storm, a potential difference of 2.7 MV was generated between a cloud and the top of the lightning conductor on the statue. A flash of lightning passed between the cloud and the lightning conductor, producing a current of 25 kA for a time of 7.5 ms.

Calculate the energy transferred by the lightning strike.

Energy transferred = ............................................
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the energy transferred by the lightning strike:

List the known quantities:

- Potential difference, *V* = 2.7 MV = 2.7 × 10<sup>6</sup> V
- Current, *I* = 25 kA = 25 × 10<sup>3 </sup>A
- Time, *t* = 7.5 ms = 7.5 × 10<sup>–3</sup> s

Use the equation defining current to calculate the charge, *Q*:

- $Q = I t = ( 25 \times 10^{3} ) \times ( 7.5 \times 10^{- 3} )$
- $Q=187.5C$ **[1 mark]**

Use the equation defining potential difference to calculate work done, *W*:

- $V=\frac{W}{Q}$
- $W = ( 2.7 \times 10^{6} ) \times 187.5$ **[1 mark]**
- $W = 5.0625 \times 10^{8} = 5.1 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{J} ( 2 \mathrm{s} . \mathrm{f} . )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

The ratio $\frac{powerdissipatedinY}{powerdissipatedinX}$ is:

- $P=IV=I^{2}R$ where $R=\frac{ρl}{A}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{P_{Y}}{P_{X}}=\frac{I^{2}R_{Y}}{I^{2}R_{X}}=\frac{\frac{ρ_{Y}l_{Y}}{A_{Y}}}{\frac{ρ_{X}l_{X}}{A_{X}}}$

**[Total: 3 marks]**

The e.m.f of a cell with internal resistance may be more than the terminal p.d. of the cell because:

- There are lost volts within the cell **OR** energy used / spent on internal resistance; **[1 mark]**
- When the cell drives a current; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd: Compare the definitions of e. m .f and p. d.
parts.solutionMd:
Comparing the definitions of e.m.f and p.d.:

- E.m.f is the transfer of (chemical) energy from the cell to (electrical) energy in the circuit; **[1 mark]**
- Whilst p.d. is the transfer of (electrical) energy from the circuit to the surroundings via the components; **[1 mark]**
- Per unit charge; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd: For a cell, explain the term *internal resistance*.

**Fig 1.1**

The current in resistor A is 400 mA and the power dissipated by it is 6 W.

Calculate *r *of the battery.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate *r* of the battery:

List the known quantities:

- Electromotive force, *E* = 15.2 V
- Current through resistor *A, I* = 400 mA = 0.4 A
- Power dissipated, *P* = 6 W

Calculate the potential difference *V *through resistor A:

- $P=IV\RightarrowV=\frac{P}{I}$
- $V=\frac{6}{0.4}=15V$ **[1 mark]**

- $E=V+Ir\Rightarrowr=\frac{E-V}{I}$
- $r=\frac{15.2-15}{0.4}$ **[1 mark]**
- $r=0.5Ω$ **[1 mark]**

Two circuits X and Y shown in Fig 1.1 were used by a student to test a battery of four identical cells. In circuit X the battery is connected to a voltmeter registering 12 V and there was no load resistor. In circuit Y a load resistor of 5.2 Ω is connected in parallel with an ammeter registering 0.41 A and a voltmeter registering 4.9 V. Assume that the meters in the circuits are ideal.

parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Terminal p.d., *V* = 4.9 V
- E.m.f., *ε* = 12 V
- Current, *I *= 0.41 A

Rearrange e.m.f. equation for internal resistance *r*:

- *ε* *= V + Ir  *therefore, *r = *$\frac{ε-V}{I}$**[1 mark]*** *

Determine the internal resistance *r*:

- *r *= $\frac{12-4.9}{0.41}$ = 17.32*  ***[1 mark]**

Internal resistance *r* of a single cell:

- There are 4 cells
- So, $\frac{r}{4}$ =* *17.32* × *$\frac{1}{4}$ = 4.329 = 4.3 Ω (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**** **

parts.problemMd:

In circuit Y a load resistor of 5.2 Ω is connected in parallel with an ammeter registering 0.41 A and a voltmeter registering 4.9 V. Assume that the meters in the circuits are ideal.

Terminal p.d., V = 4.9 V; E.m.f., ε = 12 V; Current, I = 0.41 A; r = (12 - 4.9)/0.41 = 17.32 Ω (total internal resistance); internal resistance of a single cell r/4 = 4.3 Ω.

One of the cells in the battery is reversed.

Determine the new reading on the ammeter in circuit** **Y.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Total internal resistance, *r* = 17.32 Ω (from part (b))
- p.d. across each cell, p.d. = $\frac{12}{4}$ = 3.0 V
- Resistance of load resistor, *R* = 5.2 Ω

Determine the new e.m.f., *ε*:

- Voltmeter reading in circuit** **X = 3.0 + 3.0 + 3.0 – 3.0 = 6.0 V = new e.m.f. in Y **[1 mark]**

Rearrange e.m.f. equation for current *I*:

- *ε* =* V *+* Ir *=* IR *+* Ir*
- *I *=* *$\frac{ε}{R+r}$* *

Calculate current *I *in circuit Y:

- *I *= $\frac{6.0}{5.2+17.32}$* ***[1 mark]**
- *I* = 0.27 A **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 3 marks]**** **

> *The sum of the p.d. in a closed loop must equal the sum of the e.m.f. (Kirchhoff’s second law). The e.m.f. of each cell can be treated like a vector and the vector sum gives the total e.m.f. of the four connected cells. Despite one of the cells in the battery reversing, the internal resistances are still added up in series. *

parts.problemMd:
A battery of e.m.f. 60.0 V and internal resistance, *r*, is connected in a circuit as shown in Fig. 1.1.

**Fig 1.1**

The current in the battery is 2.3 A.

Calculate the internal resistance *r*.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Current, *I* = 2.3 A
- E.m.f., *ε* = 60.0 V

Calculate total resistance *R* of the circuit:

- Resistance of parallel combination: $\frac{1}{R_{T}}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}=\frac{1}{5.0}+\frac{1}{3.0}=\frac{8}{15}$
- *R*<sub>*T*</sub>* *= $\frac{15}{8}$= 1.875 Ω
- Total resistance *R * of circuit = 1.875 + 2.0 + 7.0 = 10.875 Ω **[1 mark]**

Calculate terminal pd *V*:

- *V = I ×* *R* = 2.3 × 10.875 = 25.0125 V **[1 mark]**

Calculate the internal resistance *r*:

- *ε* *= V + Ir*, therefore *r =   *$\frac{ε-V}{I}$
- *r*  = $\frac{60.0-25.0125}{2.3}$ **[1 mark]**
- *r* = 15.2 Ω = 15 Ω (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**** **

**[Total: 4 marks]**

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Kirchhoff's first law states that:

- The sum of currents into a junctions equals the sum of the currents out of a junction;** [1 mark]** ** **

(ii) The quantity conserved by this law is:

- Charge; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *It is common to mistakenly say that 'current' is conserved in this law. Although that's true, current is just the flow of **charge**, which is the fundamental conservation linked with Kirchhoff's first law. Therefore, for part (ii), 'current' will **not** get the mark.*

parts.problemMd:

[1]

(ii) State the quantity that is conserved by this law.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Kirchhoff's second law states that:

- The sum of e.m.f's equals the sum of the p.d's around a loop / circuit;** [1 mark]** ** **

(ii) The quantity conserved by this law is:

- Energy; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *It is common to mistakenly say that 'p.d' is conserved in this law. However, p.d. is the measure of energy per unit charge transferred between two points in a circuit. Therefore, it is technically **energy **that is conserved.*

parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

  - $V=\frac{W}{Q}$
  - $W=VQ$ **[1 mark]**
  - $W = 6 \times ( 2.5 \times 10^{3} )$
  - $W=1.5\times10^{4}J$ **[1 mark]**

- % uncertainty in *E *= % uncertainty in y-intercept = 21 %

Calculate the % uncertainty in the gradient of the best flt line:

- % uncertainty = $\frac{0.026}{0.326}\times100$
- % uncertainty = 7.98 % = 8.0 % (2s.f.)

Calculate the % uncertainty in *Q*:

- % uncertainty in *Q *= 21 + 8 = 29%

Calculate the absolute uncertainty in *Q*:

- Absolute uncertainty = $\frac{29}{100}\times1.79$
- Absolute uncertainty = ±0.5191 Ω = ±0.52 Ω (2s.f.) **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A combination of identical resistors each with resistance *R*  has a total resistance of 250 Ω as shown in Fig. 1.2.

![sl-sq-5-2-hard-q1a-qun-series-resistors](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-2-kirchhoffs-laws/assets/049-sl-sq-5-2-hard-q1a-qun-series-resistors.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Show, without the use of a calculator, how to find the value of resistance of each resistor and hence determine the value of *R*.
parts.solutionMd:
Recall the pattern of resistance when identical resistors are placed in parallel:

- Single resistor, *R*<sub>*tot*</sub> = *R*
- Two resistors,  *R*<sub>*tot*</sub> = ½ *R*
- Three resistors, *R*<sub>*tot*</sub> =  ⅓ *R*
- Four resistors, *R*<sub>*tot*</sub> =  ¼ *R*

Under the diagram, write the values of the combinations as fractions:

![sl-sq-5-2-hard-q1a-ma-series-resistors](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-2-kirchhoffs-laws/assets/050-sl-sq-5-2-hard-q1a-ma-series-resistors.png)

Write the full equation for resistance in series:

- $totalresistance=250=R+\frac{1}{2}R+\frac{1}{3}R+\frac{1}{4}R$ **[1 mark]**

Write all fractions in terms of a common denominator:

- $250=\frac{12}{12}R+\frac{6}{12}R+\frac{4}{12}R+\frac{3}{12}R$

Gather the terms:

- $250=\frac{25}{12}R$

Rearrange and cancel:

- $\frac{250\times12}{25}=R$
- $R=10\times12=120$ Ω **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *If you went straight to the correct answer by identifying the combinations in terms of fractions of **R**, and then calculating for a **set of resistors in series**, as shown above, well done!*

> *But you may have laboriously worked out the value of resistance of each combination in parallel, using *$\frac{1}{R_{total}}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}+...$*, this must have taken a long time, and created the opportunity for mistakes to be made. *

> *It is important to recognise that the sum of three resistors in parallel is given by *$3R$* because:*

$\frac{1}{R_{T}}=\frac{1}{R}+\frac{1}{R}+\frac{1}{R}$

$\frac{1}{R_{T}}=\frac{1}{3R}$

$R_{T}=3R$

> *The fact that this answer is only awarded two marks is a clue that there is a quicker way.*

> *Always pause and think before starting. A moment's thought should be enough to see the pattern of the combinations, and recall the fact that since the resistors are **identical**, a pattern of resistance follows, as described in the solution above.*

> *Always be ready to apply every part of your knowledge in any situation. This-open minded approach will make you a much better scientist.*

| **Circuit** | **Voltage supplied by power source /V** | **Reading on voltmeter /V** |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8.0 | 5.0 |
| 2 | 10 | 4.0 |

Calculate the resistance of resistors $R_{1}$, $R_{2}$ and $R_{3}$.

You may assume the voltmeter has an infinitely high resistance.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Voltage supplied by power source in Circuit 1, $V_{S1}$= 8.0 V
- Voltage on voltmeter in Circuit 1, $V_{1}$= 5.0 V
- Current flowing through power supply in Circuit 1, $I_{1}$= 0.50 A
- Voltage supplied by power source in Circuit 2, $V_{S2}$= 10 V
- Voltage on voltmeter in Circuit 2, $V_{2}$= 4.0 V

Consider Circuit 1:

- If the voltmeter has an infinitely high resistance, then current will flow through both $R_{1}$and $R_{2}$:

![5-1-s-q--q2a-ma-fig-1-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-2-kirchhoffs-laws/assets/052-5-1-s-q-q2a-ma-fig-1-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

Calculate the resistance of $R_{2}$:

- Recall: *V *= *IR*
- $R_{2}$= $\frac{V_{1}}{I_{1}}$ = $\frac{5.0}{0.5}$ = 10 Ω **[1 mark]**

Calculate the resistance of $R_{1}$:

- Voltage across $R_{1}$, $V_{R1}$=$V_{S1}$ – $V_{1}$= 8.0 – 5.0 = 3.0 V
- $R_{1}$= $\frac{V_{R1}}{I_{1}}$ = $\frac{3.0}{0.5}$ = 6 Ω **[1 mark]**

Consider Circuit 2:

- If the voltmeter has an infinitely high resistance, then current will flow through both $R_{2}$ and $R_{3}$:

![5-1-s-q--q2a-ma-fig-2-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-2-kirchhoffs-laws/assets/053-5-1-s-q-q2a-ma-fig-2-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

Calculate the current, *I*, flowing through $R_{2}$:

- *I* = $\frac{V_{2}}{R_{2}}$= $\frac{4}{10}$ = 0.4 A **[1 mark]**

Calculate the resistance of $R_{3}$:

**EITHER**

- Voltage across $R_{3}$, $V_{R3}$= $V_{S2}$ – $V_{2}$ = 10 – 4.0 = 6.0 V
- $R_{3}$= $\frac{V_{R3}}{I}$ = $\frac{6.0}{0.4}$ = 15 Ω **[1 mark]**

**   ****OR**

- Total resistance of  $R_{2}+R_{3}$, $R_{2+3}$= $\frac{V_{S2}}{I}$ = $\frac{10}{0.4}$ = 25 Ω
- Resistance, $R_{3}$= $R_{2+3}$ – $R_{2}$ = 25 – 10 = 15 Ω **[1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- $R_{1}$= 6 Ω
- $R_{2}$= 10 Ω
- $R_{3}$= 15 Ω

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

There is current flowing from P to R in the resistor network shown. The potential differences across three of the resistors are 3.0 V, 6.0 V and 5.0 V as shown in Fig. 1.1. Fig. 1.1. Determine the potential difference across the other two resistors.
Mark scheme: x = 2 V (potential difference across QS branch); y = 4 V. LHS branch p.d. = 3 V + 5 V = 8 V; RHS branch p.d. = 6 V + 4 V = 10 V; QS p.d. = 2.0 V.

The current through the branch QS is 3.0 A. The total combined resistance of the resistors in the outer loop of the circuit is *r*. The resistance in the outer loop of the circuit is split according to the ratio of the magnitudes of the potential differences of the resistors on each side of the loop.

Obtain an expression, in terms of *r*, for the total resistance of all the resistors in the circuit.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Current through QS, *I*<sub>1</sub>* *= 3.0 A
- p.d. across QS, *V*<sub>QS</sub>* *= 2.0 V (from part a)
- p.d. across the LHS branch, *V*<sub>LHS</sub>* *= 3 V + 5 V = 8 V
- p.d. across the RHS branch, *V*<sub>RHS</sub>* *= 6 V + 4 V = 10 V (from part a)

Calculate the resistance of the branch QS:

- Recall: *V *= *IR*
- $R_{QS} = \frac{V_{QS}}{I_{1}}$
- $R_{QS} = \frac{2}{3}$ Ω **[1 mark]**

Determine the ratio of resistance on each side of the outer loop:

- *V*<sub>LHS</sub>* *: *V*<sub>RHS</sub>* *= *R*<sub>LHS</sub>* *: *R*<sub>RHS</sub>
- 8 : 10 = 4 : 5 **[1 mark]**

Calculate the LHS and RHS resistances as fractions of *r*:

- $R_{LHS} = \frac{4}{9} r$
**AND**
$R_{RHS} = \frac{5}{9} r$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total resistance of all the resistors in the circuit:

- The QS branch is the single shared resistor between the two loops, so it is counted once
- $R=R_{LHS}+R_{RHS}+R_{QS}$
- $R = \frac{4}{9} r + \frac{5}{9} r + \frac{2}{3}$
- $R = r + \frac{2}{3}$ Ω **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The two power supplies mean the resistors on each side of the outer loop carry different currents, but the ratio given in the question lets you partition **r** without solving for the individual resistor values. *

> *The QS branch is a single resistor in the network. When summing the resistances of the circuit, count it once — it does not appear in both loops separately. *

> *This question is probably harder than anything you will encounter in your exam, but that makes it great practice! *

parts.problemMd:
Diagram 1.2 shows a circuit where *V*<sub>*1*</sub>  is a battery of 0.5 V, *V*<sub>*2*</sub>  a battery of 1 V and *V*<sub>*3*</sub>  a battery of 2 V. Each resistor has a resistance of 0.25 Ω.

![EBd_MI14_10-2-q2c-h-sq-cie-ial-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-2-kirchhoffs-laws/assets/028-ebd-mi14-10-2-q2c-h-sq-cie-ial-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Determine the value of each current at junction A.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- *V*<sub>*1*</sub> = 0.5 V
- *V*<sub>*2*</sub> = 1 V
- *V*<sub>*3*</sub>  = 2 V
- Resistance of each resistor, *R *= 0.25 Ω

Label the diagram to show the loops, polarity of the batteries and directions of each current:

A diagram that would score 1 mark should look like this:

![img-1167](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-2-kirchhoffs-laws/assets/029-img-1167.jpeg)

- Currents *I*<sub>*1*</sub>, *I*<sub>*2*</sub>  and *I*<sub>*3  *</sub>are<sub>* *</sub>labelled as shown with arrows in the correct direction **AND**
- Positive and negative battery and resistor terminals should be indicated correctly with the positive side of the resistor the side where the current enters; **[1 mark]**

Use Kirchhoff's first law to obtain an equation for the currents at junction A:

- *I*<sub>*1*</sub>* + I*<sub>*3*</sub> = *I*<sub>*2*</sub>* ***[1 mark]**

Use Kirchhoff's second law to obtain an equation for the sum of the potential differences in loops 1 and 2:

- Recall Ohm's Law: *V *= *IR*
- Loop 1: **AND**

  - *V*<sub>*1*</sub>* *− *I*<sub>*1*</sub>*R*<sub>*1*</sub>* *− *I*<sub>*2*</sub>*R*<sub>*2*</sub> − *V*<sub>*2*</sub> − *I*<sub>*1*</sub>*R*<sub>*4*</sub> = 0
  - 0.5 − (0.25*I*<sub>*1*</sub>) − (0.25*I*<sub>*2*</sub>) − 1 − (0.25*I*<sub>*1*</sub>) = 0
  - −0.5 − 0.5*I*<sub>*1 *</sub>− 0.25*I*<sub>*2*</sub> = 0
  - 0.5*I*<sub>*1*</sub> + 0.25*I*<sub>*2*</sub> = −0.5
- Loop 2:

  - *V*<sub>*3*</sub> − *I*<sub>*3*</sub>*R*<sub>*3*</sub> − *I*<sub>*2*</sub>*R*<sub>*2*</sub> − *V*<sub>*2*</sub> = 0
  - 2 − (0.25*I*<sub>*3*</sub>) − (0.25*I*<sub>*2*</sub>) − 1 = 0
  - 1 − (0.25*I*<sub>*3*</sub>) − (0.25*I*<sub>*2*</sub>) = 0
  - 1 = 0.25*I*<sub>*3 *</sub>+ 0.25*I*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *I*<sub>*3 *</sub>+ *I*<sub>*2*</sub> = 4 **[1 mark]**

Substitute for *I*<sub>*3*</sub> into the equation for current:

- From loop 2: *I*<sub>*3*</sub><sub> </sub>=<sub> </sub>4 − *I*<sub>*2*</sub>
- Equation for current: *I*<sub>*1*</sub>* + I*<sub>*3*</sub> = *I*<sub>*2*</sub>
- So, *I*<sub>*1*</sub> + (4 − *I*<sub>*2*</sub>) = *I*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *I*<sub>*1*</sub> = 2*I*<sub>*2*</sub> − 4 **[1 mark]**

Now substitute for *I*<sub>*1*</sub>* *from above into the equation for loop 1:

- From loop 1: 0.5*I*<sub>*1*</sub> + 0.25*I*<sub>*2*</sub> = −0.5
- 0.5(2*I*<sub>*2*</sub> − 4) + 0.25*I*<sub>*2*</sub> = −0.5
- *I*<sub>*2*</sub>* *− 2 + 0.25*I*<sub>*2*</sub> = −0.5
- 1.25*I*<sub>*2*</sub> = −0.5 + 2
- *I*<sub>*2*</sub> = 1.2 A **[1 mark]**

Now substitute for *I*<sub>*2*</sub> to obtain *I*<sub>*1*</sub>:

- *I*<sub>*1*</sub> = (2 × 1.2) − 4
- *I*<sub>*1*</sub> = −1.6 A **[1 mark]**

Substitute for *I*<sub>*2*</sub> into the equation for loop 2:

- From loop 2:* I*<sub>*3 *</sub>+ *I*<sub>*2*</sub> = 4
- *I*<sub>*3*</sub> = 4 − 1.2
- *I*<sub>*3*</sub>* *= 2.8 A **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

> *You can label your circuit in any way but make sure the direction of the current is consistent all the way around.*

> *When obtaining an equation for the sum of the potential differences if you cross from:*

- *− terminal of one resistor to the + terminal of another resistor *$\rightarrow$* the change in potential difference is + *
- *+ terminal of one resistor to the − terminal of another resistor *$\rightarrow$* the change in potential difference is −*

> *It is always a good idea to check your answer at the end. Here you can do this by using the equation for current:*

- *I*<sub>*1*</sub>* + I*<sub>*3*</sub>* = **I*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *So, −1.6 + 2.8 = 1.2 which is correct*

parts.problemMd:
Fig 1.1 shows a potential divider circuit containing a fixed resistor and thermistor.

![10-2-2a-e-thermistor-potential-divider](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/062-10-2-2a-e-thermistor-potential-divider.png)

**Fig 1.1**

** **Explain what happens to *V*<sub>out</sub> as the temperature of the thermistor increases.
parts.solutionMd:
As the temperature increases:

- The resistance of the thermistor decreases; **[1 mark]**
- So *V*<sub>out</sub> increases;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Potential dividers are all about the **sharing** of the potential from the battery (hence the name). When the resistance of the thermistor decreases, this means the voltage through it also decreases (from **V** = **IR** where **I** is the same for both resistors). *

> *However, the battery has a set voltage. Therefore, the voltage of the fixed resistor must **increase** so the combined voltage of the thermistor and fixed resistor remains the same. **V*<sub>*out*</sub>* is the reading of the voltage from the fixed resistor.*

parts.solutionMd:
For *R* = 7.0 Ω, calculate the p.d. between points Y and Z

List the known quantities:

- Resistance of variable resistor, *R* = 7.0 Ω
- Resistance of resistor P, *R*<sub>P</sub> = 7.5 Ω
- E.m.f of the power supply, *V* = 32 V

Use the graph to determine the current *I* when *R* = 7.0 Ω:

![img-7305c24fc61f-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/061-img-7305c24fc61f-1.jpeg)

- *I* = 2.3 A **[1 mark]**

**Method 1: Calculating p.d from current *****I***

Calculate the p.d. across YZ:

- P.d across YZ = p.d across XZ – p.d. across XY
- P.d across YZ = 32 – (2.3 × 7.5) = 14.75 = 15 V **[1 mark]**

**Method 2: Calculate p.d. from resistance**

Determine the total resistance in the circuit, *R*<sub>T</sub>:

- $R_{T}=\frac{V}{I}=\frac{32}{2.3}=13.91Ω$

Calculate the p.d. across YZ:

- Resistance in Q-R parallel combination, *R*<sub>QR</sub> = 13.91 – 7.5 = 6.41 Ω
- P.d across YZ = *I *×* R*<sub>QR</sub>* = *2.3 × 6.41 = 14.74 = 15 V **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A circuit is set up as shown in Fig. 1.1 below. The cells in Fig. 1.1 have negligible internal resistance. The cell at the top has an e.m.f. of 5 V and the cell at the bottom has an e.m.f. of 6 V. R1 is a variable resistor with a resistance that varies between 0 and 10 Ω, and R2 and R3 are fixed resistors with a resistance of 10 Ω and 30 Ω respectively. Initially, R1 is set such that its resistance is 0 Ω.

Determine the current through the resistor $R_{2}$ .
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- $R_{1}$= 0 Ω
- $R_{2}$= 10 Ω
- $R_{3}$= 30 Ω

Apply Kirchhoff's second law to the top loop:

- Kirchhoff's second law states that, in a closed loop, the total e.m.f. is equal to the sum of potential differences

  - In the top loop, e.m.f. is 5 V so $ε=5=V_{1}+V_{3}$
- $V_{1}$ must be 0 V, as resistor 1 has no resistance so there is no change in potential across it

  - Therefore $V_{3}=5V$ **[1 mark]**

Apply Kirchhoff's second law to the bottom loop:

- In the bottom loop, e.m.f. is 6 V so $ε=6=V_{2}+V_{3}$

  - $V_{3}$ is 5 V so $6=V_{2}+5$
  - $V_{2}=1V$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the current through resistor $R_{2}$:

- Using Ohm’s law across $R_{2}$  : $V_{2}$ = $I_{2}R_{2}$
- Therefore, 1 = $I_{2}$ × 10
- $I_{2}$= $\frac{1}{10}$  = 0.10 A **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Equally, you could have applied the second law to the bottom loop then the top loop, or a loop around the whole circuit. All should produce the same potential differences across each resistor. *

parts.solutionMd:
State what happens to the potential difference across $R_{2}$ :

- The potential difference across $R_{2}$  <u>increases</u> (as the potential difference across $R_{1}$  increases); **[1 mark]**

To explain, describe how the potential difference across $R_{1}$  changes:

- As the resistance of  $R_{1}$ increases, the potential difference ($V_{1}$) across it increases; **[1 mark]**

Describe how the potential difference across $R_{1}$  affects the potential difference across $R_{3}$ :

- (Because of Kirchhoff’s second law) the potential difference across $R_{3}$= 5 V – potential difference across $R_{1}$ **AND**
- Therefore, as the potential difference across $R_{1}$ increases, the potential difference across $R_{3}$ <u>decreases</u>; **[1 mark]**

Describe how the potential difference across $R_{3}$ affects the potential difference across $R_{2}$ :

- (Because of Kirchhoff’s second law) the potential difference across $R_{2}$ = 6 V – potential difference across $R_{3}$ **AND**
- Therefore as the potential difference across $R_{3}$ decreases, the potential difference across $R_{2}$ increases<u>;</u>** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *This is a potential divider question in an unfamiliar context when you just consider the top loop. As **R*<sub>*1*</sub>* ** increases in resistance, the potential difference across it increases. There is only a total e.m.f. of 5 V in this top loop, so less is available to be 'spent' on **R*<sub>*3*</sub>*. *

> *Then, this becomes a potential divider question for the lower loop. If **R*<sub>*3*</sub>*  has a greater potential difference, there is less available for **R*<sub>*2*</sub>*  following the conservation of energy.*

> *The thought process for this question is simple, however this mark scheme is large because you needs to **explain** every step:*

- *If p.d. across **R*<sub>*1*</sub>* increases then p.d. across **R*<sub>*3*</sub>* decreases*
- *This is because the potential difference in the loop remains constant from **V = IR *
- *So, p.d. across **R*<sub>*2*</sub>* will also increase by the same logic*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A circuit is set up as shown in Fig. 1.1 below. The cells in Fig. 1.1 have negligible internal resistance. The cell at the top has an e.m.f. of 5 V and the cell at the bottom has an e.m.f. of 6 V. R1 is a variable resistor with a resistance that varies between 0 and 10 Ω, and R2 and R3 are fixed resistors with a resistance of 10 Ω and 30 Ω respectively. By labelling the direction of current on Fig. 1.1, write down the relationship between three currents I1, I2 and I3 at the junction between R1 and R2. Using Kirchhoff's first law: I1 + I2 = I3.

Calculate the current flowing through each resistor when *R*<sub>1</sub> is set to a resistance of 10 Ω.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- $R_{1}$= 10 Ω
- $R_{2}$= 10 Ω
- $R_{3}$= 30 Ω
- EMF<sub>1</sub>, $ε_{1}$ = 5 V
- EMF<sub>2</sub>, $ε_{2}$ = 6 V

Apply Kirchhoff’s second law to the loop containing EMF<sub>1</sub>:

- Kirchhoff’s second law says the total EMF in a closed circuit (loop) equals the sum of potential differences across each component
- Therefore, *ϵ*<sub>1</sub> = *V*<sub>1</sub> + *V*<sub>3 </sub>(where *V*<sub>1</sub> and *V*<sub>3</sub> are the voltages across *R*<sub>1</sub> and *R*<sub>3</sub> respectively)
- Using Ohm’s Law, *ϵ*<sub>1</sub> = *I*<sub>1</sub>*R*<sub>1</sub> + *I*<sub>3</sub>*R*<sub>3</sub>
- Therefore 5 = 10*I*<sub>1</sub> + 30*I*<sub>3</sub> (equation 1) **[1 mark]**

Apply Kirchhoff’s second law to the loop containing EMF<sub>2</sub>:

- *ϵ*<sub>2</sub> = *V*<sub>2</sub> + *V*<sub>3 </sub>(where *V*<sub>2</sub> and *V*<sub>3</sub> are the voltages across *R*<sub>2</sub> and *R*<sub>3</sub> respectively)
- Again, using Ohm’s Law, *ϵ*<sub>2</sub> = *I*<sub>2</sub>*R*<sub>2</sub> + *I*<sub>3</sub>*R*<sub>3</sub>
- Therefore 6 = 10*I*<sub>2</sub> + 30*I*<sub>3</sub> (equation 2) **[1 mark]**

Substitute the expression from part (a) into equation 1 and equation 2:

- Since there are three unknowns, there needs to be three independent equations to solve simultaneously
- Therefore, from part (a), *I*<sub>1</sub> + *I*<sub>2</sub> = *I*<sub>3</sub> can be substituted for *I*<sub>3</sub> in equation 2 and equation 1
- Equation 2 becomes: 6 = 10*I*<sub>2</sub> + 30(*I*<sub>1 </sub>+ *I*<sub>2</sub>) = 10*I*<sub>2 </sub>+ 30*I*<sub>1</sub> + 30*I*<sub>2</sub>
- Simplifying, 6 = 40*I*<sub>2 </sub>+ 30*I*<sub>1</sub> (equation 3) **AND**
- Equation 1 becomes: 5 = 10*I*<sub>1</sub> + 30(*I*<sub>1 </sub>+ *I*<sub>2</sub>) = 10*I*<sub>1 </sub>+ 30*I*<sub>1</sub> + 30*I*<sub>2</sub>

- Simplifying, 5 = 30*I*<sub>2 </sub>+ 40*I*<sub>1</sub> (equation 4) **[1 mark]**

Solve equation 3 and equation 4 simultaneously:

- (Equation 3) × 3 gives: 18 = 120*I*<sub>2 </sub>+ 90*I*<sub>1</sub> (equation 5)
- (Equation 4) × 4 gives: 20 = 120*I*<sub>2 </sub>+ 160*I*<sub>1</sub> (equation 6)
- (Equation 6) – (Equation 5) gives: (20 –18) = (120*I*<sub>2</sub> – 120*I*<sub>2</sub>) + (160*I*<sub>1</sub> – 90*I*<sub>1</sub>)
- Therefore 2 = 70*I*<sub>1</sub>
- *I*<sub>1</sub>= $\frac{2}{70}$ = 0.029 A (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

Substitute the value for *I*<sub>1</sub> into any equation to calculate *I*<sub>2</sub>:

- Any equation can be used to calculate *I*<sub>2</sub> using the value for *I*<sub>1</sub>
- Substituting *I*<sub>1</sub> = 0.029 into equation 4 gives: 5 = 30*I*<sub>2</sub> + 40(0.029)
- 5 = 30*I*<sub>2</sub> + 1.16
- *I*<sub>2</sub> = $\frac{5-1.16}{30}$ = 0.13 A (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

Calculate *I*<sub>3</sub> using values for *I*<sub>1</sub> and *I*<sub>2</sub>:

- Using the equation from part (a): *I*<sub>1</sub> + *I*<sub>2</sub> = *I*<sub>3</sub>
- Therefore, $I_{3}$ = 0.13 + 0.029 = 0.16 A (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *This question is certainly very challenging; while circuits on the A Level paper are unlikely to require this level of analysis, there is nothing here outside the scope of your physics syllabus – notice, it only requires a very careful application of Kirchhoff’s laws and Ohm’s law. The image below shows how to apply Kirchhoff’s second law to closed loops in a circuit:*

![5-3-s-q--q3d-ma-fig-1-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/041-5-3-s-q-q3d-ma-fig-1-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

> *Notice that the loops ‘go in the direction’ of conventional current in the loop, and also that EMFs (power supplies) are distinct to the potential differences across components (sometimes called voltage drops, because energy from the current is transferred away from it to the component itself).*

> *Another key takeaway from this question, which is a very useful problem-solving tool to bear in mind generally, is that there are three unknowns – i.e., the currents **I*<sub>*1*</sub>*, **I*<sub>*2*</sub>* and **I*<sub>*3*</sub>*. The number of unknown variables in any system tells you how many ‘independent’ (unique) equations you need to set up, in which every unknown appears at least once. So, in this question, we needed to set up **three** independent equations; after we did this, it was just a case of some mathematical juggling to solve for each unknown. The image below recaps the three unknowns and the three independent equations we set up:*

![5-3-s-q--q3d-ma-fig-2-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/042-5-3-s-q-q3d-ma-fig-2-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

> *There are of course multiple equivalent ways to solve simultaneous equations (depending on which variable you choose to eliminate first, and which equation to substitute into, etc.) but you should in principle be comfortable with solving simultaneous equations (two for two unknowns and three for three unknowns!). Have a look at the Save My Exam GCSE and / or A-level maths notes to refresh your knowledge on these if you are stuck!*

parts.problemMd:
Potential divider circuits generally comprise of two or more resistors in series with each other.

Some potential divider circuits have multiple branches connected in parallel, such as that shown in Fig. 1.3:

![5-3-s-q--q4b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/072-5-3-s-q-q4b-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

Show that the potential difference between X and Y, *V*<sub>*OUT*</sub> , is 1 V.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- $V_{IN}$ = 12 V
- Resistor $R_{1}$ = 4 Ω
- Resistor $R_{2}$ = 2 Ω
- Resistor $R_{3}$ = 3 Ω
- Resistor $R_{4}$ = 1 Ω

**Method 1 (clockwise current)**

Determine the potential difference across $R_{1}$ :

- The potential divider equation for resistor $R_{1}$ (which is in a series loop with resistor $R_{2}$ ) is  $V_{OUT}$ =$\frac{R_{1}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}V_{IN}$
- Therefore  p.d. across *R*<sub>*1*</sub>*  *is $V_{1}$ = $\frac{4}{4+2}$ × 12 = $\frac{4}{6}$ × 12 = 8 V **[1 mark]**

Determine the potential difference across $R_{3}$ :

- The potential divider equation for resistor $R_{3}$ (which is in a series loop with resistor $R_{4}$) is  $V_{OUT}$ = $\frac{R_{3}}{R_{3}+R_{4}}V_{IN}$
- Therefore p.d. across *R*<sub>*3*</sub>  is $V_{3}$ = $\frac{3}{3+1}$ × 12 = $\frac{3}{4}$ × 12 = 9 V **[1 mark]**

Determine the potential at X and Y:

- Charge transfers 8 V across resistors $R_{1}$
- The potential at X is therefore 12 V – 8 V = 4 V **AND**
- Similarly, charge transfers 9 V of potential across resistor $R_{3}$
- The potential at Y is therefore 12 V – 9 V = 3 V **[1 mark]**

Show the potential difference between X and Y is 1 V:

- The potential difference between X and Y is therefore *V*<sub>*OUT *</sub> = 4 V – 3 V = 1 V **[1 mark]**** **

**Method 2 (anticlockwise current)**

Determine the potential difference across $R_{2}$ :

- The potential divider equation for resistor $R_{2}$ (which is in a series loop with resistor $R_{1}$ ) is  $V_{OUT}$ =$\frac{R_{2}}{R_{2}+R_{1}}V_{IN}$
- Therefore p.d. across *R*<sub>*2*</sub> is $V_{2}$ = $\frac{2}{2+4}$ × 12 = $\frac{2}{6}$ × 12 = 4 V **[1 mark]**

Determine the potential difference across $R_{4}$ :

- The potential divider equation for resistor $R_{4}$ (which is in a series loop with resistor $R_{3}$ ) is  $V_{OUT}$ =$\frac{R_{4}}{R_{4}+R_{3}}V_{IN}$
- Therefore p.d. across *R*<sub>*4*</sub>  is $V_{4}$ = $\frac{1}{1+3}$ × 12 = $\frac{1}{4}$ × 12 = 3 V **[1 mark]**

Determine the potential at X and Y:

- Charge transfers 4 V across resistor $R_{2}$
- The potential at X is therefore 12 V – 4 V = 8 V **AND**
- Charge transfers 3 V across resistor $R_{4}$
- The potential at X is therefore 12 V – 3 V = 9 V **[1 mark]**

Show the potential difference between X and Y is 1 V:

- The potential difference between X and Y is therefore *V*<sub>*OUT*</sub>  = 9 V – 8 V = 1 V **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Method 1** assumes that the current flows in a clockwise direction through the circuit: in other words, that the terminals of the power supply are oriented as shown in the sketch below. You should work your way through the four steps, to convince yourself that the potential at point X is 4V **if the current flows clockwise** through the circuit.*

![5-3-s-q--q4b--ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/073-5-3-s-q-q4b-ma-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

> *Following this reasoning, you should be able to check and see that the potential at Y is 12 V – 9 V = 3 V, so the potential **difference **between X and Y is 1 V. *

> *Method 2** assumes the current flows in an anti-clockwise direction through the circuit; in that case, simply reverse the direction of the current in the illustration above and you should see that the potential at X is 12 V – 4 V = 8 V. Similarly, the potential at Y is 12 V – 3 V = 9 V, giving a potential difference between X and Y as 1 V again. *

> *Clearly, either assumption is valid and will give the correct **potential difference **between **X** and **Y**. This question introduces you to a fact you will explore more in A Level physics: ‘potential’ as a quantity is relative (i.e., it depends on how you define directions), but potential **difference** is always absolute – so long as your working is consistent!*

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.4 shows another potential divider circuit which includes a thermistor with resistance *R*.

![5-3-s-q--q4d-hard-aqa-a-level-physics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-physics-25/10-d-c-circuits/10-3-potential-dividers/assets/074-5-3-s-q-q4d-hard-aqa-a-level-physics.png)

**Fig. 1.4**

The battery has an EMF of 12 V, with negligible internal resistance. At room temperature, the resistance of the thermistor is 5 kΩ.

Calculate the current in the battery at room temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Resistance of the thermistor (at room temperature), *R* = 5 kΩ = 5000 Ω
- Resistance between AC = 20 kΩ = 20 000 Ω
- Resistance between CE = 20 kΩ = 20 000 Ω
- Resistance between BD = 10 kΩ = 10 000 Ω
- EMF of the battery = 12 V

Determine the series resistances:

- Resistors in series $R_{T} = R_{1} + R_{2} + R_{3} + \times \times \times$
- There are two resistors in series between** **A and E, so $R_{T}=R_{1}+R_{2}$
- Therefore, the total resistance between** **A and E = resistance between AC + resistance between CE = 20 000 + 20 000 = 40 000 Ω **AND**
- There are two resistors in series between B and F, so $R_{T}=R_{1}+R_{2}$
- Therefore, the total resistance between B and F = resistance between BD + resistance of the thermistor (at room temperature) = 10 000 + 5000 = 15 000 Ω **[1 mark]**

Determine the total resistance of the circuit:

- Resistors in parallel `1 over R subscript T equals 1 over R subscript 1 plus 1 over R subscript 2 plus 1 over R subscript 3 plus times times times`
- The resistance between** **A and E is in parallel to the resistance between B and F
- Therefore $\frac{1}{R_{T}}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}=\frac{1}{40000}+\frac{1}{15000}=\frac{11}{120000}$
- Therefore *R*<sub>T</sub> = $\frac{120000}{11}$ = 10 909 Ω **[1 mark]**

Determine the current through the battery:

- Using Ohm’s law across the battery, *V* = *IR*
- *V* is the EMF *ϵ *of the cell
- Therefore 12 = *I* × 10 909
- *I* = $\frac{12}{10909}$ = 1.1 × 10<sup>–3</sup> A **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd: A beam of α-particles produces a current of 3.5 pA. Calculate the number of α-particles per second passing a point in the beam.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the number of α-particles per second passing a point in the beam

List the known quantities:

- Current, *I* = 3.5 pA = 3.5 × 10<sup>–12</sup> A

State the equation for current, *I*:

- $Q=It\RightarrowI=\frac{Q}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine an equation for the number of α-particles, *n*:

- $I=n\times\frac{Q}{t}\Rightarrow\frac{n}{t}=\frac{I}{Q}$
- $\frac{n}{t} = \frac{3.5 \times 10^{- 12} }{2 \times ( 1.60 \times 10^{- 19} )}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{n}{t}=1.094\times10^{6}=1.1\times10^{6}s^{-1}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *An alpha particle is a helium nucleus of **2** protons and **2** neutrons. Therefore, its charge is the 2 × charge of a proton (**e** = 1.60 × 10*<sup>*–19*</sup>* C). You will be expected to remember the composition of an alpha particle, and the charge **e** is given on your data sheet.*

> *The wording 'per second' means 'every 1 second'. Therefore, the 'number of particles, **n**, per second' is represented as an equation *$\frac{n}{t}$*.*

parts.problemMd:
When a nucleus of plutonium-239 absorbs a neutron, the following reaction may take place.

$Pu_{94}^{239} + \mathrm{n} pre_{b} pre^{a} \rightarrow \text{Xe} pre_{54} pre^{x} + \text{Zr} pre_{y} pre^{103} + 3 \mathrm{n} pre_{b} pre^{a}$

State the values of *a*, *b*, *x* and *y*.
parts.solutionMd:
The values of *a*, *b*, *x* and *y* are:

`Pu _ 94 ^ 239 + n _ 0 ^ 1 -> Xe _ 54 ^ 134 + Zr _ 40 ^ 103 + 3 n _ 0 ^ 1`

- *a *= 1 **AND** *b* = 0 **[1 mark]**

Calculate *x*:

- 239 + 1 = *x* + 103 + (3 × 1)
- *x* = 240 – 106
- *x* = 134 **[1 mark]**

Calculate *y*:

- 94 + 0 = 54 + *y* + (3 × 0)
- *y* = 94 – 54
- *y* = 40 **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *On the right-hand side, *`3 n presubscript 0 presuperscript 1 space`*means that there are **3** neutrons, so **both** the mass number (1) and the atomic number (0) must be **multiplied** by 3.*

parts.problemMd:
A Plutonium-239 nucleus has a mean density of 1.3 × 10<sup>17</sup> kg m<sup>–3</sup>.

Show that the radius of a Plutonium-239 nucleus is 9.0 × 10<sup>–15</sup> m.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the radius of a Plutonium-239 nucleus

List the known quantities:

- Mean density of the Plutonium-239 nucleus,* ρ* = 1.3 × 10<sup>17</sup> kg m<sup>–3</sup>

Calculate the mass of the Plutonium nucleus, *m*:

- *m* = mass number × atomic mass unit = 239 × 1 u
- *m* = 239 × (1.66 × 10<sup>–27</sup>) = 3.9674 × 10<sup>–25</sup> kg **[1 mark]**

Calculate the radius of the Plutonium nucleus, *r*:

- $ρ=\frac{m}{V}=\frac{m}{\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}}=\frac{3m}{4πr^{3}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $r = \sqrt[3]{ \frac{3 m}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \\rho } } = \sqrt[3]{ \frac{3 \times ( 3.9674 \times 10^{- 25} )}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 1.3 \times 10^{17} )} }$ = 8.996 × 10<sup>–15</sup> = 9.0 × 10<sup>–15</sup> m **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You can approximate a nucleus as a sphere, but you must remember the equation for the volume of a sphere, as this will not be given on your data sheet! However, the value of the atomic mass unit (u) will be given.*

> *Read the question carefully, as it says 'aside from their structure'. This means answers such as 'an α-particle is two protons and two neutrons and a β-particle is an electron' will not be accepted.*

Remember to link this important discovery to questions asking about the distribution of energy of beta particles.*

parts.problemMd:

Suggest the standard form of the two possible equations that represent this decay and define all the terms used.
parts.solutionMd:
The first equation represents β− decay:

- `X _ Z ^ A -> Y _ Z + 1 ^ A + beta _ - 1 ^ 0 + v -bar _ 0 ^ 0 _ e`** [1 mark]**

The second equation represents β+ decay:

- `X _ Z ^ A -> Y _ Z - 1 ^ A + beta _ + 1 ^ 0 + v _ 0 ^ 0 _ e` **[1 mark]**

Where:

- X is the <u>parent</u> nuclei with nucleon number A and proton number Z **AND**
- Y is the <u>daughter</u> nuclei with the nucleon number A and proton number Z ±1 **AND**
- `beta _ +/- 1 ^ 0` is the beta particle **AND**
- `v -bar _ 0 ^ 0 _ e` is the (electron) anti-neutrino **AND **$v_{0}^{0}_{e}$** **the (electron) neutrino; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The question does not say whether the decay is β+ or β−, so you must include both equations. You should think of these equations automatically when considering β decay. *

> *You are asked to define all the terms in your equations so make sure you do so carefully. This is time-consuming but easy marks! Make sure you use the correct language of **parent **and **daughter **nuclei. *

parts.problemMd:
Thorium, `Th presubscript 90 presuperscript 232` decays to an isotope of Radium (Ra) through a series of transformations. The particles emitted in successive transformations are:

$αββγα$

Determine the resulting nuclide after these successive transformations.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the resulting nuclide after these successive transformations:

- During $α$ emission, an alpha particle `alpha presubscript 2 presuperscript 4` is released from each starting atom

  - The mass number decreases by 4 and the proton number decreases by 2
- During $β$ emission, an electron (or positron) is released

  - The proton number increases by 1, but there is no change in the mass number
- During $γ$ emission, electromagnetic gamma rays are emitted

  - There is no reduction in mass or proton number

A flow diagram of the processes involved is obtained using the periodic table:

- $Th_{90}^{232} \rightarrow Ra_{88}^{228} \rightarrow Ac_{89}^{228} \rightarrow Th_{90}^{228} \rightarrow Th_{90}^{228} \rightarrow Ra_{88}^{224}$

  - All $α$ decays correct; **[1 mark]**
  - All  $β$decays correct; **[1 mark]**

State the final decay product:

- `Ra presubscript 88 presuperscript 224`** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember that the proton number of each element in the periodic table is unique. Look up each proton number to obtain the correct element. *

parts.problemMd:

Explain the simplest sequence of alpha and beta decays required to do this.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the condition required for the formation of the isotope:

- For the decay sequence to result in the formation of an isotope of the original nucleus, the proton number must remain the same; **[1 mark]**

Determine the simplest sequence that can achieve this:

- (The simplest sequence is) 1 alpha (decay) **and** 2 beta (decays); **[1 mark]** **OR** In equation form: `Z _ X ^ A -> alpha _ 2 ^ 4 + 2 beta _ - 1 ^ 0 + Y _ X ^ A - 4` **[1 mark]**

An explanation is:

- Change in proton number: 2 + 2 × (–1) = 0 **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *When explaining your reasoning, make it clear why your answer is correct by backing it up with any calculations for full marks (like is done in this explanation). It is not enough just to say ‘the proton number remains the same’.*

- *Alpha decay decreases the proton number by 2*
- *Beta decay increases the proton number by 1*

**Final answer:** **Any ****one**** from:**

- uuu / three up quarks  **[1 mark]**
- ttt / three top quarks **[1 mark]**
- ccc / three charm quarks **[1 mark]**
- utc / up quark, top quark, charm quark **[1 mark]**
- $\overset{-}{d}\overset{-}{s}\overset{-}{b}$ / anti-down quark, anti-strange quark, anti-bottom quark **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *Although a meson is a type of hadron, a meson cannot have a charge of +2**e **as there is no combination of a quark and anti-quark pair that gives a charge of +2**e**.*

> *It is important you memorise the **charges** of each of the quarks, and remember that the equivalent anti-quark has the **opposite** charge. *

parts.problemMd: State the quark composition of an alpha particle.
parts.solutionMd:
The quark composition of an alpha particle is:

- (An alpha particle has) 2 protons $( u u d )$ and 2 neutrons $( u d d )$; **[1 mark]**
- (So its quark composition is) 6 up (u) **AND** 6 down (d) quarks;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *A proton would have a quark composition of uud. A neutron has udd. Therefore, uud + uud + udd + udd = 6 up and 6 down quarks.*

parts.problemMd: Use the quark model to show that the charge on the anti-neutron is 0.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the quark model to show that the charge on the anti-neutron is 0

- (The quark structure) is anti-up anti-down anti-down / $\overline{u}\overline{d}\overline{d}$; **[1 mark]**
- $- \frac{2}{3} ( e ) + 1 \frac{1}{3} ( e ) + 1 \frac{1}{3} ( e ) = 0$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *It is important you remember all the charges of each quark. An anti-quark is going to have the same magnitude but **opposite charge**.*

parts.problemMd:
A sigma baryon Σ is a hadron that consists of an up (u) quark, a down (d) quark and a strange (s) quark.

State the quark composition of Σ<sup>+</sup> , Σ<sup>0</sup> and Σ<sup>–</sup> .
parts.solutionMd:
State the quark composition of Σ<sup>+</sup> , Σ<sup>0</sup> and Σ<sup>–</sup> :

- Σ<sup>+ </sup>= uus; **[1 mark]**
- Σ<sup>0</sup> = uds; **[1 mark]**
- Σ<sup>–</sup> = dds; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The subscript for each of the Σ particles indicates its charge. Since it is a **baryon**, this means it is made up of **three** **quarks **(anti-baryons are made up of three antiquarks). It is important to remember the charge of each of these quarks to combine them in a way to get the total charge required:*

- *uus = *$+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=1$
- *uds = *$+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=0$
- *dds = *$-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=-1$

parts.problemMd: Explain why a baryon with the quark composition $u\overline{d}s$ cannot exist.
parts.solutionMd:
A baryon with the quark composition $u\overline{d}s$ cannot exist because:

- A baryon can only be made up of three quarks or three anti-quarks **OR **a baryon cannot consist of a mix of quarks and anti-quarks; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: State the number of 'up' quarks in the nucleus of `Al presubscript 13 presuperscript 27`.
parts.solutionMd:
The number of 'up' quarks in the nucleus of `Al presubscript 13 presuperscript 27` is:

Determine the number of protons and neutrons:

- There are 13 protons
- There are 27 – 13 = 14 neutrons

Calculate the number of up quarks:

- A proton (uud) has 2 up quarks and a neutron (udd) has 1 up quark
- Number of up quarks = (13 × 2) + (14 × 1) = 40 **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
The $D$ particle has a quark structure $u\overline{c}$ .

Determine

(i) the classification of the $D$ particle,

[1]

(ii) the charge on the $D$ particle.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The classification of the $D$ particle is:

- A meson; **[1 mark]** ** **

(ii) The charge on the $D$ particle is:

- $u \bar{c} = \frac{2}{3} + ( - \frac{2}{3} ) = 0$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *Just 'hadron' will not be enough to get the mark for part (i), you should be as specific as possible.*

parts.problemMd: Using the quark model, show that the magnitude of the charge of a proton is equal to the charge of an electron.
parts.solutionMd:
Using the quark model, show that the magnitude of the charge of a proton is equal to the charge of an electron

- uud (2 up quarks and 1 down quark)
- $+ \frac{2}{3} e + \frac{2}{3} e + ( - 1 \frac{1}{3} e ) = 1 e$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Using the quark model for β<sup>+</sup> decay, show that charge is conserved in this decay.
parts.solutionMd:
Using the quark model for β<sup>+</sup> decay, prove that charge is conserved

- β<sup>+</sup> decay is: $p\rightarrown+e^{+}+ν_{e}$
- Therefore, the quark changes are: $u\rightarrowd+e^{+}+ν_{e}$ **[1 mark]**

Compare charges on both sides:

- $+ \frac{2}{3} = - 1 \frac{1}{3} + ( + 1 ) + 0 = + \frac{2}{3}$ **[1 mark]**
- (LHS = RHS), therefore, the charge is conserved; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i) The quark composition of a proton is:
